paper_title: Some open questions in TDDFT: Clues from Lattice Models and Kadanoff-Baym Dynamics
original_question: How should exchange-correlation kernels for Hubbard lattice TDDFT account for qualitative features of the ALDA kernel that have no known continuum analogue, including a sign that changes with density and interaction strength, and a singularity at half filling for sufficiently large interaction U caused by the discontinuity of vxc at the Mott-Hubbard metal-insulator transition? The paper expects these features to persist when nonlocal and nonadiabatic effects are added, so a complete theory must explain how they affect density response beyond the local adiabatic limit.
self_contained_problem:
Consider lattice time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT) applied to the single-band Hubbard model

  H = -t ∑_{⟨i,j⟩,σ} (c†_{iσ} c_{jσ} + h.c.) + U ∑_i n_{i↑} n_{i↓} + ∑_i v_i(τ) n_i,

with site density n_i(τ) and on-site interaction U > 0. Within a Kohn–Sham mapping to a non-interacting lattice system, define the exchange-correlation (XC) potential v_xc[n] and the adiabatic local-density-approximation (ALDA) XC kernel

  f^{ALDA}_{xc}(n) = ∂ v^{hom}_{xc}(n)/∂ n,

where v^{hom}_{xc}(n) is the XC potential of the homogeneous Hubbard model at uniform density n, computed (e.g.) from Bethe-ansatz in 1D or from dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT) in higher dimensions.

Two qualitative features of f^{ALDA}_{xc} are observed that have no known counterpart in continuum XC kernels:

(i) Sign change: f^{ALDA}_{xc}(n;U) changes sign as a function of band filling n ∈ (0,2) and interaction strength U.

(ii) Singularity at half filling: for sufficiently large U (specifically U > U_c^{Mott} in dimension d ≥ 2, and for all U > 0 in d = 1), v^{hom}_{xc}(n) has a discontinuity at n = 1 associated with the Mott–Hubbard metal-insulator transition, inducing a Dirac-delta–like singularity in f^{ALDA}_{xc} at n = 1.

Develop a theory of the (in general nonlocal and nonadiabatic) lattice XC kernel f_{xc}[n](i,j;ω) for the Hubbard model that:

(a) reproduces the sign-change behavior of f^{ALDA}_{xc} as a function of (n,U) in the local adiabatic limit,

(b) accounts for the half-filling singularity tied to the discontinuity of v_{xc} at the Mott transition,

(c) shows that these two qualitative features survive (in an appropriate sense to be made precise) the inclusion of nonlocality in (i,j) and frequency dependence in ω, and

(d) describes quantitatively their imprint on the interacting density response function χ(i,j;ω) of the Hubbard model beyond the ALDA.

Provide either an explicit construction of such an f_{xc} (e.g., from DMFT charge susceptibilities) together with a proof/argument that properties (a)–(c) hold and a calculation establishing (d), or else a rigorous demonstration that one of these features is artifactual and disappears when nonlocal/nonadiabatic corrections are included.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has constructed nonadiabatic XC kernels for the Hubbard model via DMFT charge susceptibilities and studied the Hubbard dimer exactly, confirming strong frequency dependence and features tied to Mott physics. However, no general theory has been established that fully characterizes how the ALDA sign change and the half-filling delta-like singularity propagate into the full nonlocal, nonadiabatic kernel and the density response. The question therefore appears still open as of the latest available literature.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: In non-commutative, group-based cryptography, what class of group is the most appropriate platform group for building cryptographic schemes?
status_search_result: The question of identifying the "most appropriate" platform group for non-commutative group-based cryptography is widely regarded as an overarching open problem in the field. Since the early 2000s, many candidate platforms (braid groups, Thompson's group, polycyclic groups, free metabelian groups, right-angled Artin groups, matrix groups, self-similar groups, etc.) have been proposed and analyzed, with various attacks (length-based, linear representation, quotient) breaking or weakening many concrete proposals, but no consensus or proof of optimality for any single class has emerged. Recent surveys and research articles continue to treat the choice of platform group as an open research direction.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can one prove that a chosen group platform is secure for non-commutative cryptographic constructions such as public-key exchange protocols, digital-signature schemes, and authentication schemes?
self_contained_problem:
Let $G$ be a finitely generated non-abelian (non-commutative) group, equipped with an efficient encoding of elements and efficient algorithms for the group operations (multiplication and inversion). Such a $G$ is called a platform group for a cryptographic scheme when the security of the scheme is reduced to the computational hardness of one or more problems formulated in $G$ (for example, the conjugacy search problem, the word problem with restricted presentations, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, the decomposition problem, or a learning-with-errors analogue over $G$).

Consider three classes of non-commutative cryptographic constructions built over such a platform group $G$:
(a) public-key exchange protocols (e.g., Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld type or Ko–Lee type protocols),
(b) digital-signature schemes,
(c) identification/authentication schemes.

Develop a general methodology, together with explicit criteria on $G$ (such as growth, complexity of the word and conjugacy problems, distortion of subgroups, generic-case versus average-case complexity, distributional properties of random elements, and resistance to known attacks such as length-based attacks, linear-algebra attacks, and quantum attacks), under which one can give a rigorous reduction proving that schemes in classes (a)–(c) over $G$ are provably secure in a standard cryptographic model (e.g., IND-CPA, IND-CCA, EUF-CMA, or zero-knowledge soundness). Equivalently: identify a specific finitely presented non-abelian group $G$ together with a hard computational problem $P$ over $G$ whose average-case hardness can be established, and exhibit protocols for (a), (b), (c) whose security is provably reducible to $P$.
status_search_result: The question of identifying non-commutative platform groups together with average-case hard problems on which provably secure key exchange, signature, and authentication schemes can be based remains an active and open research area. Subsequent surveys (e.g., the polycyclic-group survey by Kahrobaei and collaborators) and ongoing projects such as the CCNY CAISS "Provable Cryptography from Non-Commutative Groups" continue to list this as a core open problem; while candidate platforms (braid groups, polycyclic groups, Grigorchuk groups, extra-special groups, matrix groups) have been proposed and partial security reductions exist, no general methodology or fully provably secure scheme has been established.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Can the security of the non-commutative cryptographic protocols surveyed in the paper be analyzed rigorously?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the family of nonabelian (i.e. non-commutative) group-based cryptographic protocols built on finitely presented infinite groups, including the following representative schemes:

1. The Ko–Lee key exchange, whose security rests on the conjugacy search problem in a braid group or other nonabelian platform group G: given g, h = x^{-1} g x ∈ G with x lying in a specified subgroup A ≤ G, recover an element x' ∈ A with x'^{-1} g x' = h.
2. The Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld commutator key exchange, whose security rests on the simultaneous conjugacy search problem with respect to two prescribed subgroups A, B ≤ G.
3. Authentication and key-agreement protocols based on the twisted conjugacy search problem, the word problem, the membership problem, the decomposition problem, and the geodesic length problem in suitable finitely presented groups.

For each such protocol, formulate and prove a rigorous reduction between the protocol's cryptographic security (e.g. one-wayness or indistinguishability of session keys against a polynomial-time adversary, in an appropriate model such as random self-reducibility or the generic-group model) and a precisely stated, well-posed algorithmic problem in the underlying platform group, taking into account the actual distribution of keys produced by the protocol. In particular, determine whether one can:

(a) Define a worst-case to average-case reduction for the relevant search problem (conjugacy, simultaneous conjugacy, twisted conjugacy, decomposition, etc.) over the key-generation distribution used by the protocol; and

(b) Prove, under a clearly stated computational assumption on this distributional problem, that no probabilistic polynomial-time adversary can break the protocol with non-negligible advantage; or, alternatively, exhibit a polynomial-time cryptanalytic algorithm (for example via length-based, linear-centralizer, linear-decomposition, or quotient attacks) that refutes such a claim for the platform group in question.

The problem is to carry out this rigorous security analysis for the standard families of platform groups proposed in nonabelian group-based cryptography (braid groups, polycyclic groups, Grigorchuk-type groups, Thompson's group, free metabelian groups, small-cancellation groups, and matrix groups over group rings).

No comprehensive rigorous security analysis covering the surveyed protocols has been established.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Given that the paper states that only three non-commutative digital-signature schemes were then known, can additional non-commutative digital-signature schemes be designed?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A digital signature scheme is a triple of probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms (KeyGen, Sign, Verify) such that:
- KeyGen(1^n) outputs a public/private key pair (pk, sk).
- Sign(sk, m) outputs a signature σ on a message m.
- Verify(pk, m, σ) outputs accept/reject, with correctness Verify(pk, m, Sign(sk, m)) = accept for all valid keys and messages, and existential unforgeability under chosen-message attack (EUF-CMA) against probabilistic polynomial-time adversaries.

A digital signature scheme is called non-commutative (or nonabelian group based) if its KeyGen, Sign, and Verify algorithms are constructed using the algebraic structure of a non-abelian (non-commutative) group, semigroup, ring, or algebra G, and if the security reduction relies on a computational problem in G that exploits non-commutativity (for example, the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy problem, the word problem, the membership/decomposition problem, or related search problems in braid groups, matrix groups over non-commutative rings, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group, or non-commutative associative algebras).

Problem. Design new non-commutative digital signature schemes beyond the previously known constructions; that is, exhibit a digital signature scheme (KeyGen, Sign, Verify) whose KeyGen, Sign, and Verify procedures use a non-abelian platform structure G and whose EUF-CMA security can be proven (or strongly argued) to reduce to a computational problem in G that essentially requires non-commutativity, and which is not equivalent to a previously published non-commutative signature construction.
status_search_result: The challenge is open-ended in nature, but multiple new non-commutative digital signature schemes have been proposed since 2011, including conjugacy-based and braid-group signatures, polynomial-based schemes over non-commutative groups and division semirings, signatures over non-commutative rings and matrix problems, KoKa-DSS (2025), EQSIGN (2024) based on the non-abelian hidden subgroup problem, and signature algorithms on non-commutative associative algebras over finite fields. Thus additional schemes have indeed been designed, partially addressing the question, while the broader research program of building secure (especially post-quantum) non-commutative signatures remains active.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: For polycyclic-group cryptographic constructions that rely on commuting subgroups, which choice of commuting subgroups makes the schemes secure?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Several non-abelian group-based cryptographic protocols (for example, the commutator key-exchange protocol and Ko–Lee-type key exchanges) use the following template. Fix a finitely generated group G, presented in a way that admits efficient multiplication and a normal form. Publish two subgroups A, B ≤ G that commute elementwise, i.e. ab = ba for every a ∈ A and b ∈ B. Alice picks secret elements a₁, a₂ ∈ A and sends to Bob an element of the form a₁ x a₂ (for the commutator scheme, x is a published element of G); Bob picks b₁, b₂ ∈ B and replies with b₁ x b₂. Using the commutation relations between A and B, both parties extract a common shared key. The security of such a protocol depends on the computational hardness, in the platform group G, of associated search problems (the simultaneous conjugacy / commutator decomposition / subgroup-membership-with-commuting-factor problems) restricted to the chosen pair (A, B).

Now restrict G to be an infinite polycyclic group (a group admitting a subnormal series with cyclic quotients), given by a polycyclic presentation so that collection yields a deterministic polynomial-time normal form.

Problem. Determine an explicit family of pairs of commuting subgroups (A, B) of polycyclic platform groups G with the following properties simultaneously:
1. A and B are finitely generated, elementwise commuting subgroups of G.
2. Membership in A and B and computation in A, B and G are efficient.
3. The associated search problems used by the commuting-subgroup key-exchange protocols are computationally hard on the family (G, A, B); in particular, no known length-based, linear-algebraic, quotient-based, or subgroup-distortion attack succeeds in polynomial time.

Equivalently: characterize, among polycyclic groups, which pairs of commuting subgroups (A, B) yield secure instantiations of the commuting-subgroup-based key-exchange schemes, or prove that no such choice exists in the polycyclic setting.
status_search_result: A 2016 survey on the status of polycyclic group-based cryptography and a 2022 survey on group-based cryptography in the quantum era both discuss the question of suitable commuting subgroups in polycyclic platforms. Specific proposed classes have been cryptanalyzed (e.g., certain polycyclic-group cryptosystems shown insecure), but no general characterization of secure commuting subgroup pairs in polycyclic groups has been established. The problem appears to remain open, with some negative results for particular classes.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Is there a quantum algorithm for the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups that lowers the complexity of solving that problem?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called polycyclic if it admits a subnormal series
$$G = G_0 \triangleright G_1 \triangleright \cdots \triangleright G_n = \{1\}$$
in which every quotient $G_i / G_{i+1}$ is cyclic. The search conjugacy problem in $G$ is the following algorithmic task: given two elements $u, v \in G$ that are known to be conjugate in $G$ (i.e., there exists $x \in G$ with $x^{-1} u x = v$), produce such a conjugating element $x$.

Classically, the search conjugacy problem in (non-virtually-abelian) polycyclic groups is believed to have high complexity, and certain families of polycyclic groups have been proposed as platforms for non-abelian group-based cryptography on this basis.

Question: Does there exist a quantum algorithm that solves the search conjugacy problem in polycyclic groups with strictly lower (worst-case or average-case) complexity than the best known classical algorithm? Equivalently, exhibit such a quantum algorithm together with a complexity analysis improving on the classical bounds, or prove that no such quantum speed-up is possible.
status_search_result: Recent surveys on group-based cryptography in the quantum era (2022) and follow-up work on the status of polycyclic group-based cryptography continue to list the existence of an effective quantum algorithm for the conjugacy search problem in polycyclic groups as an open question; quantum behavior of related hidden-subgroup-type problems on infinite, non-abelian groups remains poorly understood.

paper_title: Aspects of Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography: A Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Can the computer algebra system GAP be used as a practical and secure implementation platform for these non-commutative cryptographic schemes?
self_contained_problem:
Non-commutative (nonabelian) group-based cryptography refers to cryptographic protocols whose security relies on the computational hardness of problems formulated in nonabelian groups, such as the conjugacy search problem, the simultaneous conjugacy search problem, the word problem, the membership problem, the twisted conjugacy search problem, and related problems in groups such as braid groups, polycyclic groups, Thompson's group, matrix groups over finite rings, and finitely presented groups given by generators and relations. Examples of such protocols include the Anshel–Anshel–Goldfeld key exchange, the Ko–Lee key exchange, Stickel's protocol, and various commutator/decomposition-based key agreements.

GAP (Groups, Algorithms, Programming) is an open-source computer algebra system designed for computational discrete algebra, with particular emphasis on computational group theory. It provides a high-level programming language, a library of algorithms for finite and finitely presented groups, permutation groups, polycyclic groups, matrix groups, and finite fields, together with extensive data libraries of algebraic objects.

Determine whether GAP can serve as a practical and cryptographically secure implementation platform for nonabelian group-based cryptographic schemes. More precisely:

(a) Identify a class of nonabelian group-based protocols (key exchange, public-key encryption, digital signature, or authentication) whose group-theoretic primitives — including generation of platform groups, sampling of secret elements, normal form computation, multiplication, inversion, and rewriting — can be implemented in GAP with running times suitable for practical use at standard security parameters.

(b) Provide a quantitative analysis showing that such a GAP-based implementation resists known cryptanalytic attacks (length-based attacks, linear-algebra attacks, linear-decomposition attacks, quantum attacks where relevant) while remaining efficient, or alternatively prove that GAP's computational model imposes inherent obstructions (e.g., side-channel leakage, lack of constant-time arithmetic, performance limits in normal-form algorithms) that prevent any such implementation from being simultaneously practical and secure.
status_search_result: GAP is widely used as a research tool for computational group theory and is freely available, and several research-level implementations of nonabelian group-based cryptographic primitives (e.g., for braid groups and polycyclic groups) have been prototyped in GAP. However, no authoritative source establishes that GAP provides a practical and cryptographically secure deployment platform meeting standard security and performance requirements, nor a proof that it cannot. The question of GAP's suitability as a practical, secure implementation platform for nonabelian cryptography therefore appears to remain a generally open engineering/research question rather than a settled mathematical theorem.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: What progenitor systems actually produce the main classes of gamma-ray bursts? More specifically, which stellar or compact-object channels generate massive-star GRBs and compact-star GRBs, given that current evidence is indirect, only a small and biased subset of long GRBs have secure supernova associations, and some short-duration or high-redshift events do not fit a simple neutron-star-merger picture?
self_contained_problem:
Gamma-ray bursts (GRBs) are brief, intense flashes of gamma-ray radiation observed from cosmological distances. Phenomenologically they are divided into two main observational classes based on duration and spectral hardness: long-soft GRBs (typically with prompt-emission durations T_{90} > 2 s) and short-hard GRBs (typically with T_{90} < 2 s). It is widely conjectured that long-soft GRBs originate from the core collapse of certain rapidly rotating massive stars (the "collapsar" or massive-star channel), supported by a limited number of secure spectroscopic associations between long GRBs and Type Ic broad-lined supernovae, while short-hard GRBs originate from the merger of compact-object binaries (neutron star–neutron star or neutron star–black hole), supported only by indirect evidence such as host-galaxy demographics and offset distributions. However, only a small, observationally biased subset of long GRBs have confirmed supernova counterparts, and certain short-duration events as well as some high-redshift bursts exhibit properties that are difficult to reconcile with a simple compact-binary merger origin.

Problem. Identify the actual astrophysical progenitor systems that produce the main observational classes of gamma-ray bursts. Specifically:
(a) Determine which stellar evolutionary channels (e.g., single rapidly rotating Wolf–Rayet stars, tidally spun-up binary helium stars, chemically homogeneous massive stars, or other configurations) give rise to the massive-star (long-soft) GRB class, and characterize the conditions under which such progenitors yield a successful relativistic jet and an accompanying supernova.
(b) Determine which compact-object channels (e.g., binary neutron star mergers, neutron star–black hole mergers, accretion-induced collapse, magnetar giant flares, or other compact-star configurations) give rise to the compact-star (short-hard) GRB class, and account for short-duration or high-redshift events whose properties are not naturally explained by a binary neutron star merger.
Provide a mapping from progenitor channel to observable signatures (duration distribution, spectral properties, host galaxy demographics, offset distributions, kilonova/supernova counterparts, gravitational-wave signatures) sufficient to discriminate between the proposed channels.
status_search_result: The identification of GRB progenitors remains an active research question. While GW170817/GRB 170817A confirmed that at least some short GRBs come from binary neutron star mergers, and the long-GRB/Type Ic-BL supernova connection is established for a subset of nearby long bursts, the full mapping of progenitor channels to GRB classes is incomplete. Recent discoveries of long-duration GRBs with kilonova-like signatures (e.g., GRB 211211A, GRB 230307A) and short GRBs with apparent supernova-like emission show that the duration-progenitor correspondence is not one-to-one, and the progenitor question is still considered open.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: What is the composition of gamma-ray-burst ejecta at the prompt-emission radius: are the outflows primarily matter-dominated fireballs or magnetically dominated jets, and what are the baryon, lepton-pair, and neutron contents of the flow? Here the key quantity is the magnetization sigma, the ratio of Poynting flux to matter flux, and the problem is to determine whether sigma is much less than 1, of order 1, or much greater than 1 in the emitting region.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a relativistic outflow producing the prompt emission of a gamma-ray burst (GRB). Model the outflow as a relativistic jet carrying both baryonic matter (with possible additional lepton-pair and neutron components) and a large-scale magnetic field. Define the magnetization parameter at the prompt-emission radius as

  sigma = F_Poynting / F_matter,

i.e., the ratio of the Poynting (electromagnetic) energy flux to the matter (kinetic) energy flux through a comoving cross-section of the flow at the radius where the prompt gamma-rays are emitted.

Determine the composition of GRB ejecta at the prompt-emission radius. Specifically:

1. Decide whether the prompt-emission outflow is generically (a) matter-dominated (sigma << 1, a "fireball"), (b) of order equipartition (sigma ~ 1), or (c) magnetically/Poynting-flux dominated (sigma >> 1).

2. Determine the baryon loading, the contribution of electron–positron pairs, and the neutron content of the flow, and how these are related to sigma.

A complete solution would either provide a model-independent diagnostic that fixes sigma at the emission radius from observations, or establish theoretically which regime is realized in long and short GRBs.
status_search_result: The composition of GRB prompt-emission outflows remains an open and actively debated question. Recent studies (e.g., analyses of GRB 230307A in 2024 and GRB 160625B) provide evidence for Poynting-flux-dominated outflows (sigma > 1) in particular bursts, while other GRBs show thermal components consistent with matter-dominated fireballs. No consensus diagnostic has fixed sigma generically at the emission radius across the GRB population.

original_question: What radiation mechanism produces the prompt gamma-ray-burst spectrum that is usually fit by the empirical Band function? The unresolved possibilities include synchrotron or jitter emission from accelerated leptons, synchrotron self-Compton emission, Comptonization of thermal or photospheric photons, and hadronic emission, and the explanation must account for observed low-energy spectral slopes, cooling behavior, and peak energies.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Which components of observed post-burst gamma-ray-burst light curves are genuinely produced by the external forward or reverse shock, and how should jet breaks, chromatic behavior, and reverse-shock signatures be interpreted once internal central-engine contributions are removed? This is especially important in the Swift era, where X-ray afterglows commonly contain multiple components that complicate standard external-shock parameter inference.
self_contained_problem:
In the standard fireball model of gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), a relativistic jet launched by a central engine drives an external blast wave into the circumburst medium, producing a forward shock that heats swept-up ambient material and (during the early deceleration phase) a reverse shock that propagates back into the ejecta. Synchrotron emission from electrons accelerated at these shocks is predicted to give rise to broadband afterglow light curves whose temporal and spectral indices are linked by closure relations depending on the electron energy distribution index p, the circumburst density profile, the cooling regime, and the jet geometry. When the bulk Lorentz factor Γ of a collimated jet of half-opening angle θ_j drops below 1/θ_j, the model predicts an achromatic temporal steepening (a "jet break") observable simultaneously at all wavelengths.

In the Swift era, X-ray and optical afterglow light curves frequently exhibit multiple components — including steep decays, plateaus, flares, and chromatic breaks — that are not naturally accounted for by a single external forward-shock component, suggesting prolonged contributions from the central engine.

Provide a quantitative, observationally testable prescription that does the following:

(a) Specifies, for an arbitrary multi-wavelength GRB afterglow data set, an algorithm to decompose the observed light curve into (i) genuine external forward-shock emission, (ii) external reverse-shock emission, and (iii) emission attributable to long-lasting central-engine activity, using only temporal indices, spectral indices, closure relations, and cross-band timing.

(b) Defines a precise notion of an achromatic ("platinum") jet break — i.e., a simultaneous temporal break at all observed wavelengths consistent with the post-jet-break closure relations — and determines whether such a break exists in the current sample of well-monitored GRB afterglows once central-engine contributions identified by (a) are subtracted.

(c) Identifies clean signatures of the reverse shock (e.g., optical flash, radio flare timing, polarization) that survive after the subtraction in (a) and that allow unambiguous determination of the magnetization parameter and Lorentz factor of the ejecta.

In particular, decide whether, after removal of internal/central-engine components, the remaining afterglow emission of typical Swift-era GRBs is consistent with a single-component external forward + reverse shock model, and whether truly achromatic jet breaks occur.
status_search_result: Subsequent systematic studies (e.g., Wang et al. 2015, ApJS 219, 9; Racusin et al. 2009, ApJ 698, 43) have shown that closure-relation tests and multi-wavelength decompositions can attribute roughly half of Swift GRB afterglows to a simple external forward shock, rising to >90% when long-lasting reverse shocks, structured jets, and arbitrary medium profiles are invoked. Some achromatic breaks (e.g., short GRB 140903A) have been identified, but no universally accepted "platinum" sample of strictly achromatic jet breaks across all bands has emerged. The general decomposition and reverse-shock identification problem remains an active research area without a definitive solution.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Are massive-star gamma-ray bursts reliable tracers of the star-formation history of the universe across cosmic time, especially at high redshift?
self_contained_problem:
Long-duration gamma-ray bursts (LGRBs) are believed to arise from the collapse of certain massive stars. Let R_GRB(z) denote the comoving rate density of long-duration GRBs as a function of redshift z, and let ψ_*(z) denote the cosmic star-formation rate density. A naive "tracer" hypothesis posits that there exist a redshift-independent constant k > 0 such that R_GRB(z) = k · ψ_*(z) for all z (after correction for instrumental selection effects, beaming, and luminosity function).

Determine whether massive-star (long-duration) GRBs are reliable tracers of the cosmic star-formation history in this sense across all cosmic epochs, particularly at high redshift (z ≳ 3). Specifically:

(a) Decide whether the proportionality R_GRB(z) ∝ ψ_*(z) holds, or whether an additional redshift-dependent factor f(z) (for example arising from a metallicity threshold, an evolving initial mass function, evolving luminosity function, or evolving beaming/jet properties) is required so that R_GRB(z) = k · f(z) · ψ_*(z).

(b) If such a factor f(z) is required, characterize its functional form and identify the dominant physical mechanism (metallicity bias, IMF evolution, luminosity-function evolution, beaming-angle evolution, or a combination) responsible for the deviation.

(c) Assess whether, after correcting for any such bias, GRB-derived measurements of ψ_*(z) at high redshift are consistent with independent determinations from galaxy surveys.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Does the luminosity function of gamma-ray bursts evolve with redshift or cosmic time, so that bursts at higher redshift are systematically more luminous than those nearby?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the population of long-duration gamma-ray bursts (GRBs), modeled as point sources with isotropic-equivalent peak luminosities L distributed according to a (possibly redshift-dependent) luminosity function Φ(L, z), where z denotes cosmological redshift. Define the comoving GRB rate density ρ(z) and assume an observed sample is drawn from the joint distribution determined by Φ(L, z), ρ(z), and the survey selection function (flux-limited detection in a given energy band).

The question is whether Φ(L, z) genuinely depends on z in a non-separable or shape-changing way, in particular whether a "luminosity evolution" of the form Φ(L, z) = Φ_0(L / g(z)) / g(z) with a monotonically increasing function g(z) (for example a power law g(z) = (1+z)^δ with δ > 0) is required by the data, so that GRBs at higher redshift are systematically intrinsically more luminous than those at low redshift. Equivalently: can the observed redshift–luminosity distribution of GRBs be explained by a non-evolving luminosity function combined with a comoving rate density tracing cosmic star formation, or does consistency with observations require evolution of the luminosity function itself with cosmic time?

Determine whether such redshift evolution of the GRB luminosity function exists, and if so, characterize its functional form (e.g., the exponent δ in a (1+z)^δ parameterization).
status_search_result: Multiple statistical analyses of Swift and HETE-2 GRB samples report evidence that a non-evolving luminosity function is disfavored, with luminosity evolution roughly of the form L ∝ (1+z)^δ with δ ≈ 1.4–2.5 providing better fits, and recent (2025) work on Type II GRBs again excluding the no-evolution model. However, degeneracies between luminosity evolution and density evolution remain, and the precise form of evolution is not uniquely determined, so the question is partially resolved rather than definitively settled.

paper_title: Open Questions in GRB Physics
original_question: Do gamma-ray bursts at very high redshift arise from progenitors different from those of lower-redshift bursts, for example from an earlier stellar population that forms more massive stars and perhaps powers more energetic events?
self_contained_problem:
A gamma-ray burst (GRB) is a brief, intense flash of gamma radiation observed at cosmological distances, generally believed to be produced by a relativistic jet launched during the catastrophic collapse of a massive star (long-duration GRBs) or the merger of compact objects (short-duration GRBs). Each GRB has a measured cosmological redshift z, and the population of observed bursts spans a wide range of z, from low redshift (z ≲ 1) up to z ≳ 8.

Population III stars are a hypothesized first generation of stars formed from primordial (essentially metal-free) gas in the early universe; theoretical models suggest they may have a top-heavy initial mass function and reach significantly larger masses than typical present-day massive stars, potentially producing more energetic explosive events.

Question: Do gamma-ray bursts originating at very high redshift (e.g., z ≳ 6) arise from a class of progenitor systems that is intrinsically different from the progenitors of gamma-ray bursts observed at lower redshift? In particular, do high-redshift GRBs originate from an earlier stellar population (such as Population III or its immediate descendants) consisting of more massive stars, and does this produce systematic differences (for example higher isotropic-equivalent energies, longer intrinsic durations, or different luminosity functions) in the high-redshift GRB population compared with the low-redshift one?
status_search_result: The question of whether high-redshift GRBs arise from a distinct progenitor population (such as Population III stars) remains an open observational and theoretical question. Recent reviews and studies continue to discuss possible signatures (higher energetics, longer durations) of Pop III GRBs but no definitive observational identification has been made; current samples of z>6 GRBs are too small to robustly distinguish progenitor populations.

original_question: Can a single high-resolution semi-analytic model of galaxy formation simultaneously match the observed specific-star-formation-rate--stellar-mass relation at redshift z = 0, the stellar mass function and its evolution, galaxy two-point correlation functions, and galaxy cold-gas fractions? The model must do this without relying on unrestricted tuning of all physical recipes and while keeping its star-formation, feedback, cooling, and merging prescriptions physically plausible.

paper_title: A modified star formation law as a solution to open problems in galaxy evolution
context_brief: Baryonic recipes versus cosmology in galaxy clustering
original_question: When semi-analytic galaxy-formation models fail to match observed galaxy two-point auto-correlation functions, is the mismatch primarily caused by the baryonic recipes used to assign stellar masses and galaxy properties, or by the underlying cosmology of the dark-matter simulation? The issue is nontrivial because galaxy positions are tied to haloes and subhaloes, while stellar-mass selection and clustering predictions can change substantially when the star-formation law changes, and similar clustering matches can be obtained with different cosmological parameters depending on the baryonic recipes.
self_contained_problem:
Consider semi-analytic models (SAMs) of galaxy formation built on top of a cosmological dark-matter N-body simulation. In such a model, halos and subhalos are identified in the simulation (which is fully specified by a set of cosmological parameters, e.g. Ωm, Ωb, σ8, ns, h), and a system of "baryonic recipes" (prescriptions for gas cooling, star formation, supernova and AGN feedback, mergers, etc., parametrized by a star-formation law and associated efficiencies) is applied to populate these halos and subhalos with galaxies of given stellar mass M⋆ and other properties.

For a stellar-mass-selected sample of model galaxies, one computes the projected two-point auto-correlation function w_p(r_p), or equivalently the real-space ξ(r), which can be compared directly with the same statistic measured for observed galaxy samples (e.g., from large redshift surveys).

Let C denote the choice of cosmological parameters and B the choice of baryonic recipes (including the form of the star-formation law). It is empirically observed that there exist pairs (C, B) ≠ (C′, B′) producing comparably good fits to the observed correlation function of stellar-mass-selected galaxies, so the two ingredients are degenerate.

Problem. Determine, in a quantitatively rigorous way, whether the persistent mismatch between SAM predictions and observed galaxy two-point auto-correlation functions for stellar-mass-selected samples is primarily attributable to:
  (a) deficiencies in the baryonic recipes B (in particular, the adopted star-formation law and the resulting stellar-mass assignments), or
  (b) the cosmological parameters C of the underlying dark-matter simulation,
or to a coupled combination of (a) and (b). Equivalently, characterize and break the degeneracy between B and C in the prediction of stellar-mass-selected galaxy clustering, and identify which component must be modified to simultaneously match observed correlation functions across stellar-mass bins and redshifts.
status_search_result: The question of disentangling baryonic-recipe effects from cosmological-parameter effects in semi-analytic predictions of galaxy clustering remains an active research topic. Subsequent works (e.g., on subhalo abundance matching, emulator-based SAM calibration, and joint clustering+lensing analyses) have constrained the degeneracy but have not definitively resolved which component dominates the mismatch in stellar-mass-selected auto-correlation functions; the issue is still considered open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For a holomorphic local dynamical system f with stable set K_f, what is the dynamical structure of the induced global system (K_f, f)? More specifically, how do orbits in K_f behave asymptotically near the fixed point, can they converge or exhibit chaotic behavior, can there be dense orbits, and what proper forward-invariant subsets of K_f can occur together with their internal dynamics?
self_contained_problem:
Let f: (C^n, p) → (C^n, p) be a holomorphic local dynamical system, i.e., f is a germ of a holomorphic self-map of C^n fixing the point p (so f(p) = p). Define the stable set of f at p to be
   K_f := { z ∈ U : f^k(z) is defined for all k ≥ 0 and f^k(z) → p as k → ∞ },
where U is a neighborhood of p on which iterates of f are defined as long as they stay in U. The pair (K_f, f) is then a (global) discrete dynamical system.

Investigate the dynamical structure of (K_f, f). In particular, address the following:

(a) Describe the asymptotic behavior of orbits {f^k(z)}_{k≥0} for z ∈ K_f. Under what conditions on f (e.g., on the spectrum of df_p, resonances, formal/analytic normal forms) do all orbits in K_f converge to p, and under what conditions can they exhibit chaotic behavior?

(b) Can the system (K_f, f) admit a dense orbit? Characterize the local dynamical systems for which topological transitivity (existence of a dense forward orbit) on K_f occurs.

(c) Classify the proper, forward f-invariant subsets S ⊂ K_f that can arise (e.g., stable manifolds, parabolic basins, Siegel-type domains, attracting petals, invariant analytic sets), and describe the internal dynamics of f restricted to each such S.
status_search_result: This is a broad guiding question in local discrete holomorphic dynamics in several complex variables. While many partial results exist in specific regimes (hyperbolic, attracting, parabolic Fatou-flower-type, Siegel/Bryuno, semi-attracting cases) due to work by Abate, Bracci, Hakim, Écalle, Rivi, and others, no complete description of the dynamics on the stable set K_f is known in general; the question is regarded as a long-standing open program rather than a single solved theorem.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Associate computable invariants, ideally from a small class, to each holomorphic local dynamical system at the origin of C^n so that equality of invariants characterizes conjugacy as strongly as possible. In particular, can one construct complete invariant systems for holomorphic, smooth, C^k, or topological local conjugacy classes?
status_search_result: The classification of holomorphic local dynamical systems in $\mathbb{C}^n$ up to (holomorphic, smooth, $C^k$, or topological) conjugacy is a long-standing program. Complete invariants are known only in special cases (e.g., one-dimensional parabolic germs via Écalle–Voronin invariants; hyperbolic germs via linearization). In general dimension and for general germs the problem remains open, with active research on resonant, parabolic, and small-divisor cases.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Find natural families of one-variable elliptic holomorphic germs of the form f_{λ,a}(z)=λz+z^2 g_a(z), parametrized by a in some parameter space M, for which holomorphic linearizability is equivalent exactly to the Brjuno condition on the multiplier λ. In particular, is every elliptic polynomial, or even every elliptic cubic polynomial, holomorphically linearizable if and only if its multiplier is a Brjuno number?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C},0)$ denote the set of holomorphic germs $f:(\mathbb{C},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$. A germ $f(z)=\lambda z+O(z^2)$ with $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda$ not a root of unity is called elliptic (or irrationally indifferent). Such a germ is said to be holomorphically linearizable at $0$ if there exists a holomorphic germ $\varphi:(\mathbb{C},0)\to(\mathbb{C},0)$ with $\varphi'(0)\neq 0$ such that $\varphi^{-1}\circ f\circ\varphi(z)=\lambda z$. Writing $\lambda=e^{2\pi i\alpha}$ with $\alpha\in\mathbb{R}\setminus\mathbb{Q}$, and letting $(p_n/q_n)_{n\geq 0}$ be the continued fraction convergents of $\alpha$, the number $\lambda$ (equivalently $\alpha$) is said to satisfy the Brjuno condition if 
$$\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{\log q_{n+1}}{q_n}<\infty.$$

(a) Find natural families $\{f_{\lambda,a}(z)=\lambda z+z^2 g_a(z)\}_{a\in M}\subset\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C},0)$ of elliptic germs, parametrized by $a$ ranging over a parameter space $M$ (with $g_a$ holomorphic in a fixed neighborhood of $0$), such that for every $a\in M$ the germ $f_{\lambda,a}$ is holomorphically linearizable at $0$ if and only if $\lambda$ satisfies the Brjuno condition.

(b) In particular, decide the following: Is it true that every elliptic polynomial $P(z)=\lambda z+a_2 z^2+\cdots+a_d z^d$ (with $|\lambda|=1$, $\lambda$ not a root of unity, $d\geq 2$, $a_d\neq 0$) is holomorphically linearizable at $0$ if and only if $\lambda$ satisfies the Brjuno condition? In particular, is this true for every elliptic cubic polynomial $P(z)=\lambda z+a_2 z^2+a_3 z^3$ (with $a_3\neq 0$)?
status_search_result: The necessity of the Brjuno condition for holomorphic linearizability is known (by Yoccoz) for the quadratic family $z\mapsto\lambda z+z^2$, and sufficiency (Brjuno–Rüssmann) holds in general. Whether the Brjuno condition is necessary for linearizability of polynomials of degree $\geq 3$, and in particular for elliptic cubic polynomials, is reported in recent surveys as still open (Douady's conjecture). No proof of necessity in degree $\geq 3$ nor a counterexample appears in the literature.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For one-variable elliptic holomorphic germs with a Cremer fixed point at the origin, are two topological invariants sufficient for complete topological classification: the multiplier f'(0) and the homeomorphism class of the stable set germ K_f at the origin? Equivalently, do those two data completely determine the topological local conjugacy class of a Cremer point?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}, 0)$ be a germ of holomorphic self-map of $(\mathbb{C}, 0)$ fixing the origin, with multiplier $\lambda := f'(0)$ of the form $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \alpha}$ with $\alpha \in \mathbb{R} \setminus \mathbb{Q}$, and assume the origin is a Cremer point of $f$ (i.e., $f$ is not holomorphically linearizable at $0$). Define the (local) stable set (filled Julia set germ) of $f$ at $0$ as
$$K_f := \{\, z \in U : f^{\circ n}(z) \in U \text{ for all } n \ge 0 \,\}$$
considered as a germ at $0$, where $U$ is a sufficiently small neighborhood of $0$ on which $f$ is defined.

Two such germs $f, g$ are said to be topologically locally conjugate at $0$ if there exist neighborhoods $U_f, U_g$ of $0$ and a germ of homeomorphism $h : (U_f, 0) \to (U_g, 0)$ with $h \circ f = g \circ h$ near $0$.

Question: Is it true that two elliptic holomorphic germs $f, g \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}, 0)$ each having a Cremer point at the origin are topologically locally conjugate at $0$ if and only if
(i) $f'(0) = g'(0)$, and
(ii) the germs $(K_f, 0)$ and $(K_g, 0)$ are homeomorphic?

Equivalently, do the multiplier $f'(0)$ and the homeomorphism class of the stable set germ $K_f$ at $0$ form a complete set of topological invariants for the local topological dynamics at a Cremer fixed point?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not surface any published resolution of this classification question. Recent work on hedgehogs and neutral germs (e.g., Stony Brook IMS preprints) continues to investigate the local topology near Cremer points but does not announce a complete topological classification by multiplier and stable-set germ. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Given two one-variable parabolic germs, is there an effective decision procedure for determining whether they are holomorphically locally conjugate, taking into account the multiplier, parabolic multiplicity, iterative residue, and the usually intractable functional invariants that complete the holomorphic classification?
self_contained_problem:
Let f and g be two parabolic germs of one-variable holomorphic diffeomorphisms fixing the origin, that is, f, g ∈ C{z} with f(0)=g(0)=0 and f'(0), g'(0) roots of unity (so that some iterate has the form z + a z^{k+1} + ...). Their holomorphic local classification is given by the multiplier f'(0), the parabolic multiplicity (equivalently, the integer k), the iterative residue, and the Écalle–Voronin functional invariants (the equivalence class of the horn maps).

Problem: Devise an effective decision procedure (an algorithm taking finite descriptions of f and g as input, e.g. truncated power series with computable coefficients, plus oracle access where appropriate) that decides whether f and g are holomorphically locally conjugate at 0 — i.e., whether there exists a germ h of holomorphic diffeomorphism with h(0)=0 and h ∘ f = g ∘ h. The procedure must take into account the multiplier, the parabolic multiplicity, the iterative residue, and the (in general intractable) functional Écalle–Voronin invariants, and produce a definitive yes/no answer.
status_search_result: The classification of one-dimensional parabolic germs via multiplier, parabolic multiplicity, iterative residue, and Écalle–Voronin functional invariants (horn maps) is classical and complete. However, the Écalle–Voronin invariants are functional and generally intractable; resurgent methods (Écalle, and recent work by Dudko–Sauzin) express them as convergent numerical series, but no general effective decision algorithm for conjugacy is known. The question of an effective conjugacy-decision procedure remains open.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For a non-invertible dominant germ f in End(C^n, O), does the sequence of orders of its iterates, {c(f^k)}_{k∈N}, eventually satisfy a linear recurrence relation with integer coefficients?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ be a holomorphic germ fixing the origin, and assume $f$ is non-invertible (i.e. $df_O$ is not invertible) and dominant (i.e. $\det df \not\equiv 0$ as a germ). For a holomorphic germ $g:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$, define its order $c(g)$ to be the largest integer $c\ge 1$ such that every component of $g$ (in some, equivalently any, system of local coordinates centered at $O$) belongs to $\mathfrak{m}^c$, where $\mathfrak{m}$ is the maximal ideal of the local ring of germs at $O$. Equivalently, $c(g)$ is the minimum over the components $g_j$ of the order of vanishing of $g_j$ at $O$.

Consider the sequence $\{c(f^k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}}$ of orders of the iterates $f^k=f\circ\cdots\circ f$ ($k$ times).

Question: Does there exist an integer $K\ge 1$, an integer $r\ge 1$, and integers $a_1,\dots,a_r\in\mathbb{Z}$ such that
$$c(f^{k+r}) = a_1\, c(f^{k+r-1}) + a_2\, c(f^{k+r-2}) + \cdots + a_r\, c(f^k) \qquad \text{for all } k\ge K\,?$$

In other words, is it true that for every non-invertible dominant germ $f\in\operatorname{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$, the sequence of orders of its iterates eventually satisfies a linear recurrence relation with integer coefficients?
status_search_result: In dimension $n=2$ (for superattracting dominant germs), the analogous sequence of attraction rates is known to eventually satisfy an integral linear recursion of order at most two, established by Favre and Jonsson and extended in subsequent work (e.g., Gignac–Ruggiero, "Growth of attraction rates for iterates of a superattracting germ in dimension two", 2012). For general $n\ge 3$ and arbitrary non-invertible dominant germs, no proof or counterexample appears to be available, so the problem is partially solved (settled in dimension two, open in higher dimensions).

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Let f be a superattracting germ in End(C^n, O) with first nonzero homogeneous term H, and suppose the postcritical set of f is a topological cone near the origin. Under what additional conditions is f topologically locally conjugate to H? In particular, is the answer always yes when H is non-degenerate?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n, O)$ be a holomorphic germ fixing the origin, written as $f(z) = H(z) + \text{(higher-order terms)}$, where $H$ is the first nonzero homogeneous term of $f$ at the origin. Assume that $f$ is superattracting at $O$, i.e., the differential $df_O$ vanishes (so $\deg H \geq 2$). Recall that the critical set of $f$ is $\mathrm{Crit}(f) = \{z : \det df_z = 0\}$, and the postcritical set is $\mathrm{PC}(f) = \bigcup_{k \geq 1} f^k(\mathrm{Crit}(f))$. The homogeneous map $H$ is called non-degenerate if $H^{-1}(O) = \{O\}$.

A subset $S \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ containing $O$ is a topological cone near $O$ if there exist a neighborhood $U$ of $O$, a topological space $L$, and a homeomorphism $\Phi: U \to (L \times [0,1))/(L \times \{0\})$ sending $O$ to the cone point and sending $S \cap U$ onto a sub-cone of the form $(K \times [0,1))/(K \times \{0\})$ for some $K \subset L$.

Suppose that the postcritical set of $f$ is a topological cone near the origin. 

(a) Determine sufficient additional conditions under which $f$ is topologically locally conjugate to $H$ at $O$ (i.e., there exists a germ of homeomorphism $\varphi$ at $O$ with $\varphi(O) = O$ such that $\varphi \circ f = H \circ \varphi$).

(b) In particular, decide whether such a topological local conjugacy between $f$ and $H$ always exists whenever $H$ is non-degenerate.
status_search_result: A targeted search for a topological-cone criterion implying topological local conjugacy of a superattracting germ in $\mathbb{C}^n$ to its leading homogeneous term did not return any resolution. Surveys on local discrete holomorphic dynamics list this as an open problem, and follow-up work (e.g., on attraction rates of superattracting germs in dimension two) addresses related but distinct questions. No published proof or counterexample resolving the criterion was located.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For a non-invertible dominant germ f in End(C^3, O), under what conditions does there exist a modification π: M̃ → C^3 based at the origin, a point p in the exceptional fiber π^{-1}(O), and a holomorphic germ f̃ in End(M̃, p) that is rigid or at least weakly rigid and satisfies π ◦ f̃ = f ◦ π?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ denote the set of holomorphic germs $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ fixing the origin. A germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ is called dominant if its Jacobian determinant does not vanish identically, and non-invertible if $df_O$ is not invertible. A modification based at $O$ is a proper holomorphic map $\pi:\widetilde{M}\to\mathbb{C}^n$ from a smooth complex manifold $\widetilde{M}$ such that $\pi$ is a biholomorphism outside the exceptional fiber $E=\pi^{-1}(O)$, which is a connected divisor with simple normal crossings. 

For a germ $\widetilde{f}\in\mathrm{End}(\widetilde{M},p)$ at a point $p\in E$, denote by $C(\widetilde{f}^k)$ the critical set of the $k$-th iterate $\widetilde{f}^k$, and define the generalized critical set as the (germ at $p$ of the) union $C^\infty(\widetilde{f})=\bigcup_{k\ge 1} C(\widetilde{f}^k)$. The germ $\widetilde{f}$ is called rigid if $C^\infty(\widetilde{f})$ is (the germ of) a divisor with simple normal crossings at $p$ and is totally invariant, i.e. $\widetilde{f}^{-1}(C^\infty(\widetilde{f}))=C^\infty(\widetilde{f})$ as germs at $p$. It is called weakly rigid if $C^\infty(\widetilde{f})$ has simple normal crossings at $p$ (without requiring total invariance).

Problem. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on a non-invertible dominant germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^3,O)$ ensuring that there exist a modification $\pi:\widetilde{M}\to\mathbb{C}^3$ based at $O$, a point $p\in E=\pi^{-1}(O)$, and a holomorphic germ $\widetilde{f}\in\mathrm{End}(\widetilde{M},p)$ which is rigid (or at least weakly rigid) and which lifts $f$ in the sense that $\pi\circ\widetilde{f}=f\circ\pi$ as germs.
status_search_result: The two-dimensional analogue (rigidification of dominant superattracting germs in $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^2,O)$) has been established by Favre–Jonsson and Ruggiero using valuative techniques, but in dimension three the problem appears to remain open: searches turn up no general rigidification theorem for non-invertible dominant germs in $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^3,O)$, and known work in higher dimension only addresses partial cases (e.g. attracting rigid germs, principal resonances). No source claims a full solution.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: For a germ tangent to the identity in C^n, describe its stable set in terms of characteristic directions, directors, indices, and any additional necessary invariants. In particular, determine how those data control which points converge to the origin, including phenomena not captured merely by convergence tangent to a characteristic direction.
self_contained_problem:
Let f : (C^n, 0) → (C^n, 0) be a holomorphic germ tangent to the identity, i.e., f(z) = z + P_{k+1}(z) + P_{k+2}(z) + ⋯ where each P_j is a vector of homogeneous polynomials of degree j and P_{k+1} ≢ 0 (so k ≥ 1 is the order of f − id). The stable set of f is

   Stab(f) = { z ∈ (C^n, 0) : f^m(z) is defined for all m ≥ 0 and f^m(z) → 0 as m → ∞ }.

A characteristic direction of f is a point [v] ∈ P^{n−1}(C) such that P_{k+1}(v) = λ v for some λ ∈ C; it is non-degenerate if λ ≠ 0, and degenerate if λ = 0. Associated to a non-degenerate characteristic direction [v] one has its directors (the eigenvalues, suitably normalized, of an associated linear endomorphism of T_{[v]} P^{n−1}), and one can attach further holomorphic invariants such as residual indices along invariant subvarieties.

Problem. Give a complete description of Stab(f) in terms of the characteristic directions of f, their directors, the residual indices along the associated invariant data, and any additional holomorphic invariants required. In particular, characterize which orbits converge to 0, and account for trajectories converging to 0 whose behavior is not captured by convergence tangent to a single characteristic direction (e.g., orbits attracted along degenerate directions or arising from invariant subvarieties without tangent direction at 0).
status_search_result: The problem of giving a full description of the stable set of a germ tangent to the identity in C^n in terms of characteristic directions, directors, indices, and further invariants remains open in general. In dimension 2, results of Écalle, Hakim, Abate, and others give parabolic curves at non-degenerate characteristic directions; recent work (Lopez-Hernanz–Raissy–Ribón–Sanz Sánchez–Vivas, Mongodi–Ruggiero, 2021–2023) extends this and constructs parabolic manifolds and invariant curves in further situations, but in dimension n ≥ 3 examples are known of isolated germs whose only characteristic directions (even after blow-ups) are degenerate, showing no complete description is yet available.

paper_title: Open problems in local discrete holomorphic dynamics
original_question: Let λ⃗=(λ_1,...,λ_n) be eigenvalues for a diagonalizable differential, and suppose the Brjuno-type series Σ_{k≥0} 2^{-k} log(1/Ω_{λ⃗}(2^{k+1})) diverges. Does there then exist a formally linearizable germ f in End(C^n, O) with those eigenvalues that fails to be holomorphically linearizable?
self_contained_problem:
For a vector $\vec\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)\in\mathbb{C}^n$, define for each integer $m\ge 2$
$$\Omega_{\vec\lambda}(m)=\min\Big\{\,\big|\lambda^{Q}-\lambda_j\big|\;:\;Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^n,\;2\le |Q|\le m,\;1\le j\le n,\;\lambda^Q-\lambda_j\ne 0\,\Big\},$$
where $\lambda^Q=\lambda_1^{q_1}\cdots\lambda_n^{q_n}$ and $|Q|=q_1+\cdots+q_n$. Let $\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ denote the set of germs at the origin of holomorphic self-maps $f:(\mathbb{C}^n,O)\to(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$. Such a germ $f$ with diagonalizable differential $df_O$ having eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$ is called *formally linearizable* if there is a formal power series tangent to the identity conjugating $f$ to the linear map $\mathrm{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n)$, and *holomorphically linearizable* if such a conjugation can be taken convergent.

Suppose that
$$\sum_{k\ge 0}\frac{1}{2^{k}}\log\frac{1}{\Omega_{\vec\lambda}(2^{k+1})}=+\infty.$$
Does there necessarily exist a germ $f\in\mathrm{End}(\mathbb{C}^n,O)$ whose differential at the origin is diagonalizable with eigenvalues $\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_n$, such that $f$ is formally linearizable but not holomorphically linearizable?
status_search_result: Surveys on small divisors in discrete local holomorphic dynamics indicate that, in several variables, the necessity of the Brjuno-type condition for holomorphic linearizability remains unresolved; Yoccoz's necessity result covers only the one-dimensional case. No published proof of the multivariable necessity has been located.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Microscopic mechanisms of reentrant nematic behavior
original_question: Across liquid-crystal systems that show a reentrant nematic (RN) phase—a nematic phase that appears again at lower temperature after a smectic phase—what microscopic mechanisms cause reentrancy in the different classes of systems, and how can those mechanisms be experimentally identified and distinguished, given that reentrancy is not caused by a single mechanism but by many?
self_contained_problem:
A liquid crystal exhibits a reentrant nematic (RN) phase if, upon lowering the temperature at fixed pressure (or varying another thermodynamic control parameter such as composition or pressure at fixed temperature), the system passes through the sequence isotropic → nematic (N) → smectic (Sm) → nematic (RN), so that orientationally ordered but positionally disordered nematic order reappears below a more ordered smectic phase. Empirically, reentrant nematic behavior is observed in several distinct classes of mesogenic systems, including (a) strongly polar rod-like molecules with a terminal cyano (or similarly polar) group that form bilayer (partial-bilayer) smectic phases, (b) mixtures of polar and nonpolar mesogens, (c) single-component nonpolar mesogens, and (d) systems under applied pressure.

Problem. For each class of liquid crystal systems known to exhibit a reentrant nematic phase, identify the microscopic mechanism (formulated in terms of the intermolecular interaction potential and the resulting statistical-mechanical model — e.g. antiferroelectric dipolar pairing and frustrated dimer formation à la Berker–Walker, monomer–dimer steric/induced-force competition, packing/steric entropy effects, or other) that is responsible for the reappearance of nematic order below the smectic phase. Furthermore, propose experimental signatures (structural, thermodynamic, and dynamical — for instance X-ray structure factors, dielectric response, NMR order parameters, self-diffusion anisotropy, or rheological response) that uniquely identify each mechanism and that allow one to discriminate between the competing mechanisms in a given material, taking into account that reentrancy is not produced by a single universal mechanism but by several distinct ones depending on the details of the intermolecular potential.
status_search_result: Reviews and recent literature on reentrant nematic liquid crystals indicate that no single microscopic mechanism explains reentrancy across all systems: frustrated antiferroelectric dimerization (Berker–Walker), monomer–dimer competition, and steric/packing effects each apply to different classes, and the identification of which mechanism operates in a given system — particularly in non-dimer-forming and nonpolar single-component mesogens — remains unresolved. Experimental discriminators are still under active investigation.

context_brief: Nematic order across the SA-RN transition
original_question: How does the nematic orientational order parameter Q change when a liquid crystal crosses from a smectic-A (SA) phase, in which molecules organize in layers, into a reentrant nematic (RN) phase, and can experiments resolve whether Q increases sharply, changes only subtly, or shows no enhancement?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a thermotropic liquid crystal that, upon cooling at fixed pressure (or upon varying composition in a binary mixture), exhibits the phase sequence

  Nematic (N)  →  Smectic-A (S_A)  →  Reentrant Nematic (RN),

where the nematic phases possess long-range orientational order (described by the uniaxial scalar nematic order parameter Q = ⟨P_2(cos θ)⟩, with θ the angle between a molecular long axis and the nematic director) but no long-range translational order, and the smectic-A phase additionally has one-dimensional density modulation along the director (molecules organized in layers).

Determine the behavior of the nematic orientational order parameter Q as the system crosses the S_A → RN phase boundary. Specifically:

(a) Does Q increase discontinuously (jump) at the S_A–RN transition, change only by a small continuous amount, or remain effectively unchanged compared with its value in the adjacent S_A phase?

(b) Provide a theoretical prediction (e.g. via a Landau free energy with coupled nematic order parameter Q and smectic density-wave amplitude ψ) for the sign and magnitude of ΔQ across the transition, and identify experimental observables (e.g. optical birefringence, magnetic/diamagnetic anisotropy, NMR splittings, X-ray determinations of ⟨P_2⟩) capable of resolving this change.
status_search_result: Searches return Landau-theoretic models coupling nematic and smectic order parameters that qualitatively account for reentrant nematic behavior, but no definitive experimental determination of the change in the nematic scalar order parameter Q across the S_A–RN transition was located. The question of whether Q jumps, changes subtly, or is unchanged at this transition appears to remain unresolved.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Mechanism of reentrancy without dimer formation
original_question: For liquid crystals that exhibit reentrant nematic phases without forming dimers—for example single-component, terminal-nonpolar molecules whose smectic layer thickness equals the molecular length—what experimental microscopic mechanism drives the loss of smectic layering and the return to a nematic phase?
self_contained_problem:
Consider thermotropic liquid crystals composed of single-component, terminal-nonpolar rod-like molecules that exhibit a reentrant nematic phase, i.e. on cooling display the phase sequence isotropic → nematic → smectic-A → nematic (reentrant) (possibly continuing to lower-temperature phases). Suppose that X-ray diffraction in the smectic-A phase shows that the smectic layer spacing equals the average molecular length, so that antiparallel association into bilayer dimers does not occur. In such systems the classical frustrated-spacing/dimer mechanism (competition between monomer length and antiparallel-dimer length characteristic of strongly polar cyano- or nitro-terminated mesogens) cannot be invoked.

Identify and characterize, on the basis of direct experimental microscopic evidence, the molecular-scale mechanism that destabilizes the smectic-A layered order on cooling and drives the reappearance of the uniaxial nematic phase. The answer must specify which microscopic degrees of freedom (e.g. conformational/chain-flexibility changes, density or packing fluctuations, transverse dipolar correlations, intermolecular tilt or biaxial fluctuations, etc.) are responsible for the loss of layering, and must be supported by experimental observables (such as scattering, NMR, dielectric, or calorimetric measurements) rather than purely by lattice or mean-field theoretical models.
status_search_result: The microscopic mechanism driving reentrancy in non-dimer-forming (terminal-nonpolar, single-component) liquid crystals remains an outstanding open question. Theoretical proposals exist (e.g., Dowell's lattice theory based on chain flexibility, and more recent suggestions of repulsive-interaction-driven reentrancy that would apply to both polar and nonpolar systems), but no direct experimental microscopic mechanism has been established and the question is still listed as an open problem in recent reviews.

paper_title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?
context_brief: Experimental status of enhanced RN self-diffusivity
original_question: Do reentrant nematic phases in single-component, nonpolar molecular liquid crystals exhibit the very large self-diffusivity along the nematic director n that simulations predicted for confined reentrant nematics, and can experiments establish translational diffusion—not another relaxation mechanism—as the cause of the observed dynamical signatures?
self_contained_problem:
A liquid crystal exhibiting a reentrant nematic (RN) phase is one in which, upon isobaric cooling from the isotropic (I) phase, the system passes through a nematic (N) phase, then a smectic-A (S_A) phase, and on further cooling re-enters a nematic phase, denoted RN. In a uniaxial nematic phase, let n̂ denote the director and let D_∥ denote the molecular self-diffusion coefficient measured along n̂.

Computer simulations of confined model RN phases predict that, upon entering the RN phase, D_∥ increases by approximately an order of magnitude relative to the values found in the I, N, and S_A phases, and that this enhancement is due to a collective translational transport mode along n̂ rather than to any other (e.g. rotational or fluctuation-driven) relaxation mechanism.

Question: Does an analogous order-of-magnitude enhancement of D_∥ occur in the reentrant nematic phase of bulk, single-component, nonpolar thermotropic liquid crystals (i.e., systems composed of a single nonpolar molecular species, with no solvent and no dipolar association)? Specifically:

(a) Establish, by experiment on such single-component nonpolar materials, whether D_∥ in the RN phase is significantly larger than D_∥ in the surrounding I, N, and S_A phases.

(b) Demonstrate experimentally that the dynamical signature responsible for the observed behavior is genuine translational self-diffusion along n̂, and not some other relaxation mechanism contributing to the measured response.
status_search_result: Subsequent experimental work reports a maximum in self-diffusivity upon entering a reentrant nematic phase, with diffusivity rising by roughly an order of magnitude in the RN phase before decreasing in Arrhenius fashion (Mazza et al., "Diffusivity Maximum in a Reentrant Nematic Phase," 2012). However, a separate study of anisotropic self-diffusion across N, S_A, and RN phases found the temperature dependence of translational diffusion in the two nematic phases to be uniform within experimental error, indicating residual disagreement between simulation predictions and experiment. Whether translational diffusion (rather than another relaxation mechanism) is unambiguously responsible in single-component, nonpolar systems is therefore not fully settled.

paper_title: Some open problems on cycles
original_question: Let G be a simple Eulerian graph, meaning every vertex of G has even degree. Let cd(G) denote the smallest number of edge-disjoint circuits whose union is the entire edge set E(G). Is it always true that cd(G) ≤ |V(G)|/2 for every simple Eulerian graph G?
self_contained_problem:
A graph G = (V(G), E(G)) is called simple if it has no loops or multiple edges, and Eulerian if every vertex has even degree. A circuit (cycle) in G is a connected subgraph in which every vertex has degree 2. Define cd(G) to be the minimum number k such that E(G) can be partitioned into k pairwise edge-disjoint circuits C_1, ..., C_k with E(G) = E(C_1) ∪ ... ∪ E(C_k).

Prove or disprove: for every simple Eulerian graph G,
   cd(G) ≤ |V(G)| / 2.
status_search_result: Hajós' conjecture (1968) on cycle decompositions of Eulerian graphs remains open in general. It has been verified for restricted classes such as planar graphs, projective graphs, graphs of maximum degree at most 4, graphs of pathwidth at most 6, and small graphs (up to 12 vertices). Recent work (Girão, Granet, Kühn, Osthus) establishes an approximate version for dense graphs, but the full conjecture is still unresolved.

paper_title: Unsolved problems in particle physics
original_question: What physical mechanism generated the baryon asymmetry of the Universe, producing a matter-antimatter excess of order one unpaired quark per ten billion quark-antiquark pairs, when Standard Model electroweak baryogenesis fails because the required first-order electroweak phase transition would need an experimentally excluded light Higgs boson and CKM CP violation is insufficient?
self_contained_problem:
In standard cosmology, the observed Universe contains an asymmetry between matter and antimatter quantified by the baryon-to-photon ratio, equivalently by

  (n_q − n_{\bar q}) / (n_q + n_{\bar q}) ∼ 10^{-10},

i.e. roughly one unpaired quark for every ten billion quark–antiquark pairs at the relevant epoch. According to Sakharov's conditions, dynamically generating such an asymmetry from a baryon-symmetric initial state requires (i) baryon-number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, and (iii) a departure from thermal equilibrium.

Within the Standard Model of particle physics (gauge group SU(3)_C × SU(2)_L × U(1)_Y with the experimentally established Higgs sector and the measured CKM mixing matrix), the following two facts hold:
 (a) A first-order electroweak phase transition, needed to provide the out-of-equilibrium condition for electroweak baryogenesis, occurs only for a Higgs boson mass M_H ≲ 50 GeV, a range excluded by direct collider searches (the physical Higgs mass is ≈ 125 GeV).
 (b) The CP violation encoded in the CKM matrix is quantitatively too small to produce an asymmetry of the observed magnitude.

Problem: Identify and establish a concrete physical mechanism, beyond the minimal Standard Model, that dynamically generates the cosmological baryon asymmetry, satisfies Sakharov's three conditions, is consistent with all current experimental constraints, and quantitatively reproduces the observed value (n_q − n_{\bar q})/(n_q + n_{\bar q}) ∼ 10^{-10}, including a natural explanation of why this number is so small.
status_search_result: The origin of the baryon asymmetry of the Universe remains an open problem. While many candidate mechanisms exist (leptogenesis, electroweak baryogenesis in extensions of the Standard Model such as 2HDM/MSSM, Affleck–Dine, GUT baryogenesis, etc.), none has been experimentally confirmed, and recent reviews continue to list baryogenesis among the central unsolved problems of particle physics and cosmology.

original_question: What particle-physics model, field, or mechanism caused early-universe inflation, what is the inflaton if a new scalar field drove the exponential expansion, and what caused inflation to stop rather than continue until the present?
self_contained_problem:
Cosmological observations indicate that the very early Universe underwent a phase of nearly exponential (de Sitter–like) expansion, called inflation, during which the scale factor a(t) grew with Hubble rate H(t) satisfying ä/a = H² + Ḣ ≈ H² > 0 over many e-folds. In the standard particle-physics picture, such an expansion can be driven by a scalar field φ (the "inflaton"), absent from the Standard Model, with action
  S = ∫ d⁴x √(−g) [ ½ M_P² R − ½ g^{μν} ∂_μ φ ∂_ν φ − V(φ) ],
whose slow-roll evolution on a sufficiently flat potential V(φ) yields ε = (M_P²/2)(V'/V)² ≪ 1 and η = M_P² V''/V ≪ 1, producing inflation that subsequently terminates (when ε → 1) and reheats the Universe into a hot radiation-dominated phase consistent with Standard Model physics.

Identify, within a particle-physics framework, the field content, model, or mechanism responsible for early-universe inflation. In particular:
(i) Determine the identity of the inflaton: specify whether it is a new scalar degree of freedom beyond the Standard Model or arises from known fields, and give the form of its potential V(φ) and its couplings consistent with current cosmological constraints (spectral index n_s, tensor-to-scalar ratio r, amplitude of curvature perturbations, absence of observable non-Gaussianity).
(ii) Provide a dynamical mechanism that causes inflation to terminate after a finite number of e-folds N ≳ 50–60 rather than continue indefinitely, and that reheats the Universe to standard hot Big Bang cosmology with the observed matter–radiation content.
status_search_result: The fundamental nature of the inflaton and the precise mechanism that ended inflation remain unresolved open problems in physics. Numerous candidate models exist (e.g., Starobinsky/R² inflation, Higgs inflation, axion-monodromy, hilltop, plateau models), and current CMB data (Planck, BICEP/Keck, ACT) constrain but do not uniquely identify any model; recent 2024–2025 ACT/Planck combined analyses tighten constraints on n_s and r but still leave many viable inflaton candidates.
