paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: Extend the theory of global and local Weyl modules from currently understood cases to more general equivariant map algebras, including determining lengths, dimensions, and characters of local Weyl modules, and extending BGG reciprocity to this broader EMA setting.
self_contained_problem:
Let X be an irreducible affine scheme of finite type over an algebraically closed field k of characteristic zero, with coordinate ring A = k[X], and let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over k. Suppose a finite group Γ acts on X by automorphisms and on g by Lie algebra automorphisms. The associated equivariant map algebra is

  M(X, g)^Γ = (g ⊗_k A)^Γ,

the Lie subalgebra of Γ-fixed points in g ⊗ A under the diagonal action.

For a triangular-type decomposition of M(X,g)^Γ (when one is available, e.g. when g is reductive with a fixed Cartan and Borel preserved compatibly with Γ), one defines:
 (i) the global Weyl module W(λ) attached to a dominant integral weight λ, as the universal cyclic highest-weight module on which the positive part acts by zero and a chosen Cartan-type subalgebra acts via λ;
 (ii) the local Weyl module W_loc(λ, m), obtained from W(λ) by quotienting by the action of a maximal ideal m of the commutative algebra A_λ := End_{M(X,g)^Γ}(W(λ))^{op}.

The problem is to:

(a) For general data (X, g, Γ) as above (going beyond the cases of untwisted loop algebras, twisted loop algebras, multi-loop algebras, current algebras, and equivariant map algebras with free abelian group action treated in the existing literature), determine the length, the k-dimension, and the (graded) character of every local Weyl module W_loc(λ, m).

(b) Formulate and prove a version of Bernstein–Gelfand–Gelfand (BGG) reciprocity in the category of finite-dimensional graded (or suitably restricted) modules over M(X, g)^Γ: namely, exhibit a class of "standard" modules (e.g. global or local Weyl modules) and a class of indecomposable projective covers P(λ) of the simple objects L(λ), and prove that the projective P(λ) admits a filtration whose multiplicities [P(λ) : Δ(μ)] equal the multiplicities [Δ(μ) : L(λ)] of L(λ) as a composition factor of the standard module Δ(μ), in this general equivariant map algebra setting.
category_tag: Weyl modules for equivariant map algebras
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: local Weyl modules are understood for equivariant map algebras with free abelian group actions (Fourier–Khandai–Kus, 2011), global Weyl modules for general equivariant map algebras have been studied (Feigin–Loktev, Chari–Fourier–Khandai, and subsequent work), and BGG reciprocity has been established for current algebras (Bennett–Chari–Manning, 2012; Bennett–Bianchi–Chari et al., 2014). Recent extensions include hyper-map algebras and equivariant map Lie superalgebras (2025). However, a uniform treatment giving lengths, dimensions, and characters of local Weyl modules and BGG reciprocity for fully general equivariant map algebras remains incomplete. The problem is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: Assume g is semisimple and M = M(X,g)^Γ. Describe the first cohomology group H1(M,V) for a general M-module V, extending the partial results already known for some equivariant map algebras and locally finite modules; in particular, clarify this cohomology for the adjoint module Mad, where H1(M,Mad) = Der_k(M) / IDer(M).
self_contained_problem:
Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, let g be a finite-dimensional semisimple Lie algebra over k, and let X be a scheme of finite type over k. Let Γ be a finite group acting on X by scheme automorphisms and on g by Lie algebra automorphisms. The associated equivariant map algebra is

  M = M(X, g)^Γ = { f ∈ g ⊗_k 𝒪(X) : (id ⊗ γ*)·f = γ·f for all γ ∈ Γ },

with Lie bracket induced from that of g and pointwise multiplication on 𝒪(X). For an M-module V, let H^1(M, V) denote the first Chevalley–Eilenberg Lie algebra cohomology of M with coefficients in V, which classifies equivalence classes of abelian extensions / outer derivations valued in V.

Problem. Give an explicit description of H^1(M, V) for a general M-module V, in terms of invariants of (X, g, Γ) and of V. In particular:

(a) Specialize to the adjoint module M_ad = M (with action by the Lie bracket) and produce an explicit description of

  H^1(M, M_ad) = Der_k(M) / IDer(M),

the space of outer k-linear derivations of M (where IDer(M) denotes inner derivations).

(b) Extend the result beyond the previously known cases (such as multiloop algebras and locally finite modules) to a uniform statement covering arbitrary M-modules V and arbitrary equivariant map algebras M(X, g)^Γ with g semisimple.

paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: For a perfect equivariant map Lie algebra M = (g ⊗ A)^Γ, understand its central extensions, especially the universal central extension uce(M), and determine when the universal central extension of the fixed-point algebra agrees with the fixed points of the universal central extension of the untwisted algebra, namely when uce((g ⊗ A)^Γ) is naturally isomorphic to uce(g ⊗ A)^Γ.
self_contained_problem:
Let $k$ be a field of characteristic $0$, let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a Lie algebra over $k$, and let $A$ be a commutative associative unital $k$-algebra. Let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting by Lie algebra automorphisms on $\mathfrak{g}$ and by $k$-algebra automorphisms on $A$. The diagonal action of $\Gamma$ on the (untwisted) map algebra $\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A$ is given by $\gamma \cdot (x \otimes a) = (\gamma \cdot x) \otimes (\gamma \cdot a)$. The corresponding equivariant map algebra is the fixed-point Lie subalgebra
$$M := (\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A)^\Gamma = \{ z \in \mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A : \gamma \cdot z = z 	ext{ for all } \gamma \in \Gamma\}.$$

For any perfect Lie algebra $L$ (i.e.\ $[L,L] = L$) there exists a universal central extension $\mathrm{uce}(L) 	woheadrightarrow L$, characterized up to unique isomorphism by being a perfect central extension that uniquely covers every central extension of $L$.

Assume that $M = (\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A)^\Gamma$ is perfect. The action of $\Gamma$ on $\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A$ lifts uniquely to an action on $\mathrm{uce}(\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A)$ by Lie algebra automorphisms, so the fixed-point algebra $\mathrm{uce}(\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A)^\Gamma$ is well-defined.

Describe the universal central extension $\mathrm{uce}(M)$ explicitly. In particular, determine necessary and sufficient conditions on the triple $(\mathfrak{g}, A, \Gamma)$ under which there is a natural isomorphism
$$\mathrm{uce} igl((\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A)^\Gamma igr) \;\cong\; \mathrm{uce}(\mathfrak{g} \otimes_k A)^\Gamma.$$

status_search_result: No definitive resolution was found in the literature. Status appears to remain open or only partially understood.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: At present collider energies, for QCD processes involving partons with small longitudinal momentum fraction x and transverse momentum kT of order the saturation scale Qs(x), is the nonlinear parton-saturation description implemented by the Color Glass Condensate phenomenology actually necessary, or can the data be described adequately by purely linear gluon distributions supplemented with a non-perturbative ad hoc cutoff? Here parton saturation means the weakly coupled nonlinear QCD regime that appears when parton densities grow at small x, and Qs(x) is the momentum scale separating dense and dilute regimes.
self_contained_problem:
Consider quantum chromodynamics (QCD) processes at present-day high-energy hadron and nuclear colliders that probe partons carrying a small longitudinal momentum fraction x of their parent hadron and having transverse momentum k_T of the order of the saturation scale Q_s(x). Here "parton saturation" denotes the weakly coupled nonlinear QCD regime expected to set in when gluon densities at small x become so large that nonlinear effects (such as gluon recombination) balance linear BFKL-type growth, and Q_s(x) is the momentum scale separating the dense (k_T ≲ Q_s) from the dilute (k_T ≫ Q_s) regime, with Q_s(x) increasing as x decreases. The Color Glass Condensate (CGC) is the effective field theory implementation of this nonlinear saturation regime.

Question: Is it necessary, at currently accessible collider energies, to use the nonlinear CGC/saturation framework to describe QCD data in the kinematic region x ≪ 1, k_T ∼ Q_s(x)? Equivalently: can the relevant observables in this regime be adequately described instead by purely linear (collinear or k_T-factorized) gluon distributions supplemented by an ad hoc non-perturbative infrared cutoff, or does an adequate description of the data require properly incorporating the nonlinear dynamics at k_T ∼ Q_s(x)?

The task is to determine, on the basis of comparison with collider data, whether nonlinear saturation dynamics is unavoidable for a satisfactory phenomenological description, or whether linear-evolution descriptions with a tunable infrared cutoff suffice.
category_tag: QCD parton saturation / Color Glass Condensate
status_search_result: The question of whether nonlinear saturation/CGC dynamics is strictly necessary at current colliders, as opposed to linear gluon distributions with an ad hoc infrared cutoff, remains an active phenomenological question. Recent work (e.g. NLO CGC phenomenology with threshold resummation for forward hadron production at RHIC/LHC, and CMS observations of long-range two-particle correlations in p–Pb collisions) provides increasingly suggestive but not yet conclusive evidence for saturation. The community generally still treats this as an open question, motivating future facilities such as the Electron-Ion Collider.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: What is the transverse impact-parameter dependence of the nuclear gluon density and of the saturation scale Qs in a nucleus, and is the current phenomenological Color Glass Condensate practice of modeling a nucleus as Woods-Saxon distributed CGCs whose gluon densities are evolved independently at different impact parameters sufficient for a conceptually accurate description of small-x nuclear structure?
self_contained_problem:
In the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) effective theory of small-x QCD, a large nucleus at high energy is characterized by a transverse-position-dependent gluon distribution and a local saturation scale Q_s(x, b), where x is the longitudinal momentum fraction and b is the transverse impact parameter relative to the nuclear center. A common phenomenological prescription is to model the nucleus as an ensemble of independent CGC sources distributed in the transverse plane according to a Woods–Saxon profile

  ρ(r) = ρ_0 / (1 + exp((r - R)/a)),

and to evolve the gluon density at each impact parameter b independently in x via small-x evolution equations (e.g., the JIMWLK or BK equations), with no transverse coupling between different b.

Determine, from first principles in QCD at high parton density:

(a) the correct functional dependence of the nuclear gluon density xG_A(x, b) and of the saturation scale Q_s,A(x, b) on the transverse impact parameter b in a large nucleus at small x;

(b) whether the prescription of treating the nucleus as a Woods–Saxon distribution of independent CGC sources with b-independent (locally evolved) small-x evolution provides a conceptually accurate description of the transverse structure of nuclei at small x, or whether non-trivial transverse correlations and/or coupling between different impact parameters during small-x evolution must be included for a correct description.
category_tag: small-x QCD and Color Glass Condensate
status_search_result: The impact-parameter dependence of the nuclear gluon density and saturation scale remains a central open non-perturbative input in CGC phenomenology. While impact-parameter dependent dipole and b-CGC models have been developed and refined, and exclusive processes at the future Electron-Ion Collider are being designed precisely to image the transverse small-x structure of nuclei, no first-principles determination has been established and the question of whether independent-b evolution of Woods–Saxon-distributed CGC sources is conceptually sufficient is still under active investigation.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: In the QCD saturation regime at high parton density, does the QCD coupling run with the saturation scale Qs, the momentum scale that separates dense and dilute small-x regimes and increases as x decreases?
self_contained_problem: In quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at high parton density and small Bjorken x, the transition between the dense (high-occupancy) and dilute regimes of the gluon distribution inside a hadron or nucleus is characterized by a dynamically generated momentum scale Q_s(x), called the saturation scale, which grows as x decreases. The strong coupling α_s(μ) of QCD depends on a renormalization scale μ via the QCD β-function, and in many small-x evolution equations (e.g., the Balitsky–Kovchegov and JIMWLK equations) the choice of the scale at which α_s is evaluated is not uniquely fixed by the leading-order formalism.\n\nDetermine whether, in the saturation regime at small x, the appropriate renormalization scale for the running QCD coupling is set by the saturation scale Q_s(x) itself. Concretely: establish, from first principles within perturbative QCD beyond leading order, whether α_s should run with μ = Q_s(x) (or some specified function of Q_s) when describing observables and evolution equations in the high-parton-density regime, and characterize precisely the kinematic conditions under which such a prescription is correct.
status_search_result: This is posed as a fundamental open conceptual question in small-x/saturation QCD. While running-coupling corrections to the BK and JIMWLK equations have been computed (Balitsky; Kovchegov–Weigert) and phenomenological fits often use scales related to Q_s, there is no rigorous derivation establishing that the coupling universally runs with Q_s; the choice of scale remains a topic of ongoing research and debate. Status appears open.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: What universality properties characterize the QCD saturation regime of high-density small-x gluons, and how can proton-nucleus and electron-nucleus collisions explore those properties in the strongly correlated gluonic many-body system?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), at small Bjorken-x the gluon density inside a hadron grows rapidly and is conjectured to enter a non-linear regime, called parton saturation, characterized by a dynamically generated saturation scale Q_s(x,A) (depending on x and on the nuclear mass number A) at which non-linear gluon recombination balances linear BFKL-type growth, while the strong coupling α_s(Q_s) remains weak. In this regime the small-x gluon system is described as a strongly correlated many-body state, often modeled by classical Yang–Mills color fields (the Color Glass Condensate effective theory) with stochastic color sources.

Formulate and establish the universality properties of this saturation regime. Specifically:

(a) Identify and prove which observables (e.g., dipole scattering amplitudes, unintegrated gluon distributions, multi-parton correlators, n-point Wilson-line correlators) become universal functions of the single combination Q_s(x,A) times a transverse scale, independent of the specific hadronic target (proton vs. nucleus) and of details of the initial non-perturbative input.

(b) Determine the precise sense (geometric scaling, fixed points of the JIMWLK / Balitsky–Kovchegov non-linear evolution equations, scaling solutions of these renormalization-group equations) in which such universality holds, including the dependence on the running of α_s and on impact parameter.

(c) Specify which measurements in proton–nucleus (p+A) and electron–nucleus (e+A) collisions—such as forward single-inclusive hadron production, di-hadron azimuthal correlations, diffractive vector-meson production, inclusive and diffractive deep inelastic structure functions—can isolate and quantitatively test these universality predictions, distinguishing genuine saturation universality from leading-twist collinear-factorization expectations.

(d) Characterize how the saturation regime connects, as Q_s decreases, to the confinement regime, and whether classical color fields remain the correct effective degrees of freedom in that transition.
status_search_result: The universality of the QCD saturation regime and its experimental exploration via p+A and e+A collisions remains an active open research direction. While partial universality results (geometric scaling, BK/JIMWLK fixed-point analyses, CGC factorization theorems for limited classes of observables) have been established, a complete characterization is unresolved and is a central scientific motivation for the Electron-Ion Collider (EIC), expected to begin operations in the early 2030s.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
context_brief: EIC discriminating power of F2 and FL
original_question: At a future Electron Ion Collider, can combined measurements of the F2 and FL structure functions in inclusive electron-nucleus deep inelastic scattering discriminate between linear and nonlinear QCD evolution, as combined F2 and FL measurements are expected to do at the Large Hadron electron Collider?
self_contained_problem:
Consider inclusive deep inelastic scattering of electrons on nuclei (e+A DIS), in which the virtual-photon–nucleus cross section is decomposed into the inclusive structure function F_2(x,Q^2) and the longitudinal structure function F_L(x,Q^2), with x the Bjorken variable and Q^2 the photon virtuality. At small x, two competing theoretical descriptions of QCD evolution are available: (i) linear evolution, governed by DGLAP and/or BFKL equations, in which gluon densities grow without bound; and (ii) nonlinear evolution, governed by equations of the Balitsky–Kovchegov / JIMWLK type, which include gluon recombination and lead to saturation of the gluon density at a scale Q_s(x,A).

At a proposed Electron–Ion Collider (EIC) operating with electron–nucleus collisions in a kinematic regime that probes small x and moderate Q^2, with the capability of an e+A collision energy scan needed to extract F_L via the Rosenbluth-type separation, determine whether combined precision measurements of F_2(x,Q^2) and F_L(x,Q^2) over the accessible (x,Q^2) range have sufficient discriminating power to distinguish predictions of linear QCD evolution from those of nonlinear (saturation-based) QCD evolution. In particular, quantify the predicted relative differences ΔF_2/F_2 and ΔF_L/F_L between the two frameworks (after matching them in a control region where both are expected to be reliable) as functions of x, Q^2, and nuclear mass number A, and determine whether these differences exceed the projected combined experimental and theoretical uncertainties at the EIC, as is expected to be the case at the Large Hadron electron Collider (LHeC).
status_search_result: Recent phenomenological studies (e.g., Phys. Rev. D 105, 114017 (2022) and follow-up work) have computed F_2 and F_L within both linear collinear-factorization frameworks and nonlinear BK-based frameworks matched in a common region, finding that at EIC kinematics deviations in F_2 remain at the few-percent level while deviations in F_L can reach roughly 10%, indicating that F_L provides meaningful but not yet conclusive discriminating power. The definitive experimental discrimination depends on EIC running conditions (energy scan for F_L extraction) and final detector/luminosity performance, so the question is partially addressed theoretically but not yet experimentally settled.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: How is event-by-event initial spatial anisotropy in the transverse density of a heavy-ion collision converted by the system evolution into final-state momentum anisotropy of detected particles, and can this hydrodynamic response be understood generally enough to avoid running a separate event-by-event hydrodynamic simulation for every candidate initial condition?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as follows. At an early proper time τ₀ after impact, the transverse energy-density profile e(x,y) of the produced matter is given on the transverse plane, and fluctuates from event to event. For each integer n ≥ 1, define the complex initial spatial anisotropy (eccentricity) of harmonic order n by

  ε_n e^{i n Φ_n} = − ( ∫ d²x⊥ r^n e^{i n φ} e(x,y) ) / ( ∫ d²x⊥ r^n e(x,y) ),

with (r,φ) polar coordinates centered at the energy-weighted center of mass. Let the subsequent evolution be governed by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics with a fixed equation of state and fixed transport coefficients (e.g., shear and bulk viscosities), followed by a standard particlization prescription on a freeze-out hypersurface. The final azimuthal single-particle distribution dN/dφ admits a Fourier decomposition

  dN/dφ ∝ 1 + 2 Σ_{n≥1} v_n cos[n(φ − Ψ_n)],

defining the complex flow harmonics V_n = v_n e^{i n Ψ_n}.

Problem. Determine, on an event-by-event basis, an explicit and predictive functional map F mapping the initial energy-density profile e(x,y) (or, equivalently, a finite collection of its cumulants {ε_m e^{i m Φ_m}} together with relevant scalar moments such as ⟨r^k⟩) to the final flow vector V_n,

  V_n = F_n( {ε_m e^{i m Φ_m}}, {⟨r^k⟩}, η/s, ζ/s, equation of state, … ),

that reproduces the output of full event-by-event viscous hydrodynamic simulations to controlled accuracy across centralities and harmonic orders, so that no separate hydrodynamic simulation is required for each candidate initial condition. In particular, characterize the regime of validity of a linear response relation V_n = κ_n ε_n e^{i n Φ_n}, identify and quantify the leading nonlinear and mode-mixing corrections (e.g., cubic response in ε_n and quadratic mixings such as ε_2 ε_3 contributing to V_5), and determine to what extent the response coefficients depend only on bulk medium properties rather than on details of the initial-state model.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: for lower harmonics (n=2,3) and central/mid-central collisions, an approximately linear response V_n ≈ κ_n ε_n is well established, and explicit nonlinear/mode-mixing parametrizations (cubic response in ε_n, and quadratic mixings producing V_4, V_5, V_6 from ε_2, ε_3) have been formulated and tested against event-by-event viscous hydrodynamics with good but not perfect accuracy. A fully predictive, model-independent functional map covering all harmonics, all centralities, and all initial-condition models without running new simulations is not yet available, so the broader problem remains partially solved.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
context_brief: Interpretation and selection of new observables
original_question: What can newly measured heavy-ion observables, including new flow and particle-correlation observables, teach researchers about the quark-gluon plasma, the initial state, and the system evolution, and what additional observables should be measured?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the produced matter is modeled as a quark-gluon plasma (QGP) whose space-time evolution is commonly described by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics with fluctuating initial conditions, followed by hadronic freeze-out. Standard final-state observables include the azimuthal anisotropic flow harmonics v_n (defined via the Fourier expansion dN/dφ ∝ 1 + 2 Σ_{n≥1} v_n cos[n(φ − Ψ_n)] of the single-particle azimuthal distribution about event-plane angles Ψ_n), event-by-event distributions P(v_n), event-plane correlations between Ψ_n at different harmonics, mixed-harmonic correlators, and multi-particle cumulants v_n{2k}. The initial state is characterized by eccentricities ε_n of the transverse energy- or entropy-density profile.

Address the following:

(a) Identify which combinations of the newly available observables (event-by-event v_n distributions, mixed-harmonic event-plane correlators ⟨cos(n_1 Ψ_{m_1} + ⋯ + n_k Ψ_{m_k})⟩, higher-order cumulants v_n{4}, v_n{6}, v_n{8}, factorization-breaking ratios in p_T and rapidity, and symmetric/asymmetric cumulants SC(m,n)) most tightly constrain (i) the shear and bulk viscosity to entropy density ratios η/s and ζ/s of the QGP as functions of temperature, (ii) the statistical properties of the fluctuating initial energy/entropy density (mean, variance, and non-Gaussianity of the ε_n distributions), and (iii) the pre-equilibrium dynamics linking the initial color-field stage to the hydrodynamic stage.

(b) Propose a minimal set of additional final-state observables, beyond those listed above, whose measurement would further disentangle initial-state fluctuations from medium response, and provide a precise mathematical definition of each proposed observable together with the specific theoretical degeneracy it is designed to break.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended program-defining question about heavy-ion phenomenology. While significant progress has been made (e.g., extraction of η/s(T) and ζ/s(T) via Bayesian analyses by the JETSCAPE and Duke groups, and new symmetric cumulants and factorization-breaking measurements at the LHC), the broader question of which observables most tightly constrain initial-state fluctuations and QGP transport, and what further observables should be measured, remains an active open research direction with no definitive resolution.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: Can the various sources of event-by-event fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions, including fluctuations in nucleon or quark positions, binary interactions, finite nucleon extent, initial momentum distribution, and local energy deposition or particle production, be disentangled from one another?
self_contained_problem:
In a relativistic heavy-ion collision, the initial state of the produced fireball varies from event to event due to several distinct stochastic mechanisms. Consider the following sources of event-by-event fluctuations in the initial conditions:

(1) Fluctuations in the transverse positions of the nucleons (or constituent quarks) inside the colliding nuclei, together with the stochastic pattern of their binary interactions (which nucleon pairs scatter inelastically).

(2) The finite spatial extent of individual nucleons, modeled by a smooth profile and accompanied by a correspondingly adjusted Woods–Saxon nuclear density distribution.

(3) Fluctuations in the initial transverse momentum distribution of the produced matter (initial flow), independent of the geometric energy-density profile.

(4) Local fluctuations in the energy deposition and/or particle production at each transverse point, beyond what is dictated by the nucleon positions.

Each of these mechanisms imprints itself on observable final-state event-by-event quantities such as the harmonic flow coefficients v_n, their probability distributions P(v_n), event-plane correlations, and the correlations between flow harmonics of different orders.

Problem. Devise a set of observables, or a procedure, that uniquely disentangles the contributions of mechanisms (1)–(4) from one another using only measurable final-state correlations. More precisely: do there exist final-state observables whose dependence on these four sources is sufficiently independent that, given experimental measurements of those observables, one can separately determine (or place quantitative constraints on) the magnitude of each fluctuation source individually?
status_search_result: The question of separating the various sources of initial-state fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions remains an active research topic. Subsequent works (e.g., studies of flow cumulants, P(v_n) distributions, and symmetric cumulants by ATLAS, ALICE, CMS, and theory groups) have constrained certain combinations, but no consensus procedure fully disentangles nucleon-position, sub-nucleonic, initial-momentum, and local energy-deposition fluctuations independently. The status is best described as still open / partially constrained.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
context_brief: Rapid thermalization in initial non-equilibrium evolution
original_question: Can rapid thermalization during the initially non-equilibrium stage of a heavy-ion collision be obtained in an SU(3) Yang-Mills field-evolution framework when quantum fluctuations are included in a full 3+1-dimensional simulation?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the early, far-from-equilibrium stage of an ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as a classical-statistical SU(3) Yang–Mills field theory in 3+1 spacetime dimensions. The classical color fields are evolved from initial conditions motivated by the Color Glass Condensate, and quantum fluctuations are incorporated by sampling initial-field perturbations (e.g., with a spectrum determined by the JIMWLK/CGC framework or by linearized fluctuations on top of the classical background) and then propagating them under the full nonlinear SU(3) Yang–Mills equations on a 3+1-dimensional lattice.

Within this classical-statistical SU(3) Yang–Mills framework with quantum fluctuations included in a fully 3+1-dimensional simulation, determine whether the gauge-field system undergoes rapid thermalization on a timescale compatible with the short hydrodynamization times (of order 1 fm/c or less) inferred from heavy-ion phenomenology. Specifically, establish whether the local energy-momentum tensor isotropizes (longitudinal pressure approaching transverse pressure) and whether the gluon occupation numbers approach a thermal (Bose–Einstein) distribution rapidly, or whether the dynamics instead remain anisotropic and/or relax only on parametrically longer timescales.
status_search_result: The question of rapid thermalization in classical-statistical SU(3) Yang–Mills simulations with quantum fluctuations in full 3+1D remains an active research area. Subsequent works have shown isotropization via chromo-Weibel-like instabilities and filamentation, but classical field theory suffers from Rayleigh–Jeans divergence and does not reach quantum thermal distributions, leaving full quantum thermalization unresolved. No definitive demonstration of rapid quantum thermalization in this framework has been established.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: Beyond the first few coordinate-space Fourier coefficients ε_n used to characterize initial-state profiles, what additional quantities can represent the longitudinal structure, initial velocity profile, and other initial-state features more completely?
status_search_result: This is a programmatic open problem from heavy-ion phenomenology. paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
context_brief: Limits of simplified hydrodynamic response relations
original_question: How far can simplified response relations between initial eccentricities and final flow harmonics be pushed—for example, can all mixed-harmonic event-plane correlations be reproduced without brute-force event-by-event hydrodynamic calculations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled as follows. In each event, the transverse density of the initial-state fireball is characterized by a set of complex eccentricities
  ε_n e^{i n Φ_n} = − ⟨ r^n e^{i n φ} ⟩ / ⟨ r^n ⟩,  for n = 2, 3, 4, …,
computed from the energy density at mid-rapidity (with ⟨·⟩ the energy-density-weighted average in the transverse plane after recentering). The final-state azimuthal particle distribution dN/dφ is described by complex flow harmonics
  V_n = v_n e^{i n Ψ_n},  n = 2, 3, 4, …,
which in principle are obtained by solving the event-by-event relativistic viscous hydrodynamic equations on each fluctuating initial condition and computing the Cooper–Frye particle spectrum.

A simplified, non-event-by-event "response" model attempts to predict V_n directly from the initial eccentricities through a fixed (event-independent) functional relation, e.g. a polynomial of the form
  V_n = κ_n ε_n e^{i n Φ_n} + ∑_{m,k} χ^{(n)}_{m,k} (ε_m e^{i m Φ_m})(ε_k e^{i k Φ_k}) δ_{m+k,n} + (higher-order terms),
with response coefficients κ_n, χ^{(n)}_{m,k}, … determined once (e.g. from a small set of smooth/averaged hydrodynamic runs) and then applied event-by-event to the fluctuating eccentricities.

Question. Determine the ultimate scope of such simplified response relations for reproducing mixed-harmonic event-plane correlations, defined for integer coefficients (c_2, c_3, …) with ∑ n c_n = 0 by
  ⟨ cos( ∑_n c_n n Ψ_n ) ⟩_events.
Specifically: does there exist a closed-form, event-independent map V_n = F_n(ε_2, Φ_2, ε_3, Φ_3, …) (of polynomial type or otherwise) that, applied event-by-event to a realistic ensemble of fluctuating initial conditions, reproduces all mixed-harmonic event-plane correlations measured in heavy-ion collisions to within experimental precision, thereby eliminating the need for brute-force event-by-event hydrodynamic simulation? If such a map exists, exhibit it and characterize its accuracy and domain of validity (collision system, centrality, harmonic order); if not, identify which correlators provably cannot be captured by any such response ansatz and require full event-by-event hydrodynamic evolution.
category_tag: Relativistic hydrodynamic response in heavy-ion collisions
status_search_result: Subsequent work has shown that a substantial set of mixed-harmonic event-plane correlations can indeed be reproduced by simplified linear-plus-nonlinear (mode-coupled) response relations applied to fluctuating initial eccentricities, including single-shot and cumulant-based predictions matching ATLAS/ALICE data and RHIC predictions. Thus the program has been partially successful—linear response captures v2, v3 and many correlations involving Ψ2, Ψ3, while polynomial/mode-coupling expansions capture leading higher-harmonic correlators. However, full quantitative agreement for all correlators across systems and centralities still relies on event-by-event hydrodynamic simulations, and no proof exists that a universal closed-form response map suffices. The general question therefore remains open in its strongest form.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: Can the rapidity-even first-order event plane Ψ_1 be reconstructed experimentally, and what would such a reconstruction reveal about the corresponding rapidity-even v_1 flow observable in heavy-ion collisions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider relativistic heavy-ion collisions in which the azimuthal distribution of produced particles in each event is expanded in a Fourier series,
   dN/dφ ∝ 1 + 2 Σ_{n≥1} v_n cos[n(φ − Ψ_n)],
where Ψ_n is the n-th order event plane and v_n is the corresponding flow harmonic. Initial-state fluctuations are known to generate, in addition to the conventional rapidity-odd directed flow, a rapidity-even component of the first harmonic v_1 ("dipolar flow") associated with a fluctuation-driven first-order symmetry plane Ψ_1 that does not change sign under η → −η.

Question: Devise an experimental procedure to reconstruct, event by event, the rapidity-even first-order event plane Ψ_1 corresponding to the rapidity-even v_1 observable, accounting for the constraint of overall transverse momentum conservation, and use this reconstruction to characterize the rapidity-even v_1(p_T, η, centrality). Specifically:

(a) Define a rapidity-even weight w(η, p_T) that suppresses the rapidity-odd directed-flow contribution and the trivial momentum-conservation recoil contribution while retaining the fluctuation-driven dipolar component, and use it to construct an event-flow vector Q_1 whose phase estimates Ψ_1.

(b) Establish the resolution correction for this Ψ_1 estimator and verify, by comparison with two- and multi-particle cumulant methods (e.g., v_1{2}, v_1{4}), that the resulting v_1{Ψ_1} measures the rapidity-even dipolar flow.

(c) Determine the resulting v_1(p_T) at midrapidity, including its sign-changing behavior, its high-p_T magnitude relative to v_2 and v_3, and its centrality dependence.
status_search_result: The reconstruction has been substantially achieved. ATLAS measured the rapidity-even dipolar v_1 in Pb-Pb collisions at 2.76 TeV using a two-particle correlation/fit method that handles momentum conservation, and STAR has reported beam-energy-dependent rapidity-even dipolar v_1 in Au+Au, with later analyses studying v_1{Ψ_1} versus rapidity, p_T, centrality, and energy. Thus the broad goal of reconstructing the corresponding Ψ_1 and characterizing rapidity-even v_1 has been carried out, although refinements (event-plane resolution, decorrelation in η, baryon-rich regimes) remain active.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: Can theory calculations of three-particle correlations with a high-transverse-momentum trigger particle and low-transverse-momentum associated particles, in Δφ–Δφ, Δφ–Δη, and Δη–Δη angular spaces, disentangle jet-medium effects from the underlying pure medium response?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collision modeled by a fluctuating initial energy-density profile evolved hydrodynamically into a hot, expanding QCD medium, together with hard partons that traverse and interact with this medium ("jet-medium" interactions). For each event, define the single-particle azimuthal angle φ and pseudorapidity η of produced hadrons. Fix a high-transverse-momentum trigger hadron with p_T ∈ [6, 8] GeV, and consider associated hadrons with p_T below approximately 2 GeV. Define the three-particle correlation functions C(Δφ₁, Δφ₂), C(Δφ, Δη), and C(Δη₁, Δη₂), where the differences are computed between each associated particle and the trigger (or between the two associated particles, as appropriate), after subtracting combinatorial backgrounds.

Provide theoretical predictions for these three-particle correlation functions in the three angular spaces (Δφ–Δφ, Δφ–Δη, and Δη–Δη), both:
(a) from a pure hydrodynamic medium evolution baseline (no hard trigger; only collective response to initial-state fluctuations), and
(b) from a full calculation including a high-p_T trigger and its energy/momentum deposition into the medium.

Determine whether the structures in (a) and (b) differ in a quantitatively distinguishable way, and thus whether such three-particle correlation observables can disentangle jet-medium-induced contributions from the pure collective medium response.
status_search_result: No comprehensive theoretical calculation of three-particle correlations in all three angular spaces (Δφ–Δφ, Δφ–Δη, Δη–Δη) with a hard trigger and soft associates that cleanly disentangles jet-medium response from pure hydrodynamic flow has been established. While two-particle correlations and event-by-event hydrodynamics with hard probes have advanced substantially since 2012, the specific three-particle disentanglement program remains a largely open theoretical and experimental challenge.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
original_question: Let x'=f(x,u) be a real-analytic control system. If the system is small-time locally controllable at a state x0, must it also be small-time locally reachable at x0? The source explicitly notes that the converse implication, from small-time local reachability to small-time local controllability, is known to hold.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a control system $\dot{x} = f(x,u)$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$, where $f$ is real-analytic in $(x,u)$, $u$ takes values in a fixed control set $U \subset \mathbb{R}^m$, and admissible controls are measurable functions $u(\cdot)$ with values in $U$. Fix an equilibrium state $x_0$ (so that there exists $u_0 \in U$ with $f(x_0,u_0)=0$). For $T>0$, let $\mathcal{R}^{\le T}(x_0)$ denote the set of points reachable from $x_0$ by admissible trajectories in time at most $T$.

The system is called small-time locally controllable (STLC) at $x_0$ if for every $T>0$ the set $\mathcal{R}^{\le T}(x_0)$ contains an open neighborhood of $x_0$. The system is called small-time locally reachable at $x_0$ if for every $T>0$ the interior of $\mathcal{R}^{\le T}(x_0)$ is nonempty and $x_0$ lies in its closure (equivalently, $x_0$ is normally self-reachable in arbitrarily small time).

It is known that small-time local reachability at $x_0$ implies small-time local controllability at $x_0$ in the analytic setting. Question: Does the converse hold? That is, if a real-analytic control system is small-time locally controllable at $x_0$, must it also be small-time locally reachable at $x_0$?
status_search_result: A 1995 paper by Krastanov ("On the relation between small-time local controllability and normal self-reachability", MCSS) shows that under a nontangency condition—satisfied automatically by all real-analytic systems—small-time local controllability implies normal self-reachability of the initial state. This appears to give a positive answer in the analytic case, but it is not entirely clear from accessible summaries whether this exactly matches the formulation of small-time local reachability asked in the original question, so the status is reported as unknown pending verification.

The class of systems satisfying nontangency includes all real-analytic systems.", "claim": "For real-analytic systems, STLC implies normal self-reachability of the initial state, which strongly suggests the analytic-case question is answered affirmatively."}, {"title": "On small-time local controllability (Jafarpour, Lewis)", "url": "https://arxiv.org/abs/1604.02432", "snippet": "Survey of small-time local controllability conditions for nonlinear systems.", "claim": "Subsequent literature continues to investigate STLC characterizations, indicating the area remains active."}]

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
original_question: Is the one-dimensional Burgers equation globally controllable?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional viscous Burgers equation on a bounded interval (0,1) with boundary controls:
   u_t - u_{xx} + u u_x = 0,   (t,x) ∈ (0,T) × (0,1),
   u(t,0) = v_0(t),   u(t,1) = v_1(t),   t ∈ (0,T),
   u(0,x) = u_0(x),   x ∈ (0,1),
where v_0, v_1 are scalar control functions and u_0 is a given initial state.

The equation is said to be globally controllable in time T if, for every pair of states u_0, u_1 in a suitable function space (e.g. L^2(0,1) or H^1(0,1)) without any smallness assumption, there exist boundary controls v_0, v_1 such that the corresponding solution satisfies u(T,·) = u_1.

Question: Is the one-dimensional Burgers equation globally controllable in this sense (possibly with the freedom to choose T > 0 depending on u_0 and u_1)?
status_search_result: The question has been substantially clarified. Guerrero and Imanuvilov produced a counterexample showing that global exact boundary controllability fails for the 1-D viscous Burgers equation in general (and recent work establishes lack of controllability in the L^∞ setting). On the positive side, small-time global null controllability has been proved (Marbach and collaborators), as well as global exact controllability to nonzero constant states uniformly in viscosity, and small-time global controllability via bilinear controls. Thus the original yes/no question has been resolved negatively for exact boundary controllability while several positive partial results exist, so the problem is best described as partially solved.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
context_brief: small-time controllability for nonlinear heat equation
original_question: For a one-dimensional heat equation with a cubic nonlinearity, is the equation small-time controllable?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional semilinear heat equation with cubic nonlinearity on a bounded interval (say (0,1)) with a distributed (or boundary) control:

  y_t(t,x) - y_{xx}(t,x) + y(t,x)^3 = u(t,x) 1_{\omega}(x),  (t,x) ∈ (0,T) × (0,1),
  y(t,0) = y(t,1) = 0,
  y(0,x) = y_0(x),

where ω ⊂ (0,1) is a nonempty open control region (or, alternatively, the control acts on the boundary), and u is the control.

The equation is said to be small-time globally controllable (to a target state y_1, or to trajectories) if for every T > 0 and every pair of states y_0, y_1 in the natural energy space (e.g. L^2(0,1) or H^1_0(0,1)), there exists a control u such that the corresponding solution satisfies y(0,·) = y_0 and y(T,·) = y_1.

Question: Is this cubic semilinear heat equation small-time controllable in the above sense?
status_search_result: Recent work has obtained partial progress on small-time controllability for nonlinear heat equations with polynomial (including cubic) nonlinearities, mainly via bilinear controls (e.g., small-time approximate controllability between states of the same sign and small-time exact controllability to the ground state for positive data). For the standard distributed/boundary-controlled 1D heat equation with cubic nonlinearity, full small-time global controllability does not appear to be established in the literature, and the problem is generally regarded as still open.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: In quantum control of a primary quantum system coupled either reversibly to an auxiliary system through a unitary interaction Hamiltonian or irreversibly to a bath or quantum field through a damping process, can the strength of reversible coupling and the strength of irreversible coupling be compared quantitatively so that they count as one common resource for control, or must they be treated as fundamentally distinct control resources?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a primary quantum system that an experimenter wishes to control. Suppose the system can be coupled to its surroundings in two distinct ways:

(a) Reversibly, via a unitary interaction with an auxiliary quantum system, generated by a time-independent interaction Hamiltonian H_int. A natural scalar measure of the strength of this reversible coupling is the spectral spread of H_int, i.e. the difference between its largest and smallest eigenvalues, λ_max(H_int) − λ_min(H_int). This quantity bounds the rate at which information (and hence entropy) can be extracted from the system through the auxiliary.

(b) Irreversibly, via Markovian coupling to a zero-temperature bath or quantum field, modeled by a Lindblad-type dissipator with a characteristic damping rate γ > 0. The natural scalar measure of the strength of this irreversible coupling is γ.

Question: Does there exist a quantitative comparison between the reversible coupling strength λ_max(H_int) − λ_min(H_int) and the irreversible damping rate γ — for example, an exchange rate, a conversion protocol, or a unified figure of merit — under which the two can be regarded as manifestations of a single underlying control resource? Or must reversible and irreversible couplings be treated as fundamentally distinct, mutually irreducible resources for quantum control?

Formulate either (i) a quantitative equivalence (with explicit conversion) demonstrating that they constitute one common resource, or (ii) a no-go result showing that no such equivalence is possible and that the two are fundamentally distinct resources.
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not turn up any work that quantitatively reconciles unitary interaction strength (spectral spread of an interaction Hamiltonian) with Markovian damping rate as a single quantum-control resource, nor a no-go result establishing their fundamental distinctness. General resource-theoretic reversibility results (e.g., probabilistic interconversion of quantum resources) address related but different questions. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Quantum auxiliary resources for classical record processing
original_question: In coherent feedback control mediated by quantum fields, where the measurement record that would be classically processed in continuous measurement-based control must instead be represented and processed through the dynamics of a quantum auxiliary system, what size of auxiliary Hilbert space and what auxiliary dynamics are required to approximate different kinds of classical information processing of that measurement record?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum control setting in which a primary quantum system is coupled, via quantum fields (e.g., input/output bosonic channels in the Hudson–Parthasarathy framework), to a quantum auxiliary system. The composite "plant + auxiliary" undergoes purely unitary/dilated Markovian dynamics, with feedback realized coherently through the field interconnections (no measurement is performed). This coherent feedback architecture is to play the role of measurement-based continuous feedback control, in which a continuous weak measurement produces a classical stochastic record r(t) that is then processed by a classical filter/controller F (for example: linear filtering such as a Kalman–Bucy filter or stochastic master equation update; nonlinear filtering; threshold detection; finite-state automata; or more general digital signal processing) before being fed back to drive the plant.

Formulate and solve the following resource problem. Given a target classical processing map F acting on the measurement record (specified, e.g., as a causal operator on the space of trajectories with a prescribed approximation tolerance ε in an appropriate norm on the resulting closed-loop dynamics or on the controlled state of the plant over a time horizon T):

(a) Determine the minimal dimension d(F, ε, T) of the auxiliary Hilbert space H_aux needed so that there exists an auxiliary Hamiltonian and system–auxiliary–field coupling (Lindblad/SLH parameters) producing a coherent feedback loop whose induced action on the plant approximates, to within ε, the closed-loop dynamics that would be obtained by classically processing the measurement record through F and feeding the result back.

(b) Characterize the auxiliary dynamics (Hamiltonian, coupling operators, and field interconnections) that achieve this approximation, and identify the scaling of d(F, ε, T) with ε, T, and natural complexity measures of F (such as the dimension of the state space of the optimal classical filter, its Lipschitz/bandwidth parameters, or, in the discrete case, the number of internal states of the automaton).

Address in particular the cases where F is (i) a linear time-invariant filter, (ii) a nonlinear stochastic-master-equation filter for state estimation, and (iii) a finite-state classical controller.
status_search_result: No general resolution was located. Subsequent works (e.g., schemes replacing measurement feedback with coherent feedback for specific state-preparation tasks, and pedagogical reviews of continuous monitoring and feedback) provide partial constructions and case studies rather than a general theory quantifying the auxiliary Hilbert-space size and dynamics required to emulate arbitrary classical processing of a continuous measurement record. The general resource question therefore appears still open, with only partial/task-specific progress.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: In the regime of good quantum control, where the protocol keeps the state-preparation fidelity close to one because entropy is extracted much faster than environmental noise creates it, what is the optimal protocol for preparing a target state by unitary interaction with a system when both the norm of the interaction Hamiltonian and the rate at which that Hamiltonian may be changed are bounded?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a finite-dimensional quantum system with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$, evolving unitarily under a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H(t)$ acting on $\mathcal{H}$. The associated unitary $U(t)$ satisfies $i\,\dot U(t) = H(t)\,U(t)$ with $U(0)=I$ (units $\hbar=1$). Fix an initial pure state $|\psi_0\rangle\in\mathcal{H}$ and a target pure state $|\psi_*\rangle\in\mathcal{H}$, and consider the regime of "good control": the protocol is operated so that the preparation fidelity $F(T)=|\langle\psi_*|U(T)|\psi_0\rangle|^2$ is close to one (entropy is extracted from the system much faster than environmental noise generates it).

Impose the following two constraints on the control Hamiltonian:
(i) a bound on the operator norm, $\|H(t)\|\le E$ for all $t\ge 0$;
(ii) a bound on the rate at which the Hamiltonian may be changed, $\|\dot H(t)\|\le R$ for all $t\ge 0$,
for fixed positive constants $E$ and $R$.

Determine the optimal protocol $H(t)$ that prepares $|\psi_*\rangle$ from $|\psi_0\rangle$ — i.e., that maximizes the fidelity $F(T)$ at a given time $T$, or equivalently minimizes the time $T$ required to reach a prescribed fidelity threshold — subject to constraints (i) and (ii). Characterize this optimal protocol explicitly and derive the resulting quantum speed limit.
category_tag: quantum optimal control and speed limits
status_search_result: Standard quantum speed limits (Mandelstam–Tamm, Margolus–Levitin) and various works on time-optimal state preparation under a bounded Hamiltonian norm exist, and recent papers (e.g., on bang-off control in two-qubit systems and geometric speed limits for many-body state preparation) address related but distinct settings. No source was found that gives the optimal state-preparation protocol simultaneously under a bound on the Hamiltonian norm and a bound on its rate of change in the good-control regime; the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Bounding measurement-based feedback using coherent feedback
original_question: In the regime of good quantum control, can one derive bounds on the performance of continuous measurement-based feedback control by solving optimal coherent-feedback-control problems that use resources equivalent to the irreversible coupling resources available to the measurement-based controller?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider an open quantum system whose controller can interact with the system through a single dynamical resource: a coupling between the system and a one-way traveling-wave field (e.g., a transmission line) via some system observable, characterized by a maximum irreversible coupling rate κ. Two feedback paradigms can be built on this resource:

(i) Continuous measurement-based feedback control (MBC): the output field is continuously measured (e.g., via homodyne or photon counting), producing a classical record that is processed by a classical controller, which then drives the system via classical control Hamiltonians.

(ii) Coherent feedback control (CFC): the output field is fed, without measurement, into an auxiliary quantum controller that processes it coherently and then couples back to the system through another such traveling-wave channel; the controller is allowed unrestricted internal quantum dynamics, but its irreversible coupling resources to the system are constrained to be equivalent to those available to the MBC scheme (same set of system observables and same maximum coupling rate κ).

Let J be a control performance functional (for example, steady-state expectation of a target observable, fidelity to a target state, or a quadratic cost averaged over time), and let
  J*_MBC(κ) = optimum of J achievable by any MBC protocol using coupling rate ≤ κ,
  J*_CFC(κ) = optimum of J achievable by any CFC protocol using equivalent coupling resources ≤ κ.

Since CFC subsumes MBC (any MBC protocol can be implemented as a CFC by adjoining a measurement and classical processor as part of a coherent ancilla), one has J*_CFC(κ) ≥ J*_MBC(κ) (for a maximization).

Question. In the regime of "good quantum control" (e.g., high coupling rate or near-optimal stabilization), develop a general method that, by solving an optimal coherent-feedback-control problem with coupling resources equivalent to those of the measurement-based controller, yields nontrivial upper bounds on J*_MBC(κ). Specifically, exhibit a procedure that, for a given system, target functional J, and resource bound κ, produces a computable bound B(κ) ≥ J*_MBC(κ) derived from the optimum over CFC protocols using equivalent irreversible coupling resources, and characterize the conditions under which this bound is tight.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has compared coherent and measurement-based feedback for specific systems (notably single-qubit stabilization), showing numerically that coherent feedback can match or exceed MBC performance under equivalent irreversible coupling resources, and proving no-go theorems separating the two paradigms in some control tasks. However, a general framework that produces analytic bounds on MBC performance by solving optimal CFC problems with equivalent resources has not been established in full generality, so the problem appears partially addressed rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Linear networks and protection of non-Gaussian states
original_question: For quantum linear networks, can one prove that they cannot protect non-Gaussian quantum states from linear noise, even in the easier setting where the states to be protected are known rather than arbitrary unknown states?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum linear network: a continuous-variable quantum system whose dynamics is generated by a Hamiltonian that is at most quadratic in the canonical mode operators (creation and annihilation operators of a finite collection of bosonic modes), possibly coupled to external bosonic reservoirs through linear (i.e. mode-operator–linear) Lindblad jump operators. Such evolutions form the class of Gaussian (linear) quantum dynamics: they map Gaussian states to Gaussian states and preserve the linear span of canonical operators in the Heisenberg picture.

A "linear noise" channel on the system is any completely positive trace-preserving map arising from coupling the system, via at most quadratic system–bath Hamiltonians, to a (possibly thermal) Gaussian environment, so that the joint reduced dynamics on the system is a Gaussian channel.

Let ρ be a fixed, known non-Gaussian state of the bosonic system (for instance a Fock state, a Schrödinger-cat state, or any state whose Wigner function is not a Gaussian). A "protection protocol using a linear network" consists of:
 (i) an encoding Gaussian channel E that embeds ρ into a (possibly larger) bosonic system,
 (ii) the action of the linear noise channel N on the encoded system, and
 (iii) a decoding Gaussian channel D,
all of which are Gaussian (linear) operations, possibly involving ancillary modes prepared in arbitrary Gaussian states, Gaussian measurements, and Gaussian feed-forward.

Prove the following statement, or exhibit a counterexample:

For every non-Gaussian state ρ and every nontrivial linear noise channel N (i.e. one that is not the identity on the relevant modes), there exist no Gaussian encoding E, ancillary Gaussian resources, and Gaussian decoding D such that
   D ∘ N ∘ E (ρ) = ρ.
Equivalently, quantum linear networks cannot perfectly protect any known non-Gaussian state from linear noise.
category_tag: Gaussian quantum channels and non-Gaussian state protection
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not return any paper that explicitly proves or refutes the claim that quantum linear (Gaussian) networks cannot protect known non-Gaussian states from linear noise. Related results on Gaussian no-go theorems (e.g. no-distillation and no-error-correction for Gaussian states with Gaussian operations by Eisert–Scheel–Plenio and Niset–Fiurášek–Cerf) are known, but a direct resolution of this specific protection question for known non-Gaussian inputs was not located. Status appears unverified.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Direct coupling versus field-mediated coupling in linear networks
original_question: For linear quantum feedback networks, what performance advantage is provided by direct reversible coupling between systems compared with field-mediated irreversible coupling, and how does that advantage change when external time-dependent control is either allowed or disallowed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider linear quantum feedback networks consisting of interconnected open quantum harmonic oscillators. Two interconnection mechanisms are available:

(i) Direct (reversible) coupling, modeled by a bilinear interaction Hamiltonian of the form H_int = i(a^† K b − b^† K^* a) between the canonical mode operators of the component systems, which preserves unitarity and introduces no additional bath.

(ii) Field-mediated (irreversible) coupling, in which subsystems are connected via bosonic quantum field channels in the (S,L,H) / SLH framework, so that any such connection necessarily comes with coupling to a vacuum bath via Lindblad/quantum-stochastic terms.

For a fixed target class of input–output linear quantum stochastic systems and a fixed performance measure (e.g. coherent H^∞ disturbance attenuation, coherent LQG cost, or fidelity of a desired Gaussian input–output map), let

P_direct := the optimal performance achievable using a network in which both direct and field-mediated couplings are permitted,
P_field  := the optimal performance achievable using a network restricted to field-mediated couplings only,

each evaluated under two regimes:
(a) static, time-invariant interconnections only;
(b) augmented by arbitrary external time-dependent classical control inputs applied to each component.

Problem. Quantify the gap between P_direct and P_field in regimes (a) and (b). Specifically:

1. Provide a sharp, explicit bound (or exact formula) for the performance improvement that admitting direct coupling provides over restricting to field-mediated coupling, in terms of intrinsic parameters of the target linear network (e.g. system matrices, number of modes, channel dimensions).

2. Determine how this gap changes when external time-dependent control is allowed versus disallowed, and identify whether time-dependent control can fully or partially compensate for the absence of direct coupling.

3. Characterize the class of target linear quantum input–output maps that are realizable with field-mediated coupling alone versus those requiring direct coupling, and relate this realizability gap to the quantitative performance advantage in (1).
status_search_result: Existing work (e.g. on direct and indirect couplings in coherent feedback of linear quantum stochastic systems) shows that direct coupling can strictly improve LQG/H∞ performance and characterizes stability, dissipation and passivity via Lyapunov / LMI conditions, and provides multistep synthesis algorithms. However, no general sharp quantification of the performance advantage of direct over field-mediated coupling, nor a systematic comparison with and without time-dependent control, appears to have been established. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Control limits with equally noisy controllers
original_question: What are the fundamental limits of quantum control when the controller or auxiliary system is subject to noise as strong as the noise affecting the controlled system itself, and how do those limits scale as the size of the auxiliary controller is increased relative to the size of the system?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system S (the "target") undergoing open-system dynamics generated by some Hamiltonian together with a noise process (e.g., a Lindblad master equation with dissipators of a fixed strength). One attempts to control S by coupling it to an auxiliary quantum system A (the "controller"), and the joint system S+A evolves under some controllable Hamiltonian interaction. Assume that the auxiliary controller A is itself subject to noise of the same type and strength as the noise acting on S (so that, per degree of freedom, the controller is just as noisy as the system).

Define a control task by a target operation or target state on S, and define the achievable control error as the infimum, over all admissible joint Hamiltonians and initial states of A, of a suitable distance (e.g., diamond-norm or fidelity-based error) between the realized reduced dynamics on S and the target.

Questions:
(a) Determine the fundamental lower bound on the achievable control error for S as a function of the noise strength, given that the auxiliary A is subject to noise of equal strength per subsystem.
(b) Determine how this lower bound scales with the size (Hilbert-space dimension, or number of qubits/degrees of freedom) of the auxiliary A relative to the size of S. In particular, can the control error be driven to zero by enlarging A while keeping the per-subsystem noise rate fixed, and if so at what rate; if not, what is the asymptotic floor?
status_search_result: Recent work (e.g., information-theoretical bounds on quantum optimal control with noisy channels, Sci. Rep. 2022; works on mitigating controller noise via optimal control, Quantum 2024) provides partial bounds and channel-capacity-based scaling laws relating control error to noise on the controller/auxiliary, but no general resolution of the fundamental limits when the controller is as noisy as the system, nor a complete scaling law with auxiliary size, has been established. The problem appears to remain open in its full generality.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Noisy-controller comparison of coherent and measurement-based feedback
original_question: When the quantum controller used in a feedback protocol is damped, noisy, or both, how do coherent feedback and measurement-based feedback compare in performance, and at what controller-noise level is the performance advantage of coherent feedback erased strongly enough to matter for practical applications?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum feedback-control setup in which a quantum "plant" system $P$ is to be regulated (e.g., stabilized to a target state, cooled, or have a target observable optimized) by a controller $C$. Two paradigms are to be compared:

(a) Measurement-based feedback (MBF): the plant is continuously monitored by a measuring device, producing a classical record on which a classical controller acts to apply control fields back on the plant.

(b) Coherent feedback control (CFC): the controller $C$ is itself an auxiliary quantum system, coherently coupled to the plant through quantum channels (no measurement is performed); control is implemented via Hamiltonian and dissipative interaction between $P$ and $C$.

Model the controller $C$ as an open quantum system that is itself subject to damping and noise. Concretely, suppose in case (b) the joint plant–controller dynamics are described by a Lindblad master equation
$$\dot\rho_{PC} = -i[H_{PC},\rho_{PC}] + \mathcal{D}[L_{\text{ctrl}}]\rho_{PC} + \kappa\,\mathcal{D}[a_C]\rho_{PC} + \gamma\,(\bar n+1)\mathcal{D}[a_C]\rho_{PC} + \gamma\,\bar n\,\mathcal{D}[a_C^\dagger]\rho_{PC},$$
where $\kappa$ parameterizes controller damping and $(\gamma,\bar n)$ parameterize controller thermal noise; in case (a) the analogous noise is absent on the (now classical) controller but the plant suffers measurement back-action and detector inefficiency.

For a fixed control task (e.g., minimization of steady-state plant entropy, minimization of an observable variance, or maximization of fidelity to a target pure state), do the following:

1. Determine, as a function of the controller noise parameters $(\kappa,\gamma,\bar n)$, the comparative performance of optimal MBF and optimal CFC protocols.

2. Identify the threshold values of the controller noise level at which any performance advantage of CFC over MBF is eliminated.

3. Characterize whether such thresholds occur in regimes that are physically relevant for realistic experimental implementations.
status_search_result: Several works since 2013 have begun to address the comparison. Hamerly and Mabuchi, and later studies including a unified collision-model framework (Phys. Rev. A 108, 042413, 2023) and recent works on atoms coupled to semi-infinite waveguides (arXiv:2307.16876), provide partial results: coherent feedback tends to be superior at low temperatures and weak coupling and for operator control, while measurement-based feedback can outperform coherent feedback in strong-coupling/noisy regimes and for state stabilization; controllers in the maximally mixed state nullify any CFC advantage. However, a general quantitative threshold answer for arbitrary noisy controllers and tasks of practical relevance remains incomplete, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Complex measurement-based protocols for small systems
original_question: For continuous-measurement-based feedback control of small quantum systems, including even a single qubit, can more complex protocols than those previously tried—especially protocols that modify the measurement as part of feedback—improve performance, and when they do improve performance, does the improvement reveal anything about coherent feedback control?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a small open quantum system $S$ (for example, a single qubit with Hilbert space $\mathbb{C}^2$) coupled to an environment and subject to a continuous quantum measurement whose record is fed back, in real time, into the system's Hamiltonian and/or into the choice of measurement itself. Formally, the conditional state $\rho_t$ evolves according to a stochastic master equation
$$d\rho_t = -i[H(u_t),\rho_t]\,dt + \mathcal{D}[L(v_t)]\rho_t\,dt + \mathcal{H}[L(v_t)]\rho_t\,dW_t,$$
where $\mathcal{D}[L]\rho = L\rho L^\dagger - \tfrac{1}{2}\{L^\dagger L,\rho\}$, $\mathcal{H}[L]\rho = L\rho + \rho L^\dagger - \mathrm{Tr}[(L+L^\dagger)\rho]\rho$, $dW_t$ is a Wiener increment associated with the measurement record, and the control parameters $u_t$ (Hamiltonian control) and $v_t$ (measurement-basis/operator control) are causal functionals of the past measurement record. Fix a control objective such as the steady-state fidelity with a target pure state $|\psi\rangle$, i.e.\ maximize
$$J[u,v] = \liminf_{T\to\infty}\,\mathbb{E}\!\left[\tfrac{1}{T}\int_0^T \langle\psi|\rho_t|\psi\rangle\,dt\right].$$

(a) Construct continuous-measurement-based feedback protocols for such small systems—in particular for a single qubit—that are strictly more general than those considered to date by allowing the measurement operator $L(v_t)$ itself to be modified in feedback, and determine whether such protocols can strictly improve $J[u,v]$ over the best known protocols that use only a fixed measurement and Hamiltonian feedback.

(b) For any protocol that does yield such an enhancement, determine what the structure of the enhancement implies about coherent feedback control, in which the controller is itself a quantum system coupled to $S$ without any classical measurement step.

Identify, where possible, the optimal feedback protocol for the single-qubit case under physically natural noise models and control constraints.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature (e.g. Wiseman–Bouten-style analyses, the 2014 candidate optimal-protocol proposal arXiv:1407.8172, and the 2016 comparative study of coherent vs. measurement-based feedback for a single qubit, arXiv:1606.06507, plus experimental work in superconducting and NV-diamond systems) has produced candidate protocols, partial optimality arguments in the "good control" regime, and empirical comparisons, but truly optimal continuous-measurement feedback protocols—especially those that adapt the measurement itself—remain unknown even for a single qubit, and a general principled connection to coherent feedback has not been established. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: On Completions, neat atom structures, and omitting types
context_brief: Elementary status of weak-unit complete representability
original_question: Is the class of countable completely representable algebras of countably infinite dimension, when representability is taken on weak units (equivalently, via weak representations or weak models rather than square units), an elementary class; that is, can this class be characterized by first-order sentences and shown to be closed under elementary equivalence?
self_contained_problem:
Work in the framework of algebraic logic. For a countably infinite ordinal α, let CA_α denote the variety of cylindric algebras of dimension α. A representation of an algebra 𝔄 ∈ CA_α on a square unit is an embedding into a cylindric set algebra whose unit is a Cartesian power ^αU for some non-empty set U. A representation on a weak unit (also called a weak representation, or representation on a weak space) is an embedding into a generalized cylindric set algebra whose unit is a weak space ^αU^{(p)} = { s ∈ ^αU : |{ i ∈ α : s(i) ≠ p(i) }| < ω } for some fixed p ∈ ^αU. Such a representation is called complete if it preserves all existing infinitary suprema and infima of the algebra.

Let CRCA_α^w denote the class of all atomic algebras 𝔄 ∈ CA_α that admit a complete representation on a weak unit, where α is countably infinite and 𝔄 is countable.

Question: Is CRCA_α^w an elementary class? Equivalently, can membership in CRCA_α^w be characterized by a set of first-order sentences in the signature of CA_α, so that CRCA_α^w is closed under elementary equivalence?
status_search_result: It is known (Hirsch–Hodkinson) that the class of completely representable cylindric algebras of dimension ≥ 3 with square units is non-elementary, and that for infinite-dimensional polyadic algebras the class of completely representable algebras is elementary. The variant for weak units (weak representations) in countably infinite dimension does not have a clearly identified resolution in the available sources; the Hirsch–Hodkinson cardinality argument is noted not to transfer to weak units, and no later paper located in the search definitively settles whether the weak-unit version is elementary. Status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Nonlinear Schrödinger equation on graphs: recent results and open problems
original_question: Can one derive an effective one-dimensional Gross–Pitaevskii or nonlinear Schrödinger dynamics on graph-like structures, such as a Y-junction, directly from a many-body Bose system or another first-principles model? In particular, if one starts from an N-body theory on a graph and takes the many-particle limit with suitable scalings, how should the vertex or defect boundary conditions be handled in the limiting equation, given that even the corresponding problem for a line with a single defect is still open?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{G}$ be a metric graph consisting of a single vertex $v$ to which $k\ge 2$ half-lines (edges) $e_1,\dots,e_k$ are attached (e.g., $k=3$ corresponds to a Y-junction; $k=2$ corresponds to the real line with a single point defect at $v$). On each edge $e_j$ identified with $[0,\infty)$, consider an $N$-body bosonic Hamiltonian
$$H_N = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl(-\Delta_{x_i}\bigr) + \sum_{1\le i<j\le N} N^{2}V\bigl(N(x_i-x_j)\bigr),$$
acting on the symmetric $N$-fold tensor product of $L^2(\mathcal{G})$, where $-\Delta$ on $\mathcal{G}$ is the self-adjoint Laplacian determined by a prescribed family of vertex (matching) conditions at $v$ (for example Kirchhoff, $\delta$-type with strength $\alpha$, or a general self-adjoint coupling parametrized by a unitary matrix), and $V\ge 0$ is a short-range, spherically symmetric, compactly supported pair potential.

Question. Starting from a sequence of $N$-particle states whose one-particle reduced density matrices converge to a pure condensate $|\varphi\rangle\langle\varphi|$ with $\varphi\in L^2(\mathcal{G})$, derive rigorously, in the mean-field/Gross–Pitaevskii scaling limit $N\to\infty$, an effective one-dimensional nonlinear Schrödinger (Gross–Pitaevskii) equation
$$i\partial_t \varphi = -\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}\varphi + g|\varphi|^{2}\varphi$$
on $\mathcal{G}$, identifying the effective coupling constant $g$ in terms of the scattering length of $V$, and—crucially—determine which self-adjoint vertex condition at $v$ the limiting one-particle operator $-\Delta_{\mathcal{G}}$ must satisfy as a function of the microscopic vertex condition imposed on $H_N$. Treat in particular the case $k=2$ (a line with a single point defect) and the case $k=3$ (Y-junction).
category_tag: Mean-field limits and NLS on metric graphs
status_search_result: Rigorous derivations of the 1D Gross–Pitaevskii equation from many-body bosonic dynamics are well established on the line and on strongly confined 3D domains, but no derivation appears in the literature for metric graphs with non-trivial vertex (defect) conditions. Even on the line with a single point defect, the corresponding mean-field/Gross–Pitaevskii limit does not appear to have been carried out, consistent with the problem being posed as open.
