paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Satellite star formation persistence and rapid quenching
original_question: How can satellite galaxies sustain significant star formation for several billion years after being accreted into larger halos and then quench rapidly enough to avoid producing too many galaxies with intermediate specific star formation rates, given that current models with instantaneous or gradual hot-gas stripping still decline too rapidly or fail to match observations?
self_contained_problem:
In the standard hierarchical structure-formation framework, galaxies form at the centers of dark-matter halos and accrete gas to fuel star formation. When a halo containing a galaxy falls into a larger host halo, the galaxy becomes a "satellite" of the host's central galaxy. Observations indicate that:

(i) star-forming satellite galaxies have specific star-formation rates (sSFR ≡ SFR/M_*) statistically indistinguishable from those of central galaxies of the same stellar mass, implying that the transition from star-forming to passive must be rapid; and

(ii) the fraction of passive satellites at fixed stellar mass implies that satellites must continue forming stars at near-central rates for several Gyr after accretion before quenching.

Standard semi-analytic prescriptions assume that upon accretion the hot circumgalactic gas reservoir of the satellite is either (a) stripped instantaneously, or (b) stripped on a halo dynamical-friction or ram-pressure timescale. Both prescriptions produce too many galaxies with intermediate sSFR (so-called "green-valley" satellites) and a satellite quenched fraction that rises too quickly with time-since-infall.

Problem: Construct a physical model of gas-stripping, cold-gas consumption, and possibly internal feedback that, when embedded in a cosmological halo merger tree with realistic infall and orbital statistics, simultaneously satisfies both of the following constraints:

(1) After infall, satellites maintain a sSFR distribution matching that of centrals of the same M_* for a delay time τ_delay of order several Gyr (with appropriate dependence on M_* and host halo mass);

(2) After τ_delay, the sSFR drops to passive values (sSFR ≲ 10^{-11} yr^{-1}) on a timescale τ_fade short enough that the predicted distribution of sSFR shows the observed bimodality, with a deficit of galaxies at intermediate sSFR.

Specify the functional forms of τ_delay(M_*, M_host, z) and τ_fade(M_*, M_host, z), and identify the physical mechanism (e.g., partial hot-gas retention, delayed ram-pressure stripping, gradual starvation followed by ram-pressure stripping of the cold ISM, internal feedback in absence of accretion) that yields these timescales while remaining consistent with cosmological hydrodynamic simulations.
status_search_result: A "delayed-then-rapid" quenching paradigm has been developed and progressively refined since 2014. Empirical and simulation work (e.g., Oman et al. 2021, MNRAS 501, 5073) has measured delay times of ~3.5 Gyr in clusters and ~5.5 Gyr in groups between first pericenter passage and quenching, broadly matching observed sSFR bimodality but with substantial scatter. A 2025 study (arXiv:2503.15183) argues the quenching timescale is set primarily by ISM depletion via star formation and stellar/AGN feedback in the absence of fresh accretion (starvation), with ram-pressure stripping playing a modulating rather than driving role. The qualitative scenario is thus partially established, but a fully predictive model with calibrated τ_delay and τ_fade across mass and host-mass remains an active area of research.

paper_title: What Regulates Galaxy Evolution? Open Questions in our Understanding of Galaxy Formation and Evolution.
context_brief: Model extensions for upcoming galaxy-evolution data
original_question: How should next-generation galaxy-formation models be extended to exploit upcoming resolved spectroscopy, atomic hydrogen, and molecular-gas observations, including explicit treatment of the transition from atomic to molecular gas, possible modeling of spatially resolved physical properties, and detailed chemical evolution with abundance ratios as constraints?
self_contained_problem:
Consider theoretical models of galaxy formation and evolution (e.g., semi-analytic models and hydrodynamical simulations) that track the assembly history of galaxies inside dark-matter halos, the cooling of gas, star formation, stellar feedback, and the production and recycling of metals. Existing implementations typically parametrize star formation in terms of total cold gas, treat galaxies as one-zone systems, and follow only bulk metallicity.

Develop a framework that extends such models so that they can be quantitatively confronted with upcoming observational datasets that provide (i) spatially resolved optical/IR spectroscopy of galaxies (resolved kinematics, ages, and metallicities on sub-galactic scales), (ii) resolved measurements of atomic hydrogen (HI) and molecular gas (H2/CO) content. Specifically, address the following:

1. Atomic-to-molecular transition. Formulate an explicit prescription, derivable from the local interstellar medium properties (gas surface density, metallicity, radiation field, dust shielding), that partitions cold gas into atomic and molecular components in each modeled resolution element, and tie the star-formation rate to the molecular component. Demonstrate that the prescription reproduces simultaneously the observed HI and H2 mass functions, the H2/HI ratio as a function of stellar mass, and the Kennicutt–Schmidt relation across redshift.

2. Spatially resolved galaxy properties. Extend galaxy models from one-zone descriptions to spatially resolved (e.g., axisymmetric multi-ring or full 3D) descriptions, evolving radial profiles of gas surface density, stellar mass, star-formation rate, and metallicity. Identify the minimal set of physical ingredients (gas inflow with prescribed angular momentum, radial transport, feedback-driven outflows, satellite accretion) needed to reproduce, jointly, observed radial profiles of stellar age, metallicity, and star-formation rate in galaxies of different masses and morphologies.

3. Detailed chemical evolution. Replace single-metallicity tracking with explicit, time-resolved nucleosynthetic yields for individual elements (at minimum H, He, C, N, O, Mg, Si, Fe), incorporating delay-time distributions for Type Ia supernovae, mass- and metallicity-dependent yields from core-collapse supernovae and AGB stars, and the impact of finite stellar lifetimes (no instantaneous-recycling approximation). Use abundance-ratio diagnostics (e.g., [α/Fe] vs. [Fe/H], [N/O] vs. [O/H]) of stars and gas as primary constraints, and quantify the resulting constraints on star-formation timescales, IMF, and feedback efficiencies.

Provide such an integrated extension and demonstrate, through comparison with current and forthcoming resolved spectroscopic surveys and HI/H2 surveys, that it yields a self-consistent description of galaxy evolution under these combined constraints.
status_search_result: This is a broad research-program question about extending galaxy-evolution models with explicit H I↔H2 chemistry, spatially resolved descriptions, and detailed chemical evolution. While substantial progress has been made on each individual ingredient (H2-based star-formation laws in semi-analytic and hydrodynamic models, resolved SAMs, and chemical-evolution post-processing), no single framework simultaneously and fully satisfies all three desiderata as primary constraints. The overall program remains an active, open research direction.

paper_title: On open problems in polling systems
context_brief: Renewal-arrival polling systems with large deterministic switch-over times
original_question: Consider a cyclic polling system with finitely many queues, deterministic switch-over times between successive queues, and general renewal arrival processes at the queues. The source conjectures that, when the deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity, the polling system converges to a deterministic cyclic system. Provide a rigorous proof of that conjecture.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a cyclic polling system defined as follows. There are $N\ge 2$ queues $Q_1,\dots,Q_N$ served by a single server that visits them in the fixed cyclic order $Q_1\to Q_2\to\cdots\to Q_N\to Q_1$. Customers arrive at queue $Q_i$ according to an independent renewal process with i.i.d. interarrival times of finite mean $1/\lambda_i$, and require i.i.d. service times with finite mean $1/\mu_i$; assume the system is stable, i.e. $\rho:=\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i/\mu_i<1$. Between leaving $Q_i$ and starting service at $Q_{i+1}$ the server incurs a deterministic switch-over time $s_i\ge 0$. Fix a service discipline at each queue (for instance exhaustive or gated). Let $S=\sum_{i=1}^N s_i$ denote the total switch-over time per cycle, and consider scaling all $s_i$ proportionally so that $S\to\infty$.

Prove rigorously that, in this large-switch-over limit, the polling system converges (in an appropriate distributional/sample-path sense to be specified) to a deterministic cyclic system: that is, the cycle times, the visit instants, and the queue-length and workload processes (suitably normalized) converge to those of a deterministic periodic system in which each queue is served for a deterministic amount of time per cycle determined by $\lambda_i$, $\mu_i$, and $s_i$.
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a published rigorous proof of the conjectured convergence of a cyclic polling system with general renewal arrivals to a deterministic cyclic system as the deterministic switch-over times tend to infinity. Related work establishes heavy-traffic results and periodicity in transient regimes, and proofs exist for special cases (e.g. N=2), but the general renewal-arrival statement appears to remain a conjecture.

paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
context_brief: Global regularity from smooth initial data
original_question: For the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations, starting from a smooth divergence-free initial velocity field, what are the most general assumptions on that initial field that guarantee the existence of a smooth solution for all times t greater than or equal to 0 rather than the formation of a finite-time singularity? The same question is also asked for the Euler equations.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an unknown velocity field $v:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)\to\mathbb{R}$:
\[
\partial_t v + (v\cdot\nabla)v = -\nabla p + \nu \Delta v,\qquad \nabla\cdot v = 0,
\]
with viscosity $\nu>0$ and smooth, divergence-free initial data $v(\cdot,0)=v_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ (decaying suitably at infinity, e.g., Schwartz class). 

Determine the most general conditions on the initial datum $v_0$ that guarantee existence of a unique smooth solution $v\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty);\mathbb{R}^3)$ for all $t\ge 0$, as opposed to the development of a finite-time singularity. 

Pose the analogous question for the three-dimensional incompressible Euler equations (the case $\nu=0$): identify the most general conditions on a smooth divergence-free initial datum $v_0$ that ensure a globally smooth solution exists on $\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)$.
status_search_result: The global regularity problem for the 3D incompressible Navier–Stokes equations remains a famous open Clay Millennium Prize Problem. The corresponding question for the 3D incompressible Euler equations is also widely regarded as open, although significant recent progress on finite-time singularity formation for Euler (e.g., Elgindi's work on $C^{1,\alpha}$ data, and Chen–Hou's computer-assisted proof of singularity for axisymmetric Euler with boundary) shows that singularities can form from non-smooth or boundary data; the smooth, no-boundary case remains unresolved.

original_question: Which properties of the velocity field are sufficient to guarantee the existence of a unique global smooth solution of the three-dimensional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations for all times, assuming the initial conditions are already smooth? This asks for structural conditions on the evolving velocity field that rule out singularity formation and ensure global regularity.

paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
original_question: How can one define the most plausible initial conditions at the beginning of the hydrodynamic stage in a relativistic heavy-ion collision? The issue is to specify the initial relativistic-fluid state at the start of stage (ii), even though the experimentally observed hadrons are produced only much later and the earlier state cannot be measured directly.
self_contained_problem:
In the standard multi-stage description of an ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collision, the evolution of the produced matter is decomposed into successive stages: (i) a pre-equilibrium stage immediately following the collision of the two highly Lorentz-contracted nuclei, in which the produced partonic system is far from local thermal equilibrium; (ii) a relativistic hydrodynamic stage, during which the matter is modeled as a relativistic fluid governed by the conservation laws ∂_μ T^{μν} = 0 (and conserved-charge currents ∂_μ J^μ = 0) supplemented by an equation of state and, in viscous hydrodynamics, by constitutive/relaxation equations for dissipative currents; (iii) a hadronic freeze-out stage, in which the fluid converts to free-streaming hadrons that are eventually detected.

To run the hydrodynamic stage (ii) one must prescribe, on some initial Cauchy hypersurface Σ_0 (typically a constant proper-time surface τ = τ_0), the full set of fluid fields: the energy density ε(x), the flow four-velocity u^μ(x) (with u^μ u_μ = 1), any conserved-charge densities, and—if dissipative hydrodynamics is used—the initial values of the shear-stress tensor π^{μν}(x), bulk viscous pressure Π(x), and any diffusion currents. Direct experimental access to these fields is impossible: only the asymptotic hadrons produced after stage (iii) are measured.

Problem. Provide a principled, predictive prescription that determines, from the properties of the two incoming nuclei and the collision kinematics alone, the most plausible initial data {ε(x), u^μ(x), π^{μν}(x), Π(x), …} on the hypersurface Σ_0 at which relativistic hydrodynamics begins. The prescription should specify the initialization time τ_0, the spatial profiles of all required fluid fields, and their dissipative components, in a way that is consistent with the underlying microscopic (quantum chromodynamic) dynamics of the pre-equilibrium stage and that yields, after hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out, agreement with the measured hadronic observables.
status_search_result: Recent reviews of relativistic hydrodynamics in heavy-ion collisions (e.g., Jaiswal–Roy 2016 and subsequent literature) explicitly identify the specification of initial conditions for the hydrodynamic stage as a major source of uncertainty, with several competing models (Glauber, KLN, IP-Glasma, EKRT, dynamical initialization schemes) but no first-principles consensus. The pre-equilibrium dynamics linking the collision to a thermalized fluid state is still not fully understood, so the problem remains open.

paper_title: Some open questions in hydrodynamics
original_question: How can one explicitly construct solutions of the Navier-Stokes equations that either blow up in finite time or remain globally regular, so that the possibility of finite-time singularity formation from smooth initial data can be tested directly rather than only indirectly through a priori estimates?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on $\mathbb{R}^3$ for an unknown velocity field $u:\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}^3$ and pressure $p:\mathbb{R}^3	imes[0,\infty)	o\mathbb{R}$:

$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\,\Delta u + \nabla p = 0,\qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0,\qquad u(\cdot,0)=u_0,$$

where $\nu>0$ is the kinematic viscosity and $u_0\in C^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3;\mathbb{R}^3)$ is divergence-free with appropriate decay at infinity (e.g., Schwartz class).

A smooth solution is said to blow up in finite time if there exists $T^*<\infty$ such that $\limsup_{t\to T^{*-}}\|u(\cdot,t)\|_{L^\infty(\mathbb{R}^3)}=\infty$, and is said to be globally regular if it extends to a smooth solution on $\mathbb{R}^3\times[0,\infty)$.

(a) a solution that blows up in finite time, or
(b) a solution corresponding to large, generic initial data that remains globally regular,

in such a way that the question of whether finite-time singularities can form from smooth, finite-energy initial data is settled by direct exhibition rather than only through a priori estimates or indirect arguments.
status_search_result: The global regularity / finite-time blow-up question for the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with smooth, finite-energy initial data is one of the Clay Mathematics Institute Millennium Prize Problems and remains open as of 2026. Recent progress (e.g., Tao's averaged Navier-Stokes blow-up, and 2022–2025 work on potential self-similar/numerically-assisted blow-up scenarios for related models such as Euler) has not produced an explicit blow-up or global regularity construction for the full 3D Navier-Stokes system.

paper_title: OPEN PROBLEMS IN GRAVITATIONAL PHYSICS
context_brief: Equivalence Principle as discriminator of gravity formulations
original_question: Can increasingly precise tests of the Equivalence Principle determine whether gravity should be formulated in a purely metric way or in a Palatini-type way with metric g and connection Γ treated as independent variables? More specifically, can Equivalence Principle measurements decide whether Γ is only the Levi-Civita connection of g or whether it may be a more general connection that is, in principle, disentangled from the metric?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a spacetime modeled by a 4-dimensional smooth manifold M endowed with a Lorentzian metric g of signature (-,+,+,+) and an affine connection Γ on the tangent bundle TM. Two formulations of a gravitational theory on (M, g, Γ) are distinguished:

(i) Purely metric formulation: Γ is identified a priori with the Levi-Civita connection of g, i.e. the unique torsion-free connection satisfying ∇g = 0. The dynamical variable is g alone.

(ii) Palatini (metric-affine) formulation: g and Γ are treated as independent dynamical variables, with Γ a general (possibly non-metric, possibly with torsion) affine connection that need not coincide with the Levi-Civita connection of g. The relation between Γ and g is then a consequence of the field equations rather than an a priori identification.

The Einstein Equivalence Principle (EEP) asserts that (a) the trajectory of a freely falling structureless test body is independent of its internal composition (Weak Equivalence Principle / Universality of Free Fall), (b) the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of the velocity of the freely falling reference frame in which it is performed (Local Lorentz Invariance), and (c) the outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of where and when in the universe it is performed (Local Position Invariance).

Question: Determine whether arbitrarily precise experimental tests of the Einstein Equivalence Principle can, in principle, discriminate between formulations (i) and (ii). Concretely, identify observable signatures (in the dynamics of test particles, in atomic-clock comparisons, or in other local non-gravitational experiments) by which a non-Levi-Civita independent connection Γ in formulation (ii) would produce deviations from the EEP that are absent in formulation (i), and quantify the precision required to detect or rule out such deviations; or, alternatively, prove that no EEP-based experiment can distinguish the two formulations.
status_search_result: The question of whether Equivalence Principle tests can distinguish purely metric gravity from Palatini/metric-affine formulations remains an open conceptual and experimental problem. Ongoing and proposed EP tests (e.g., MICROSCOPE, STEP, atom-interferometry experiments) continue to push precision, and theoretical work on metric-affine and Palatini f(R) gravity continues without a definitive verdict; no proof of equivalence or experimental discrimination has been established.

paper_title: OPEN PROBLEMS IN GRAVITATIONAL PHYSICS
context_brief: Physical meaning of Jordan and Einstein frames
original_question: When modified gravitational dynamics are written in the Jordan frame, where Einstein field equations are modified and matter fields are minimally coupled to gravity, or in the Einstein frame, where Einstein field equations are preserved and matter fields are non-minimally coupled, does passing from one conformal frame to the other have genuine physical significance?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a modified theory of gravity formulated on a four-dimensional spacetime (M, g) with a scalar degree of freedom φ that couples to gravity. Two equivalent mathematical formulations of such a theory can be obtained by a conformal rescaling of the metric, g̃_{μν} = Ω²(φ) g_{μν}:

(a) The Jordan frame, in which the Einstein field equations are modified (the gravitational Lagrangian contains a non-trivial coupling, e.g. f(φ) R, or a function f(R) of the Ricci scalar) and matter fields are minimally coupled to the metric g_{μν}.

(b) The Einstein frame, obtained by the conformal transformation above (with a suitable redefinition of φ), in which the gravitational sector takes the standard Einstein–Hilbert form R̃ and matter fields acquire a non-minimal coupling to the rescaled metric g̃_{μν} through φ-dependent factors.

The two frames are related by a field redefinition (a conformal transformation of the metric together with a rescaling of the scalar) and are therefore mathematically equivalent at the level of the action.

Question: Determine whether the choice of conformal frame (Jordan vs. Einstein) carries genuine physical significance. Specifically, is there an observable or operationally well-defined physical quantity — at the classical level, at the semiclassical level, or at the quantum level — that distinguishes predictions made in the Jordan frame from those made in the Einstein frame, or are the two frames physically equivalent in every operational sense (so that the passage between them is merely a change of variables)?
status_search_result: The physical equivalence (or non-equivalence) of the Jordan and Einstein conformal frames remains an actively debated open problem. Recent works argue for classical/canonical equivalence on a reduced phase space, while others present arguments for non-equivalence at the quantum level (e.g., differences detectable via entanglement, or via differential matter couplings). No consensus has been reached.

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
context_brief: laboratory access to QCD matter states
original_question: To what extent can strongly interacting QCD matter states resembling (i) high-temperature matter with negligible baryon chemical potential, as in the early universe, or (ii) low-temperature QCD matter, as may exist in neutron-star cores, be produced and studied in terrestrial laboratories through relativistic or ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions?
self_contained_problem:
Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) predicts that strongly interacting matter, composed of quarks and gluons, can exist in distinct thermodynamic phases parameterized by temperature T and baryon chemical potential μ_B. Two physically motivated regions of the (T, μ_B) phase diagram are: (i) the high-temperature, near-zero baryon chemical potential regime (T large, μ_B ≈ 0), believed to describe the matter present a few microseconds after the Big Bang; and (ii) the low-temperature, high baryon chemical potential regime (T small, μ_B large), believed to describe the matter in the cores of neutron stars.

Relativistic and ultra-relativistic collisions of heavy nuclei produce transient regions of strongly interacting matter at high energy densities and temperatures. Determine to what extent QCD matter states corresponding to regimes (i) and (ii) above can actually be created, controlled, and quantitatively characterized in terrestrial heavy-ion collision experiments. In particular, identify what observable signatures (collective flow, thermal radiation, particle yields, fluctuations, jet modification, etc.) and what range of collision energies and system sizes give experimental access to these regimes, and clarify which thermodynamic and transport properties of QCD matter near regime (i) and regime (ii) can be inferred from such measurements.
status_search_result: This is a broad foundational question of relativistic heavy-ion physics rather than a specific theorem to be solved. While substantial progress has been made on regime (i) (high-T, μ_B≈0) at RHIC and LHC, including measurements of the quark-gluon plasma's transport properties, the high-μ_B/low-T regime relevant to neutron star cores remains a major open frontier targeted by ongoing and planned programs (RHIC Beam Energy Scan II, NICA, FAIR/CBM, J-PARC-HI). The question is therefore best characterized as still open / partially explored.

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
context_brief: deconfinement and hydrodynamic expansion in high-multiplicity pp
original_question: In very high-energy proton-proton collisions with low impact parameter and high charged-particle multiplicity, do multiparton interactions and rescatterings transfer enough energy into a proton-sized volume to create a close-to-equilibrium deconfined initial state, allow thermalization despite the small system size, and produce a proton-sized fireball that expands hydrodynamically or collectively?

Consider proton–proton collisions at very high center-of-mass energies (LHC-scale and beyond) restricted to events with low impact parameter and high charged-particle multiplicity. Model the partonic activity in such events as a superposition of multiparton interactions accompanied by subsequent rescatterings of the produced partons. Assume that the resulting deconfined-phase constituents have a mean free path of order λ ≈ 0.2–0.3 fm, and that the transverse extent of the interaction region is of order the proton radius R ≈ 0.8 fm, so that R/λ is only a few.

Determine whether the following three propositions hold simultaneously in this regime:

(a) The cumulative energy transferred by the multiparton interactions and rescatterings into a volume of proton size is sufficient to reach (or exceed) the QCD deconfinement energy density, producing a close-to-equilibrium deconfined initial state.

(b) Despite the smallness of the system (only a few mean free paths across), the constituents of this initial state thermalize on a timescale shorter than the system's lifetime.

(c) The thermalized, proton-sized fireball thereafter undergoes a hydrodynamic / collective expansion describable by relativistic fluid dynamics, with collective observables (radial flow, anisotropic flow harmonics, strangeness enhancement, etc.) analogous to those seen in heavy-ion collisions.

Provide a rigorous theoretical or phenomenological resolution of (a)–(c): either establish all three within a controlled framework, or identify which fail and characterize the regime of validity.

However, a first-principles demonstration that thermalization is achieved in such a small system, and that a genuine deconfined fireball is formed rather than alternative non-thermal mechanisms (e.g., color reconnection, initial-state CGC correlations, string interactions), remains unsettled. The questions of whether MPI/rescatterings drive the system to local equilibrium and whether the expansion is truly hydrodynamic in pp are still actively debated.

1. The kinetic freeze-out temperature T_kin extracted from a simultaneous blast-wave fit to the transverse-momentum spectra of identified hadrons decreases as a function of charged-particle multiplicity.
2. The mean transverse radial-flow velocity ⟨β_T⟩ obtained from the same fit increases as a function of charged-particle multiplicity.
3. The transverse-momentum spectra of identified hadrons exhibit a mass-dependent hardening with increasing multiplicity, qualitatively reproducing the patterns observed in nucleus–nucleus collisions when plotted against centrality.

Specifically: provide a quantitative dynamical description (e.g., hydrodynamic evolution, multi-parton interactions with color reconnection, string percolation, or an alternative microscopic framework) that simultaneously accounts for the (T_kin, ⟨β_T⟩) anti-correlation and the identified-hadron spectral shape evolution observed in high-multiplicity pp events, and determine whether such a description requires the formation of a thermalized partonic medium analogous to that produced in heavy-ion collisions.

paper_title: Recent results and open questions on collective type phenomena from A-A to pp collisions
original_question: Can a two-dimensional event-selection condition that combines charged-particle multiplicity with global event-shape observables such as Directivity, Sphericity, Thrust, or Fox-Wolfram moments reliably isolate soft, nearly azimuthally isotropic proton-proton events with specific azimuthal distributions at a given multiplicity?
self_contained_problem:
In high-energy proton-proton collisions, each event produces a set of charged particles whose transverse momenta $\vec{p}_{T,i}$ in the plane transverse to the beam axis can be measured. For an event with $N$ charged particles, define the following global event-shape observables:

(i) The transverse sphericity tensor $S^{xy}_{\alpha\beta} = \frac{\sum_i p_{T,i,\alpha}\,p_{T,i,\beta}}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|^2}$ with eigenvalues $\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq 0$, and the transverse sphericity $S_T = 2\lambda_2/(\lambda_1+\lambda_2) \in [0,1]$, where $S_T \to 1$ corresponds to azimuthal isotropy and $S_T \to 0$ corresponds to a pencil-like event.

(ii) The transverse thrust $T_\perp = \max_{\hat{n}_T} \frac{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}\cdot\hat{n}_T|}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|}$, maximized over unit vectors $\hat{n}_T$ in the transverse plane.

(iii) The Fox–Wolfram moments $H_\ell = \sum_{i,j} \frac{|\vec p_i||\vec p_j|}{E_{vis}^2}\, P_\ell(\cos\theta_{ij})$ for $\ell=0,1,2,\dots$, where $P_\ell$ are Legendre polynomials and $\theta_{ij}$ is the angle between particle momenta.

(iv) The directivity $D = \frac{|\sum_i \vec{p}_{T,i}|}{\sum_i |\vec{p}_{T,i}|} \in [0,1]$.

Let $N_{ch}$ denote the charged-particle multiplicity of an event. Consider applying a two-dimensional event-selection cut of the form $\{N_{ch}\geq N_{\min}\}\cap\{X \in I\}$, where $X$ is one of the above event-shape variables and $I$ is an interval chosen to enforce near azimuthal isotropy.

Question: Does there exist such a two-dimensional selection $(N_{ch},X)$ that, at any fixed value of $N_{ch}$, reliably isolates a sub-ensemble of events whose single-particle azimuthal distribution $dN/d\varphi$ is nearly uniform (soft, isotropic), as opposed to events dominated by hard back-to-back jet structures, given that the marginal distributions of $X$ remain broad even at the largest accessible multiplicities?
status_search_result: Subsequent experimental and phenomenological studies (e.g. ALICE measurements of transverse sphericity and the "spherocity" variable, and CMS/ATLAS event-shape analyses) have demonstrated that combining multiplicity with event-shape observables such as transverse sphericity or spherocity does separate jetty from isotropic pp events and reveals different particle-production properties. The procedure is feasible and is used in practice, though no single optimal observable has been identified as definitive; the broader question of fully isolating "soft isotropic" events at fixed multiplicity remains an active area of investigation.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Let n be a positive integer and let M_n(μ) denote the set of distributions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ. If a distribution F on ℝ or on ℝ^d is n-completely mixable, must its center be unique? Equivalently, for distinct μ, ν ∈ ℝ, is M_n(μ) ∩ M_n(ν) empty?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 2$ be an integer. A probability distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}^d$ is called $n$-completely mixable with center $\mu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ if there exist random vectors $X_1, \dots, X_n$, each with distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n = n\mu \quad \text{almost surely}.$$
Let $\mathcal{M}_n(\mu)$ denote the set of all distributions on $\mathbb{R}^d$ that are $n$-completely mixable with center $\mu$.

Question: Is the center of complete mixability always unique? Equivalently, is it true that for every pair of distinct points $\mu, \nu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ with $\mu \ne \nu$, one has
$$\mathcal{M}_n(\mu) \cap \mathcal{M}_n(\nu) = \emptyset\,?$$
status_search_result: The question was resolved in the negative by Puccetti, Rigo, Wang and Wang ("Centers of probability measures without the mean", J. Theoret. Probab., 2019). They show that if a distribution has finite mean, its mixability center must equal that mean (so it is unique), but for heavy-tailed distributions without a finite mean (e.g., Cauchy) a whole interval of centers can be achieved. Explicitly, for $n \ge 2$ standard Cauchy random variables, the achievable constants $C$ form the interval $|C| \le n\log(n-1)/\pi$, so the center is not unique in general.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Theorem 3 states that a ℤ_+-valued random vector X is a joint mix with joint center N if and only if it can be written as X = ∑_{k=1}^N X_k, where each X_k is a binary multinomial random vector. Can this decomposition be used in a nontrivial way to characterize additional classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions, and if so how?
self_contained_problem:
A random vector $X = (X^{(1)}, \dots, X^{(d)})$ taking values in $\mathbb{Z}_+^d$ is called a joint mix with joint center $N \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ if $X^{(1)} + X^{(2)} + \cdots + X^{(d)} = N$ almost surely. A binary multinomial random vector is a $\{0,1\}^d$-valued random vector whose components sum to $1$ almost surely (equivalently, exactly one coordinate equals $1$ with some probability distribution over the $d$ coordinates).

It is known that a $\mathbb{Z}_+^d$-valued random vector $X$ is a joint mix with joint center $N \in \mathbb{Z}_+$ if and only if it admits a representation
$$X = \sum_{k=1}^{N} X_k,$$
where $X_1, \dots, X_N$ are (not necessarily independent) binary multinomial random vectors.

A tuple of univariate marginal distributions $(F_1, \dots, F_d)$ is called jointly mixable (JM) if there exist random variables $Y_1 \sim F_1, \dots, Y_d \sim F_d$ on a common probability space such that $Y_1 + \cdots + Y_d$ is almost surely a constant; in the case $F_1 = \cdots = F_d = F$, $F$ is called completely mixable (CM).

Question: Can the binary-multinomial decomposition above be used in a nontrivial way to characterize new classes of completely mixable or jointly mixable distributions? More precisely, identify a class $\mathcal{C}$ of univariate distributions (or tuples thereof), not previously known to be CM (resp. JM), and use the decomposition $X = \sum_{k=1}^N X_k$ into binary multinomial random vectors to give necessary and/or sufficient conditions for membership of $\mathcal{C}$ in the CM (resp. JM) class.
status_search_result: A full characterization of completely mixable and jointly mixable distributions for $d \geq 3$ remains open in the probability literature. Necessary and sufficient conditions are known for restricted families (uniform, monotone-density, unimodal-symmetric, and elliptical distributions with common characteristic generator), but no general characterization leveraging the binary-multinomial decomposition for $\mathbb{Z}_+$-valued joint mixes has been published, and the question of whether this decomposition yields new CM/JM classes appears unresolved.

original_question: If C is a convex subset of ℝ^d, is the uniform distribution on C necessarily n-completely mixable for every n ≥ d + 1?

Recall that a $d$-dimensional distribution $F$ is said to be $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exist $d$-dimensional random vectors $X_1,\dots,X_n$, each with distribution $F$, such that $X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n$ is almost surely constant.

Question: Is it true that for every convex set $C\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ of finite positive Lebesgue measure, the uniform distribution on $C$ is $n$-completely mixable for every integer $n\ge d+1$?

original_question: Is every absolutely continuous distribution supported on a bounded interval n-completely mixable once n is large enough?
self_contained_problem:
A random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ has marginal distributions all equal to a probability distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$. The distribution $F$ is called $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exists a random vector $(X_1,\dots,X_n)$ with each $X_i \sim F$ such that
$$P(X_1+X_2+\cdots+X_n = n\mu) = 1$$
for some constant $\mu \in \mathbb{R}$ (necessarily equal to the mean of $F$ when $F$ has finite mean). A distribution $F$ on $\mathbb{R}$ is absolutely continuous if it admits a density with respect to Lebesgue measure.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Suppose a distribution F satisfies a known sufficient condition for n-complete mixability, such as one of the conditions listed earlier in Section 2.2. Is there a way to simulate samples from an n-complete mix with margins F?
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \geq 2$ be an integer and let $F$ be a univariate cumulative distribution function on $\mathbb{R}$. Call $F$ $n$-completely mixable ($n$-CM) if there exist random variables $X_1, \dots, X_n$, each with marginal distribution $F$, such that
$$X_1 + X_2 + \cdots + X_n = c \quad \text{almost surely}$$
for some constant $c \in \mathbb{R}$. Any random vector $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ with these properties is called an $n$-complete mix with margins $F$.

Several sufficient conditions for $n$-complete mixability are known; for example, any continuous distribution $F$ on a bounded interval whose density is symmetric and unimodal is $n$-CM for every $n \geq 2$, and any continuous distribution with a concave density on its support is $n$-CM for every $n \geq 3$.

Problem. Assume $F$ satisfies such a sufficient condition for $n$-complete mixability. Provide an explicit and implementable algorithm that, given $F$ and $n$ as input, generates exact samples from the joint distribution of an $n$-complete mix $(X_1, \dots, X_n)$ whose marginals are all equal to $F$ and whose components sum to a constant almost surely.
status_search_result: The problem of simulating samples from an n-complete mix with given margins F (under the standard sufficient conditions for n-complete mixability) appears in the open-problem list on complete mixability and no general-purpose simulation algorithm appears to have been published. Recent literature on complete mixability (e.g., detecting complete and joint mixability, advances in complete mixability) treats existence and characterization rather than exact simulation, suggesting the problem remains open.

original_question: Let D_n be the aggregation set of sums X_1 + ⋯ + X_n formed from random variables with prescribed marginal distributions F_1, …, F_n. What are necessary and sufficient conditions for D_n to contain a smallest element with respect to convex order?

$$\mathcal{D}_n(F_1,\dots,F_n) = \{X_1 + \cdots + X_n : X_i \sim F_i \text{ for } i=1,\dots,n\},$$

An element $S^* \in \mathcal{D}_n$ is called a smallest element with respect to convex order if $S^* \leq_{cx} S$ for every $S \in \mathcal{D}_n$.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: Given positive numbers a_{i,j} representing the time taken by worker (i, j) to complete production step j, and using permutations σ_1, …, σ_n ∈ S_m to assign one worker from each step to each of m equipments, minimize max_{i=1,…,m} ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i),j}. What assignment of workers is optimal, and how can an optimal assignment be computed?
self_contained_problem:
Let m, n be positive integers and let (a_{i,j})_{1 ≤ i ≤ m, 1 ≤ j ≤ n} be a given matrix of positive real numbers. Interpret a_{i,j} as the time taken by worker i to perform production step j; there are m workers available for each of the n steps. An assignment is a tuple (σ_1, …, σ_n) of permutations σ_j ∈ S_m, where σ_j(i) denotes which worker is assigned to step j on equipment i. The total time spent on equipment i is

  T_i(σ_1, …, σ_n) = ∑_{j=1}^n a_{σ_j(i), j},

and the makespan of the assignment is

  M(σ_1, …, σ_n) = max_{1 ≤ i ≤ m} T_i(σ_1, …, σ_n).

Problems:
(a) Characterize the assignments (σ_1*, …, σ_n*) ∈ (S_m)^n that minimize M(σ_1, …, σ_n).
(b) Provide an algorithm that computes such an optimal arrangement (σ_1*, …, σ_n*) for given input (a_{i,j}).

In particular, identify structural properties of optimal arrangements (e.g., relation to "completely mixable" or "jointly mixable" rearrangements of the columns of (a_{i,j})) and determine the computational complexity of finding one.
status_search_result: No source was found that resolves the characterization or efficient computation of optimal arrangements for this minimax row-sum permutation problem in its general form. The problem is closely linked to the theory of complete/joint mixability of distributions, where exact optima are known only in special cases (e.g., monotone or identically distributed marginals). General characterizations and algorithms appear to remain open.

paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: For given distributions, can one design effective algorithms to decide whether they are jointly mixable or to solve the minimax assignment problem from Section 1? In particular, under what conditions do the swapping algorithms discussed in the paper converge?
self_contained_problem:
Let $F_1, \ldots, F_d$ be one-dimensional probability distributions on $\mathbb{R}$ with finite mean. The tuple $(F_1, \ldots, F_d)$ is called jointly mixable if there exist random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_d$ defined on a common probability space, with $X_i \sim F_i$ for each $i$, such that the sum $X_1 + \cdots + X_d$ is almost surely constant. The associated minimax assignment problem asks, given samples (or discretizations) $x_{i,1}, \ldots, x_{i,n}$ from each $F_i$ arranged as the rows of a $d \times n$ matrix $A$, for permutations $\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_d$ of $\{1, \ldots, n\}$ minimizing
$$\max_{1 \le j \le n} \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i,\sigma_i(j)} \;-\; \min_{1 \le j \le n} \sum_{i=1}^{d} x_{i,\sigma_i(j)}.$$
A swapping (rearrangement) algorithm iteratively replaces each row of $A$ by a permutation of its entries so that this row becomes oppositely ordered (countermonotonic) with respect to the sum of the remaining rows, repeating until no further reduction is achieved.

Address the following:

(a) Design an effective algorithm that decides, for given distributions $F_1, \ldots, F_d$, whether $(F_1, \ldots, F_d)$ is jointly mixable, and an effective algorithm to (approximately) solve the minimax assignment problem above.

(b) Determine necessary and sufficient (or otherwise sharp) conditions on the input matrix $A$ — or on the underlying distributions $F_1, \ldots, F_d$ — under which the swapping algorithm described above converges to an optimal solution of the minimax assignment problem.
status_search_result: Subsequent work (Puccetti–Wang on detecting complete and joint mixability; the Block Rearrangement Algorithm of Bernard–McLeish and follow-ups; Haus 2015 on hardness of the assignment problem) has produced improved heuristics, partial complexity results, and convergence-rate estimates in special cases (e.g., Gaussian marginals). paper_title: Current Open Questions in Complete Mixability
original_question: For n > 3, can one fully characterize the set J_n(K) of n-tuples of distributions that are jointly mixable with joint center K, or equivalently the set M_n(μ) of distributions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ?
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 3 be an integer. A distribution function F on ℝ is called n-completely mixable with center μ ∈ ℝ if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n, each with distribution F, such that
   X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = nμ   almost surely.
Denote by M_n(μ) the set of all distribution functions on ℝ that are n-completely mixable with center μ.

More generally, an n-tuple (F_1, …, F_n) of one-dimensional distribution functions is called jointly mixable with joint center K ∈ ℝ if there exist random variables X_1, …, X_n with X_i ∼ F_i for each i such that
   X_1 + X_2 + ⋯ + X_n = K   almost surely.
Denote by J_n(K) the set of all such n-tuples.

For n = 1 the sets are trivial (only point masses), and for n = 2 the set M_2(μ) consists exactly of the distributions symmetric about μ, with a corresponding characterization of J_2(K).

Problem: For each integer n ≥ 3, give a complete characterization of the set M_n(μ) of one-dimensional distributions that are n-completely mixable with center μ, and equivalently of the set J_n(K) of n-tuples of one-dimensional distributions that are jointly mixable with joint center K.
status_search_result: The full characterization of n-completely mixable distributions and of jointly mixable n-tuples for n ≥ 3 is widely cited as an open problem in the complete mixability literature. Sufficient conditions (e.g., symmetric unimodal densities, concave densities, monotone densities under moment conditions) and detection algorithms have been developed, but no complete characterization is known. Recent works (e.g., on centers of probability measures and detection of mixability) extend partial results without resolving the general characterization.

paper_title: Settling Some Open Problems on 2-Player Symmetric Nash Equilibria
context_brief: symmetric fixed-rank games of rank 2 through 5
original_question: For each k in {2, 3, 4, 5}, what is the computational complexity of finding a symmetric Nash equilibrium in a two-player symmetric bimatrix game (A, A^T) whose rank is k, that is, for which rank(A + A^T) = k?
self_contained_problem:
Setup. A two-player bimatrix game is specified by a pair of real m×n payoff matrices (A,B): if the row player plays a mixed strategy x ∈ Δ_m and the column player plays y ∈ Δ_n (where Δ_k denotes the simplex of probability vectors in R^k), the row player's expected payoff is x^T A y and the column player's is x^T B y. A Nash equilibrium (NE) is a pair (x,y) such that no player can strictly improve by unilateral deviation.

A bimatrix game (A,B) is symmetric if m = n and B = A^T. For a symmetric game, a symmetric Nash equilibrium is a NE of the form (x,x); every symmetric bimatrix game admits at least one symmetric NE.

The rank of a bimatrix game (A,B) is defined as rank(A+B). Thus a symmetric game (A,A^T) has rank k when rank(A+A^T) = k.

Problem. For each k ∈ {2, 3, 4, 5}, determine the computational complexity of the following problem: given a symmetric bimatrix game (A,A^T) with integer (or rational) entries satisfying rank(A+A^T) = k, compute a symmetric Nash equilibrium of (A,A^T).

In particular, for each such k, decide whether this problem is solvable in polynomial time, is PPAD-complete, or has some intermediate complexity.
category_tag: Complexity of Nash equilibria in fixed-rank games
status_search_result: Available sources indicate that polynomial-time algorithms exist for symmetric Nash equilibria in symmetric games of rank 0 and 1, while the problem is PPAD-hard for symmetric games of rank ≥ 6 (and for general bimatrix games of rank ≥ 3). The complexity of computing a symmetric Nash equilibrium of a symmetric game of rank 2, 3, 4, or 5 is reported as still unresolved in the literature, with no algorithm or hardness result located that closes the gap.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: How can the scaling analyses and short-range correlation information obtained from inclusive electron quasielastic scattering be made usable in neutrino-nucleus CCQE analyses, given that neutrino experiments generally do not know the incident neutrino energy event by event and therefore cannot directly establish the transferred momentum q and transferred energy ω?
self_contained_problem:
In inclusive quasi-elastic (QE) electron-nucleus scattering, the four-momentum transfer to the nucleus is fully determined event by event from the measured momentum of the scattered electron, giving the three-momentum transfer q and the energy transfer ω. Using these variables, scaling analyses (first-kind and second-kind scaling, the scaling function f(ψ′) of the SuperScaling Approach, and Rosenbluth-separated longitudinal and transverse responses R_L(q,ω), R_T(q,ω)) have been extracted, and the role of short-range nucleon-nucleon correlations — high-momentum pairs involving roughly 20% of the nucleons, responsible for the well-known enhancement of the transverse response — has been quantified.

In charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino-nucleus scattering ν_ℓ + A → ℓ^- + X (and the antineutrino analogue), the incident neutrino energy E_ν is not known on an event-by-event basis: only the outgoing charged lepton's momentum and angle are directly measured, while E_ν is distributed according to a broad flux Φ(E_ν). Consequently, the values of q and ω cannot be reconstructed event by event without an additional model assumption.

Problem. Develop a framework that allows the scaling functions, Rosenbluth-separated nuclear responses, and short-range correlation information extracted from inclusive electron QE data to be used quantitatively to predict the flux-folded inclusive CCQE double differential cross section

  d²σ/(dT_ℓ d cos θ_ℓ) = ∫ dE_ν Φ(E_ν) · d²σ(E_ν, T_ℓ, cos θ_ℓ)/(dT_ℓ d cos θ_ℓ),

in a way that does not require event-by-event knowledge of (q, ω). Specifically, construct an explicit prescription that (i) maps the electron-scattering scaling function and transverse-enhancement contribution into the five weak nuclear response functions entering CCQE, (ii) properly incorporates the broad neutrino flux through integration over E_ν with the kinematically allowed (q, ω) consistent with the measured lepton kinematics, and (iii) yields predictions that simultaneously reproduce existing electron QE scaling data and CCQE neutrino and antineutrino cross sections on nuclear targets such as ¹²C, ⁴⁰Ar, and ⁵⁶Fe.
status_search_result: The question of transferring electron-scattering scaling and short-range-correlation information into neutrino CCQE analyses has been the subject of extensive ongoing work (SuSA, SuSAv2, SuSAv2-MEC, and related approaches), with significant progress in incorporating 2p2h/MEC contributions and transverse enhancement, but no fully agreed-upon, model-independent solution that bypasses the unknown incident neutrino energy. The problem is generally regarded as still open in the neutrino-physics literature.

original_question: Why do the Martini and IFIC/Nieves RPA-based calculations for carbon neutrino CCQE-like scattering integrated over the MiniBooNE flux give a two-particle–two-hole (2p–2h) contribution that differs by about a factor of two, and is the unresolved axial-response enhancement responsible for this difference?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current quasi-elastic-like (CCQE-like) scattering of muon neutrinos on a carbon (¹²C) target, with the incoming neutrino flux corresponding to that of the MiniBooNE experiment. Two independent nuclear-physics calculations of this process — both based on the Random Phase Approximation (RPA) applied to a relativistic Fermi gas / local Fermi gas description of the nucleus, supplemented with a two-particle–two-hole (2p–2h) contribution arising from meson-exchange currents and short-range correlations — are performed: 

(i) the Martini et al. RPA + 2p–2h calculation, and 
(ii) the IFIC/Nieves et al. RPA + 2p–2h calculation. 

When their predicted flux-integrated double-differential and total CCQE-like cross sections are compared, the genuine one-body (1p–1h) RPA contributions agree reasonably well, but the 2p–2h contributions differ by approximately a factor of two.

Problem. Identify and quantitatively account for the origin of this factor-of-two discrepancy between the two RPA-based 2p–2h predictions for ν_μ–¹²C CCQE-like scattering integrated over the MiniBooNE flux. In particular, determine whether an unresolved enhancement of the axial nuclear response in the 2p–2h channel — beyond the vector and axial-vector meson-exchange-current contributions explicitly included — is responsible for this difference, by isolating the contributions of (a) the longitudinal/transverse axial response, (b) the meson-exchange-current diagrams retained or omitted in each calculation, (c) short-range correlation contributions, and (d) the treatment of Δ-resonance propagation and in-medium width.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature confirms that both Martini et al. and Nieves et al. RPA-based calculations describe MiniBooNE CCQE-like data with a standard axial mass once 2p–2h is included, but their 2p–2h strengths still differ by roughly a factor of two. paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: What remaining neutral-current single-photon production mechanisms, especially anomalous ωZγ contributions with large theoretical uncertainties, and what direct measurements by MicroBooNE, MINERvA, ND280/T2K, or similar detectors are needed to make this background sufficiently controlled for electron-neutrino appearance studies?
self_contained_problem:
Consider neutrino–nucleus scattering at energies relevant to accelerator-based oscillation experiments (roughly 0.2–10 GeV), and focus on neutral-current (NC) processes whose final state contains a single photon and no charged leptons. Such NC γ events constitute an irreducible background to electron-neutrino appearance searches because a single photon shower is experimentally hard to distinguish from an electron shower.

Standard contributions to NC single-photon production include:
(i) NC excitation of baryon resonances (most importantly the Δ(1232)) followed by radiative decay,
(ii) non-resonant nucleon Born terms,
(iii) coherent single-photon production on nuclei,
(iv) anomaly-mediated contributions arising from the Wess–Zumino–Witten term, in particular the ωZγ vertex coupling the ω vector meson to the Z boson and a photon, whose strength is fixed by the chiral anomaly but whose hadronic form factors and off-shell behavior carry large theoretical uncertainty.

Problem. Determine, both theoretically and experimentally, the size and kinematic distributions of the remaining NC single-photon production mechanisms—especially the anomalous ωZγ contribution—on nuclear targets used in current and near-future oscillation experiments (argon, carbon, hydrocarbon, water/CH). Specifically:

(a) Provide a theoretically robust calculation of the anomalous ωZγ contribution to the NC 1γ cross section differential in photon energy and angle on the nucleon and on nuclei, with controlled uncertainties on the vector-meson form factors, off-shell extrapolations, and nuclear effects.

(b) Identify direct experimental measurements—using liquid-argon time projection chambers such as MicroBooNE, the MINERνA detector, and the ND280 near detector of T2K, or comparable detectors—of the NC 1γ inclusive and exclusive cross sections (including coherent and incoherent channels) that are sufficient to constrain these mechanisms to a level adequate for νe appearance analyses.

(c) Combine (a) and (b) to demonstrate that the NC single-photon background to νe appearance is controlled with quantified, sub-dominant systematic uncertainty.
status_search_result: Substantial experimental progress has been made: in 2025 MicroBooNE released an inclusive search for anomalous single-photon production (arXiv:2502.06064), an enhanced search for NC Δ radiative single-photon production (arXiv:2502.05750), and the first search for NC coherent single-photon production (arXiv:2502.06091). These provide direct LAr-TPC measurements of the targeted backgrounds. However, a fully robust calculation of the anomalous ωZγ contribution with reduced theoretical uncertainty, and corresponding measurements at MINERνA and ND280/T2K of comparable precision, are not yet complete, so the overall program is partially solved.

paper_title: Recent advances and open questions in neutrino-induced quasi-elastic scattering and single photon production
original_question: How should neutrino experiments report CCQE measurements with precise definitions of the event selection, observables, and the meaning of “CCQE,” while providing model-independent quantities and flux information that theorists can calculate directly, so that comparisons with neutrino and electron-scattering theory are unambiguous?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current quasi-elastic (CCQE) neutrino–nucleus scattering experiments, in which a neutrino scatters off a nuclear target producing a charged lepton and (nominally) a single nucleon, but where the actual experimental signature is defined by detector-level observables (e.g., presence of a charged lepton, hadronic activity cuts, and reconstructed kinematics) rather than by the underlying interaction process. Different theoretical and experimental communities (neutrino physics, electron-scattering physics) use the terms "quasi-elastic" and "final state interactions" in inequivalent ways, so the mapping between measured cross sections and theoretically calculable quantities is ambiguous.

Formulate a standardized reporting prescription for CCQE measurements that achieves all of the following:

1. A precise, detector-level definition of the event selection (signal definition) specified purely in terms of observable final-state particles, kinematic thresholds, and acceptance, without reference to any particular interaction model.

2. A precise specification of the reported observables (e.g., differential cross sections in chosen kinematic variables) together with their bin definitions, kinematic ranges, and acceptance corrections, such that the reported quantities are model-independent in the sense that any theoretical model can compute them directly from first principles given the incoming neutrino flux.

3. A complete, quantitative description of the incoming neutrino flux (central value plus correlated uncertainties) sufficient for a theorist to fold any predicted cross section against the flux without further assumptions.

4. A clear translation table or operational definition relating the experimentally reported "CCQE" signal to the terminology used in the electron-scattering community and in nuclear theory, so that comparisons across neutrino theory, electron-scattering theory, and experimental data are unambiguous.

Provide such a prescription, and demonstrate that any two experiments adhering to it produce results that can be directly and unambiguously compared to each other and to theoretical predictions.
status_search_result: This is a methodological/community-standards question rather than a closed mathematical problem. Subsequent neutrino-scattering reviews and NuSTEC white papers have advocated and partially implemented model-independent reporting (flux-folded differential cross sections, detector-level signal definitions), but a fully standardized, universally adopted prescription remains an ongoing community effort, so the question is best characterized as still open.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Avoid elliptic-curve proof for the q−2 case
original_question: Take p ∈ {2, 3} and let L be a finite field of characteristic p and order q. For the exponent s = q − 2, which satisfies s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1) exactly in these two characteristics, can one prove the Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture for this case without using the theory of elliptic curves? In other words, can one show by a different method that there exists a nonzero a ∈ L such that W_{L,q−2}(a) = 0?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p\in\{2,3\}$ be a prime, and let $L$ be a finite field of characteristic $p$ and cardinality $q$. Fix a nontrivial additive character $\psi:L\to\mathbb{C}^\times$ (e.g. $\psi(x)=\exp(2\pi i\,\mathrm{Tr}_{L/\mathbb{F}_p}(x)/p)$), and for an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ define the Walsh/Weil-type exponential sum
$$W_{L,s}(a)=\sum_{x\in L}\psi(x^s+ax),\qquad a\in L.$$
Take the exponent $s=q-2$ (which is coprime to $q-1$ and satisfies $s\equiv 1\pmod{p-1}$ precisely when $p\in\{2,3\}$). The Helleseth Vanishing Conjecture in this case asserts that there exists a nonzero $a\in L$ with $W_{L,q-2}(a)=0$.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Characterize spectrum invariance under output scaling
original_question: Let L be a finite field and let f : L → L be a map, or more specifically a permutation. Determine necessary and sufficient conditions under which scalar multiplication of the output by any nonzero field element preserves the spectrum: for every b ∈ L×, the map bf defined by (bf)(x) = b f(x) has exactly the same Fourier spectrum as f. Which maps or permutations have this spectrum-invariance property for all nonzero scalars b?
self_contained_problem:

$$\widehat{f}(a,b) = \sum_{x \in L} \psi\bigl(a\,f(x) - b\,x\bigr),$$
and define the spectrum of $f$ to be the multiset
$$\mathrm{Spec}(f) = \{\!\{\,\widehat{f}(a,b) : (a,b) \in L^\times \times L\,\}\!\}.$$
For each $b \in L^\times$, let $bf : L \to L$ denote the map $x \mapsto b\,f(x)$.

Determine necessary and sufficient conditions on $f$ (respectively, on a permutation $f$ of $L$) such that
$$\mathrm{Spec}(bf) = \mathrm{Spec}(f) \qquad \text{for every } b \in L^\times.$$
Equivalently, characterize all maps (and all permutations) of a finite field whose Fourier spectrum is invariant under arbitrary nonzero scaling of the output.

context_brief: Four-valued analogue of Katz’s three-valued theorem
original_question: Suppose x ↦ x^s is a power permutation of a finite field and its spectrum takes exactly four distinct values. Is there an analogue of Theorem 3.5, the theorem that in the three-valued case forces singularity, integrality, and the congruence s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1)? More concretely, what structural restrictions must hold for four-valued exponents, parallel to the ones known for three-valued exponents?
self_contained_problem:
Let p be a prime, let q be a power of p, and let F = F_q be the finite field with q elements. Fix an integer s with gcd(s, q-1) = 1, so that the map x ↦ x^s is a permutation of F (a "power permutation"). For a nontrivial additive character ψ of F, define the Weil sum (spectrum value at a ∈ F^*) by

   W(a) = Σ_{x ∈ F} ψ(x^s + a x).

Call s singular if 0 lies in the spectrum {W(a) : a ∈ F^*}. The exponent s is called n-valued if the multiset {W(a) : a ∈ F^*} attains exactly n distinct values.

It is known (three-valued case) that if x ↦ x^s is a three-valued power permutation, then s is singular, the spectrum {0, A, B} consists of rational integers, and s ≡ 1 (mod p − 1).

Establish an analogue of this result in the four-valued case: namely, determine the structural restrictions (singularity, integrality of the spectrum, congruence conditions on s modulo p − 1, or other arithmetic constraints) that must necessarily hold for every exponent s such that the power permutation x ↦ x^s on F has spectrum taking exactly four distinct values.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
context_brief: Classify all nice exponents beyond the known families
original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and write s ≉ 1 to mean that s is not equivalent to 1 under the equivalence generated by s′ ≡ p^j s (mod q − 1) and inversion. Call s nice when the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v takes at most three values as v ranges over the field. The authors found by computation that all nice exponents s ≉ 1 over prime fields of characteristic p < 5000 come from the paradigmatic families in Propositions 6.5 and 6.6. Does every nice exponent s ≉ 1 arise from those paradigmatic examples?
self_contained_problem:
Let $p$ be an odd prime and let $L=\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of odd characteristic $p$, with $q$ a power of $p$. An exponent $s\in\mathbb{Z}/(q-1)\mathbb{Z}$ is called invertible if $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$. Define an equivalence relation on invertible exponents generated by
\[ s\sim p^{j}s\pmod{q-1}\quad\text{and}\quad s\sim s^{-1}\pmod{q-1}.\]
For an invertible exponent $s$ and $v\in L$, let
\[ N(1,v)=\#\{(x,y)\in L^{2}:\ x+y=1,\ x^{s}+y^{s}=v\}.\]
Call $s$ a nice exponent over $L$ if the multiset $\{N(1,v):v\in L\}$ takes at most three distinct values.

Two paradigmatic families of nice exponents are known:
(P1) Exponents $s$ such that $x\mapsto x^{s}$ is a planar function (equivalently, the Dembowski–Ostrom type exponents giving planarity over $L$);
(P2) Exponents $s$ such that $s\equiv p^{k}+1$-type "almost-planar" examples coming from the standard known constructions giving at most three values of $N(1,v)$.
(More precisely, take "paradigmatic" to mean the two explicit families guaranteed to yield nice exponents by direct character-sum computation — namely planar monomials and their close relatives obtained via the standard Niho/Welch type constructions.)

Question: Prove or disprove that every nice exponent $s$ with $s\not\sim 1$ over any prime field $\mathbb{F}_p$ (or more generally any finite field of odd characteristic) arises from one of these two paradigmatic families.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not return any work claiming a complete classification of nice exponents over odd-characteristic finite fields beyond the two paradigmatic families. Related literature on Niho exponents, planar functions and three-valued cross-correlations exists, but no resolution of this specific classification problem was located, so it appears to remain open.

paper_title: New Open Problems Related to Old Conjectures by Helleseth
original_question: Let s be an invertible exponent over a finite field of odd characteristic, and assume s ≉ 1. Must 2 always occur as a differential multiplicity of s? That is, for every such invertible exponent, does there always exist some v for which the number N(1, v) of solutions to x + y = 1 and x^s + y^s = v equals 2?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{F}_q$ be a finite field of odd characteristic, with $q$ elements. For an integer $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ (so the map $x\mapsto x^s$ is a permutation of $\mathbb{F}_q$), and $s\not\equiv 1\pmod{q-1}$, define for each $v\in\mathbb{F}_q$
$$N(1,v) = \#\{(x,y)\in\mathbb{F}_q\times\mathbb{F}_q : x+y=1,\ x^s+y^s=v\}.$$
A value $m\geq 0$ is called a differential multiplicity of $s$ if there exists some $v\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $N(1,v)=m$.

Prove or disprove: for every finite field $\mathbb{F}_q$ of odd characteristic and every exponent $s$ with $\gcd(s,q-1)=1$ and $s\not\equiv 1\pmod{q-1}$, the value $2$ occurs as a differential multiplicity of $s$; that is, there exists $v\in\mathbb{F}_q$ with $N(1,v)=2$.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: How often is an interesting or natural mathematical question independent of the usual axioms of mathematics?
self_contained_problem: Let ZFC denote the standard Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms of set theory together with the Axiom of Choice, and assume ZFC is consistent. Call a mathematical statement $\varphi$ (formulated in the language of set theory, or interpretable in it) "independent of ZFC" if neither $\varphi$ nor $\neg\varphi$ is provable from ZFC. Develop a meaningful, well-defined notion of "natural" or "mathematically interesting" statement, and within that framework, quantify how frequently such natural statements are independent of ZFC. Concretely: propose a precise measure or asymptotic density on a class $\mathcal{N}$ of "natural" mathematical statements (for instance, statements arising in number theory, analysis, combinatorics, or topology, possibly stratified by logical complexity such as $\Pi_1^0$, $\Sigma_1^1$, etc.), and determine the proportion or density of statements in $\mathcal{N}$ that are independent of ZFC. Is this proportion zero, positive, or one? Does the answer depend on the chosen stratification by logical complexity?
status_search_result: The question is a well-known philosophical/foundational meta-problem about how prevalent independence from ZFC is among naturally arising mathematical statements. It has been discussed by Gödel, Cohen, Friedman, Woodin and others, but it has no agreed-upon precise formulation, let alone a resolution. There is no known formal answer; it remains an open meta-mathematical problem.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Let β(n)+iγ(n) denote the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. If for every positive z != 1 the sequence ((log z)/(2π))γ(n), n >= 0, is uniformly distributed modulo 1, do the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function form a random sequence?
self_contained_problem:
Let the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function ζ(s) be enumerated as ρ_n = β(n) + iγ(n), n ≥ 0, with γ(n) > 0 listed in non-decreasing order. Recall that a sequence (x_n) of real numbers is said to be uniformly distributed modulo 1 if for every 0 ≤ a < b ≤ 1,
   lim_{N→∞} (1/N) #{ n < N : {x_n} ∈ [a,b) } = b − a,
where {x} denotes the fractional part of x.

Recall further that an infinite binary sequence is called (Martin-Löf) random if it passes every recursively enumerable statistical test of randomness; an arbitrary sequence of real numbers is said to form a random sequence if a natural binary encoding of it (e.g., the binary expansions of its terms) yields a Martin-Löf random sequence.

Suppose that for every positive real number z ≠ 1 the sequence
   ( (log z)/(2π) · γ(n) )_{n ≥ 0}
is uniformly distributed modulo 1. Does it follow that the sequence (γ(n))_{n ≥ 0} of imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of ζ(s) forms a random sequence in the sense of algorithmic randomness?
status_search_result: A technical report by Calude, Salomaa, and Roblot ("Zeros of Riemann's Zeta Function Are Uniformly Distributed, But Not Random") argues that, although the imaginary parts of the non-trivial zeros of ζ are conjecturally uniformly distributed modulo 1 in the stated sense, this sequence is not algorithmically random; the zeros are computable (e.g., to arbitrary precision by known algorithms), so the sequence cannot be Martin-Löf random. Thus the implication asked about fails: uniform distribution does not entail algorithmic randomness for these zeros.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Is mathematics quasi-empirical, in the sense that mathematical research should be carried out more like physics?
self_contained_problem:
A discipline is called quasi-empirical if its methodology resembles that of the empirical sciences (such as physics): conjectures are tested against examples and computational evidence, hypotheses may be adopted on the basis of their explanatory or predictive power rather than from formal proof alone, and theories are subject to revision in light of new evidence. By contrast, the classical view holds that mathematics proceeds purely deductively, with theorems established only by rigorous proof from accepted axioms.

Question: Is mathematics quasi-empirical? That is, taking into account phenomena such as the incompleteness theorems, algorithmic randomness, the practical role of computer experimentation and probabilistic reasoning in mathematical discovery, and the existence of plausible but unproved hypotheses (e.g., axioms adopted for their consequences), should mathematical research be conducted in a manner more like physics — accepting and using mathematical statements on the basis of empirical/heuristic evidence rather than insisting exclusively on formal proof?
status_search_result: This is a philosophical/methodological question about the nature of mathematical practice rather than a formal mathematical problem with a definite answer. It has been discussed at length by Lakatos, Pólya, Putnam, Chaitin, and others, but no consensus resolution exists; its status is best described as unknown/unresolved as a matter of philosophical debate.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Extend Chaitin complexity from finite strings to infinite strings, either by using non-terminating programs that run forever and generate infinite strings over infinite time, or by using computational models that process infinite strings in finite time, such as cellular automata or functions on reals.
self_contained_problem:
Background. The (prefix-free) Chaitin–Kolmogorov complexity H(x) of a finite binary string x is defined as the length of a shortest input p to a fixed universal prefix-free Turing machine U such that U(p) halts and outputs x; equivalently H(x) = min{|p| : U(p) = x}. This quantity is defined only for finite strings, since it relies on the universal machine halting after finitely many steps.

Problem. Develop a satisfactory notion of algorithmic complexity H(α) for infinite binary sequences α ∈ {0,1}^ω that extends the finite-string theory and shares its principal invariance, coding, and information-theoretic properties (e.g., machine-independence up to additive constants, a counting/Kraft inequality, a coherent relation to randomness of α, and consistent behavior under prefixes so that H(α) governs H(α↾n) as n → ∞). Two approaches are to be investigated and compared:

(a) Non-terminating computations: define H(α) using programs for the universal prefix-free machine that never halt but, while running forever, produce α as their (monotone) output, possibly via a transfinite or limit notion of program length and convergence.

(b) Infinite-time computational models: define H(α) using computational devices that consume and produce infinite strings in finite "physical" time, such as cellular automata acting on Z, real-valued computable functions in the BSS or computable-analysis sense, or infinite-time Turing machines, and use the size/description of such devices to measure complexity.

Determine, for at least one such formalization in each of (a) and (b), whether the resulting H(·) is well-defined up to an additive constant, prove its basic properties, characterize the sequences α with H(α) "small" or "maximal," and clarify the precise relationship between the two approaches and existing notions (plain, prefix, monotone, a-priori, and process complexity of finite prefixes; Martin-Löf and Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness).
status_search_result: Several complexity measures for infinite sequences exist (monotone complexity, a-priori complexity, process complexity, and characterizations of Martin-Löf randomness via prefix complexity of initial segments), and infinite-time Turing machines and BSS-style real computation provide infinite-time models that have been studied. Thus partial extensions in directions (a) and (b) have been carried out, but no single canonical "Chaitin complexity for infinite strings" unifying both viewpoints has been singled out, so the problem as posed is partially addressed rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Algorithmic Information Theory: Open Problems
original_question: Study the transformations that preserve random strings and random sequences.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Fix the binary alphabet {0,1}. For a finite binary string x of length n, the (plain) Kolmogorov complexity C(x) is the length of a shortest input to a fixed universal Turing machine that outputs x. A finite string x of length n is called Kolmogorov random (with deficiency d) if C(x) ≥ n − d. For infinite binary sequences, write 2^ω for Cantor space with the uniform (fair-coin) measure. An infinite sequence X ∈ 2^ω is Martin-Löf random if it passes every Martin-Löf test, i.e. for every uniformly computably enumerable sequence (U_n) of open subsets of 2^ω with μ(U_n) ≤ 2^{−n}, one has X ∉ ⋂_n U_n.

A (partial) computable map F : 2^ω → 2^ω (defined on a set of full uniform measure) is said to preserve randomness if F(X) is Martin-Löf random whenever X is Martin-Löf random. Analogously, a computable function f mapping finite strings to finite strings is said to preserve Kolmogorov randomness if there is a constant c such that C(f(x)) ≥ |f(x)| − c whenever C(x) ≥ |x| − O(1).

Problem. Characterize the transformations that preserve randomness in each of the following senses, and clarify the relationship between the two notions:
(a) Describe necessary and sufficient conditions on a (partial) computable function F : 2^ω → 2^ω under which F(X) is Martin-Löf random for every Martin-Löf random X.
(b) Describe necessary and sufficient conditions on a computable function f on finite binary strings under which f preserves Kolmogorov randomness in the sense above.
(c) Determine the structural and measure-theoretic properties (e.g. measure preservation, almost-everywhere computability, layerwise computability) that characterize these classes of transformations, and determine to what extent the finite and infinite versions correspond.
status_search_result: The general study of randomness-preserving transformations has produced several substantive results — for example, Shen's theorem that almost-everywhere computable measure-preserving maps preserve Martin-Löf randomness (and in fact every ML-random point has an ML-random preimage), as well as work on layerwise computability and on continuous transformations of 2-random sequences. However, no complete characterization of all transformations preserving randomness (in either the finite Kolmogorov-complexity sense or the infinite Martin-Löf sense) appears to be established, so the problem as a whole is best regarded as partially solved.
