paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If Γ is a continuum that recedes to ∞, it is known (see Hayman [386]) that as z → ∞ on Γ, log |f (z)| lim sup ≥ −A, r→∞ log M (|z|) where A is an absolute constant. Is it true that A = 1? This is certainly the case if Γ is a ray through the origin, see Beurling [96]. If A > 1, is it possible to obtain a good numerical estimate for A?
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function, and let
$$M(r) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, \qquad r > 0.$$
Let $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a continuum (a connected closed set) that recedes to infinity, i.e., $\Gamma$ is unbounded. It is known that there exists an absolute constant $A > 0$ such that for every such $f$ and $\Gamma$,
$$\limsup_{\substack{z \to \infty \\ z \in \Gamma}} \frac{\log |f(z)|}{\log M(|z|)} \;\geq\; -A.$$
When $\Gamma$ is a ray emanating from the origin, the optimal value is $A = 1$.

(a) Determine whether $A = 1$ is admissible for every continuum $\Gamma$ receding to infinity; equivalently, decide whether the inequality above holds with $A = 1$ for all non-constant entire $f$ and all unbounded continua $\Gamma$.

(b) If the optimal absolute constant satisfies $A > 1$, obtain a sharp (or good) numerical estimate for $A$.
status_search_result: Hayman and Kjellberg ("On the minimum of a subharmonic function on a connected set", 1983) gave a positive answer: for any non-constant subharmonic function $u$ and any $A > 1$, the set $\{z : u(z) + A\,B(|z|) < 0\}$ (with $B(r) = \max_{|\zeta|=r} u(\zeta)$) has no unbounded component, which implies $A = 1$ is the correct constant. Thus the problem is solved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It was shown by Kjellberg [475] that if 0 < α < 1 and log m0 (r, f ) < cos(φα) log M (r, f ) + O(1), as r → ∞, then log M (r, f ) lim = β, r→∞ rα where 0 < β ≤ ∞. If α = 1, it was shown by Hayman [406] that unless f (z) = AeBz , the corresponding result holds with β = ∞. Examples constructed by Hayman show that m0 (r, f )M (r, f ) → ∞ as r → ∞ can occur for a function of order 1 + ε for every positive ε. The case of functions of order 1 and maximal type remains open.
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a transcendental entire function. For r>0, write
  M(r,f) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|,   m_0(r,f) = min_{|z|=r} |f(z)|.
Recall that f has order 1 and maximal type if
  limsup_{r→∞} (log M(r,f))/r = ∞   and   limsup_{r→∞} (log log M(r,f))/(log r) = 1.

Background: Kjellberg proved that if 0 < α < 1 and
  log m_0(r,f) < cos(πα) · log M(r,f) + O(1)   as r → ∞,
then lim_{r→∞} (log M(r,f))/r^α exists in (0, ∞]. The analogue at α = 1 (with the natural condition log m_0(r,f) < log M(r,f) + O(1), i.e. m_0(r,f) M(r,f) ≤ C for some constant C, or more generally that m_0(r,f) does not grow with M(r,f)) was established by Hayman for entire functions of order strictly less than 1 and for order exactly 1 of finite type, where unless f(z) = A e^{Bz} one obtains lim_{r→∞} (log M(r,f))/r = ∞. Examples are known showing that m_0(r,f) M(r,f) → ∞ can occur for entire functions of order 1+ε for every ε > 0.

Problem: Determine whether there exists an entire function f of order 1 and maximal type, other than A e^{Bz}, satisfying
  m_0(r,f) · M(r,f) → ∞   as r → ∞,
or, equivalently, decide whether for every entire function f of order 1 and maximal type one must have
  liminf_{r→∞} m_0(r,f) · M(r,f) < ∞.

original_question: Suppose that f (z) has finite order, and that Γ is a rectifiable path on which f (z) → ∞. Let ℓ(r) be the length of Γ in |z| < r. Find such a path for which ℓ(r) grows as slowly as possible, and estimate ℓ(r) in terms of M (r, f ). If f (z) has zero order, or more generally, finite order, can a path be found for which ℓ(r) = O(r) as r → ∞? If log M (r, f ) = O(log2 r) as r → ∞, but under no weaker growth condition, it is shown by Hayman [394] and Piranian [635] that we may choose a ray through the origin for Γ. If f (z) has a finite asymptotic value a, the corresponding question may be asked for paths on which f (z) → a. (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be an entire function of finite order, and let $M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$. Suppose $\Gamma$ is a rectifiable path in the complex plane along which $f(z)\to\infty$, and let $\ell(r)$ denote the length of the portion of $\Gamma$ inside the disc $|z|<r$.

(a) Find a path $\Gamma$ for which $\ell(r)$ grows as slowly as possible, and obtain an estimate of $\ell(r)$ in terms of $M(r,f)$.

(b) If $f$ has order zero, or more generally finite order, determine whether one can always choose such a path $\Gamma$ with $\ell(r)=O(r)$ as $r\to\infty$.

(c) Formulate and answer the analogous questions when $f$ has a finite asymptotic value $a$ and $\Gamma$ is required to be a rectifiable path along which $f(z)\to a$.

It is known that if $\log M(r,f)=O(\log^2 r)$ as $r\to\infty$ (and under no weaker growth hypothesis), then $\Gamma$ may be chosen to be a ray through the origin.
status_search_result: Hayman showed that if $\log M(r,f)\ll(\log r)^2$ one may take $\ell(r)=O(r)$ along a ray. Gol'dberg and Eremenko disproved the corresponding conjecture for faster-growing functions: for any $\varphi(r)\to\infty$ there is an entire function with $\log M(r)\ll\varphi(r)(\log r)^2$ admitting no path with $f\to\infty$ and $\ell(r)\ll r$, and such examples exist of any prescribed finite order. Sharp estimates of $\ell(r)$ in terms of $M(r,f)$ and the asymptotic-value version remain only partially understood.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that an entire function f has exactly one curve Γ of maximum modulus (that is, Γ is connected, joins 0 to ∞, and f has no other maximum modulus points). What can be said about the minimum rate of growth of M (r, f ), if one is given information about the geometry of the curve Γ, for example, that Γ is a given infinitely-spiralling spiral? If Γ is a radial line, clearly nothing much can be said. (In a sense, this is the opposite of a Phragmén-Lindelöf principle). (D. A. Brannan)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a non-constant entire function, and write M(r,f) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)| for its maximum modulus. A point z is called a maximum modulus point of f if |f(z)| = M(|z|, f). Suppose that the set of maximum modulus points of f is a single connected curve Γ that joins 0 to ∞ (i.e., Γ is a connected, unbounded curve with 0 ∈ Γ and Γ contains points of arbitrarily large modulus, and there are no maximum modulus points of f outside Γ).

Determine, in terms of the geometry of Γ, the slowest possible rate of growth of M(r,f) as r → ∞. In particular:

(a) If Γ is a radial half-line, no nontrivial lower bound on the growth of M(r,f) is to be expected; confirm this.

(b) If Γ is a prescribed infinitely-spiralling curve (for example, a logarithmic spiral about the origin), establish the sharp lower bound on the growth rate of M(r,f) imposed by the requirement that Γ is the unique curve of maximum modulus of an entire function f.

More generally, find a quantitative relationship between the geometric/spiralling behaviour of Γ and the minimal possible growth of M(r,f).

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: For entire or, more generally, meromorphic functions f and g, let ‘f ≤ g’ mean that, for any sequence {zn }∞ 1 for which |f (zn )| → ∞, then |g(zn )| → ∞. For entire functions, it can be proved that, if f ′ ≤ f , then f is of exponential type; what can be said if f ′′ ≤ f ? Does f ′′ ≤ f imply that f is normal (that is, that |f ′ (z)|(1 + |f (z)|2 )−1 is bounded)? (An analogue in the case of the unit disc D has been proved by Pommerenke [652]). In the above ordering, does there exist f ∧ g and f ∨ g for any two entire functions f and g? That is, given f and g, does there exist an h such that h ≤ f and h ≤ g, and so that if k ≤ f and k ≤ g, then k ≤ h? Similarly, for f ∨ g. Finally, if f is meromorphic and f ′ ≤ f , does this imply a growth restriction on f , e.g. is the order of f at most two? Note: Any constant c satisfies c ≤ f for all entire f , and any non-constant polynomial p satisfies f ≤ p for any entire f . Observe also that ecz are all equivalent if c > 0. (L. A. Rubel and J. M. Anderson)
self_contained_problem:
For meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$ on the complex plane, write $f \preceq g$ to mean: for every sequence $\{z_n\}_{n=1}^\infty \subset \mathbb{C}$ with $|f(z_n)| \to \infty$, one has $|g(z_n)| \to \infty$. A meromorphic function $f$ is called normal if the spherical derivative $|f'(z)|/(1+|f(z)|^2)$ is bounded on $\mathbb{C}$. It is known that for entire $f$, the relation $f' \preceq f$ implies that $f$ is of exponential type.

(a) Suppose $f$ is entire and $f'' \preceq f$. What can be deduced about the growth of $f$? In particular, does $f'' \preceq f$ imply that $f$ is normal?

(b) Does the partial preorder $\preceq$ on the set of entire functions admit binary meets and joins? That is, given any two entire functions $f$ and $g$, does there exist an entire function $h$ such that $h \preceq f$ and $h \preceq g$, and such that whenever an entire $k$ satisfies $k \preceq f$ and $k \preceq g$ then $k \preceq h$ (a greatest lower bound $f \wedge g$)? Likewise, does a least upper bound $f \vee g$ always exist?

(c) If $f$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb{C}$ and $f' \preceq f$, does this imply a growth restriction on $f$? In particular, is the order of $f$ necessarily at most $2$?

No source was found that settles whether $f''\preceq f$ implies normality, whether the preorder admits meets/joins on entire functions, or whether $f'\preceq f$ forces a meromorphic $f$ to have order $\le 2$. The status therefore appears unverified.

When ρ = 0, Sρ is a sector with vertex at z = 0, and the conjecture is a consequence of results of Carlson [144], which were later generalised by Rosenbloom [671], Ganelius [286], and Korevaar and McCoy [487]. denote its $n$-th partial sum. Suppose that there exist a constant $K>0$ and a real number $\rho\ge 0$ such that every partial sum $S_n(z)$, $n=1,2,3,\dots$, is non-zero throughout the region

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f denote a rational or entire function of a complex variable, and f n , n = 1, 2, . . ., the n-th iterate of f , so that f 1 = f, f n+1 = f ◦ f n = f n ◦ f . Provided that f is not rational of degree 0 or 1, the set C of those points where {f n } forms a normal family is a proper open subset of the plane, and is invariant under the map z 7→ f (z). A component G of C is a wandering domain of f if f k (G) ∩ f n (G) = ∅ for all {k, n | k ≥ 1, n ≥ 1, k 6= n}. Jakobson has asked whether it is possible for a rational function f to have a wandering domain. Baker [50] gave a transcendental entire function which does have such domains. (I. N. Baker)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be a rational function of degree at least $2$, and define its iterates by $f^1=f$ and $f^{n+1}=f\circ f^n$ for $n\ge 1$. The Fatou set $\mathcal C$ of $f$ is the set of points $z\in\widehat{\mathbb C}$ in a neighborhood of which the family $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}$ is normal; it is an open, completely invariant subset of $\widehat{\mathbb C}$. A connected component $G$ of $\mathcal C$ is called a wandering domain of $f$ if $f^k(G)\cap f^n(G)=\emptyset$ for all integers $k,n\ge 1$ with $k\ne n$ (equivalently, no iterate $f^n(G)$ lies in a periodic component of $\mathcal C$).

Question: Can such a rational function $f$ possess a wandering domain?
status_search_result: Solved by Dennis Sullivan in 1985 ("Quasiconformal homeomorphisms and dynamics I"): a rational map of the Riemann sphere of degree at least 2 has no wandering Fatou components. Every Fatou component is eventually periodic. This resolved the question (originally posed by Fatou and raised by Jakobson) in the negative.

original_question: Let f be an entire function, and let D be a component of the set in C where the family of iterates {fn } is normal. Can this family have an infinite bounded set of constant limit functions? Eremenko and Lyubich [248] have shown that the set of constant limit functions may be infinite. (A. Eremenko)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a transcendental entire function, and consider the family $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}$ of iterates of $f$. The Fatou set $F(f)$ is the maximal open subset of $\mathbb{C}$ on which $\{f^n\}$ is a normal family (in the sense of Montel, where convergence to $\infty$ is allowed). Let $D$ be a connected component of $F(f)$. A constant limit function of $\{f^n\}$ on $D$ is a constant $c\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ such that some subsequence $f^{n_k}$ converges locally uniformly on $D$ to the constant function $c$. Let $L(D)\subset\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ denote the set of all such constant limit functions on $D$.

It is known that $L(D)$ may be infinite for some choice of $f$ and $D$. The question is: does there exist a transcendental entire function $f$ and a Fatou component $D$ of $f$ such that $L(D)$ is infinite and contained in a bounded subset of $\mathbb{C}$ (in particular, $\infty\notin L(D)$)?
status_search_result: The question is closely tied to the existence of "dynamically bounded" wandering domains, whose existence is a major open problem in transcendental dynamics. Recent work (e.g., on classifying simply connected wandering domains and on limit sets of iterates in wandering domains, 2021–2023) discusses the classification of limit functions but does not exhibit an entire function with an infinite bounded set of constant limit functions on a Fatou component. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let H be an entire function, let f1 , f2 be linearly independent solutions of the differential equation w′′ + Hw = 0, and let E = f1 f2 . Clearly f1 , f2 and E are entire. Also, it is well-known that if H is a polynomial of degree n, then the orders of f1 and f2 are ρ(f1 ) = ρ(f2 ) = 21 (n + 2). Furthermore, the exponent of convergence of the zeros of E is λ(E) = 21 (n + 2), provided that n > 1. If H is transcendental then ρ(f1 ) = ρ(f2 ) = +∞ and one might hope that, by analogy with the previous remarks, λ(E) = +∞. However, examples by Bank and Laine [53] showed that this is not necessarily the case if ρ(H) is a positive integer or +∞. They also asked whether λ(E) = +∞ if ρ(H) is non-integral and finite and they showed that this is indeed the case if ρ(H) < 21 , a result improved to ρ(H) ≤ 21 by Rossi [672]. What happens in general? (S. Hellerstein and J. Rossi)
self_contained_problem:
Let $H$ be a transcendental entire function, and let $f_1, f_2$ be two linearly independent entire solutions of the second-order linear differential equation
$$w'' + H w = 0.$$
Define the entire function $E = f_1 f_2$, and let $\lambda(E)$ denote the exponent of convergence of the zero sequence of $E$, i.e.
$$\lambda(E) = \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log n(r,1/E)}{\log r},$$
where $n(r,1/E)$ counts the zeros of $E$ in $\{|z|\le r\}$. Let $\rho(H)$ denote the order of $H$.

It is known that if $\rho(H)$ is a positive integer or $+\infty$, then $\lambda(E)$ may be finite, while if $\rho(H) \le 1/2$, then $\lambda(E) = +\infty$. 

Question: Suppose $\rho(H)$ is finite and non-integral (in particular $\rho(H) > 1/2$). Must one always have $\lambda(E) = +\infty$?
status_search_result: The question is the Bank–Laine conjecture. It was disproved by Bergweiler and Eremenko, who constructed a transcendental entire coefficient $H$ of finite non-integral order admitting linearly independent solutions $f_1, f_2$ of $w''+Hw=0$ such that $E=f_1 f_2$ has finite exponent of convergence of its zeros. Their paper "On the Bank–Laine conjecture" appeared in J. Eur. Math. Soc.

original_question: Suppose that f (z) = 1 + a1 z + a2 z 2 + . . . ∈ U2p . If p = 0 (so that f ∈ U0 ) and if f is not a polynomial, it is well-known that f cannot have two consecutive Taylor coefficients equal to zero. If p > 0, can an analogous assertion be made? Is it true, for example, that the Taylor series of f in U2p cannot have 2p + 2 consecutive coefficients equal to zero? (J. Williamson)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathcal{L}-\mathcal{P}$ denote the Laguerre–Pólya class, i.e. the class of entire functions that are uniform limits on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ of real polynomials having only real zeros. For each integer $p \ge 0$, let $U_{2p}$ denote the class of entire functions $f$ that are uniform limits on compact subsets of $\mathbb{C}$ of real polynomials having at most $2p$ non-real zeros (counted with multiplicity); in particular $U_0 = \mathcal{L}-\mathcal{P}$.

It is a classical fact that if $f(z) = 1 + a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + \cdots \in U_0$ and $f$ is not a polynomial, then $f$ cannot have two consecutive Taylor coefficients equal to zero (i.e. there is no $n \ge 1$ with $a_n = a_{n+1} = 0$).

Question: For $p \ge 1$, formulate and prove an analogous statement for the class $U_{2p}$. In particular, decide whether the following holds: if $f(z) = 1 + a_1 z + a_2 z^2 + \cdots \in U_{2p}$ and $f$ is not a polynomial, then the Taylor series of $f$ at $0$ cannot have $2p+2$ consecutive coefficients equal to zero, i.e. there is no integer $n \ge 1$ such that $a_n = a_{n+1} = \cdots = a_{n+2p+1} = 0$.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any published resolution of Williamson's question about $2p+2$ consecutive zero Taylor coefficients for functions in the class $U_{2p}$. Related recent work concerns Taylor-coefficient conditions for membership in the Laguerre–Pólya class and the number of non-real zeros of derivatives, but does not appear to settle this specific gap-coefficient problem. Status is therefore unverified.

original_question: Let Ω be a component of the normal set of an entire function (under iteration). Is dim(∂Ω) > 1? Or is ∂Ω a circle/line? (D. Hamilton)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a transcendental entire function, and consider the dynamical system generated by iteration of $f$. The Fatou set (also called the normal set) of $f$ is
$$F(f)=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:\{f^n\}_{n\ge 1}\text{ is a normal family in some neighborhood of }z\},$$
where $f^n$ denotes the $n$-th iterate of $f$. Let $\Omega$ be a connected component of $F(f)$, and let $\partial\Omega$ denote its topological boundary in $\mathbb{C}$. Let $\dim$ denote Hausdorff dimension.

Determine whether the following dichotomy must hold for every such component $\Omega$ of every transcendental entire function $f$: either
\[ \dim(\partial\Omega) > 1, \]
or else $\partial\Omega$ is a (round) circle or a straight line.
status_search_result: The dichotomy is known to hold in important cases but remains open in general. Recent work (2025) establishes that for components of attracting or parabolic basins of transcendental entire maps, the boundary has hyperbolic dimension strictly greater than 1 under conditions such as the immediate component being bounded or having infinite degree (in the Eremenko–Lyubich class). However, the full question is not fully resolved in general, particularly for Siegel disks and wandering domains, where examples with boundary dimension exactly 1 are known but the precise geometry has not been settled.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: (Fatou’s conjecture) Show that the subset U of functions g in Rd , such that all the critical points of g are in the basins of attraction of periodic sinks, is dense in Rd . The property ‘g ∈ U ’ is also sometimes called Axiom A. See also Fatou [259]. (P. Fatou; communicated by M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $d \geq 2$ and let $R_d$ denote the space of rational maps $g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}} \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ of degree $d$ from the Riemann sphere to itself, equipped with its natural topology (e.g., as a subset of complex projective space via coefficients). A periodic point $z_0$ of period $p$ of $g$ is called a (periodic) sink (attracting periodic point) if $|(g^p)'(z_0)| < 1$, and its basin of attraction is the set of points whose forward orbits converge to the cycle of $z_0$. A critical point of $g$ is a point where the derivative vanishes (in suitable local coordinates on the sphere). Let
$$U = \{ g \in R_d : \text{every critical point of } g \text{ lies in the basin of attraction of some periodic sink}\}.$$
(Maps in $U$ are also called hyperbolic, or said to satisfy Axiom A.) Prove or disprove: $U$ is dense in $R_d$.
status_search_result: The general Fatou conjecture on density of hyperbolic maps in the space of degree-$d$ rational maps remains open and is regarded as the central open problem in iterated rational dynamics. It has been established in several special settings: for the real quadratic family (Lyubich; Graczyk–Świątek) and more generally for real polynomials (Kozlovski–Shen–van Strien, "Density of hyperbolicity in dimension one", Annals of Math.), and for non-hyperbolic rational maps with Cantor Julia sets. The full complex version in $R_d$ is unresolved.

original_question: Let the function g in Rd have the property that its Julia set J(g) = Ĉ. Is the dimension k of the space of Beltrami forms on Ĉ, invariant under g, at most one? self_contained_problem:
Let $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote the Riemann sphere and let $g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a rational map of degree $d\ge 2$ whose Julia set $J(g)$ equals all of $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$. A measurable Beltrami form on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is an essentially bounded measurable section $\mu$ of $\overline{TC}/TC$, i.e. a measurable assignment $\mu(z)\,d\bar z/dz$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty\le 1$; it is called $g$-invariant if $g^*\mu=\mu$ almost everywhere. (a) Is $k(g)\le 1$ for every such $g$?

(b) Among rational maps $g$ of degree $\ge 2$ with $J(g)=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, are the (flexible) Lattès examples — those rational maps semiconjugate via a holomorphic map from a torus to itself given by an affine endomorphism — the only ones for which $k(g)\ne 0$?

original_question: Consider the class of functions subharmonic in the unit disc D, and satisfying u(z) ≤ 0 there. Suppose also that A(r, u) ≤ −1, for r lying on a set E consisting of a finite number of straight line segments. Then it is known (see e.g. Nevanlinna [598, p.100]) that B(r, u) is maximal, when u(z) = uE (z), where uE (z) is harmonic in D, except on a set E of the positive real axis, and u(z) assumes boundary values 0 on |z| = 1, and −1 on E. This is the solution to the so-called Carleman-Milloux problem [598]. For 0 < r < 1, 0 < K < 1, let C(r, K) be the set of all θ such that u(reiθ ) < −K. Is it true that C(r, K) has minimal length only if u(z) = uE (z)? The special case where E consists of the whole interval [0, 1] has particular interest. (T. Kövari)

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disc. For a function $u$ subharmonic in $\mathbb{D}$ and $0<r<1$, define
$$A(r,u)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}u(re^{i\theta})\,d\theta,\qquad B(r,u)=\sup_{|z|=r}u(z).$$
Consider the class $\mathcal{F}_E$ of functions $u$ subharmonic in $\mathbb{D}$ satisfying
\begin{enumerate}
\item $u(z)\le 0$ for all $z\in\mathbb{D}$,
\item $A(r,u)\le -1$ for every $r$ in a prescribed set $E\subset[0,1)$ that is a finite union of straight line segments.
\end{enumerate}
It is classical (the Carleman–Milloux problem) that $B(r,u)$ is maximized within $\mathcal{F}_E$ by the extremal function $u_E$, where $u_E$ is harmonic in $\mathbb{D}\setminus E^*$ (with $E^*$ the corresponding subset of the positive real axis), takes boundary values $0$ on $\{|z|=1\}$ and $-1$ on $E^*$.

For $0<r<1$ and $0<K<1$, and for $u\in\mathcal{F}_E$, define
$$C(r,K;u)=\{\theta\in[0,2\pi):u(re^{i\theta})<-K\},$$
and let $|C(r,K;u)|$ denote its Lebesgue measure (length).

Question: Is it true that, among all $u\in\mathcal{F}_E$, the length $|C(r,K;u)|$ is minimized only when $u=u_E$? In particular, settle the case in which $E$ is the entire interval $[0,1]$.

$$\omega(\zeta)=\frac{1}{\pi r(\zeta)^2}\iint_{D_\zeta}\omega(x+iy)\,dx\,dy,$$

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It is known that the set E of least capacity C and given volume is a ball. If E displays some measure of asymmetry (for instance, if every ball with the same volume as E in space contains a minimum proportion δ in the complement of E), can one obtain a lower bound for the capacity of E which exceeds C by some positive function of δ? (E. Fraenkel; communicated by W. K. Hayman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 2$ and let $E \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a compact set. Denote by $|E|$ its Lebesgue measure (volume) and by $\operatorname{cap}(E)$ its (Newtonian, for $n \ge 3$, or logarithmic, for $n=2$) capacity. The classical isocapacitary inequality asserts that among all compact sets of a fixed volume $V$, the capacity is minimized uniquely by the ball $B$ with $|B|=V$; write $C := \operatorname{cap}(B)$.

Define the Fraenkel asymmetry of $E$ by
$$\delta(E) \;=\; \inf_{x \in \mathbb{R}^n} \frac{|E \,\triangle\, B(x)|}{|E|},$$
where $B(x)$ denotes the ball centered at $x$ with $|B(x)|=|E|$. Equivalently, $\delta$ measures the minimum, over all balls of the same volume as $E$, of the relative volume of the symmetric difference (so that, up to normalization, it captures the minimum proportion of any equal-volume ball lying outside $E$).

Question: Does there exist a function $\Phi : [0,2] \to [0,\infty)$ with $\Phi(\delta) > 0$ whenever $\delta > 0$, depending only on $n$ and $V$, such that for every compact $E \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $|E|=V$ one has
$$\operatorname{cap}(E) \;\ge\; C + \Phi(\delta(E))\,?$$
That is, can the isocapacitary deficit $\operatorname{cap}(E) - C$ be bounded below by a positive function of the asymmetry $\delta(E)$?
status_search_result: A sharp quantitative isocapacitary inequality has been established: the isocapacitary deficit of a set with fixed volume is bounded below by a constant times the square of the Fraenkel asymmetry. This answers Fraenkel's question affirmatively, with $\Phi(\delta) \asymp \delta^2$. Extensions to $p$-capacity and fractional capacity have also been proved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that you have a continuous real function u(x) on Rn , and you want to know whether a homeomorphism φ : Rn → Rn and a harmonic function v on Rn exist, such that v(x) = u(φ(x)). Is it necessary and sufficient that there should exist mappings µ1 , µ2 , . . . , µn so that U = (u, µ1 , µ2 , . . . , µn ) is a light open mapping of Rn into Rn ? The case n = 2 is a result of Stoilow which is in [788], for example. (L. A. Rubel, communicated by D. A. Brannan)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\geq 2$ and let $u:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ be a continuous function. A continuous map $F:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ is called *light* if for every $y\in\mathbb{R}^n$ the fiber $F^{-1}(y)$ is totally disconnected, and *open* if it sends open sets to open sets. A function $v:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ is *harmonic* if $\Delta v=0$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$.

Question: Is it true that there exist a homeomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$ and a harmonic function $v:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ with
$$u(x)=v(\varphi^{-1}(x)) \quad\text{(equivalently, } v(x)=u(\varphi(x))\text{)}$$
if and only if there exist continuous real-valued functions $\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_{n-1}$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ such that the map
$$U=(u,\mu_1,\mu_2,\ldots,\mu_{n-1}):\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^n$$
is a light open mapping?

(The case $n=2$ is known via Stoïlow's theorem: a continuous light open map of the plane factors as a homeomorphism followed by a holomorphic map, and the real part of a holomorphic map is harmonic. The problem asks whether the analogous characterization of "harmonizable" continuous functions $u$ via the existence of light-open-mapping completions holds for all $n\geq 2$.)

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let D be a domain containing the origin whose ‘outer boundary’ is T and whose ‘inner boundary’ is a closed set E in D. If every radius of the unit disc meets E, determine the supremum of the harmonic measure at 0 of T with respect to D. (W. H. J. Fuchs)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disc and $\mathbb{T}=\{z:|z|=1\}$ its boundary. Consider a domain $D\subset\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ such that:
- $0\in D$,
- the "outer boundary" of $D$ is $\mathbb{T}$,
- the "inner boundary" of $D$ is a closed set $E\subset\overline{\mathbb{D}}$ contained in $D^c\cap\mathbb{D}$ (so that $\partial D=\mathbb{T}\cup E$),
- every radius $\{re^{i\theta}:0\le r\le 1\}$ ($\theta\in[0,2\pi)$) of the closed unit disc meets $E$.

Let $\omega(0,\mathbb{T},D)$ denote the harmonic measure at $0$ of $\mathbb{T}$ with respect to $D$, i.e. the value at $0$ of the bounded harmonic function on $D$ with boundary values $1$ on $\mathbb{T}$ and $0$ on $E$.

Determine
$$\sup\bigl\{\,\omega(0,\mathbb{T},D)\,:\, D \text{ as above}\bigr\}.$$
Equivalently, determine the infimum of $\omega(0,E,D)$ taken over all closed sets $E\subset\overline{\mathbb{D}}\setminus\{0\}$ that meet every radius of the closed unit disc, where $D$ is the component of $\overline{\mathbb{D}}\setminus E$ containing $0$.
category_tag: Harmonic measure in the unit disc
status_search_result: The problem, attributed to W. H. J. Fuchs, is closely tied to Hall's lemma and to sharp lower bounds for the harmonic measure of a set in the closed unit disc whose radial projection has prescribed length. FitzGerald–Rodin–Warschawski, and later Marshall–Sundberg, established sharp results for continua meeting every radius (with the extremal configuration described via quadratic differentials and a numerical constant arising from a 3:1 rectangle), and further refinements were given by Solynin and others. The exact value of the supremum in the original generality (closed sets, not necessarily continua) appears not to be definitively pinned down in the literature surveyed; partial sharp bounds are known.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Is there a harmonic polynomial P (x1 , x2 , x3 ), P 6≡ 0 that is divisible by x41 + x42 + x43 ? (H. S. Shapiro)
self_contained_problem: A polynomial $P(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ in three real variables is called harmonic if $\Delta P = \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x_1^2} + \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x_2^2} + \frac{\partial^2 P}{\partial x_3^2} = 0$ identically on $\mathbb{R}^3$. Determine whether there exists a nonzero harmonic polynomial $P(x_1,x_2,x_3)$ such that $P$ is divisible (in the polynomial ring $\mathbb{R}[x_1,x_2,x_3]$) by $x_1^4 + x_2^4 + x_3^4$.
status_search_result: The problem is resolved in the negative: a theorem of Brelot and Choquet states that any nontrivial polynomial divisor of a harmonic polynomial on $\mathbb{R}^n$ must take both positive and negative values. Since $x_1^4+x_2^4+x_3^4$ is nonnegative (and vanishes only at the origin), it cannot divide any nonzero harmonic polynomial.

must be identically zero on $D$?

- For $n = 2$, such a function $\varepsilon$ always exists.

original_question: Let K(z, z ′ ) denote the kernel of the double layer potential occurring in Fredholm’s theory where z, z ′ ∈ Γ, Γ being a smooth Jordan curve. original_question: Let Ω be a bounded open subset of Rn , n ≥ 2, and suppose that y ∈ ∂Ω. Denote the open ball of centre y and radius r by B(r). A point y is said to be B-regular for Ω if, for each resolutive function f on ∂Ω that is bounded in B(R) ∩ ∂Ω for some positive R, the Perron-Wiener-Brelot solution H Ω of the Dirichlet problem is bounded in B(r) ∩ Ω for some positive r. Also, a point y is said to be lB-regular for Ω if there exists a positive null sequence {rm }∞ 1 , such that y is B-regular for B(rm ) ∩ Ω for all m. original_question: Is there a function f (k) of the positive integer k, so that the square of every polynomial having at least f (k) terms has a least k terms? Erdös proved that at any rate, f (k) > k 1+c for a positive constant c. (P. Erdös)

For a polynomial $P(x) \in \mathbb{C}[x]$, let $Q(P)$ denote the number of nonzero terms (monomials) appearing in $P$. The question concerns the relationship between $Q(P)$ and $Q(P^2)$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a function $f : \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \to \mathbb{Z}_{>0}$ such that for every positive integer $k$ and every polynomial $P(x) \in \mathbb{C}[x]$ with $Q(P) \ge f(k)$, the square satisfies $Q(P^2) \ge k$.

Equivalently, defining
$$ g(k) := \min\{ Q(P^2) : P(x) \in \mathbb{C}[x],\ Q(P) \ge k \}, $$

original_question: Let W + be the Banach algebra P∞ of power series f (z) = n=0 an z n absolutely convergent in |z| ≤ 1, with kf k = n=0 |an |. Which functions generate W + ? More precisely, for which functions f is it true that the polynomials in f are dense in W + ? It is clear that a necessary condition is that f be univalent in D. self_contained_problem:
Let $W^+$ denote the Banach algebra of all power series $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} a_n z^n$ that converge absolutely on the closed unit disc $\overline{\mathbb{D}}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\le 1\}$, equipped with the norm $\|f\|=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}|a_n|$. Say that $f\in W^+$ generates $W^+$ if the set of polynomials in $f$ (i.e.\ the algebra $\{P\circ f : P\in\mathbb{C}[z]\}$) is dense in $W^+$ with respect to this norm. It is known that:

(i) A necessary condition for $f$ to generate $W^+$ is that $f$ be univalent on the open unit disc $\mathbb{D}$.

(ii) If $f$ is univalent on $\mathbb{D}$ and $f'\in H^1(\mathbb{D})$ (the Hardy space), then $f$ generates $W^+$.

(iii) If $f(z)=\sum a_n z^n$ is univalent on $\mathbb{D}$ and there exists $\varepsilon>0$ such that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} n|a_n|^2 (\log n)^{1+\varepsilon}<\infty$, then $f$ generates $W^+$.

Conditions (ii) and (iii) are independent.

Question: Is univalence on $\mathbb{D}$ alone sufficient? That is, does every $f\in W^+$ which is univalent on $\mathbb{D}$ generate $W^+$?

original_question: It was proved by Hall that every Bloch function has (possibly infinite) angular limits on an uncountably dense subset of |z| = 1. Do there always exist angular limits on a set of positive measure relative to some fixed Hausdorff measure, such as logarithmic measure for example? (J. E. McMillan, Ch. Pommerenke)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disc, and let $\mathbb{T} = \{z : |z| = 1\}$ denote its boundary. A holomorphic function $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ is called a Bloch function if 
$$\|f\|_{\mathcal{B}} := \sup_{z \in \mathbb{D}} (1-|z|^2)\,|f'(z)| < \infty.$$
For $\zeta \in \mathbb{T}$, the angular (non-tangential) limit of $f$ at $\zeta$ is, when it exists in $\mathbb{C} \cup \{\infty\}$, the common value of $\lim_{z \to \zeta} f(z)$ taken as $z \to \zeta$ inside any Stolz angle with vertex at $\zeta$. It is known (Hall) that every Bloch function admits a (possibly infinite) angular limit on an uncountably dense subset of $\mathbb{T}$.

Given a Hausdorff measure function $h : [0,\infty) \to [0,\infty)$ (for example $h(t) = 1/\log(1/t)$, giving the logarithmic measure), let $\Lambda_h$ denote the associated Hausdorff measure on $\mathbb{T}$.

Question: Does there exist a Hausdorff measure function $h$ such that for every Bloch function $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$, the set of points $\zeta \in \mathbb{T}$ at which $f$ has an angular limit (finite or infinite) has positive $\Lambda_h$-measure?

\item if $\delta > 2^{-1/2}$, then $\delta$ is admissible.
\end{itemize}

$$\delta^{*}=\inf\{\delta\in(0,1] : \delta \text{ is admissible}\}.$$
(In particular, is $\delta^{*}=\tfrac{1}{2}$?)

original_question: A non-constant function f analytic in D, is said to be in the MacLane class A if the set of points of the unit circle T at which f has an asymptotic value is a dense subset of T (see MacLane [547]). A function f is said to have an arc tract if there exists a sequence {γn } of arcs, γn ⊂ D, and a non-degenerate subarc γ of T such that γn → γ (in the obvious fashion) and min{|f (z)| : z ∈ γn } → ∞ as n → ∞. self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disc and $\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}$ the unit circle. For a non-constant analytic function $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$, a point $\zeta\in\mathbb{T}$ is said to be a point at which $f$ has an asymptotic value if there exist a value $\alpha\in\mathbb{C}\cup\{\infty\}$ and a continuous path $\gamma:[0,1)\to\mathbb{D}$ with $\gamma(t)\to\zeta$ as $t\to1^-$ such that $f(\gamma(t))\to\alpha$ as $t\to1^-$. Define the MacLane class $\mathcal{A}$ to be the set of non-constant analytic functions $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ such that the set of points of $\mathbb{T}$ at which $f$ has an asymptotic value is dense in $\mathbb{T}$.

Say that $f$ has an arc tract if there exist a sequence of arcs $\{\gamma_n\}$ with $\gamma_n\subset\mathbb{D}$ and a non-degenerate subarc $\gamma\subset\mathbb{T}$ such that $\gamma_n\to\gamma$ (in the Hausdorff sense) and $\min\{|f(z)|:z\in\gamma_n\}\to\infty$ as $n\to\infty$.

Question: Does there exist a function $f\in\mathcal{A}$ that has an arc tract and whose derivative $f'$ does not vanish anywhere in $\mathbb{D}$?

No subsequent resolution has been found.

original_question: It can be shown that there exists a Blaschke product B(z) with B(0) = 0 such that 1 + B(z) 1 − B(z) is a Bloch function. Give an explicit construction for such a product. (F. Holland)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disc. A Blaschke product is a function of the form
$$B(z) = z^m \prod_{n} \frac{|a_n|}{a_n}\,\frac{a_n - z}{1 - \overline{a_n} z},$$
where $m \in \{0,1,2,\dots\}$ and $\{a_n\} \subset \mathbb{D}\setminus\{0\}$ is a (possibly empty, finite, or infinite) sequence satisfying the Blaschke condition $\sum_n (1-|a_n|) < \infty$. A holomorphic function $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ is said to be a Bloch function if
$$\|f\|_{\mathcal{B}} := \sup_{z \in \mathbb{D}} (1 - |z|^2) |f'(z)| < \infty.$$

It is known that there exists a Blaschke product $B$ with $B(0) = 0$ such that the function
$$F(z) = \frac{1 + B(z)}{1 - B(z)}$$
is a Bloch function on $\mathbb{D}$.

Problem: Give an explicit construction of such a Blaschke product $B$ (i.e., specify its zero sequence, or equivalently a closed-form expression) for which $B(0) = 0$ and $\dfrac{1 + B(z)}{1 - B(z)}$ belongs to the Bloch space.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: The ratio R of two Blaschke products B(z, an ), B(z, bn ) is of bounded characteristic, but need not be a normal meromorphic function. That is, if an is ‘close’ to bn for infinitely many n we can arrange that the spherical derivative of R is too large for R to be normal. When is R a normal function? Cima and Colwell [157] have shown that if {an } and {bn } are both interpolating sequences, then R is normal if and only if {an } ∪ {bn } is also an interpolating sequence. What happens if the sequences are not interpolating sequences? (J. M. Anderson)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disc. Recall that for a sequence $\{a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ satisfying the Blaschke condition $\sum_n(1-|a_n|)<\infty$, the associated Blaschke product is
$$B(z,\{a_n\})=\prod_n \frac{|a_n|}{a_n}\cdot\frac{a_n-z}{1-\overline{a_n}z}.$$
A meromorphic function $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ is called normal if the family $\{f\circ\varphi:\varphi\in\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D})\}$ is normal in the sense of Montel as a family of meromorphic functions; equivalently, the spherical derivative
$$f^{\#}(z)=\frac{|f'(z)|}{1+|f(z)|^2}$$
satisfies $\sup_{z\in\mathbb{D}}(1-|z|^2)f^{\#}(z)<\infty$. A sequence $\{a_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$ is called an interpolating (Carleson) sequence if for every bounded sequence $\{w_n\}\subset\mathbb{C}$ there exists $f\in H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ with $f(a_n)=w_n$ for all $n$.

Given two Blaschke sequences $\{a_n\},\{b_n\}\subset\mathbb{D}$, form the quotient
$$R(z)=\frac{B(z,\{a_n\})}{B(z,\{b_n\})},$$
which is meromorphic of bounded characteristic in $\mathbb{D}$. It is known that when both $\{a_n\}$ and $\{b_n\}$ are interpolating sequences, $R$ is a normal meromorphic function on $\mathbb{D}$ if and only if the union $\{a_n\}\cup\{b_n\}$ is also an interpolating sequence.

Problem. Find necessary and sufficient conditions, expressed in terms of the geometry of the sequences $\{a_n\}$ and $\{b_n\}$ in $\mathbb{D}$, for the quotient $R$ to be a normal meromorphic function on $\mathbb{D}$, without the assumption that $\{a_n\}$ or $\{b_n\}$ is an interpolating sequence.

Math. paper "Ratios of interpolating Blaschke products" and later results of Garnett–Nicolau approximating inner functions by such ratios), as well as work on Blaschke products and normality. However, no source was found that gives a complete geometric characterization of normality for the quotient $R$ in the general (non-interpolating) case, so the problem appears unresolved in full generality.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that f is univalent and zero-free in D. It has been shown by Baernstein [40] that, for each p ∈ (0, 12 ), f admits a factorisation f = Bp (Fp )1/p , where Bp ∈ H ∞ , 1/Bp ∈ H ∞ , and Re Fp > 0. Is it possible to pass to the limit p = 12 , and thus factor f into a bounded function times a function subordinate to a map onto a slit plane? (A. Baernstein II)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disc, and let $H^\infty=H^\infty(\mathbb{D})$ denote the Banach algebra of bounded holomorphic functions on $\mathbb{D}$. Suppose $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ is univalent (i.e. holomorphic and injective) and zero-free on $\mathbb{D}$. It is known that for each $p\in(0,\tfrac{1}{2})$ there exist holomorphic functions $B_p,F_p$ on $\mathbb{D}$ such that
$$f = B_p\,(F_p)^{1/p},$$
where $B_p\in H^\infty$, $1/B_p\in H^\infty$, and $\operatorname{Re} F_p>0$ on $\mathbb{D}$.

Recall that a holomorphic function $g:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ is said to be subordinate to a holomorphic function $h:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{C}$ (with $h$ univalent) if $g(\mathbb{D})\subset h(\mathbb{D})$ and $g(0)=h(0)$; equivalently, there is a holomorphic self-map $\omega:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ with $\omega(0)=0$ and $g=h\circ\omega$. By a "slit plane" we mean a domain of the form $\mathbb{C}\setminus L$ where $L$ is a closed half-line.

Question: Is it always possible to take the limit $p\to\tfrac{1}{2}$ in the above factorisation? More precisely, can every univalent zero-free $f$ on $\mathbb{D}$ be factored as
$$f = B\cdot G,$$
where $B\in H^\infty$ with $1/B\in H^\infty$ and $G$ is subordinate to a conformal map of $\mathbb{D}$ onto a slit plane?

original_question: One of the many equivalent norms on BMOA on D is defined by kf kh = inf sup |f (z) + q(z)|, q z∈D the infimum being taken over all functions analytic in D. Given f in BMOA, does there exist a q such that |f (z) + q(z)| ≡ kf kh a.e. on |z| = 1? The answer is ‘yes’ when f is a rational function. (J. A. Hempel)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ and let $\mathrm{BMOA}$ denote the space of analytic functions on $\mathbb{D}$ whose boundary values lie in $\mathrm{BMO}$ on the unit circle $\partial\mathbb{D}$. For $f\in\mathrm{BMOA}$, define
$$\|f\|_h \;=\; \inf_{g}\;\sup_{z\in\mathbb{D}}\,\bigl|f(z)+\overline{g(z)}\bigr|,$$
where the infimum is taken over all functions $g$ analytic in $\mathbb{D}$ (so that $\overline{g}$ ranges over conjugate-analytic functions). It is known that $\|\cdot\|_h$ is an equivalent norm on $\mathrm{BMOA}$.

$$\bigl|f(z)+\overline{g(z)}\bigr| \;=\; \|f\|_h \qquad \text{for almost every } z \text{ with } |z|=1\,?$$

(It is known that the answer is affirmative whenever $f$ is a rational function. The problem asks whether the same holds for arbitrary $f\in\mathrm{BMOA}$.)

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disc. Suppose

$$\hat\mu(n)=\int_0^{2\pi}e^{-inx}\,d\mu(x)$$
are nonnegative for all $n\in\mathbb{Z}$. Is it true that $(\hat\mu(n))_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}\in\ell^2$?

with $a_1=1$.

$$\mathcal{A}(c)=\inf\{A(f): f\in S,\ a_2(f)=c\}.$$

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let O be a subset of D = {|ω| < 1}. Find a characterisation of those O that are of the form (C \ f (D)) ∩ D for some f in S. What is the maximum area of O ? Given that ω1 , ω2 ∈ {|ω| < 1}, how does one tell whether there exists such an f with ω1 , ω2 ∈ Of ? The same question could be asked for ω1 , ω2 , ω3 etc. (A. W. Goodman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk, and let $S$ denote the class of functions $f : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{C}$ that are holomorphic and univalent on $\mathbb{D}$ and normalized by $f(0) = 0$ and $f'(0) = 1$. For $f \in S$, define the omitted set inside the unit disk by
$$O_f = (\mathbb{C} \setminus f(\mathbb{D})) \cap \mathbb{D},$$
i.e., the set of points $\omega$ with $|\omega| < 1$ that are not in the image $f(\mathbb{D})$.

Address the following questions:

(a) Characterise intrinsically those subsets $O \subseteq \mathbb{D}$ for which there exists $f \in S$ with $O_f = O$.

(b) Determine
$$A^* = \sup_{f \in S} \operatorname{Area}(O_f),$$
the maximum possible Lebesgue area of $O_f$, and find an extremal function (or describe the extremal configuration) for which the supremum is attained.

(c) Given two prescribed points $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in \mathbb{D}$, give a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of $f \in S$ such that both $\omega_1, \omega_2 \in O_f$. More generally, for any finite collection $\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n \in \mathbb{D}$, give a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence of $f \in S$ with $\{\omega_1, \dots, \omega_n\} \subseteq O_f$.
status_search_result: Part (b) is the well-known Goodman omitted area problem (1949). The exact value of $A^*$ remains unknown; rigorous bounds give roughly $0.240005\pi < A^* < 0.31\pi$, while numerical computations suggest $A^* \approx 0.2385813248\pi$. The companion characterisation problems in (a) and (c) (when can a prescribed set, or finite set of points, be the omitted-in-disk set of some $f \in S$) do not appear to have a complete solution in the literature. The problem is therefore still open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose f in S and define h(z) = {f (z 2 )} 2 = z + c3 z 3 + c5 z 5 + . . . Robertson’s conjecture (see Sheil-Small [708]) asserts that 1 + |c3 |2 + |c5 |2 + . . . + |c2n−1 |2 ≤ n. This is known to be true if f is star-like; is it true if f has real coefficients, or if f is close-to-convex? (P. L. Duren)
self_contained_problem:
Let $S$ denote the class of functions $f$ that are holomorphic and univalent on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ and normalized by $f(0)=0$, $f'(0)=1$. For $f\in S$, define
$$h(z) = \bigl\{f(z^2)\bigr\}^{1/2} = z + c_3 z^3 + c_5 z^5 + \cdots,$$
the odd univalent function associated with $f$ (with the branch chosen so that $h'(0)=1$).

Robertson's conjecture asserts that for every $f\in S$ and every integer $n\geq 1$,
$$1 + |c_3|^2 + |c_5|^2 + \cdots + |c_{2n-1}|^2 \le n.$$

This inequality is known to hold whenever $f$ is starlike (i.e., $f(\mathbb{D})$ is starlike with respect to the origin). 

Question: Does Robertson's inequality
$$\sum_{k=1}^{n} |c_{2k-1}|^2 \le n \qquad (\text{with } c_1 = 1)$$
hold under either of the following weaker hypotheses?
(a) $f\in S$ has real Taylor coefficients;
(b) $f\in S$ is close-to-convex (i.e., there exists a convex univalent function $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$ such that $\operatorname{Re}\bigl(f'(z)/g'(z)\bigr)>0$ on $\mathbb{D}$).
status_search_result: Robertson's conjecture for the full class S was established by Louis de Branges in 1985 as part of his proof of the Bieberbach conjecture: de Branges proved the Milin conjecture, which implies Robertson's conjecture for all of S, which in turn implies Bieberbach's. Hence the inequality holds for every f in S, in particular for f with real coefficients and for close-to-convex f, so the special cases asked about are subsumed by de Branges' theorem.

$$V_n(D) = \{\, a_n(f) : f \in S(D) \,\} \subset \mathbb{C},$$
and analogously $V_n^*(D)$ for the subclass $S^*(D)$.

Question. Does there exist some integer $n \ge 2$ for which the coefficient region $V_n(D)$ is geometrically similar to the boundary curve $C$ (i.e. has the same shape as $C$)? If not, does this hold at least for the starlike coefficient region $V_n^*(D)$?

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let D be a plane domain containing ∞. Let there be given a continuous assignment of numbers (thought of as angles) to the components of C \ D. Consider conformal mappings of D onto the complement in the extended plane of straight line segments. Show that one of these mappings is such that the straight line segments make angles with the positive real axis equal to the corresponding preassigned angles. In other words, under the mapping, each component of C \ D is associated with a slit in its preassigned direction. (B. Rodin; communicated by C. FitzGerald)
self_contained_problem:
Let $D \subset \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a plane domain with $\infty \in D$, and let $\mathcal{K}$ denote the family of connected components of $\widehat{\mathbb{C}} \setminus D$ (equipped with, say, the Hausdorff topology on compact subsets of $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$). Suppose we are given a continuous assignment $\theta : \mathcal{K} \to \mathbb{R}/\pi\mathbb{Z}$ of angles to the components of the complement of $D$.

A rectilinear slit map of $D$ is a conformal (i.e. univalent holomorphic) map $f : D \to \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ with $f(\infty) = \infty$ such that $\widehat{\mathbb{C}} \setminus f(D)$ consists of (possibly degenerate) straight line segments, one corresponding to each component $K \in \mathcal{K}$.

Prove that there exists a rectilinear slit map $f$ of $D$ such that, for every component $K \in \mathcal{K}$, the corresponding image slit makes angle $\theta(K)$ with the positive real axis.
status_search_result: For domains of finite connectivity the result is classical (Koebe). C. H. FitzGerald proved a uniqueness result for domains of countable connectivity with arbitrary angle assignments, and an existence result for arbitrary domains under the additional assumption that the continuous angle assignment has finite range, using a crossing-module extremal length tool. The full conjecture (continuous angle assignment, no finite-range hypothesis, on arbitrary plane domains) does not appear to be fully resolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let D1 , D2 be Jordan domains bounded by rectifiable curves C1 , C2 of equal length. Suppose that an isometric sewing of C1 and C2 is everywhere conformally admissible, thus generating a Riemann surface equivalent to a sphere S. Is the curve C on S which corresponds to C1 (and C2 ) necessarily rectifiable? (A. Huber)
self_contained_problem: Let $D_1, D_2 \subset \mathbb{C}$ be Jordan domains whose boundaries $C_1 = \partial D_1$ and $C_2 = \partial D_2$ are rectifiable Jordan curves of equal (finite) length $L$. Fix orientation-preserving arc-length parametrizations $\gamma_i:[0,L]\to C_i$ ($i=1,2$), and consider the identification (isometric sewing) $\gamma_1(s)\sim\gamma_2(s)$ for every $s\in[0,L]$. Assume that this isometric sewing is everywhere conformally admissible, in the sense that the topological sphere obtained from the disjoint union $\overline{D_1}\sqcup\overline{D_2}$ by identifying $C_1$ with $C_2$ via $\gamma_2\circ\gamma_1^{-1}$ carries a complex structure making it conformally equivalent to the Riemann sphere $S$, and such that the restrictions of the two uniformizing maps to $D_1$ and $D_2$ are conformal. Let $C\subset S$ be the simple closed curve that is the image of the identified $C_1\cong C_2$ under this uniformization. Question: Must $C$ be a rectifiable curve in $S$?
status_search_result: The problem is the classical Huber question on isometric conformal welding (cf. A. Huber, "Isometrische und konforme Verheftung", 1976). A web search confirms that for rectifiable curves of equal length with an arc-length isometric identification, rectifiability of the welded curve is known to hold under the stronger chord-arc hypothesis, while mere rectifiability does not even guarantee existence/uniqueness in general. No source found definitively resolves Huber's original question (rectifiability of the welded curve given conformal admissibility) in full generality, so its status is treated here as unknown.

is itself hyperbolic?

Suppose $f(z)=z+a_2 z^2+a_3 z^3+\cdots$ is holomorphic on $\mathbb{D}$ and maps $\mathbb{D}$ univalently onto a simply connected domain $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}$. Let $F:\Omega\to\mathbb{D}$ denote the inverse map of $f$, so that $F$ is conformal on $\Omega$ with $F'$ its complex derivative. Consider the intersection of $\Omega$ with the real axis $\mathbb{R}$, which is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$, and the integral
$$ I_p(\Omega) \;=\; \int_{\Omega\cap\mathbb{R}} |F'(x)|^p\, dx. $$
It is known that $I_1(\Omega)$ is finite, with a bound independent of $f$ (Hayman–Wu theorem), and that $I_2(\Omega)$ can be infinite (for instance for slit disks of suitable radius).

Question: Is it true that for every such univalent $f$ and every $p$ with $1\le p<2$,
$$ \int_{\Omega\cap\mathbb{R}} |F'(x)|^p\, dx \;<\; \infty\, ? $$
status_search_result: Searches for the $L^p$ extension of the Hayman–Wu theorem (finiteness of $\int_{\Omega\cap\mathbb{R}}|F'|^p$ for $1\le p<2$) returned only the classical Hayman–Wu theorem ($p=1$) and refinements of its sharp constant by Øyma, Rohde, and Brown Flinn. No source confirming or refuting the $1<p<2$ case was located, so the current status appears unresolved from available evidence.

Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ denote the open unit disk. A function $f$ holomorphic in $\mathbb{D}$ is called $p$-valent in $\mathbb{D}$ (where $p$ is a positive integer) if $f$ takes no value more than $p$ times in $\mathbb{D}$ and takes some value exactly $p$ times.

Fix positive integers $p$ and $q$ with $1\le q\le p$, and let
$$f(z)=z^{q}+\sum_{n=q+1}^{\infty}a_{n}z^{n}$$
be $p$-valent in $\mathbb{D}$. Suppose $f$ has exactly $s$ zeros (counted with multiplicity) $\beta_{1},\beta_{2},\dots,\beta_{s}$ in $\mathbb{D}\setminus\{0\}$, so that $0<|\beta_k|<1$ for each $k$, and assume $t:=p-q-s\ge 0$.

Define the comparison function
$$F(z)=\frac{z^{q}}{(1-z)^{2q+2s}}\Big(1+\frac{z}{1-z}\Big)^{2t}\prod_{k=1}^{s}\bigl(1+|\beta_{k}|z\bigr)\bigl(1+|\beta_{k}|^{-1}z\bigr)\cdot\prod_{k=1}^{s}|\beta_k|,$$
written so that
$$F(z)=z+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}A_{n}z^{n}.$$

Prove or disprove: under the above hypotheses,
$$|a_{n}|\le |A_{n}|\quad\text{for every } n\ge q+1.$$
status_search_result: Goodman's conjecture (1948) on coefficient bounds for p-valent functions in terms of their zeros remains open in general. It has been verified in special cases, including when t=0 and f is p-valent starlike with respect to the origin, for p-valent typically-real functions, and for certain generalizations of convex-in-one-direction univalent classes, but the full conjecture is still unresolved.

there exist $f,g\in S$ for which both $F$ and $G$ have infinite valence in $\mathbb{D}$.

self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk. For a function $g$ analytic in $\mathbb{D}$, the valence of $g$ is defined as
$$v(g) = \sup_{w \in \mathbb{C}} \#\{z \in \mathbb{D} : g(z) = w\} \in \{1, 2, 3, \dots\} \cup \{\infty\}.$$
A sequence $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of positive integers (allowing the value $\infty$) is called a valence sequence if there exists a function $f$ analytic in $\mathbb{D}$ such that, for every $n \geq 1$, the $n$-th derivative $f^{(n)}$ has valence $v_n$ in $\mathbb{D}$, i.e. $v(f^{(n)}) = v_n$ for all $n \geq 1$.

Problem: Find non-trivial necessary conditions on a sequence $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ for it to be a valence sequence, and find non-trivial sufficient conditions on $\{v_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ that guarantee it is a valence sequence. Ideally, characterize valence sequences completely.
status_search_result: A web search did not turn up any modern results that fully characterize valence sequences of derivatives of analytic functions on the unit disk, nor any explicit resolution of this problem. Some partial results due to Goodman exist, but no definitive solution was located.

Let $\mathcal{S}_H$ denote the class of complex-valued harmonic functions $f = h + \overline{g}$ on the unit disk $\mathbb{D} = \{z\in\mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ that are univalent and sense-preserving, normalized so that $h(0) = g(0) = 0$ and $h'(0) = 1$. $$h(z) = z + \sum_{n\ge 2} a_n z^n, \qquad g(z) = \sum_{n\ge 1} b_n z^n.$$

It is known that for every $f\in\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ one has $\{w : |w| < 1/16\} \subset f(\mathbb{D})$, and that the function
$$k_0(z) = \mathrm{Re}\!\left(\frac{z + \tfrac{1}{3}z^3}{(1-z)^3}\right) + i\,\mathrm{Im}\!\left(\frac{z}{(1-z)^2}\right)$$
belongs to $\mathcal{S}_H^{\,0}$ and maps $\mathbb{D}$ onto the plane slit along the real axis from $-1/6$ to $-\infty$.

(b) Determine the value of
$$\alpha := \sup\{|a_2| : f \in \mathcal{S}_H\}.$$

(It is known that the Koebe constant $d$ for $\mathcal{S}_H$ satisfies $d \ge 1/(2\alpha)$, and the best known bound is $\alpha < 57.05$.)

original_question: Let Γ be a rectifiable curve, and let E be a subset of Γ having zero length. If Ω is any simply-connected domain and z ∈ Ω, is it true that the harmonic measure satisfies the equation ω(z, E, Ω) = 0? (B. Øksendal; R. Kaufman and J.-M. G. Wu; communicated by D. Hamilton)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb{C}$ be a rectifiable curve, and let $E\subset\Gamma$ be a Borel subset with one-dimensional Hausdorff measure (length) zero. Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}$ be any simply connected domain (with $E$ contained in the boundary or in $\overline{\Omega}$ in the relevant boundary sense), and let $z\in\Omega$. Denote by $\omega(z,\,\cdot\,,\Omega)$ the harmonic measure on $\partial\Omega$ from the point $z$. Is it always true that
$$\omega(z,E,\Omega)=0?$$
Equivalently: is harmonic measure on a simply connected domain absolutely continuous with respect to arclength on every rectifiable curve meeting its boundary?
status_search_result: The conjecture (due to Øksendal) was established affirmatively for simply connected planar domains by Bishop, Carleson, Garnett, and Jones in "Harmonic measures supported on curves" (Pacific J. Math., 1989), and is also presented in C. Bishop's "Harmonic measure and arclength" (Annals of Math., 1990): for a rectifiable curve $\Gamma$ and a simply connected domain $\Omega$, harmonic measure restricted to $\Gamma$ is absolutely continuous with respect to arclength, so subsets of zero length have zero harmonic measure.

original_question: Let G be a domain in C that contains the origin 0 and is axially- symmetric with respect to the real axis, that is, if a point z ∈ G then the line segment with endpoints z and z̄ also lies in G. (In particular it follows that G is simply- connected.) For t > 0, let Gt and G′t be the components of the domains {z : z ∈ G, Im z < t} and {z : z ∈ G, Re z < t} containing 0. Let ωt and ωt′ denote the harmonic measure at 0 of the sets ∂Gt ∩ {Im z = t} and ∂G′t ∩ {Re z = t} with respect to the domains Gt and G′t respectively. Now let D1 and D2 be two domains in C of this type, and use for each the notation just described. Then: (a) If ωt (D1 ) ≡ ωt (D2 ) for each t > 0, is it true that D1 = D2 ? (b) If ωt′ (D1 ) ≡ ωt′ (D2 ) for each t > 0, is it true that D1 = D2 ? (c) If both (a) and (b) fail, is it true that D1 = D2 if ωt (D1 ) ≡ ωt (D2 ) for each t > 0 and ωt′ (D1 ) ≡ ωt′ (D2 ) for each t > 0? If the answer to (a) or (b) is ‘yes’, in that case, how few t’s does one need for the con- clusion to hold? (For example, infinitely many t’s such that {Im z = t} or {Re z = t} meet the domains? Or do the t’s need to be dense?) If the answer to (a), (b) or (c) is ‘yes’, in that case can one replace ‘axially-symmetric’ by ‘simply-connected’, or perhaps drop this requirement completely? (D. A. Brannan)
self_contained_problem:
Let $G \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a domain containing the origin $0$ that is axially symmetric with respect to the real axis: whenever $z \in G$, the closed line segment from $z$ to its complex conjugate $\bar z$ also lies in $G$ (in particular, $G$ is simply connected). For each $t > 0$, define
- $G_t$ to be the connected component containing $0$ of $\{z \in G : \operatorname{Im} z < t\}$,
- $G'_t$ to be the connected component containing $0$ of $\{z \in G : \operatorname{Re} z < t\}$.

Let $\omega_t(G)$ denote the harmonic measure, evaluated at $0$, of $\partial G_t \cap \{\operatorname{Im} z = t\}$ relative to the domain $G_t$, and let $\omega'_t(G)$ denote the harmonic measure, evaluated at $0$, of $\partial G'_t \cap \{\operatorname{Re} z = t\}$ relative to the domain $G'_t$.

Now suppose $D_1$ and $D_2$ are two such axially symmetric domains. Investigate the following:

(a) If $\omega_t(D_1) = \omega_t(D_2)$ for every $t > 0$, must $D_1 = D_2$?

(b) If $\omega'_t(D_1) = \omega'_t(D_2)$ for every $t > 0$, must $D_1 = D_2$?

$$\sum_{n=0}^{\infty} |a_n|^2 = \infty.$$
Define the random analytic function on the open unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ by
$$F(z) = \sum_{n=0}^{\infty} \varepsilon_n a_n z^n.$$
(It is known that $F$ is almost surely an analytic function on $\mathbb{D}$ that is unbounded.) Determine, in terms of the sequence $(a_n)$, whether the following hold:

(a) With probability one, the image $F(\mathbb{D})$ is dense in $\mathbb{C}$.

(b) With probability one, $F(\mathbb{D}) = \mathbb{C}$.

(c) For each fixed $w_0 \in \mathbb{C}$, with probability one $w_0 \in F(\mathbb{D})$.

In particular, characterize the sequences $(a_n)$ for which (a), (b), and (c) hold. (As a benchmark, when $a_n = n^{\lambda}$, statement (b) holds for $\lambda > 1/2$ and statement (a) holds for $-1/2 < \lambda < 1/2$.)
status_search_result: The problem has seen substantial progress. Offord (1987, Annals of Probability) proved that a Gaussian Taylor series with $\sum|a_n|^2=\infty$ almost surely takes every complex value with at most one exception, addressing Kahane's question in the Gaussian case. More recently (arXiv:2403.19380, 2024), it was shown via a branching-process method that any unbounded random Taylor series with rotationally invariant coefficients has a.s. dense image, and that for complex Gaussian coefficients with sufficiently regular variances the image is a.s. all of $\mathbb{C}$. The full characterization for the Rademacher (random sign) case as posed remains not completely resolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Is it possible to express each K-quasiconformal map in 3-space as the composition of two quasiconformal maps with maximal dilatation less than K? The corresponding plane result is true. (F. W. Gehring)
self_contained_problem:
Let $K \geq 1$. A homeomorphism $f \colon \Omega \to \Omega'$ between domains in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is called $K$-quasiconformal if $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{1,n}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its dilatation
$$ K(x,f) = \frac{\max_{|h|=1}|Df(x)h|^n}{|\det Df(x)|} $$
satisfies $K(x,f) \leq K$ for almost every $x \in \Omega$ (equivalently, the maximal dilatation of $f$ is at most $K$). The composition of a $K_1$-quasiconformal map and a $K_2$-quasiconformal map is $K_1 K_2$-quasiconformal.

It is known that in dimension $n=2$, every $K$-quasiconformal map of a planar domain can be written as the composition $f = g \circ h$ of two quasiconformal maps $g$ and $h$ whose maximal dilatations are both strictly less than $K$.

Question: Does the analogous statement hold in dimension $n=3$? That is, can every $K$-quasiconformal homeomorphism between domains in $\mathbb{R}^3$ be expressed as a composition of two quasiconformal homeomorphisms each having maximal dilatation strictly less than $K$?

Standard references on quasiconformal mappings in space (Gehring, Väisälä, Heinonen) discuss the multiplicativity of dilatation under composition and the planar case, but no source found confirms a positive or negative answer in dimension three.

original_question: It was proved by Boyarskiı̆ [111] that the partial derivatives of a plane K-quasiconformal mapping are locally L-integrable for 2 ≤ p < 2 + c, where c = c(K) > 0. self_contained_problem:
Let $K \geq 1$. A homeomorphism $f: \Omega \to \Omega'$ between planar domains $\Omega, \Omega' \subset \mathbb{C}$ is called $K$-quasiconformal if $f$ belongs to the Sobolev space $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and its complex partial derivatives satisfy the Beltrami inequality
$$|\partial_{\bar z} f(z)| \leq \frac{K-1}{K+1}\, |\partial_z f(z)| \quad \text{for almost every } z \in \Omega.$$
It is known (Bojarski) that there exists a constant $c = c(K) > 0$ such that the partial derivatives $\partial_z f$ and $\partial_{\bar z} f$ belong to $L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every $p$ with $2 \leq p < 2 + c$.

Prove that one may take 
$$c(K) = \frac{2}{K-1},$$
i.e., that for every $K$-quasiconformal mapping $f$ defined on a planar domain $\Omega$, the partial derivatives of $f$ belong to $L^p_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ for every $p$ with
$$2 \leq p < \frac{2K}{K-1}.$$
The example $f(z) = z\, |z|^{1/K - 1}$ shows that the exponent $\frac{2K}{K-1}$ cannot in general be replaced by anything larger, so such a result would be sharp.
status_search_result: This is Gehring's sharp higher integrability conjecture for planar K-quasiconformal mappings. It was solved by Kari Astala in his 1994 Acta Mathematica paper "Area distortion of quasiconformal mappings", which established the sharp local integrability exponent p(K) = 2K/(K-1) for the derivatives of planar K-quasiconformal maps.

$$b_n=\sum_{\nu=1}^{n}a_\nu,\qquad c_n=\sum_{\nu=1}^{n}b_\nu.$$
It is known that $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(a_n/c_n)^{\alpha}<\infty$ whenever $\alpha>\tfrac{1}{2}$.

Characterize the class of functions $f:(0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ for which the implication
$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f(n^2)<\infty\ \Longrightarrow\ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} f(c_n/a_n)<\infty$$
holds for every admissible sequence $(a_n)$ as above. In particular, determine whether, under suitable smoothness/monotonicity conditions on $f$ (for example, an analogue of the Borwein-type hypothesis that $xf(x)$ be positive and non-increasing on $[a,\infty)$ for some $a>0$), the convergence of $\sum f(n^2)$ implies the convergence of $\sum f(c_n/a_n)$.

(For comparison, it is known that if $xf(x)$ is positive and non-increasing for $x\ge a>0$ and $\sum f(n)<\infty$, then $\sum f(c_n/b_n)<\infty$.)

self_contained_problem:
Let $N\ge 2$ be an integer and let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\ldots,\lambda_N$ be pairwise distinct real numbers. Define the trigonometric exponential sum
$$P(\theta)=\sum_{n=1}^{N} e^{i\lambda_n \theta},\qquad \theta\in\mathbb{R},$$
and set
$$\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)=\inf_{\theta\in\mathbb{R}}|P(\theta)|.$$
A direct computation gives $|P(\theta)|^2=N+2\sum_{m\ne n}\cos((\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\theta)$, and an averaging argument (using that the mean value of $\cos((\lambda_m-\lambda_n)\theta)$ is $0$) yields the bound
$$\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)\le (N-1)^{1/2}.$$
Determine the best possible upper bound for $\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N)$ as $\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N$ range over all $N$-tuples of distinct real numbers; that is, find
$$M(N)=\sup\bigl\{\mu(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N):\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_N\in\mathbb{R}\text{ distinct}\bigr\},$$
and in particular decide whether $M(N)=(N-1)^{1/2}$ or whether a smaller upper bound holds. The corresponding question when all $\lambda_n$ are rational reduces to bounding $\inf_\theta|Q(\theta)|$ for trigonometric polynomials $Q$ with $0/1$ coefficients.

original_question: (Subadditivity problem for analytic capacity) Prove or disprove the existence of a constant M such that γ(K1 ∪ K2 ) ≤ M {γ(K1 ) + γ(K2 )} for all compact sets K1 , K2 in C. Even the case where γ(K2 ) = 0 is open. For background, see Garnett [290]. (J. Korevaar)
self_contained_problem:
For a compact set $K \subset \mathbb{C}$, the analytic capacity of $K$ is defined by
$$\gamma(K) = \sup\{|f'(\infty)| : f : \mathbb{C}_\infty \setminus K \to \mathbb{C} \text{ is holomorphic, } \|f\|_\infty \le 1\},$$
where $f'(\infty) = \lim_{z\to\infty} z(f(z) - f(\infty))$.

Determine whether there exists an absolute constant $M > 0$ such that
$$\gamma(K_1 \cup K_2) \le M\bigl(\gamma(K_1) + \gamma(K_2)\bigr)$$
for every pair of compact sets $K_1, K_2 \subset \mathbb{C}$ (semiadditivity of analytic capacity). The special case in which $\gamma(K_2) = 0$ should also be addressed.
status_search_result: The semiadditivity of analytic capacity was proved by Xavier Tolsa (Acta Math. 190 (2003), 105–149), establishing the existence of an absolute constant M such that γ(K₁ ∪ K₂) ≤ M(γ(K₁) + γ(K₂)) for all compact K₁, K₂ ⊂ ℂ. The special case γ(K₂)=0 (countable semiadditivity / Painlevé's problem) is also a consequence of Tolsa's work.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: A bounded simply-connected domain D is said to be conformally rigid if there is some ε > 0 such that if f is a conformal self-map of D satisfying |f (z) − z| < ε, then f (z) ≡ z. Clearly, if each prime end of D is a singleton, then D is not conformally rigid. Show the converse. (P. M. Gauthier)
self_contained_problem:
Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}$ be a bounded simply-connected domain. Call $D$ **conformally rigid** if there exists $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every conformal (i.e. holomorphic and injective) self-map $f \colon D \to D$ satisfying $\sup_{z \in D} |f(z) - z| < \varepsilon$ must be the identity, $f(z) \equiv z$.

Recall the notion of prime ends in the sense of Carathéodory: if $\varphi \colon \mathbb{D} \to D$ is a Riemann map from the open unit disk onto $D$, the prime ends of $D$ are equivalence classes of chains of cross-cuts and correspond bijectively to points of $\partial \mathbb{D}$. The **impression** of a prime end $p$ is the set of all limit points in $\overline{D}$ of $\varphi(z_n)$ for sequences $z_n \in \mathbb{D}$ converging to the corresponding boundary point. We say a prime end is a *singleton* when its impression consists of a single point.

It is known that if every prime end of $D$ has singleton impression, then $D$ is not conformally rigid. Prove the converse: if $D$ has at least one prime end whose impression is not a singleton, then $D$ is conformally rigid; equivalently, $D$ is conformally rigid if and only if not every prime end of $D$ is a singleton.

original_question: Let D be the unit disc cut along p radial slits from the outer boundary, all of the same given length. Let u be the harmonic measure of {|z| = 1} in D. Find the configuration of slits which makes u(0) minimal, when p is fixed. (A. A. Gonchar, communicated by M. Essén)
self_contained_problem:
Fix an integer $p\ge 1$ and a length $\ell\in(0,1)$. For each choice of angles $\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p\in[0,2\pi)$, let
$$D=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}\setminus\bigcup_{k=1}^{p}\{re^{i\theta_k}:1-\ell\le r\le 1\},$$
i.e. the open unit disc with $p$ radial slits of common length $\ell$ removed, each emanating inward from the outer boundary $\{|z|=1\}$. Let $u$ be the bounded harmonic function on $D$ with boundary values $1$ on the part of $\partial D$ lying on $\{|z|=1\}$ (the "outer" arcs not removed) and $0$ on the two sides of every radial slit; equivalently, $u(z)=\omega(z,\{|\zeta|=1\}\cap\partial D,D)$ is the harmonic measure of the circular boundary arcs from the point $z$.

Determine the configuration $(\theta_1,\dots,\theta_p)$ that minimizes $u(0)$.
status_search_result: The problem, posed by Gonchar, was resolved by V. N. Dubinin using his method of dissymmetrization: among all configurations of $p$ radial slits of equal length emanating from the unit circle, the symmetric (equally spaced) configuration minimizes the harmonic measure of the circle at the origin. Baernstein later extended this to general compact radial sets.

original_question: A domain D ⊆ Rn is said to be linearly accessible, if each point in the complement of D can be joined to ∞ by a ray which does not meet D. self_contained_problem:
A domain $D \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ (with $n \geq 2$) is called linearly accessible if for every point $y \in \mathbb{R}^n \setminus D$ there exists a ray emanating from $y$ and going to $\infty$ that does not meet $D$. Fix $x_0 \in D$ and let $g(\,\cdot\,, x_0)$ denote the Green's function of $D$ with pole at $x_0$ (i.e., the function harmonic in $D \setminus \{x_0\}$ that vanishes on $\partial D$ in the appropriate sense, with the standard fundamental-solution singularity at $x_0$). 

Assume $D$ is a linearly accessible domain. Prove or disprove: for every $t \in (0, \infty)$, the superlevel set 
$$\{x \in D : g(x, x_0) > t\}$$
is itself a linearly accessible domain. (The conclusion is known to hold when $n = 2$; the question concerns general $n \geq 3$.)

Let $D \subset \mathbb{C}^n$, $n > 1$, be a bounded strictly pseudo-convex domain with smooth boundary. original_question: It is known that any quasi-conformal homeomorphism of B n = {x : x ∈ Rn , |x| < 1} onto a Jordan domain D in Rn can be extended to a homeomorphism of B n onto D. If ∂D is rectifiable (in the sense that Λn−1 (∂D) < ∞), is f |∂B n absolutely continuous (in the sense that Λn−1 f (E) = 0 for every set E in ∂B n with |E| = 0)? One can also ask the analogous question about f −1 . When n = 2, the answer to both questions is ‘yes’ for conformal mappings, but ‘no’ for quasi-conformal mappings. When n = 3, Gehring [299] has proved that, if in addition the function f has a quasi-conformal extension to Rn , then f |∂B n is absolutely continuous; but, even in this special case, it is not known if f −1 |∂D is absolutely continuous. (A. Baernstein II)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 2$ and let $B^n = \{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : |x| < 1\}$ be the open unit ball, with boundary $\partial B^n = S^{n-1}$. Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a Jordan domain (a domain whose boundary $\partial D$ is homeomorphic to $S^{n-1}$). Suppose $f : B^n \to D$ is a quasi-conformal homeomorphism; it is known that $f$ extends to a homeomorphism $\overline{B^n} \to \overline{D}$, still denoted $f$. Let $\Lambda^{n-1}$ denote $(n-1)$-dimensional Hausdorff measure, and let $|\cdot|$ denote the surface measure on $\partial B^n$. Assume that $\partial D$ is rectifiable in the sense that $\Lambda^{n-1}(\partial D) < \infty$.

(a) Is $f|_{\partial B^n}$ absolutely continuous, in the sense that $\Lambda^{n-1}(f(E)) = 0$ for every set $E \subset \partial B^n$ with $|E| = 0$?

(b) Is $f^{-1}|_{\partial D}$ absolutely continuous, in the analogous sense?

(c) For $n = 3$, suppose in addition that $f$ admits a quasi-conformal extension to all of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Is $f^{-1}|_{\partial D}$ absolutely continuous in this case?

Determine the answers to (a), (b), and (c).
status_search_result: Heinonen ("The boundary absolute continuity of quasiconformal mappings (II)", Rev. Mat. Iberoamericana 12 (1996), 697–725) constructed, for each n ≥ 3, examples of quasi-conformal maps of B^n onto Jordan domains with (n−1)-rectifiable boundary whose boundary values are not absolutely continuous, settling parts (a) and (b) negatively in general. For n = 3 with a global quasi-conformal extension, Gehring's result gives absolute continuity of f|_{∂B^n}, but the question whether f^{-1}|_{∂D} is absolutely continuous in this setting does not appear to be definitively resolved in the literature located.

original_question: Let W be a hyperbolic Riemann surface, Gω the Green’s function with pole ω ∈ W, and Γ = {[γn ]} the fundamental group. Let Γ̃ be the subgroup of equivalence classes [γ] such that, for every ω ∈ W, the harmonic conjugate G∗ω of Gω changes by an integral multiple of 2π on a representative path in [γ]. Certainly [Γ, Γ] ⊳ Γ̃ ⊳ Γ. Is it true that, if [Γ, Γ] 6= Γ̃, then W is necessarily of the form V \ A where V is a hyperbolic surface and A 6= ∅ is a relatively closed subset of zero logarithmic capacity? The conjecture is true if Γ̃ = Γ and V is the unit disc; and it is false if [Γ, Γ] = Γ̃. (The conjecture arises from work in [735].) (K. Stephenson)
self_contained_problem:
Let $W$ be a hyperbolic Riemann surface, and for each $\omega \in W$ let $G_\omega : W \setminus \{\omega\} \to (0,\infty)$ denote the Green's function of $W$ with pole at $\omega$, and let $G_\omega^*$ denote a (locally defined, multi-valued) harmonic conjugate of $G_\omega$. Let $\Gamma$ denote the fundamental group of $W$, with elements written as homotopy classes $[\gamma]$ of closed loops. Define the subgroup
$$\widetilde{\Gamma} = \{[\gamma] \in \Gamma : \text{for every } \omega \in W, \text{ the period of } G_\omega^* \text{ along any representative of } [\gamma] \text{ is an integer multiple of } 2\pi\}.$$
Then $\widetilde{\Gamma}$ is a normal subgroup of $\Gamma$ containing the commutator subgroup $[\Gamma,\Gamma]$, so that
$$[\Gamma,\Gamma] \trianglelefteq \widetilde{\Gamma} \trianglelefteq \Gamma.$$
Conjecture: If $[\Gamma,\Gamma] \neq \widetilde{\Gamma}$, then $W$ is conformally equivalent to $V \setminus A$, where $V$ is a hyperbolic Riemann surface and $A \subset V$ is a non-empty relatively closed subset of zero logarithmic capacity. Decide whether this conjecture holds in general. (It is known to be true in the special case $\widetilde{\Gamma} = \Gamma$ with $V$ the unit disc, and it is known to fail when $[\Gamma,\Gamma] = \widetilde{\Gamma}$.)
