paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let V be the zero set of some analytic function in a strictly pseudo- convex domain Ω in C2 . If V has finite area inside Ω, is it necessarily true that V is the zero set of some bounded analytic function on Ω? Bo Berndttson (no citation) has shown that the answer is ‘yes’ when Ω is the ball; and easy examples show that the answer is ‘no’ for strictly pseudo-convex domains in C when n > 2. Skoda ([719], [720]) and independently Henkin [433] have shown (under some cohomology condition on Ω) for all n that V is the zero set of a function of Nevanlinna class only if V satisfies the Blaschke condition. (R. Zeinstra)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{C}^2$ be a strictly pseudoconvex domain (a bounded domain admitting a $C^2$ defining function $\rho$ with $\Omega = \{\rho < 0\}$, $d\rho \neq 0$ on $\partial\Omega$, and the Levi form of $\rho$ strictly positive on the complex tangent space at every boundary point). Let $f$ be a holomorphic function on $\Omega$, not identically zero, and let $V = \{z \in \Omega : f(z) = 0\}$ be its zero set, regarded as a (pure $1$-dimensional) analytic subvariety of $\Omega$. Assume that $V$ has finite $2$-dimensional Hausdorff area inside $\Omega$, i.e.
$$\mathrm{Area}(V) = \int_{V_{\mathrm{reg}}} dA < \infty,$$
where $dA$ is the induced Euclidean area measure on the regular part of $V$.

Question: Must there exist a bounded holomorphic function $g \in H^\infty(\Omega)$, not identically zero, whose zero set (with multiplicities) equals $V$?

It is known that the answer is affirmative when $\Omega$ is the unit ball of $\mathbb{C}^2$, and that the corresponding statement fails in strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^n$ for $n > 2$. Decide whether the affirmative answer extends to all strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$.

status_search_result: A web search did not surface a definitive resolution of the question for general strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$. The affirmative answer for the unit ball in $\mathbb{C}^2$ (Berndtsson) and the failure for $n>2$ are well documented, but no source clearly establishes (or refutes) the result for arbitrary strictly pseudoconvex domains in $\mathbb{C}^2$. Status appears unknown based on available sources.

We call a function f : U ⊆ V → A a left analytic function if k X ∂f ej (x) = 0 ∂xj j=1 for all x ∈ U . Ryan [692] has shown that there is a generalised Cauchy integral formula Z k X f (x0 ) = G(x, x0 ) (−1)j ej dx̂j f (x), ∂M j=1 with real-analytic kernel G(x, x0 ), where M is an arbitrary, compact real n-dimensional manifold lying in U ; and x0 ∈ M̊ if and only if there are elements {pj }kj=1 ⊆ A satisfying the relation pj el + pl ej = 2δjl . Let $A$ be an associative algebra over $\mathbb{R}$ with identity $1$ and a countable basis, and let $V \subseteq A$ be a finite-dimensional real subspace with basis $\{e_1,\dots,e_k\}$. Define the Dirac-type differential operator
$$D = \sum_{j=1}^{k} e_j \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}$$
acting on differentiable functions $f : U \to A$ defined on open sets $U \subseteq V$ (with coordinates $x = \sum_j x_j e_j$). A function $f : U \to A$ is called left analytic if $Df(x) = 0$ for every $x \in U$.

It is known that there exists a generalized Cauchy integral formula
$$f(x_0) = \int_{\partial M} G(x, x_0) \sum_{j=1}^{k} (-1)^j e_j \, d\hat x_j \, f(x),$$
valid for every left analytic $f$, where $M \subset U$ is an arbitrary compact real $n$-dimensional manifold (with boundary), $x_0 \in \mathring{M}$, $d\hat x_j = dx_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge \widehat{dx_j} \wedge \cdots \wedge dx_k$, and $G(x,x_0)$ is a real-analytic $A$-valued kernel; this holds if and only if there exist elements $\{p_1,\dots,p_k\} \subseteq A$ satisfying
$$p_j e_l + p_l e_j = 2\delta_{jl} \quad (1 \le j,l \le k).$$

(a) Does the same representation formula remain valid when the kernel $G(x,x_0)$ is only assumed to be of class $C^1$ rather than real-analytic?

(b) Formulate and establish the analogue of this generalized Cauchy integral formula in the case where the algebra $A$ is allowed to be non-associative.

original_question: Given a domain of holomorphy Ω ⊆ Cn , n ≥ 2, what conditions are required on Ω to admit an analytic function p : Ω → C which cannot be analytically extended beyond the boundary of Ω, and satisfies the complex version n X ∂2 p(z) = 0 ∂zj2 k=1 of Laplace’s equation? (J. Ryan)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{C}^n$ with $n \geq 2$ be a domain of holomorphy, that is, an open connected set for which there exists a holomorphic function on $\Omega$ that cannot be holomorphically continued to any strictly larger connected open set. A holomorphic function $p : \Omega \to \mathbb{C}$ is called complex harmonic if it satisfies the complex Laplace equation
$$\sum_{j=1}^{n} \frac{\partial^2 p}{\partial z_j^2}(z) = 0 \quad \text{for all } z \in \Omega.$$

original_question: In their famous Acta paper [377], Hardy and Littlewood introduced the celebrated Hardy-Littlewood maximal function in connection with complex function theory. Let B be a convex compact symmetric body in Rn , normalised to have Euclidean volume 1. Let the Hardy-Littlewood maximal functions be Z  M f (x) = sup n |f (x + y)| dy t>0 t tB and Z  M̃ f (x) = sup kn |f (x + y)| dy . k∈Z 2 2k B (a) If B is the Euclidean ball in Rn , does there exist a constant C such that meas{x : M̃ f (x) > λ} ≤ Cλ−1 kf k1 for all λ > 0, with C independent of n? (b) If so, what is the answer to the same question for M f ? (c) In the case that n = 1, a conjecture of F. Sonia and the proposer is that the best constant in the inequality meas{x : M f (x) > λ} ≤ Cλ−1 kf k1 is C = 23 . Prove this. (d) Let 1 < p ≤ 32 . Can the best constant in the inequality kM f kp ≤ Cp kf kp be taken to be independent of n and the body B? Even if B = [− 21 , 12 ]n , can the constant be chosen independent of n? The following relevant facts are known. For (a) and (b), the best known constants are found in [729]. For (c), Sonia and the proposer have shown that the answer is ‘yes’ if 2 < p ≤ ∞; for B with suitably-curved boundary, the answer is ‘yes’ for 1 < p ≤ ∞; for the sphere, see [728]. (A. Carbery)
self_contained_problem:
Let $B \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a convex compact symmetric body normalised so that its Lebesgue measure equals $1$. Define the centered Hardy–Littlewood maximal function with respect to $B$ by
$$M f(x) = \sup_{t>0} \frac{1}{t^n}\int_{tB} |f(x+y)|\, dy,$$
and its dyadic analogue by
$$\widetilde{M} f(x) = \sup_{k\in\mathbb{Z}} \frac{1}{2^{kn}}\int_{2^k B} |f(x+y)|\, dy.$$

Answer the following questions.

(a) Suppose $B$ is the Euclidean unit ball (suitably normalised). Does there exist a finite constant $C$, independent of the dimension $n$, such that for every $f\in L^1(\mathbb{R}^n)$ and every $\lambda>0$,
$$\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n : \widetilde{M} f(x) > \lambda\}\bigr| \le \frac{C}{\lambda}\,\|f\|_1\;?$$

(b) Under the same hypothesis on $B$, does the analogous weak-type $(1,1)$ inequality
$$\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n : M f(x) > \lambda\}\bigr| \le \frac{C}{\lambda}\,\|f\|_1$$
hold with a constant $C$ independent of $n$?

(c) For $n=1$ (so $B$ is a centered interval), prove that the best constant $C$ in the weak-type $(1,1)$ inequality
$$\bigl|\{x\in\mathbb{R} : M f(x) > \lambda\}\bigr| \le \frac{C}{\lambda}\,\|f\|_1$$
equals $\tfrac{3}{2}$.

(d) For $1 < p \le \tfrac{3}{2}$, can the best constant $C_p$ in
$$\|M f\|_p \le C_p \|f\|_p$$
be chosen independent of $n$ and of the convex symmetric body $B$? In particular, can it be chosen independent of $n$ when $B = [-\tfrac{1}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}]^n$?
status_search_result: Part (a) (dimension-free weak-(1,1) bound for the dyadic maximal function over Euclidean balls) is known to hold (Stein–Strömberg type results). Part (c) — the conjecture that the best weak-(1,1) constant on $\mathbb{R}$ equals $3/2$ — was disproved by Aldaz (1998), who showed the constant is strictly greater than $3/2$; the exact value was further studied by Melas. For cubes, Aldaz (Annals 2011) proved that the weak-type $(1,1)$ constants grow to infinity with the dimension, settling the cube version of (b)/(d) negatively for weak type. The strong-type dimension-free question for general convex symmetric bodies (parts (b) and (d) for $p>1$) remains a long-standing open problem; only partial progress is known (Bourgain, Carbery, Müller, and more recent work).

original_question: Prove or disprove the following statement: If K is a compact subset of C with continuous analytic capacity α(K) = 0, then α(E \ K) = α(E) for all compact subsets E of C. An interesting special case is when K is a C 1 -arc. The case when K is a C 1+ε -arc has already been settled. (A. G. O’Farrell)
self_contained_problem:
For a compact set $K\subset\mathbb{C}$, let $\alpha(K)$ denote the continuous analytic capacity of $K$, defined by
$$\alpha(K)=\sup\{|f'(\infty)|:f\in C(\mathbb{C}),\ f\ \text{is holomorphic on}\ \mathbb{C}\setminus K,\ |f|\le 1\ \text{on}\ \mathbb{C}\},$$
where $f'(\infty)=\lim_{z\to\infty} z(f(z)-f(\infty))$.

Prove or disprove: if $K\subset\mathbb{C}$ is compact and $\alpha(K)=0$, then for every compact set $E\subset\mathbb{C}$,
$$\alpha(E\setminus K)=\alpha(E).$$

A case of particular interest is when $K$ is a $C^1$-arc. (The corresponding statement is known when $K$ is a $C^{1+\varepsilon}$-arc for some $\varepsilon>0$.)

original_question: Let f be an inner function, with f (0) = 0; then f induces an ergodic (Lebesgue-) measure-preserving map of the circle onto itself. What is the entropy, h(f ), of f ? It is conjectured that h(f ) < ∞ if and only if f ′ belongs to the Nevanlinna class; and that, in that case, then Z 2π h(f ) = log f ′ (eiθ ) dθ. 2π 0 (See [266] and [657].) (J. L. Fernandez)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|<1\}$ be the open unit disc and let $\mathbb{T}=\partial\mathbb{D}$ with normalized Lebesgue measure $dm(\theta)=d\theta/(2\pi)$. A bounded holomorphic function $f:\mathbb{D}\to\mathbb{D}$ is called inner if its radial boundary values $f^*(e^{i\theta})=\lim_{r\to 1^-}f(re^{i\theta})$ satisfy $|f^*(e^{i\theta})|=1$ for almost every $\theta$. Then $f^*$ induces a Lebesgue measure-preserving ergodic transformation of $\mathbb{T}$, and one may consider its measure-theoretic (Kolmogorov–Sinai) entropy $h(f)$.

The Nevanlinna class $N(\mathbb{D})$ consists of holomorphic functions $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$ for which 
$$\sup_{0<r<1}\int_0^{2\pi}\log^+|g(re^{i\theta})|\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}<\infty.$$

Prove or disprove the following two assertions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item $h(f)<\infty$ if and only if $f'\in N(\mathbb{D})$.
\item Whenever $h(f)<\infty$, one has
$$h(f)=\int_0^{2\pi}\log\bigl|f'(e^{i\theta})\bigr|\,\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}.$$
\end{enumerate}

Let $L=\{L_k\}_{k=0}^{\infty}$ be a non-negative increasing sequence satisfying
$$\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} L_k r^k < \infty \quad \text{for every } 0<r<1.$$
For functions $f(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} a_k z^k$ and $P(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{n} b_k z^k$ analytic in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z:|z|<1\}$, denote by
$$(P*f)(z) = \sum_{k=0}^{n} a_k b_k z^k$$
the Hadamard (coefficient-wise) product. For an analytic function $g$ on $\mathbb{D}$, write $\|g\|_\infty = \sup_{z\in\mathbb{D}} |g(z)|$.

Define the space $P_L$ to consist of all functions $f$ analytic in $\mathbb{D}$ for which there exists a constant $A\geq 0$ such that, for every integer $n\geq 0$ and every polynomial $P_n$ of degree at most $n$,
$$\|P_n * f\|_\infty \leq A\, L_n\, \|P_n\|_\infty.$$
Equip $P_L$ with the norm $\|f\|_{P_L} = \inf\{A : \text{the above inequality holds}\}$, under which $P_L$ becomes a Banach space.

It is known that for $L_k\equiv 1$, the space $P_L$ coincides with the space of Cauchy–Stieltjes transforms, and for any convex sequence $\{L_k\}$ (e.g. $L_k=k$), the function $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} L_k z^k$ lies in the closed unit ball of $P_L$.

Problem: Determine the relationship between the spaces $P_L$ and the classical Hardy spaces $H^p$ for $0<p<1$. Specifically, identify, for given sequences $L$, inclusions, embeddings, or equivalences between $P_L$ and $H^p$ ($0<p<1$).

original_question: Let f be continuous on a compact subset K of C. If there exists a sequence {fn }∞ 2 1 of functions analytic near K for which gn → f uniformly on K, ∞ does there necessarily exist a sequence {hn }1 of functions analytic near K for which hn → f uniformly on K? Paramanov has proved this under the stronger hypothesis that f ∈ Lip ( 12 ); it is also true under the hypothesis that f ∈ W 1,p (p > 2). (A. G. O’Farrell)
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a compact subset of the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and let $f:K\to\mathbb{C}$ be a continuous function. Recall that a function $g$ defined on an open neighborhood $U$ of $K$ is said to be bianalytic on $U$ if $\bar\partial^{\,2} g \equiv 0$ on $U$, equivalently if $g(z)=a(z)+\bar z\, b(z)$ for some functions $a,b$ holomorphic on $U$; and $g$ is said to be analytic near $K$ if it is holomorphic on some open neighborhood of $K$.

Suppose there exists a sequence $\{f_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of functions, each bianalytic on some open neighborhood of $K$, such that $f_n \to f$ uniformly on $K$.

Question: Must there then exist a sequence $\{h_n\}_{n=1}^{\infty}$ of functions, each analytic (holomorphic) on some open neighborhood of $K$, such that $h_n \to f$ uniformly on $K$?

It is known that the answer is affirmative under the additional hypothesis that $f$ is Lipschitz of order $\tfrac12$ on $K$, and also under the hypothesis that $f \in W^{1,p}$ for some $p>2$. The problem is to decide whether the implication holds for arbitrary continuous $f$ with no additional regularity assumption.

paper_title: Initial boundary value problem for Korteweg-de Vries equation: a review and open problems
context_brief: Global well-posedness and blow-up for finite-interval KdV IBVP
original_question: For the Korteweg-de Vries initial-boundary value problem on a finite interval, with equation u_t + u_x + u_{xxx} + u u_x = 0 on 0 < x < L and t > 0, initial data u(x,0)=φ(x), and general boundary conditions B_k u = h, determine whether the problem is globally well-posed in the Sobolev space H^s(0,L) for some s ≥ 0. Equivalently, determine whether solutions can blow up in H^s(0,L) in finite time, and in particular whether one can prove a global a priori L^2(0,L) bound for all times.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Korteweg–de Vries initial-boundary value problem on a finite interval (0, L) with L > 0:
  u_t + u_x + u_{xxx} + u u_x = 0,   for 0 < x < L, t > 0,
  u(x, 0) = φ(x),   for 0 < x < L,
together with a set of (linear) boundary conditions of the form
  B_k u(t) = h_k(t),   k = 1, 2, 3,   t > 0,
where {B_k} is a triple of boundary operators (involving traces of u, u_x, u_{xx} at x = 0 and x = L) chosen so that the linearized problem is well-posed, and h_k are prescribed boundary data. Assume that the problem is locally well-posed in the Sobolev space H^s(0, L) for some s ≥ 0, with sufficiently smooth (or zero) boundary data h_k and initial data φ ∈ H^s(0, L) satisfying the natural compatibility conditions.

Question: Determine whether this initial-boundary value problem is globally well-posed in H^s(0, L) for some s ≥ 0; equivalently, decide whether every solution remains in H^s(0, L) for all t ≥ 0 or whether some solution can blow up in H^s(0, L) in finite time. In particular, establish (or disprove) a global a priori L^2 bound
  sup_{0 ≤ t < ∞} ‖u(·, t)‖_{L^2(0, L)} < ∞
for solutions of this IBVP, which would yield global well-posedness in H^s(0, L) for all s ≥ 0 in the locally well-posed range.
status_search_result: The problem is known to be locally well-posed in H^s(0,L) for many boundary configurations, and global well-posedness has been established for several specific classes of homogeneous/dissipative boundary conditions (e.g., Bona–Sun–Zhang and related works). However, for general boundary conditions, no global a priori L^2 estimate is known and the question of global well-posedness vs. finite-time blow-up remains open in the broader formulation.

context_brief: Subcritical low-regularity KdV IVP on the line
original_question: For the pure initial value problem for the Korteweg-de Vries equation on the whole line, u_t + u u_x + u_{xxx} = 0 with x,t ∈ R and initial data u(x,0)=φ(x), determine whether the problem is well-posed in H^s(R) for some s < -3/4. The paper notes well-posedness for s ≥ -3/4 and conditional ill-posedness below that threshold in the sense that the solution map is not uniformly continuous, but says the existence of a well-posed theory below s = -3/4 is still open.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the pure initial value problem for the Korteweg–de Vries equation on the real line:
  u_t + u u_x + u_{xxx} = 0,  (x,t) ∈ ℝ × ℝ,
  u(x,0) = φ(x),  x ∈ ℝ.

For s ∈ ℝ, let H^s(ℝ) denote the L^2-based Sobolev space of order s. It is known that this initial value problem is locally (and globally) well-posed in H^s(ℝ) for s ≥ −3/4, and that for s < −3/4 the data-to-solution map fails to be uniformly continuous on bounded sets of H^s(ℝ).

Question: Does there exist some s < −3/4 for which the initial value problem above admits a well-posed theory in H^s(ℝ) (in the sense of existence, uniqueness, and continuous dependence of the solution on the initial data, in a suitable sense)? Equivalently, determine the largest range of negative Sobolev exponents s for which a well-posed theory in H^s(ℝ) exists.
status_search_result: Killip and Vișan (Annals of Mathematics, 2019) proved that the KdV equation on the real line is globally well-posed in H^s(ℝ) for all s ≥ −1, using a new method based on commuting flows of the integrable hierarchy. This extends well-posedness well below the previous s = −3/4 threshold and resolves the question of well-posedness for some s < −3/4 in the affirmative. Moreover, H^{-1}(ℝ) is sharp within the H^s(ℝ) scale, since the data-to-solution map cannot be continuously extended below s = −1.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Are there general principles that determine which renormalization-group domain wall or conformal boundary state is selected from the set of possible interfaces or boundary states connecting the ultraviolet and infrared endpoints of a renormalization-group flow in boundary or defect conformal field theory?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a renormalization-group (RG) flow in d-dimensional quantum field theory connecting an ultraviolet (UV) conformal field theory CFT_UV to an infrared (IR) conformal field theory CFT_IR. To such a flow one can associate:

(a) An "RG domain wall" (or RG interface): a conformal interface in the d-dimensional product theory CFT_UV × \overline{CFT_IR} (equivalently, in CFT_UV on a half-space glued to CFT_IR on the complementary half-space) obtained by triggering the relevant deformation that drives the flow only on one side and flowing to the IR there.

(b) A conformal boundary state |B⟩ of the folded theory CFT_UV × \overline{CFT_IR}, which (by the folding trick) encodes the same data as the conformal interface.

In general, given fixed UV and IR conformal endpoints, the set of conformal interfaces / boundary states between them is large and not unique: many distinct conformal boundary conditions of CFT_UV × \overline{CFT_IR} exist, and only specific ones arise as RG domain walls of an actual flow.

Question. Formulate and establish general principles (intrinsic to the data of CFT_UV, CFT_IR, and the deformation) that single out, from the full set of conformal interfaces/boundary states between CFT_UV and CFT_IR, those that are realized as the RG domain wall(s) / RG boundary state(s) of the flow. In particular, identify a characterization (e.g., variational, entropic via the boundary g-theorem, algebraic via fusion with bulk/topological defects, or representation-theoretic) that, given any candidate conformal boundary state of CFT_UV × \overline{CFT_IR}, determines whether it corresponds to the RG flow under consideration.
category_tag: Boundary and defect CFT / RG domain walls
status_search_result: No general selection principle is known. Algebraic constructions of RG domain walls have been proposed in special cases (e.g., between successive two-dimensional Virasoro minimal models, including recent work on A_2^{(p)} minimal models in 2023), and these examples reproduce conformal-perturbation-theory mixing of UV operators. However, no overarching principle determining the RG-selected interface/boundary state for general UV–IR flows has been established; the question is still listed as open in surveys of boundary and defect CFT.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Do there exist monotonicity theorems for boundaries or defects in dimensions higher than two that generalize the two-dimensional g-theorem for boundary conformal field theories?
self_contained_problem:
Background. A boundary conformal field theory (bCFT) on a manifold with boundary is a unitary conformal field theory equipped with a conformal boundary condition. In two-dimensional bCFT, Affleck and Ludwig defined the boundary entropy g (the boundary g-function), the logarithm of the universal contribution of the boundary to the partition function on a strip; the g-theorem (proved by Friedan and Konechny) asserts that g is monotonically non-increasing along any unitary boundary renormalization group (RG) flow that preserves bulk conformal invariance, and is stationary only at boundary fixed points.

More generally, a conformal defect of dimension p in a D-dimensional CFT is a (D−p−1)-codimensional submanifold supporting a non-trivial conformal boundary condition for the ambient theory; a boundary corresponds to p = D−1.

Problem. For each pair of integers (p, D) with 1 ≤ p ≤ D−1 and (p, D) ≠ (1, 2), determine whether there exists a real-valued quantity C_{p,D}(\mathcal D), defined for every conformal defect \mathcal D of dimension p in a unitary D-dimensional CFT, such that:
(i) C_{p,D} is intrinsic to the defect (independent of the choice of bulk fixed point in any continuous family fixing \mathcal D);
(ii) C_{p,D}(\mathcal D_{UV}) ≥ C_{p,D}(\mathcal D_{IR}) for every unitary defect-localized RG flow connecting a UV defect fixed point \mathcal D_{UV} to an IR defect fixed point \mathcal D_{IR}, with equality only when the flow is trivial;
(iii) at conformal fixed points C_{p,D} reduces to a universal local quantity (e.g. a defect Weyl-anomaly coefficient, a sphere free energy, or a generalization of the boundary entropy).

In particular, for the boundary case p = D − 1 with D ≥ 3, exhibit such a monotone, or prove that no quantity satisfying (i)–(iii) exists.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed. Defect/boundary monotonicity theorems have been established in several cases: a defect a-theorem for 4-dimensional defects (Wang, 2021), a boundary/defect F-theorem in 3 dimensions, and more recently Casini–Salazar Landea–Torroba and Cuomo–Komargodski–Mezei–Raviv-Moshe established irreversibility of RG flows on planar defects of dimension d ≤ 4 using entanglement-entropy / QNEC methods, unifying known defect c-, F- and a-theorems. So the question is partially solved: monotones exist and are proved for defect dimensions p ≤ 4 (and conjecturally for boundaries via the b-anomaly in higher D), but a fully general all-dimensional defect c-theorem remains open.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Can the techniques surveyed in the proceedings be used to discover new conformal boundary conditions, new defects, or even qualitatively new ways of formulating what quantum field theory itself is?
self_contained_problem:
Let a quantum field theory (QFT) be a conformal field theory (CFT) on a d-dimensional manifold, possibly with boundaries or with embedded submanifolds (defects). A conformal boundary condition for a CFT on a half-space $\mathbb{R}^{d-1}	imes\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}$ is a boundary condition that preserves the subgroup of the conformal group fixing the boundary hyperplane, while a conformal defect of dimension $p<d$ is an insertion supported on a $p$-dimensional submanifold preserving the conformal subgroup fixing that submanifold.

Using modern techniques developed for boundary and defect CFT — including the conformal bootstrap (with crossing equations and unitarity bounds applied to boundary/defect channel decompositions), large-charge and large-spin expansions, the analytic structure of correlators with defects, holographic constructions of boundaries/defects in AdS, and integrability or symmetry-based constraints — address the following:

(a) Construct, or prove the existence of, previously unknown conformal boundary conditions for natural CFTs (for example, the d=3 critical Ising model, free scalar/free fermion theories in various dimensions, or four-dimensional gauge theories) beyond those already classified.

(b) Construct, or prove the existence of, previously unknown conformal defects (of various codimensions) in such theories beyond those already known.

(c) Determine whether the resulting structures (e.g., the algebra of boundaries, defects, and their fusion) suggest a qualitatively new axiomatic or constructive formulation of quantum field theory itself, distinct from the standard Wightman/Osterwalder–Schrader, algebraic (Haag–Kastler), and functorial/cobordism formulations.

Produce concrete new examples or, conversely, classification/no-go results.
category_tag: Boundary and defect conformal field theory
status_search_result: The question is a broad open research direction in boundary and defect CFT. While many new boundary conditions and defects have been discovered since 2018 (e.g., via the numerical conformal bootstrap, large-charge expansions, and holography), no comprehensive classification exists and the broader question of whether such studies lead to a qualitatively new formulation of QFT remains open.

original_question: What dynamical mechanism is responsible for the complicated, almost fractal structures in the phase diagram of late-time boundary scattering outcomes for the sine-Gordon model with non-integrable Robin boundary conditions?

$$\partial_t^2 \phi - \partial_x^2 \phi + \sin\phi = 0, \qquad x<0,\; t\in\mathbb{R},$$
with the one-parameter family of Robin boundary conditions
$$\partial_x \phi(0,t) = -2k\,\sin\!\big(\phi(0,t)/2\big), \qquad k\in\mathbb{R}.$$
For $k\notin\{0,\pm\infty\}$ this boundary condition breaks integrability (the integrable cases being the Neumann limit $k=0$ and Dirichlet-type limits).

Send in an antikink with initial velocity $v\in(0,1)$ from $x=-\infty$ and let it collide with the boundary. Record the late-time outcome (e.g.\ a reflected antikink, a kink, a kink–antikink pair, one or more breathers, breather emission accompanying a soliton, or trapping at the boundary) as a function of the pair $(v,k)$ in some chosen region of the parameter plane.

Numerical experiments reveal that the resulting outcome diagram contains regions with an extremely intricate, apparently fractal pattern of nested resonance windows.

Problem: Identify and rigorously characterize the dynamical mechanism responsible for these almost fractal structures in the late-time outcome diagram of antikink–boundary scattering for the sine-Gordon model with Robin boundary conditions. In particular, explain the origin, scaling, and self-similar organization of the nested resonance windows in terms of the internal dynamics of intermediate excitations (such as breathers or boundary-bound modes) created during the collision and their subsequent re-collision with the boundary.
status_search_result: Numerical work by Arthur, Dorey, and Parini (2016) attributes the intricate, fractal-like resonance windows in the antikink–Robin-boundary scattering phase diagram to the creation of an intermediate breather whose recollision with the boundary is highly sensitive to its phase, producing nested resonance windows analogous to the kink–antikink resonance phenomenon. While this gives a qualitative dynamical mechanism, a complete rigorous characterization (e.g. of the self-similar scaling and a full quantitative theory) does not appear to have been established, so the problem is best regarded as partially solved.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Can the residual or asymptotic integrability of the sine-Gordon problem on the quarter-plane be exploited more deeply, for example through methods such as the Fokas approach, to analyze boundary-induced breaking of integrability?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the sine-Gordon equation
  u_{tt} − u_{xx} + sin(u) = 0
posed on the quarter-plane Q = {(x,t) : x < 0, t > 0}, with prescribed initial data u(x,0), u_t(x,0) for x ≤ 0 and a boundary condition imposed at x = 0 of Robin type
  u_x(0,t) + 2 M sin(u(0,t)/2) = 0, t ≥ 0,
where M ∈ ℝ is a real parameter. For generic M the boundary condition breaks the bulk integrability of the sine-Gordon equation, while distinguished values of M (including M = 0 and the integrable Ghoshal–Zamolodchikov family) preserve infinite hierarchies of conserved quantities.

The Fokas (unified transform) method represents the solution of the sine-Gordon equation on Q via a matrix Riemann–Hilbert problem whose jump matrices are built from four spectral functions associated with the initial and boundary data, related through a global relation.

Develop the unified transform / Fokas approach to extract residual or asymptotic integrability of the sine-Gordon equation on the quarter-plane with Robin boundary conditions of the above form, and use it to analyze quantitatively how the boundary induces breaking of integrability. Specifically:
  (a) Formulate the matrix Riemann–Hilbert problem corresponding to the Robin boundary condition above and derive the corresponding global relation between the spectral functions determined by the initial data and those determined by the boundary data.
  (b) Identify, via this Riemann–Hilbert / global-relation framework, those features of the dynamics (e.g. soliton trajectories, reflection coefficients, infinite families of approximately conserved charges, long-time asymptotics on rays x/t = const) that remain controllable for general Robin parameter M, and quantify the obstruction to full integrability when M is generic.
  (c) Determine the long-time asymptotic behaviour of u(x,t) on Q for generic Robin M, including the leading dispersive contribution and any soliton/breather content reflected from the boundary.
status_search_result: The Fokas/unified-transform analysis of the sine-Gordon equation on the quarter-plane has been substantially developed: a Riemann–Hilbert formulation and global relation are available, nonlinear Fourier transforms and long-time asymptotics have been studied (Its, Kotlyarov, Lenells and others), and Robin-type boundary conditions breaking integrability have been analyzed perturbatively. However, a complete quantitative theory of how Robin boundary conditions break integrability and the full long-time asymptotics for generic parameters remain partially understood; thus the broad program is partially solved.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Can extended chiral or superconformal algebras be used systematically to construct new non-topological, non-factorizing conformal defects in tricritical Ising theory and related models?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the tricritical Ising minimal model, the unitary Virasoro minimal model M(4,5) with central charge c = 7/10, and analogous rational two-dimensional conformal field theories that admit extended chiral or superconformal symmetry algebras (for example, an N=1 super-Virasoro algebra, a W-algebra, or a coset extension of the Virasoro algebra). A conformal defect on the cylinder is a line operator that commutes with the diagonal Virasoro generators L_n − \bar L_{-n} but need not commute with L_n + \bar L_{-n}. Such a defect is called:
  • topological if it commutes with both holomorphic and antiholomorphic stress tensors (equivalently, it is fully transmissive);
  • factorizing if it is a tensor product of a conformal boundary state with its conjugate (equivalently, it is fully reflective);
  • non-topological and non-factorizing otherwise.

Equivalently, by the folding trick, a conformal defect in a CFT C corresponds to a conformal boundary condition of the doubled theory C ⊗ \bar C, and a topological (resp. factorizing) defect corresponds to a boundary preserving the full diagonal (resp. fully decoupled) chiral algebra.

Question: Develop a systematic construction principle whereby boundary states of C ⊗ \bar C that preserve only an extended chiral or superconformal subalgebra of the full chiral symmetry — but not the full chiral algebra of C ⊗ \bar C — yield genuinely new conformal defects of C that are neither topological nor factorizing. Concretely:

(a) For the tricritical Ising model, exhibit conformal defects obtained by imposing gluing conditions for an extended (e.g. N=1 superconformal or coset) chiral algebra on the folded theory, and prove that the resulting defects are not expressible as superpositions of topological defects and factorizing defects.

(b) Compute their reflection and transmission coefficients and verify 0 < T < 1.

(c) Extend the construction to a broader family of rational CFTs (e.g. other unitary Virasoro minimal models, super-Virasoro minimal models, or WZW models) and characterize when extended-algebra-preserving boundary states of the doubled theory produce new non-topological, non-factorizing conformal defects.
status_search_result: Subsequent work has constructed new non-topological, non-factorizing conformal defects in the tricritical Ising model via the folding trick and boundary conditions in a fermionic c=7/10 theory, showing they are not superpositions of topological and factorizing defects. Extended-algebra (Fibonacci ⊗ Ising decomposition, super-Virasoro) viewpoints have been used in related constructions and in duality-defect studies. However, a fully systematic, general construction principle using extended chiral/superconformal algebras across broad families of rational CFTs has not been completed, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: How can one- and two-point functions in defect conformal field theory be exploited more fully as input to the boundary conformal bootstrap, and what additional structure of the three-dimensional theory living on the defect must be understood in order to make that program work for the present AdS/dCFT system?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a four-dimensional conformal field theory (specifically, a setup of AdS/dCFT type in which a half-BPS codimension-one defect supports a three-dimensional defect theory) in the presence of a flat planar boundary or codimension-one defect. In such a defect conformal field theory the basic bootstrap data include: (i) bulk one-point functions ⟨O(x)⟩ = a_O / (2 x_⊥)^{Δ_O}, where x_⊥ is the distance to the defect and Δ_O is the scaling dimension of the bulk operator O; and (ii) bulk two-point functions ⟨O_1(x) O_2(y)⟩ which, by conformal symmetry preserved by the defect, depend on a single cross-ratio and admit two channel decompositions — a bulk channel into bulk operators and a defect channel into operators living on the three-dimensional defect — whose equality gives the boundary/defect conformal bootstrap equations.

Develop a systematic framework that uses the one- and two-point function data {a_O} and the bulk-to-defect couplings as input to the boundary/defect conformal bootstrap equations, sufficient to constrain or determine the spectrum and OPE coefficients of the three-dimensional defect theory. Concretely:

(a) Identify the structural data of the three-dimensional defect CFT (operator content, symmetries, OPE coefficients, possible integrability or supersymmetry constraints) needed so that the crossing equations relating bulk and defect channels become a closed, solvable system.

(b) Show how to combine these inputs with the bulk-channel decomposition to extract nontrivial bootstrap constraints on this defect theory, and demonstrate the procedure on the half-BPS codimension-one defect in the relevant AdS/dCFT example.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction: using one- and two-point functions of a defect CFT as input to the boundary conformal bootstrap requires further understanding of the 3D theory on the defect. Subsequent literature (e.g., on dCFT bootstrap, half-BPS codimension-one defects in N=4 SYM, and bulk-defect crossing) has made partial progress, but no complete bootstrap solution of the 3D defect theory in this AdS/dCFT system is available. Status appears to remain open.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Can one perform a genuine string-theoretic computation of the one-point function of a non-protected operator in the defect AdS/CFT setup?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the defect conformal field theory obtained from the D3–D5 brane intersection in type IIB string theory: a stack of N D3-branes ending on a single D5-brane that wraps an AdS$_4 \times S^2$ submanifold of AdS$_5 \times S^5$, with $k$ units of background magnetic flux through the $S^2$. The dual gauge theory is $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang–Mills on $\mathbb{R}^{1,3}$ with a codimension-one defect across which the gauge group rank jumps by $k$, and three of the six adjoint scalars acquire $x_3$-dependent classical expectation values determined by an $\mathfrak{su}(2)$ representation of dimension $k$. Local single-trace gauge-invariant operators $\mathcal{O}(x)$ in this background have nonvanishing one-point functions of the form
$$ \langle \mathcal{O}(x) \rangle = \frac{C_{\mathcal{O}}}{x_3^{\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}}}, $$
where $\Delta_{\mathcal{O}}$ is the scaling dimension of $\mathcal{O}$.

On the string-theory side, one-point functions of $\tfrac{1}{2}$-BPS (protected) operators have been computed by evaluating classical supergravity fields, sourced by the probe D5-brane, against the appropriate bulk-to-boundary propagators. For non-protected (non-BPS) operators, however, no such gravity computation suffices, and a genuine worldsheet string computation is required.

Problem. Develop a worldsheet string-theoretic prescription, in the D3–D5 probe-brane background of AdS$_5 \times S^5$, that computes the holographic one-point function coefficient $C_{\mathcal{O}}$ for a non-protected single-trace operator $\mathcal{O}$ (for example, an operator dual to a massive string state outside the supergravity spectrum), and use it to obtain $C_{\mathcal{O}}$ at strong 't Hooft coupling for at least one such non-protected operator. Match the result, where applicable, with the integrability-based gauge-theory predictions expressed as overlaps of Bethe eigenstates with a matrix product state.
status_search_result: Searches indicate that one-point functions of non-protected operators in the D3–D5 defect CFT have been computed extensively on the gauge-theory side (tree level, loop corrections, integrability/matrix-product-state overlaps in SU(2), SU(3) and beyond), but a genuine string-worldsheet computation of such non-protected one-point functions in the probe D5-brane background has not been reported. Related worldsheet techniques exist for heavy–light correlators and giant-graviton one-point functions, but no direct worldsheet result for non-protected single-trace one-point functions in D3–D5 dCFT was found, suggesting the problem remains open.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: How can the analytic-bootstrap approach used for loop corrections in AdS5 × S5 be combined either with direct one-loop Witten-diagram computations or with integrability-based methods, so that the different approaches constrain and check one another?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the holographic dual of $\mathcal{N}=4$ super Yang–Mills theory at large $N$, namely type IIB string theory on $\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5$. In the supergravity (large 't Hooft coupling) limit, four-point functions of half-BPS single-trace operators admit a $1/N^2$ expansion whose successive orders correspond to tree-level, one-loop, two-loop, ... Witten diagrams in the bulk. Three complementary techniques have been developed to access the one-loop (and higher-loop) order:

(a) An analytic conformal bootstrap approach, in which crossing symmetry, the Lorentzian inversion formula, and the structure of the double-trace anomalous-dimension spectrum are used to fix the loop-level correlators up to a finite number of contact-term ambiguities.

(b) Direct computation of one-loop Witten diagrams in $\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5$ using bulk Feynman rules together with the spectral/Mellin representation.

(c) Integrability-based methods (e.g. the hexagon form-factor program, octagons, and integrated correlators tied to localization), which compute correlators or specific integrated observables exactly in the planar coupling.

Problem. Develop a unified framework that combines the analytic-bootstrap method (a) with either the direct one-loop Witten-diagram computation (b) or the integrability-based approach (c), in such a way that:

  (i) the contact-term and other crossing-symmetric ambiguities left undetermined by the analytic bootstrap are fixed by inputs from (b) or (c);
  (ii) results obtained by each approach provide independent, mutually consistent checks of the others; and
  (iii) the framework extends to higher loops and to half-BPS operators of arbitrary Kaluza–Klein weight on $S^5$.

Concretely, exhibit such a combined procedure (or prove an obstruction to it) and use it to determine the one-loop four-point function of four half-BPS single-trace operators in $\mathrm{AdS}_5\times S^5$ supergravity, including all contact-term coefficients, in agreement with both bulk Witten-diagram computations and integrability/localization predictions.
category_tag: AdS/CFT analytic bootstrap and loop corrections
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the question was posed: direct one-loop Witten-diagram computations in AdS5×S5 (via spectral/Mellin methods) and integrability-based approaches (hexagons, octagons, integrated correlators from localization, and "bootstrability") have been combined with analytic-bootstrap methods to fix contact-term ambiguities and provide cross-checks for one-loop and higher-loop half-BPS four-point functions. Examples include hidden 10D conformal symmetry results for tree-level correlators, loop-correlator constructions using the spectral representation, and integrability+localization bootstrap programs for N=4 SYM correlators. A fully systematic, all-Kaluza–Klein, all-loop unification is not yet complete, so the broader program is best described as partially solved/active.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Can one construct explicit families of local quasi-holomorphic curves from the complex disk into a quasi Riemann surface, for example when the ambient 2n-dimensional space is the sphere S^{2n}, so that local conformal-field-theoretic structure can be studied there?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let M be a closed oriented Riemannian 2n-manifold. A quasi Riemann surface Q(M) is, informally, a higher-dimensional analogue of an ordinary Riemann surface built from M, in which the role of meromorphic functions is played by certain "harmonic" data on M and which is locally probed by maps from a complex disk that play the role of holomorphic curves in M. More precisely, fix the unit disk Σ ⊂ ℂ. A local quasi-holomorphic curve into Q(M) is a smooth one-parameter family of geometric data on M (for example, a family of currents, harmonic forms, or sections of an appropriate bundle over M) parametrized by Σ that satisfies a Cauchy–Riemann–type equation on Q(M), so that its pullback represents the local function theory of Q(M) as ordinary meromorphic-function theory on Σ.

Problem. Take M = S^{2n} (the round 2n-sphere, identified with ℝ^{2n} ∪ {∞}). Construct explicit families of local quasi-holomorphic curves f : Σ → Q(S^{2n}) — i.e., write down concrete representatives of such Cauchy–Riemann solutions, parametrized by the unit disk (or by the Riemann sphere) — sufficient to exhibit and study the local conformal-field-theoretic structure on Q(S^{2n}). Equivalently, give an explicit local parametrization of the quasi-holomorphic curves through a basepoint of Q(S^{2n}) and describe the induced ordinary meromorphic function theory on Σ.
status_search_result: Daniel Friedan's "Quasi Riemann surfaces II" (2017) explicitly raises the need for explicit constructions of local quasi-holomorphic curves, in particular for M = S^{2n}, as an open question/speculation. No subsequent construction appears in the search results, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Boundary and Defect CFT: Open Problems and Applications
original_question: Can standard two-dimensional conformal-field-theory constructions, such as orbifolding and perturbation theory, be reproduced or generalized on quasi Riemann surfaces so as to generate new theories of higher-dimensional defects?
self_contained_problem:
A quasi Riemann surface is a higher-dimensional generalization of a Riemann surface designed so that two-dimensional conformal field theory data can be transported to higher-dimensional defect settings: it is equipped with analogues of complex structure, holomorphic differentials, period pairings, and a notion of conformal/biholomorphic equivalence sufficient to support correlators of local insertions and extended defects. On such a quasi Riemann surface, develop higher-dimensional analogues of the standard two-dimensional CFT constructions, namely:

(a) Orbifolding: given a CFT on a quasi Riemann surface together with a global symmetry group G acting on it, formulate a consistent gauging procedure that produces a new theory, including the prescription of twisted sectors, modular-invariant (or appropriately covariant) partition functions, and operator content; and

(b) Perturbation theory: given a CFT on a quasi Riemann surface, formulate a deformation by a (quasi-)marginal operator and prove existence of, and compute, perturbative corrections to correlators and to the spectrum of defect operators.

Show that these two constructions, when applied on quasi Riemann surfaces, generate genuinely new conformal theories describing higher-dimensional defects, and identify the resulting families of defect CFTs.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface a construction that systematically reproduces 2d CFT orbifolding and conformal perturbation theory on quasi Riemann surfaces to generate new higher-dimensional defect CFTs. While related work exists on defects, symmetric orbifolds, and CFTs on Riemann surfaces, no source verifies that the proposed program has been carried out, so the question appears to remain open.

original_question: When N > 4 and the positive parameters a and b satisfy a^((N-4)/2) b < C1(N), do the conclusions of Theorem 1.1 still hold? In other words, for each sufficiently large lambda > 0 and each convex set C subset of L2(Omega) whose closure in L2(Omega) contains H1_0(Omega), does there exist some v* in C such that the associated Kirchhoff problem has at least three weak solutions, two of which are global minima in H1_0(Omega) of the corresponding energy functional?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^N$ be a bounded domain with smooth boundary, with $N > 4$. Consider the Kirchhoff-type problem
$$
(P_\lambda)\quad -\Bigl(a + b\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx\Bigr)\Delta u \;=\; \lambda\bigl(|u|^{2^*-2}u + g(x,u)\bigr) + h(x,v(x)) \quad\text{in }\Omega,\qquad u = 0 \text{ on }\partial\Omega,
$$
where $a\ge 0$, $b>0$ are positive parameters, $\lambda>0$, $2^* = 2N/(N-2)$ is the critical Sobolev exponent, and $g,h$ are suitable subcritical Carathéodory perturbations (with $v$ a fixed function entering as a parameter through $h$). The associated energy functional on $H^1_0(\Omega)$ is
$$
J_\lambda(u) \;=\; \tfrac{a}{2}\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx \;+\; \tfrac{b}{4}\Bigl(\int_\Omega |\nabla u|^2\,dx\Bigr)^2 \;-\; \tfrac{\lambda}{2^*}\int_\Omega |u|^{2^*}\,dx \;-\; \lambda\!\int_\Omega G(x,u)\,dx \;-\; \int_\Omega H(x,v(x))u\,dx,
$$
with $G,H$ the antiderivatives of $g,h$ in the second variable.

There exist explicit dimensional constants $0 < C_1(N) \le C_2(N)$ such that the following multiplicity result is known: if
$$
a^{(N-4)/2}\,b \;>\; C_2(N),
$$
then for every sufficiently large $\lambda>0$ and every convex set $\mathcal{C}\subset L^2(\Omega)$ whose closure in $L^2(\Omega)$ contains $H^1_0(\Omega)$, there exists $v^*\in\mathcal{C}$ such that problem $(P_\lambda)$ admits at least three weak solutions, two of which are global minima in $H^1_0(\Omega)$ of the energy functional $J_\lambda$.

Question. When $N>4$, does the same conclusion remain valid for all $a\ge 0$, $b>0$ satisfying the below-threshold condition
$$
a^{(N-4)/2}\,b \;<\; C_1(N)\,?
$$
That is, under this condition, prove or disprove that for every sufficiently large $\lambda>0$ and every convex set $\mathcal{C}\subset L^2(\Omega)$ whose closure in $L^2(\Omega)$ contains $H^1_0(\Omega)$, there exists $v^*\in\mathcal{C}$ such that $(P_\lambda)$ has at least three weak solutions, two of which are global minima of $J_\lambda$ in $H^1_0(\Omega)$.

paper_title: The Statistical Model of Nuclear Reactions: Open Problems
context_brief: Brink-Axel validity for significant gamma transitions
original_question: The statistical model underpredicts the mean total gamma decay widths observed for neutron resonances and therefore appears to be missing gamma strength. The open question is whether the Brink-Axel hypothesis actually remains valid for all gamma transitions that contribute significantly to the gamma decay of those neutron resonances, since failure of that hypothesis could explain why the model does not reproduce the observed total gamma decay-width data.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Consider a compound nucleus formed by s-wave neutron capture on a target nucleus, producing neutron resonances at excitation energies near the neutron separation energy S_n. Each resonance λ has a total radiative (gamma) decay width Γ_γ(λ) = Σ_f Γ_γ(λ → f), where the sum runs over all energetically accessible final states f.

In the statistical model of nuclear reactions, the partial gamma decay widths from a resonance λ at excitation energy E_λ to a final state f at energy E_f are computed using a gamma-ray strength function f_XL(E_γ) (for multipolarity XL and gamma-ray energy E_γ = E_λ − E_f) together with a level density ρ(E_f, J_f, π_f). The Brink–Axel hypothesis asserts that the gamma-ray strength function f_XL(E_γ) depends only on the gamma-ray energy E_γ and is independent of the properties (excitation energy, spin, parity) of the initial and final nuclear states involved in the transition. Under this hypothesis one obtains theoretical mean total gamma decay widths ⟨Γ_γ⟩_theory.

Empirical observation. The mean total gamma decay widths ⟨Γ_γ⟩_exp measured for ensembles of neutron resonances are systematically larger than the predictions ⟨Γ_γ⟩_theory of the statistical model based on the Brink–Axel hypothesis, indicating missing gamma strength in the model.

Problem. Determine whether the Brink–Axel hypothesis (in its generalized form, asserting independence of f_XL(E_γ) from initial- and final-state properties) holds for all gamma transitions that contribute significantly to the gamma decay of neutron resonances. Specifically, identify whether a violation of the Brink–Axel hypothesis for the dominant contributing transitions (for instance through dependence of the strength function on excitation energy, spin, parity, or temperature, or through additional structure such as low-energy enhancements, scissors modes, or pygmy resonances built on excited states) can quantitatively account for the observed underprediction of ⟨Γ_γ⟩ by the statistical model.
status_search_result: Recent experimental and theoretical work gives a mixed, nucleus- and energy-dependent picture. Several Oslo-method studies (e.g., on Sn isotopes and on 238Np) report that the generalized Brink–Axel hypothesis holds reasonably well for dipole strength below the neutron separation energy, supporting its use in statistical-model calculations. However, clear violations have been documented at low gamma-ray energies (low-energy enhancement/upbend, scissors-mode discrepancies between decay and absorption) and in finite-temperature regimes, and a comprehensive 2021 test in the pygmy dipole region as well as 2025 work on the upbend resonance demonstrate that the hypothesis cannot be assumed universally. Whether such violations are sufficient to fully explain the underpredicted mean total gamma decay widths of neutron resonances remains unresolved.

paper_title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics
context_brief: Bosonic occupation factors in α gas states
original_question: Can the α-condensate character of α gas states be tested more broadly by calculating bosonic occupation factors, especially the occupation of the same 0S single-α orbit? In the carbon-12 Hoyle state, the benchmark is whether the three α particles occupy the same 0S orbit at a high fraction; the source reports existing Hoyle-state calculations giving about 70–80% occupation, but says that only three calculations of this quantity exist.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a self-conjugate even-even nucleus consisting of N alpha particles (each alpha treated as a four-nucleon cluster of two protons and two neutrons in its internal 0s ground state). An "alpha-gas" (alpha-condensate) trial state is the fully antisymmetrized N-alpha product wave function in which the center-of-mass coordinate of each alpha occupies the same lowest harmonic-oscillator-type single-alpha orbit, denoted 0S. Given a microscopic many-body wave function Psi for such a state, define the bosonic single-alpha density matrix
  rho(r, r') = <Psi | a_alpha^dagger(r) a_alpha(r') | Psi>,
where a_alpha^dagger(r) creates a (properly antisymmetrized) alpha cluster centered at r, and let {n_i} denote its eigenvalues (the bosonic occupation numbers of the natural alpha orbits phi_i), normalized so that sum_i n_i = N. The "0S occupation fraction" is f_{0S} = n_{0S}/N, the fraction of alpha particles occupying the lowest natural alpha orbit.

Problem. Develop and carry out microscopic calculations of the bosonic alpha occupation numbers {n_i}, and in particular of the 0S occupation fraction f_{0S}, for candidate N-alpha gas states in self-conjugate even-even nuclei. As the principal benchmark, compute f_{0S} for the second 0+ (Hoyle) state of 12C (N = 3) and decide whether it attains a value (typically reported to be of order 70–80%) consistent with an alpha-condensate interpretation. Extend the analysis to heavier candidate alpha-gas states (e.g., N = 4 in 16O, N = 5 in 20Ne, and beyond) to test how broadly the alpha-condensate character, as quantified by a dominant 0S bosonic occupation, persists.
status_search_result: Several microscopic calculations confirm a large 0S bosonic occupation (~70–80%) for the Hoyle state of 12C, supporting an alpha-condensate interpretation. More recent work has extended such occupation-number analyses to heavier systems (e.g., a 5α condensate state in 20Ne reported in 2023), but systematic calculations of bosonic alpha occupation factors across alpha-gas candidates remain scarce, so the broader program is only partially completed.

paper_title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics
context_brief: Excited Hoyle condensate and breathing mode
original_question: Is the third 0+ state of carbon-12 at 10.08 MeV an excited Hoyle-family Bose condensate in which the three α particles move in relative 1S orbits, making it a higher-nodal breathing analogue of the Hoyle state, and what is the direct three-α decay behavior of such an excited condensate?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the carbon-12 nucleus as a system of three α particles (each α being a tightly bound 4-nucleon cluster treated as a structureless boson). The Hoyle state is the second 0⁺ excited state of ¹²C, located at about 7.65 MeV above the ground state, and is interpreted as a dilute Bose-condensate-like configuration in which all three α particles occupy the same lowest (0S) relative orbital.

Let the third 0⁺ state of ¹²C, denoted 0₃⁺, be the 0⁺ resonance observed near 10.08 MeV excitation energy.

(a) Determine whether the 0₃⁺ state can be characterized as a higher-nodal "breathing-mode" excitation of the Hoyle condensate, in the precise sense that all three α particles occupy a common relative 1S orbital (one radial node) so that the state still qualifies as an α-particle Bose condensate but with a higher-nodal single-particle wave function than the Hoyle state.

(b) Determine the branching pattern of the three-α decay of this 0₃⁺ resonance: in particular, quantify the probability of direct (democratic) breakup into three α particles versus the sequential decay through the ⁸Be(0⁺) + α channel, and identify any qualitative differences between the direct three-α decay of the breathing 0₃⁺ state and that of the Hoyle state.
status_search_result: Microscopic 3α cluster model calculations (e.g., Phys. Rev. C 94, 044319; Phys. Rev. C 107, 044304; Eur. Phys. J. A 60 (2024)) and recent neural-network analyses (arXiv:2406.15060) support the interpretation of the 0₃⁺ state near ~10 MeV in ¹²C as a breathing-mode excitation of the Hoyle state with a 1S-like relative motion (8Be(0⁺)+α 2S-wave configuration), giving theoretical backing to part (a). The direct three-α decay branching of this state remains under active experimental and theoretical study and is not yet conclusively determined, so the question as a whole is partially solved.

paper_title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics
context_brief: Rotational bands and spinning triangle picture in carbon-12
original_question: Does carbon-12 really have a ground-state rotational band describable as a permanent spinning triangular α-cluster configuration, and does the proposed Hoyle band have a well-defined band head, given that mean-field calculations without projection find a round oblate shape and the transition strengths from the second 2+ state to the second and third 0+ states are similar?
self_contained_problem:
The nucleus carbon-12 ($^{12}$C), consisting of six protons and six neutrons, is often modeled as a system of three $\alpha$-particle clusters. Two phenomenological pictures of its low-energy spectrum are:

(a) a ground-state rotational band built on the $0^+_1$ ground state, interpreted as a rigid, permanently spinning equilateral triangular $\alpha$-cluster configuration with $D_{3h}$ symmetry;

(b) a so-called "Hoyle band," a rotational band built on the second $0^+$ state (the Hoyle state, $0^+_2$ at $\approx 7.65$ MeV), with the $0^+_2$ acting as the band head.

Settle the following questions about the structure of $^{12}$C:

1. Is the ground-state band of $^{12}$C correctly described as a permanent (rigid) spinning triangular three-$\alpha$ configuration? In particular, mean-field (Hartree–Fock or Hartree–Fock–Bogoliubov) calculations without angular-momentum or parity projection produce only a perfectly round oblate intrinsic shape rather than a triangular one; reconcile this with, or refute, the rigid spinning-triangle interpretation.

2. Does the "Hoyle band" constitute a genuine rotational band with a well-defined band head at the $0^+_2$ state? In particular, the measured electromagnetic transition strengths $B(E2)$ from the second $2^+$ state to the $0^+_2$ and to the $0^+_3$ states are comparable in magnitude, which is in tension with the existence of a unique band-head assignment for the $2^+_2$ within the Hoyle band.

Provide a definitive theoretical and/or experimental determination of (1) and (2).
status_search_result: The structure of low-lying $^{12}$C states remains under active debate. Experimental work (e.g., Marín-Lámbarri et al., 2014) has been interpreted as evidence for a $D_{3h}$ spinning-triangle ground-state band, while recent ab-initio lattice and no-core shell model calculations (e.g., Shen et al., Nature Commun. 2023) support an emergent triangular/obtuse-triangle geometry but reinterpret the Hoyle state as a "bent-arm" or breathing mode rather than a rigidly spinning triangle. Whether the Hoyle band is a genuine rotational band with a well-defined band head is still disputed, with the $B(E2)$ ratios from $2^+_2$ being a key piece of conflicting evidence. The questions are therefore not definitively settled.

paper_title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics
original_question: Can the sixth 0+ state of oxygen-16 near 15.1 MeV, or the experimentally observed peak near 15.2 MeV in the 20Ne + α inverse-kinematics reaction, be confirmed as the four-α Hoyle-analog gas state by measuring the inelastic form factor and assigning the spin of the 15.2 MeV state?
self_contained_problem:
In nuclear cluster physics, the Hoyle state of carbon-12 is the second 0+ state at approximately 7.65 MeV, lying just above the three-α breakup threshold, and it is interpreted as a dilute three-α "gas-like" condensate; its α-condensate character is supported by precise measurement of the (e,e') inelastic form factor, whose magnitude and shape are sensitive to the spatial extension of the state.

For oxygen-16, an analogous picture predicts a four-α gas-like 0+ state lying close to the four-α breakup threshold (≈14.4 MeV). The sixth 0+ state of 16O, located at about 15.1 MeV (roughly 700 keV above the four-α threshold), has been proposed as such a Hoyle-analog state, and a peak observed near 15.2 MeV in the inverse-kinematics reaction 20Ne + α has been suggested as a candidate for the four-α gas state.

Problem. Establish whether either (a) the 0+ state of 16O at ≈15.1 MeV, or (b) the resonance observed near 15.2 MeV in 20Ne + α, can be confirmed as the four-α Hoyle-analog (α-condensate) gas state. Specifically:

1. Determine the inelastic electron-scattering form factor F(q) from the 16O ground state to the 0+ state at 15.1 MeV, and compare its magnitude and momentum-transfer dependence with the prediction of a four-α condensate (THSR-type) wave function representing a dilute, spatially extended four-α gas, to decide whether the 15.1 MeV state has the large radius and condensate character expected for the Hoyle analog.

2. Assign the spin and parity of the 15.2 MeV resonance observed in 20Ne + α and determine whether it is the same state as, or distinct from, the 0+ state at 15.1 MeV, thereby confirming or refuting its identification as the four-α gas state.
status_search_result: Recent experimental work has searched for the Hoyle analogue in 16O using inelastic α scattering with complete-kinematics detection of the four-α breakup. These measurements did not confirm the giant radius predicted by the α-particle condensate model for the 0+_6 state near 15.1 MeV, suggesting the state may not have a rarefied four-α gas structure. However, the precise (e,e') inelastic form factor — the most direct probe analogous to the Hoyle-state measurement — has not been reported, and a definitive spin assignment for the 15.2 MeV peak in 20Ne + α has not been firmly established. The question is therefore only partially resolved.

paper_title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics
context_brief: Negative-parity configurations missing from THSR oxygen-16 calculations
original_question: Can the extended THSR description of oxygen-16 be enlarged to include negative-parity carbon-12 cluster configurations so that the missing 0+ state, described as an α particle orbiting the first 1− state of carbon-12, appears in the calculated oxygen-16 spectrum?
self_contained_problem:
In the cluster description of light nuclei, the Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke (THSR) wave function is a fully antisymmetrized product ansatz in which α particles are placed in a common deformed Gaussian orbital, designed to capture nonlocalized, gas-like α-clustering. In its standard "extended" form for $^{16}$O, the nucleus is described as a $^{12}$C core plus an α particle, where the $^{12}$C subsystem is restricted to positive-parity intrinsic configurations (notably the ground state and the Hoyle-like $0^+_2$ state of $^{12}$C).

Comparison of the resulting $^{16}$O spectrum with experiment and with other microscopic calculations indicates that one $0^+$ state of $^{16}$O is absent from the extended THSR spectrum, namely the state naturally interpreted as an α particle orbiting the first $1^-$ excited state of $^{12}$C.

Problem. Construct an enlargement of the extended THSR framework for $^{16}$O that incorporates negative-parity intrinsic configurations of the $^{12}$C subsystem (in particular, the $1^-_1$ state of $^{12}$C coupled with relative orbital angular momentum yielding a $0^+$ total state), and demonstrate, by explicit microscopic calculation with full antisymmetrization, that the resulting $^{16}$O spectrum contains the missing $0^+$ state describable as an α particle orbiting the $1^-_1$ state of $^{12}$C. Determine its excitation energy and structure (in particular, whether it has the character of an α-gas state).
status_search_result: Searches reveal extensions of the THSR wave function (e.g., explicit spin-orbit inclusion, applications to $^{18}$O and $^{20}$Ne), but no published work appears to have explicitly enlarged the extended THSR scheme for $^{16}$O to include negative-parity $^{12}$C cluster configurations and recover the missing $0^+$ state corresponding to an α orbiting the $1^-_1$ of $^{12}$C. The status therefore appears unresolved based on available evidence.

paper_title: Recent Theoretical Advances and Open Problems in Nuclear Cluster Physics
context_brief: Microscopic α preformation and α-decay pocket models
original_question: Can a fully microscopic description of α preformation in α decay be developed for a heavy nucleus such as lead-208 plus an α particle, including the transition from an identifiable α cluster at the nuclear surface to four shell-model nucleons at higher density, and can the THSR/local-density approximation and double-folding pocket calculations be connected?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the α-decay system $^{212}\mathrm{Po} \to {}^{208}\mathrm{Pb} + \alpha$, viewed as a four-nucleon (two protons and two neutrons) cluster moving in the mean field of a doubly-magic $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ core. Two complementary descriptions of this system are:

(i) A quartetting/THSR-type wave-function approach in which the α-cluster is described by a Tohsaki–Horiuchi–Schuck–Röpke product ansatz for four nucleons, combined with a local-density approximation. In this picture the four nucleons form an identifiable bound α cluster at low matter density (the nuclear surface), but at a critical core density the four-body intrinsic bound state dissolves and the nucleons must be described as four independent shell-model quasiparticles. This yields an effective potential pocket for the α coordinate.

(ii) A double-folding procedure in which a phenomenological effective nucleon–nucleon interaction (e.g.\ M3Y) is folded with the density distribution of the α particle and that of the $^{208}\mathrm{Pb}$ core, again producing an α–core potential exhibiting a pocket that supports a quasibound resonance whose width gives the α-decay width.

Develop a fully microscopic, quantum-mechanical description of α preformation in $^{212}\mathrm{Po}$ that:

(a) treats consistently the transition, as a function of the local nuclear density, of the four-nucleon wave function from a bound α cluster at the surface to four uncorrelated shell-model nucleons in the high-density interior;

(b) reproduces the measured α-decay width of $^{212}\mathrm{Po}$;

(c) establishes a quantitative correspondence between the THSR/local-density-approximation pocket potential of approach (i) and the double-folding pocket potential of approach (ii), explaining under what assumptions the two approaches give equivalent α–core potentials and decay widths.
status_search_result: A quartetting wave-function approach combining THSR-type four-nucleon correlations with a local-density approximation has been implemented for $^{212}$Po, using the measured $^{208}$Pb density and an M3Y double-folding mean field, and reproduces the measured α-decay width fairly well (Po-Schuck-Röpke et al., arXiv:1511.07584 and follow-ups). This represents substantial progress, but a fully ab initio microscopic treatment of the cluster–to–shell-model transition and a complete formal equivalence between the THSR/LDA and pure double-folding pocket approaches have not been fully established, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Engineering and Quality Assurance of Safety Critical Machine Learning Systems
original_question: How can safety-critical automated-driving systems define their operational design domain by efficiently collecting real-world driving scenarios from past field operational tests and customer data, and how can they define evaluation criteria such as test coverage to determine whether the collected scenarios are sufficient for safety and security assurance?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a safety-critical automated driving system that must operate within a specified operational design domain (ODD), defined as the set of environmental, geographical, temporal, and traffic conditions under which the system is designed to function safely. Suppose one has access to large logs of real-world driving data obtained from past field operational tests and from customer vehicles, where each log can be segmented into discrete "driving scenarios" (each scenario being a tuple consisting of road geometry, surrounding agents and their trajectories, weather and lighting conditions, ego-vehicle state, and triggering events).

(a) Propose a methodology for efficiently collecting and curating, from such large-scale logs, a finite scenario set S that adequately represents the ODD, including a formal model of the scenario space and a sampling/selection procedure that is tractable on industrial-scale datasets.

(b) Define a quantitative evaluation criterion (a notion of "test coverage") C(S) for any such finite collection S, together with a threshold or sufficiency condition under which one may certify that S is adequate to provide safety and security assurance for the system within its declared ODD. The coverage notion must be well-defined on the scenario model from (a) and must support an argument linking C(S) ≥ threshold to a bound on residual risk.

The problem is to provide such a methodology and coverage definition, or to prove that no such procedure can simultaneously satisfy tractability of collection and a meaningful residual-risk guarantee.
category_tag: safety assurance of autonomous driving systems
status_search_result: Defining ODD scenario coverage and sufficiency criteria for automated-driving safety assurance remains an active and open research area. Standards and frameworks (ISO 21448 SOTIF, UL 4600, PEGASUS, Safety Pool) and numerous recent papers propose partial scenario-based testing methods and coverage metrics, but no universally accepted solution that links scenario coverage to a residual-risk bound has been established.

paper_title: Open Problems in Engineering and Quality Assurance of Safety Critical Machine Learning Systems
original_question: How can developers describe the uncertainty introduced by machine-learning models inside safety-critical subsystems as statistical measures suitable for requirements, design, and assurance activities?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a safety-critical system that contains one or more subsystems whose behavior is determined by a trained machine-learning model f: X -> Y (e.g., a classifier or regressor) obtained from a finite training sample drawn from an unknown data-generating distribution D over X x Y. Because f is learned from finite data and operates in possibly shifted environments at deployment, its predictions carry uncertainty arising from (i) aleatoric noise inherent in D, (ii) epistemic uncertainty due to limited training data and model class mis-specification, and (iii) distributional shift between training and operational distributions.

Develop a principled framework that, for such a learned subsystem, expresses the predictive uncertainty as explicit statistical measures (e.g., calibrated probability distributions over outputs, prediction intervals with guaranteed coverage, conditional risk bounds, false-positive/false-negative rates, or distributionally robust performance bounds) such that:

1. The measures admit precise mathematical definitions and estimable quantities from data.
2. The measures can be incorporated as quantitative requirements (e.g., "Pr[ loss(f(X), Y) > tau ] <= epsilon under operational distribution D'") that are verifiable during design and assurance.
3. The framework provides composition rules for propagating these uncertainty measures through a larger system containing both ML and non-ML components, yielding system-level statistical guarantees.

Formally specify such a set of statistical measures, the assumptions on D and f under which they are well-defined and estimable with finite-sample guarantees, and the propagation rules through system composition.
status_search_result: The problem of providing rigorous statistical descriptions of ML uncertainty suitable for safety-critical requirements and assurance remains an active open research area. paper_title: Open Problems in Engineering and Quality Assurance of Safety Critical Machine Learning Systems
original_question: Before expensive machine-learning model training, how can a redundant subsystem architecture be verified under a predetermined probabilistic uncertainty model so that engineers can know whether the uncertainty of the entire system is absorbed or mitigated?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a system S composed of n component modules M_1, ..., M_n arranged in a redundant architecture described by a directed acyclic graph G = (V, E), where each component M_i is intended to implement a (yet-to-be-trained) machine-learning model. Suppose that for each component M_i a probabilistic uncertainty model is given a priori in the form of a conditional output distribution P_i(y_i | x_i, theta_i), where theta_i parameterizes a stochastic error model (for example, a bound on the misclassification probability, a noise distribution on outputs, or a confidence-calibrated error rate). The redundant architecture specifies a deterministic combination rule F that maps the joint outputs (y_1, ..., y_n) to a system output Y = F(y_1, ..., y_n) (e.g., majority voting, weighted ensembling, or a safety monitor with fallback).

Given a system-level safety specification phi (for instance, "Pr[Y is incorrect on input X] <= epsilon" for a stipulated input distribution D over X), develop a verification procedure that, using only the per-component uncertainty models {P_i} and the architecture (G, F) — and without training any of the actual machine-learning models — decides whether the redundant architecture absorbs or mitigates the per-component uncertainty so that the system satisfies phi. Formally:

(a) Define a precise mathematical framework (composition semantics) under which the joint distribution of (y_1, ..., y_n) given X is determined by the {P_i} and a specified dependence structure (e.g., conditional independence given X, or a copula constraint).

(b) Provide an algorithm that, given (G, F, {P_i}, D, phi), outputs YES if the induced distribution of Y satisfies phi, and otherwise outputs NO together with a witness assignment of component behaviors consistent with {P_i} that violates phi.

(c) Establish soundness, completeness, and computational complexity of the procedure, and characterize the class of redundant architectures (G, F) for which uncertainty absorption can be certified in polynomial time before training.
category_tag: probabilistic verification of redundant ML architectures
status_search_result: The question is posed in a list of open engineering/quality-assurance challenges for safety-critical ML systems. No general-purpose, sound-and-complete pre-training verification method for arbitrary redundant ML architectures under predetermined probabilistic uncertainty models is known; related work on probabilistic ensemble verification, assurance cases, and assume-guarantee contracts addresses only restricted special cases. The problem appears to remain open in the general formulation.
