paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: Let X be an affine scheme with coordinate algebra A, let a be a finite-dimensional algebra, and let an algebraic group Γ act completely reducibly on both A and a by automorphisms. For the resulting equivariant map algebra M(X,a)^Γ, classify the irreducible finite-dimensional representations when Γ is allowed to be more general than a finite group.
self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an affine scheme over an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, with coordinate algebra $A = \mathcal{O}(X)$, and let $\mathfrak{a}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra. Suppose $\Gamma$ is an algebraic group acting on $A$ and on $\mathfrak{a}$ by automorphisms (as an algebra and as a Lie algebra, respectively), and assume that the action of $\Gamma$ is completely reducible on both $A$ and $\mathfrak{a}$. Form the equivariant map algebra
$$M(X,\mathfrak{a})^{\Gamma} := (A \otimes \mathfrak{a})^{\Gamma} = \{f \in A \otimes \mathfrak{a} \mid \gamma \cdot f = f \text{ for all } \gamma \in \Gamma\},$$
viewed as a Lie algebra under the pointwise bracket. 

Classify, up to isomorphism, all irreducible finite-dimensional representations of $M(X,\mathfrak{a})^{\Gamma}$ in this generality where $\Gamma$ is permitted to be an arbitrary (not necessarily finite) algebraic group acting completely reducibly.
status_search_result: The classification of irreducible finite-dimensional representations of equivariant map algebras was carried out by Neher–Savage–Senesi (arXiv:0906.5189) in the case where Γ is a finite abelian group acting freely on the maximal spectrum of A, and subsequent work has extended results to map superalgebras and to extensions/block decompositions. A general classification when Γ is an arbitrary algebraic group acting completely reducibly does not appear to have been established in the search results, so the status remains unclear.

paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: Generalize equivariant map superalgebras by allowing the target to be any finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra, replacing the commutative coordinate algebra A by a supercommutative algebra so that X becomes a superscheme, and replacing Γ by a Z2-graded group; then determine the resulting representation theory in this broader super setting.
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. By a Lie superalgebra over k we mean a Z/2Z-graded vector space g = g_0 ⊕ g_1 equipped with a bilinear bracket satisfying graded skew-symmetry and the graded Jacobi identity. A finite-dimensional Lie superalgebra g is called simple if it has no nonzero proper graded ideals and [g, g] ≠ 0.

By a supercommutative algebra we mean an associative, unital, Z/2Z-graded k-algebra A = A_0 ⊕ A_1 such that ab = (−1)^{|a||b|} ba for homogeneous elements. Such an A is the coordinate algebra of an affine superscheme X = Spec A.

By a Z/2Z-graded group Γ we mean an affine group superscheme over k, equivalently a representable functor from supercommutative k-algebras to groups whose representing Hopf superalgebra is Z/2Z-graded. Suppose Γ acts on X (equivalently, on A by Z/2Z-graded automorphisms) and on g by Z/2Z-graded Lie superalgebra automorphisms.

The equivariant map superalgebra is then defined as
   M(X, g)^Γ := (A ⊗ g)^Γ,
the Z/2Z-graded subspace of Γ-invariants, with the Lie superbracket
   [a ⊗ x, b ⊗ y] = (−1)^{|x||b|} ab ⊗ [x, y]
extended by linearity.

Problem. Develop the representation theory of the Lie superalgebra M(X, g)^Γ in this generalized super setting, where:
 (i) g is allowed to be any finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra over k (not restricted to the basic classical types);
 (ii) A is a (possibly nontrivially Z/2Z-graded) supercommutative k-algebra, so that X is a superscheme;
 (iii) Γ is a Z/2Z-graded group acting compatibly on X and g.

Specifically, classify the irreducible finite-dimensional (graded) modules of M(X, g)^Γ in terms of suitable equivariant evaluation data on X, and describe their extensions and tensor structure, generalizing the classification known when g is basic classical, A is an ordinary commutative algebra, and Γ is an ordinary (ungraded) group.
status_search_result: The classical equivariant map superalgebra case (g basic classical, A ordinary commutative, Γ ordinary finite group) was treated by Savage and collaborators. Subsequent work has extended the theory in particular directions, e.g. equivariant map queer Lie superalgebras (Calixto–Savage, 2014) and irreducible modules and their extensions (Bagci–Calixto–Macedo). However, the full generalization simultaneously allowing arbitrary finite-dimensional simple Lie superalgebra targets, supercommutative coordinate algebras (superscheme X), and Z/2Z-graded group symmetries does not appear to have a complete representation-theoretic classification in the literature, so the program remains only partially carried out.

paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: For equivariant map algebras M(X,a)^Γ, determine classification criteria and invariants for the isomorphism problem by extending known results for loop algebras and certain two-variable multiloop algebras to the full multiloop setting and then to more general equivariant map algebras.
self_contained_problem:
Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let X be a scheme of finite type over k, and let g be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over k. The map algebra M(X, g) is the Lie algebra of regular maps from X to g, which can be identified with g ⊗_k A, where A is the coordinate ring of X, equipped with the pointwise bracket. Let Γ be a finite group acting on X by automorphisms and on g by Lie algebra automorphisms. The equivariant map algebra is the fixed-point subalgebra
  M(X, g)^Γ = { α ∈ g ⊗_k A : (γ·α) = α for all γ ∈ Γ },
where Γ acts diagonally on g ⊗_k A.

Important special cases:
(i) Multiloop algebras: X = (k^×)^n with the action of Γ = Z/m_1 Z × ⋯ × Z/m_n Z generated by commuting finite-order automorphisms σ_1, …, σ_n of g, where the i-th generator acts on the i-th coordinate of (k^×)^n by multiplication by a primitive m_i-th root of unity. For n = 1 these are the (twisted) loop algebras.
(ii) The two-variable case (n = 2) of (i).

The isomorphism problem asks: give explicit classification criteria and a complete set of invariants determining when two equivariant map algebras M(X, g)^Γ and M(X', g')^{Γ'} are isomorphic as Lie algebras.

Problem: Extend the known classification of (twisted) loop algebras (n = 1) and of two-variable multiloop algebras (n = 2) to:
(a) the full multiloop setting for arbitrary n ≥ 1, providing necessary and sufficient conditions, in terms of the data (g, σ_1, …, σ_n, m_1, …, m_n), for two such multiloop algebras to be isomorphic; and
(b) the broader class of equivariant map algebras M(X, g)^Γ, providing classification criteria and invariants in terms of the triple (X, g, Γ).
status_search_result: The isomorphism problem for equivariant map algebras is described as a fundamental open problem. Partial results exist: complete classifications are known for (twisted) loop algebras and for two-variable multiloop algebras (via Lie torus / centreless Lie torus isotopy methods and Galois cohomology over Laurent polynomial rings). paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: When a is an associative algebra and M = M(X,a)^Γ, go beyond the classification of irreducible finite-dimensional M-modules and describe all indecomposable finite-dimensional modules, together with the block decomposition of the corresponding module category.
self_contained_problem:
Let k be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Let X be a scheme of finite type over k, let a be a finite-dimensional associative k-algebra, and let Γ be a finite group acting on X by scheme automorphisms and on a by k-algebra automorphisms. Define the equivariant map algebra
   M = M(X, a)^Γ = { f ∈ a ⊗ k[X] : (γ·f)(x) = γ·f(γ^{-1}x) for all γ ∈ Γ, x ∈ X }
with multiplication induced from that of a and k[X]. Consider the category of finite-dimensional left M-modules.

(a) Classify, up to isomorphism, all indecomposable finite-dimensional M-modules.

(b) Determine the block decomposition of the category of finite-dimensional M-modules; that is, describe explicitly the equivalence classes of indecomposable objects under the equivalence relation generated by the existence of nontrivial extensions, and give a structural description of each block.
status_search_result: The block decomposition of the category of finite-dimensional representations of equivariant map (Lie) algebras has been described in terms of spectral characters by Neher–Savage (Transformation Groups, 2015), and analogous block results exist for equivariant map superalgebras. However, a complete classification of indecomposable finite-dimensional modules remains open in general (the representation type is typically wild), so the full problem is only partially resolved.

original_question: For an equivariant map Lie algebra M = M(X,g)^Γ, compute the higher Ext groups between finite-dimensional M-modules, explain how these Ext groups interact with both the representation theory of g and the geometry of X, and determine how the global dimension of the category of finite-dimensional M-modules is governed by that geometry.

Let $\Bbbk$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero. Define the equivariant map algebra
$$M = M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma} = \{\,f \in \mathfrak{g}\otimes_{\Bbbk}\mathcal{O}(X) : (\gamma\cdot f)(\gamma\cdot x) = \gamma\cdot f(x)\ \text{for all}\ \gamma\in\Gamma,\, x\in X\,\},$$
viewed as a Lie algebra under the pointwise bracket. Let $\mathcal{F}(M)$ denote the category of finite-dimensional $M$-modules.

$$\mathrm{Ext}^{n}_{M}(V,W),$$
giving an explicit description in terms of the representation theory of $\mathfrak{g}$ and of geometric invariants of $X$ (such as tangent spaces, cotangent complexes, or other local data of $X$ at the support points of $V$ and $W$).

paper_title: A survey of equivariant map algebras with open problems
original_question: Develop representation-theoretic categories for equivariant map algebras beyond finite-dimensional modules, including analogues of category O, categories of integrable highest-weight representations, categories of quasifinite representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces, and other suitable infinite-dimensional module categories.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{g}$ be a finite-dimensional Lie algebra over $\mathbb{C}$, let $X$ be an affine scheme of finite type over $\mathbb{C}$, and let $\Gamma$ be a finite group acting on $X$ by automorphisms of schemes and on $\mathfrak{g}$ by Lie algebra automorphisms. The associated equivariant map algebra is
$$M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma} = \{\, \alpha \in \mathfrak{g}\otimes_{\mathbb{C}}\mathcal{O}(X) : (\gamma\cdot\alpha)=\alpha \text{ for all } \gamma\in\Gamma\,\},$$
where $\Gamma$ acts diagonally on $\mathfrak{g}\otimes\mathcal{O}(X)$ via its actions on $\mathfrak{g}$ and on $\mathcal{O}(X)$. This class includes (twisted and untwisted) loop algebras and current algebras as special cases.

The finite-dimensional representation theory of $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ has been developed in considerable generality. The problem is to develop a representation theory of $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ in infinite-dimensional settings, by introducing and studying natural module categories that extend the known frameworks for loop and current algebras to arbitrary equivariant map algebras. Specifically:

(a) Define and study an analogue of the Bernstein–Gelfand–Gelfand category $\mathcal{O}$ for $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$, including a suitable triangular decomposition, characters, Verma-type modules, and classification of simple objects.

(b) Define and classify the integrable highest-weight representations of $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$, generalising the integrable highest-weight theory available for affine Kac–Moody (loop) algebras.

(c) Define and classify the quasifinite representations of $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$, that is, weight modules all of whose weight spaces are finite-dimensional, with respect to an appropriate Cartan-type subalgebra.

(d) Identify and study other natural infinite-dimensional module categories for $M(X,\mathfrak{g})^{\Gamma}$ (for example, smooth modules, restricted modules, or global/local Weyl module categories) and relate them to the categories in (a)–(c).
status_search_result: The program is broad and ongoing. Partial progress exists: integrable representations have been studied for equivariant map algebras associated with Borel–de Siebenthal pairs and for root-graded Lie algebras (which include EMAs); global/local Weyl modules and uniformly bounded weight modules have been investigated for various map algebras (e.g., map Witt, map Virasoro, map extended special/Hamiltonian). However, a uniform development of category O, integrable highest-weight, and quasifinite categories for arbitrary EMAs has not been completed, so the overall problem remains open in general.

self_contained_problem:

(b) Compute the abelianization $H_0(M, M_{\mathrm{ad}}) = M/[M,M]$, where $M_{\mathrm{ad}}$ denotes $M$ acting on itself by the adjoint action.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: How fast, and by what QCD dynamics, does a high-energy nuclear collision observable transition from the nonlinear saturation regime to the high-transverse-momentum leading-twist regime, given that current running-coupling Balitsky-Kovchegov small-x evolution equations do not include the DGLAP limit and predict that proton-nucleus nuclear-modification observables return to unity only at unrealistically large transverse momentum pT?
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of small-$x$ QCD evolution for high-energy nuclear collisions, the running-coupling Balitsky–Kovchegov (rcBK) equation governs the nonlinear evolution of the dipole scattering amplitude $N(r,x)$ in the saturation regime, while DGLAP evolution governs the linear, leading-twist regime at large transverse momentum $p_T \gg Q_s(x)$, where $Q_s(x)$ is the saturation scale. The nuclear modification factor for proton–nucleus collisions is defined as
$$R_{pA}(p_T,y) = \frac{1}{A}\,\frac{d^2N_{pA}/dp_T\,dy}{d^2N_{pp}/dp_T\,dy},$$
which by collinear-factorization expectations should approach unity for $p_T \gg Q_s$. Current rcBK-based predictions, however, do not embed the DGLAP limit and yield $R_{pA}\to 1$ only at unrealistically large $p_T$, especially at forward rapidities where small-$x$ evolution has acted.

Determine, within QCD, the dynamics and rate of the transition from the nonlinear saturation regime to the high-$p_T$ leading-twist DGLAP regime. Specifically:

(i) Construct a small-$x$ evolution scheme for the unintegrated gluon distribution (or dipole amplitude) that simultaneously reduces to rcBK in the saturation regime ($p_T \lesssim Q_s$) and to DGLAP evolution in the leading-twist regime ($p_T \gg Q_s$), with a controlled matching at intermediate $p_T$.

(ii) Quantify, in this scheme, how rapidly $R_{pA}(p_T,y)\to 1$ as $p_T$ grows above $Q_s(x)$, identifying the parametric dependence of the transition scale on $x$ (or rapidity $y$), $A$, and the strong coupling $\alpha_s$.

(iii) Show that the resulting predictions are consistent with proton–nucleus collider data and, where available, electron–nucleus deep-inelastic scattering data.
category_tag: Small-x QCD evolution and gluon saturation
status_search_result: Recent literature confirms that the precise matching between nonlinear (rcBK/JIMWLK) small-$x$ evolution and linear DGLAP leading-twist evolution remains phenomenologically unsettled: theoretical arguments only establish each framework in its asymptotic limit, and the intermediate-$(x,Q^2)$ kinematics relevant to $R_{pA}$ at the LHC is still unclear. Various DGLAP-improved saturation models (e.g., color-dipole DGLAP-improved fits) and unified evolution proposals exist, but no consensus solution embeds DGLAP into rcBK so that $R_{pA}\to 1$ at realistic $p_T$.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: How does QCD make the transition from the high-parton-density saturation regime, where small-x gluons form a weakly coupled nonlinear many-body system, to the confinement regime of QCD?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD), the dynamics of hadrons probed at very small Bjorken-x is governed by a high-density system of gluons. In this regime, nonlinear gluon recombination effects balance linear gluon emission, leading to the phenomenon of parton saturation, characterized by a dynamically generated saturation scale Q_s(x) that grows as x decreases. When Q_s is large compared to Lambda_QCD, the strong coupling alpha_s(Q_s) is small, so the saturated gluon system can be described as a weakly coupled but highly nonlinear many-body system (e.g., via the Color Glass Condensate effective theory, the JIMWLK/BK evolution equations, and classical Yang-Mills fields as the relevant degrees of freedom). At the opposite extreme, when momentum scales approach Lambda_QCD, QCD becomes strongly coupled and exhibits color confinement, with hadrons rather than gluons as the appropriate degrees of freedom.

Provide a quantitative theoretical description of how QCD interpolates between these two regimes. Specifically:

(a) Determine how the small-x, high-density (saturation) description of hadronic matter, formulated in terms of weakly coupled nonlinear classical color fields, evolves into the confining regime of QCD as the saturation scale Q_s is decreased toward Lambda_QCD.

(b) In particular, characterize whether classical color fields remain the correct effective degrees of freedom throughout the transition, determine whether and how the QCD coupling should be taken to run with Q_s in this crossover, and describe the universality properties (if any) of observables in the transition region.
status_search_result: The question of how QCD transitions from the weakly coupled small-x saturation regime to the strongly coupled confining regime is a long-standing open conceptual problem in high-energy QCD. It remains an active research topic addressed by Color Glass Condensate, JIMWLK/BK evolution studies, and ongoing experimental programs (p+A at the LHC and forthcoming e+A at the EIC), with no complete theoretical solution reported.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
context_brief: Effective degrees of freedom in high-density QCD
original_question: Are classical fields still the correct effective degrees of freedom for describing the many-body system of strongly correlated gluons in QCD at high parton density, especially in the parton-saturation regime explored by proton-nucleus and electron-nucleus collisions?
self_contained_problem:
In quantum chromodynamics (QCD) at high parton densities, hadrons and nuclei are dominated by gluons whose occupation numbers grow until nonlinear interactions balance gluon emission, producing a characteristic saturation momentum scale $Q_s$. In the Color Glass Condensate (CGC) framework, fast partons are treated as static color sources with random color charge density $\rho^a(x_\perp)$ governed by a weight functional $W_Y[\rho]$ (with rapidity $Y$ evolution given by the JIMWLK equation), while slower gluons are described by classical Yang–Mills fields $A^\mu_a$ obeying $[D_\mu, F^{\mu\nu}]_a = J^\nu_a$ sourced by $\rho^a$. Observables are computed as path integrals $\langle \mathcal{O}\rangle = \int \mathcal{D}\rho\, W_Y[\rho]\, \mathcal{O}[A_{\rm cl}[\rho]]$ together with quantum fluctuations on top of these classical solutions.

Determine whether classical color fields, in the sense above, remain the correct effective degrees of freedom for the strongly correlated many-gluon system of QCD in the saturation regime probed by proton–nucleus and electron–nucleus collisions. Concretely: identify a parametric regime (in terms of $Q_s$, $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$, the strong coupling $\alpha_s(Q_s)$, the atomic number $A$, and the rapidity $Y$) and an observable for which the leading-order classical-field description, supplemented by the standard small-$x$ quantum evolution, either (i) provides a controlled approximation to full QCD with quantifiable corrections, or (ii) demonstrably fails, requiring a different effective description (for instance, one in which the relevant degrees of freedom are not classical fields).
category_tag: Color Glass Condensate and parton saturation
status_search_result: The question of whether classical color fields are the correct effective degrees of freedom in saturated QCD is conceptual and remains an active research direction. The CGC effective theory continues to be developed and tested phenomenologically at RHIC and the LHC, and is a central motivation for the Electron-Ion Collider, but no definitive proof of its validity (or its replacement) in the strongly correlated saturation regime has been established. The status is therefore best characterized as open.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
context_brief: Linear versus nonlinear description of inclusive e+A DIS
original_question: If nonlinear running-coupling Balitsky-Kovchegov evolution successfully predicts nuclear-to-proton structure-function ratios in inclusive electron-nucleus deep inelastic scattering, can the linear EPS09 nuclear parton-distribution approach simultaneously accommodate both F2 and FL electron-nucleus data when saturation sets in according to the rcBK prediction, or would failure to do so make the rcBK-based description uniquely favored? Here F2 and FL are the two structure functions whose linear combination gives the total virtual-photon–nucleus cross section and which provide access to integrated quark and gluon distributions, respectively.
self_contained_problem:
Consider inclusive deep inelastic scattering of electrons off a nucleus A, e + A → e + X, whose total virtual-photon–nucleus cross section is determined by the two structure functions F2(x, Q^2) and FL(x, Q^2). These provide access, respectively, to the integrated quark and gluon distributions of the nucleus at small Bjorken x and photon virtuality Q^2.

Two theoretical descriptions are considered:

(i) A nonlinear small-x description in which the dipole–nucleus scattering amplitude evolves according to the running-coupling Balitsky–Kovchegov (rcBK) equation,
    ∂_Y N(r, Y) = ∫ d^2 r1 K_rc(r, r1, r2) [N(r1, Y) + N(r2, Y) − N(r, Y) − N(r1, Y) N(r2, Y)],
where r = r1 + r2, Y = ln(1/x), and K_rc is the Balitsky running-coupling kernel; this approach implements gluon saturation with a nuclear saturation scale Q_s,A^2(x).

(ii) A linear collinear-factorization description using the EPS09 nuclear parton distribution functions at next-to-leading order, in which F2 and FL are obtained from convolutions of nuclear quark and gluon PDFs with the standard DIS coefficient functions.

Assume that, at sufficiently small x and moderate Q^2, the rcBK framework correctly predicts the nuclear-to-proton ratios F2^A/F2^p (and the corresponding FL ratio), with saturation effects setting in at the rcBK-predicted values of Q_s,A^2(x).

Question. In the kinematic regime where the rcBK prediction implies the onset of saturation, can the linear EPS09 nuclear PDF framework be tuned, within its uncertainty bands, to simultaneously reproduce both the F2 and FL electron–nucleus data that are consistent with the rcBK prediction? If no choice of nuclear PDFs within the EPS09 (linear DGLAP) framework can describe F2 and FL simultaneously under these conditions, then the rcBK-based nonlinear description provides the unique consistent data description; determine whether such a simultaneous linear description is possible.
status_search_result: Comparisons of EPS09 nuclear PDFs with rcBK-based saturation predictions for inclusive e+A DIS structure functions are an active area of Electron-Ion Collider physics studies. Definitive electron–nucleus F2 and FL data at small x do not yet exist (the EIC is under construction), so the discriminating measurement that would resolve whether linear EPS09 can simultaneously accommodate F2 and FL when saturation sets in has not been performed; the question remains open.

paper_title: Open questions in QCD at high parton density
original_question: In electron-nucleus diffractive vector-meson production or deeply virtual Compton scattering, can the incoherent diffractive background from nuclear breakup be removed efficiently enough to access the first minimum and maximum of the momentum-transfer distribution, thereby enabling extraction of transverse spatial distributions and correlations of partons from the t dependence of the cross section?
self_contained_problem:
Consider exclusive diffractive vector-meson production in electron–nucleus scattering, e + A → e' + V + A', where V is a vector meson (e.g., J/ψ or φ), or, when the produced particle is a real photon, deeply virtual Compton scattering e + A → e' + γ + A'. Let t denote the square of the four-momentum transferred to the nuclear target. The coherent component of the cross section, in which the nucleus remains intact, is related by a two-dimensional Fourier transform in the transverse momentum to the spatial distribution (and correlations) of partons in the transverse plane of the nucleus. The incoherent component, in which the nucleus breaks up into its constituent nucleons, contributes a background that grows relative to the coherent signal at moderate and large |t|, and tends to obscure the diffractive minima and secondary maxima of dσ_coh/dt.

For diffractive J/ψ and φ production off a heavy nucleus such as gold, determine whether there exists an experimentally realizable procedure (for instance, vetoing on emitted nucleons, neutrons, or nuclear fragments, or otherwise tagging nuclear breakup) that suppresses the incoherent diffractive contribution to a level small enough, over the relevant range of |t|, that the first diffractive minimum and the subsequent maximum of the coherent t-distribution can be cleanly resolved. If such a procedure exists, quantify the required rejection efficiency, and demonstrate that the resulting measurement permits the extraction, via Fourier transformation in t, of the transverse spatial distribution and parton–parton transverse correlations in the nucleus.
category_tag: diffractive vector-meson production in eA collisions
status_search_result: The question concerns whether incoherent nuclear-breakup background can be suppressed enough at a future electron-ion collider to expose the first diffractive minimum/maximum in coherent J/ψ (and φ) production off heavy nuclei. EIC Yellow Report studies and subsequent simulations (e.g., using BeAGLE and zero-degree-calorimeter / forward-neutron vetoing) indicate this is considered feasible in principle, with rejection at the 1–2% level needed; however a definitive experimental demonstration awaits EIC operations, so the question remains open as of the present.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
context_brief: Initial-state model selection and data constraints
original_question: In relativistic heavy-ion collisions that aim to create and characterize a quark-gluon plasma, what is the best model for the fluctuating initial state, and what constraints can existing flow and particle-correlation data already place on that model?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions (such as Au+Au at RHIC or Pb+Pb at the LHC), the early-time configuration of energy/entropy density deposited in the transverse plane—the "initial state"—fluctuates event by event due to nucleon positions, sub-nucleonic structure, and color-charge fluctuations. This initial state is then evolved by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics and hadronic transport to produce final-state observables such as the azimuthal flow harmonics v_n (Fourier coefficients of the single-particle azimuthal distribution) and multi-particle azimuthal correlations.

Formulate and identify the best physical model for this fluctuating initial state. Concretely:

(a) Within the broad space of candidate frameworks—including independent-nucleon Glauber Monte Carlo models, constituent-quark/sub-nucleonic Glauber variants, Color Glass Condensate–based descriptions (e.g., KLN, MC-KLN, IP-Glasma), parametric ansätze interpolating between wounded-nucleon and binary-collision scaling (e.g., reduced-thickness/TRENTo-type entropy depositions), and saturation-based pQCD minijet approaches (e.g., EKRT)—determine which choice of geometry, fluctuation spectrum, and entropy/energy deposition rule best reproduces measured observables across collision systems and energies.

(b) Quantify what constraints currently available flow data—including the centrality dependence of v_2, v_3, v_4, …, event-by-event v_n distributions, event-plane correlations, two- and multi-particle cumulants, and transverse-momentum-dependent correlations—place on (i) the eccentricity spectrum {ε_n} of the initial state, (ii) the granularity/correlation length of fluctuations, and (iii) the parameters (e.g., entropy-deposition exponent, nucleon width, sub-nucleonic structure) of such models, when convolved with viscous hydrodynamic response.

State the best-fitting model and the resulting allowed region of its parameters.

Bayesian inference studies (e.g., using TRENTo + viscous hydrodynamics) have substantially narrowed the allowed parameter space, and newer frameworks (IP-Glasma, MC-EKRT, sub-nucleonic Glauber) continue to be proposed and tested at Quark Matter 2025. No single model has been established as definitively "best"; multiple candidates remain compatible with data within current uncertainties, so the problem is partially constrained but still open.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: What is the current uncertainty in the viscosity and transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma inferred from anisotropic-flow observables, and what strategy would best reduce that uncertainty?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision modeled by viscous relativistic hydrodynamics, in which the produced quark-gluon plasma is described as a fluid with temperature-dependent specific shear viscosity η/s(T) and specific bulk viscosity ζ/s(T). The initial state of the fluid at proper time τ_0 is given by a (fluctuating) energy-density profile ε(x,y) determined by a chosen initial-condition model (e.g. Glauber, KLN, or IP-Glasma type), and the fluid evolves until freeze-out, after which produced hadrons are sampled and their azimuthal momentum distribution is analyzed. For each event, the anisotropic flow coefficients v_n (n = 2, 3, 4, …) are defined as the Fourier coefficients of the single-particle azimuthal distribution dN/dφ ∝ 1 + 2 Σ_n v_n cos[n(φ − Ψ_n)], and one further considers their event-by-event distributions, mixed cumulants, and correlations between event-plane angles Ψ_n.

(a) Given the family of physically admissible initial-state models and the freedom in η/s(T) and ζ/s(T), determine the present quantitative uncertainty (i.e. the range of values consistent with measured anisotropic-flow observables across collision systems and beam energies) in the transport coefficients η/s(T) and ζ/s(T) of the quark-gluon plasma inferred from anisotropic-flow data.

(b) Identify an optimal strategy — specifying which combinations of flow observables (e.g. v_n at multiple harmonics, event-by-event distributions, multi-particle cumulants, symmetric cumulants, event-plane correlations, system-size and beam-energy scans) and which model-comparison methodology — that would most effectively reduce the joint uncertainty on η/s(T) and ζ/s(T) by disentangling initial-state fluctuations from medium response.
status_search_result: Bayesian global analyses of heavy-ion data (e.g. Duke/JETSCAPE collaborations, 2019–2024) have constrained η/s(T) and ζ/s(T) of the QGP to within roughly a factor of 2–3, with sizable residual uncertainties driven by initial-state model ambiguity. The problem of fully separating initial-state fluctuations from transport is widely regarded as still open; ongoing work uses higher harmonics, symmetric cumulants, and event-plane correlations as discriminators, but no unique optimal strategy has been established.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: How can experimental measurements and theoretical calculations distinguish correlations caused by initial-state effects from correlations generated by collective final-state evolution in relativistic heavy-ion collisions?
self_contained_problem:
In a relativistic heavy-ion collision, two nuclei collide at ultra-relativistic energies and produce a fireball of strongly interacting matter whose subsequent evolution can be modeled hydrodynamically. The azimuthal distribution of produced particles in the transverse plane is conventionally expanded in a Fourier series,

dN/dφ ∝ 1 + 2 Σ_{n≥1} v_n cos[ n(φ − Ψ_n) ],

where the harmonic flow coefficients v_n and event-plane angles Ψ_n fluctuate event by event. Two-particle azimuthal correlations are characterized by the harmonics V_{nΔ}(p_T^a, p_T^t) = ⟨cos[n(φ_a − φ_t)]⟩ as functions of the trigger and associated transverse momenta p_T^t and p_T^a. These correlations may originate either from initial-state geometric and quantum fluctuations of the colliding nuclei (e.g., fluctuating positions of nucleons, color-charge fluctuations, gluon-saturation effects encoded in spatial eccentricities ε_n) or from the collective final-state evolution of the produced medium (hydrodynamic response converting initial spatial anisotropies into momentum-space anisotropies v_n).

Formulate and analyze observables and theoretical procedures that can unambiguously separate these two sources of correlation. Specifically:

(a) Identify a set of measurable correlation functions (including factorization tests of V_{nΔ}(p_T^a, p_T^t) into a product v_n(p_T^a) v_n(p_T^t), multi-particle cumulants v_n{2k}, event-by-event distributions P(v_n), symmetric cumulants SC(m,n), and event-plane correlations ⟨cos(m Ψ_m + n Ψ_n + …)⟩) whose values discriminate between an initial-state-only origin and a collective hydrodynamic origin.

(b) Determine theoretically, within a chosen initial-condition model (e.g., Glauber, KLN, IP-Glasma) coupled to a hydrodynamic + hadronic-cascade description, which features of these observables are robust signatures of final-state collectivity rather than artifacts of initial-state correlations.

(c) Establish quantitative criteria (e.g., breakdown of factorization, system-size dependence, multiplicity dependence in small collision systems such as p+p and p+Pb) under which collective behavior can be claimed to dominate over initial-state correlations.
status_search_result: Distinguishing initial-state from final-state collective effects remains an actively studied open question in heavy-ion physics. Substantial progress has been made (e.g., factorization tests of V_{nΔ}, symmetric cumulants, event-plane correlations, and observation of collective-like signals in small systems), but no consensus, fully model-independent separation has been established, especially in small collision systems.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: How should the longitudinal direction in fluctuating initial-state profiles be modeled and constrained in 3+1-dimensional viscous hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions, given that existing studies of longitudinal fluctuations remain exploratory and η- and Δη-dependent particle correlations may provide useful information?
self_contained_problem:
In the framework of 3+1-dimensional viscous relativistic hydrodynamic simulations of ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions, the transverse profile of fluctuating initial conditions has been extensively studied, while the modeling of the longitudinal direction (along the beam axis, parametrized by spacetime rapidity η) remains far less constrained. Develop and constrain a model of the longitudinal structure of the fluctuating initial energy/entropy density (and any associated initial flow profile) such that:

1. The model specifies, on an event-by-event basis, the η-dependence of the local energy density and the correlations between transverse fluctuations at different values of η (including any rapidity-dependent decorrelation of the transverse geometry).
2. The model is implemented as initial data for a 3+1-dimensional viscous hydrodynamic evolution with realistic transport coefficients and a hadronic freeze-out prescription.
3. The resulting predictions for pseudorapidity-dependent particle correlations — in particular the single-particle pseudorapidity distribution dN/dη, two-particle correlations C(η₁, η₂) and their dependence on the rapidity gap Δη = η₁ − η₂, and the longitudinal decorrelation of anisotropic flow harmonics vₙ between separated pseudorapidity windows — are quantitatively reproduced and used to fix the parameters of the longitudinal initial-state model.

Provide such a model together with the constraints on its parameters extracted from η- and Δη-dependent observables, and a comprehensive characterization of longitudinal initial-state fluctuations within 3+1-dimensional viscous hydrodynamics.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made since the question was posed: 3+1D viscous hydrodynamic codes (e.g., CLVisc) coupled with longitudinally resolved initial-state models (e.g., McDIPPER, sub-nucleonic fluctuation models) now produce quantitative predictions for longitudinal flow decorrelation and directed flow, and η- / Δη-dependent correlations have been used to constrain longitudinal fluctuations. However, a fully comprehensive, predictive model of longitudinal initial-state fluctuations is not yet established, and the topic remains an active area of research.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: What are the size and importance of initial flow—the initial velocity or momentum fields produced before hydrodynamic evolution—and how should the complete energy-momentum tensor, including shear-stress components, be used to initialize hydrodynamic simulations of heavy-ion collisions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a relativistic heavy-ion collision in which a hydrodynamic description of the produced quark–gluon medium is initialized at some proper time τ₀ from a pre-equilibrium stage. The full local energy–momentum tensor T^{μν}(x) at τ₀ admits a Landau decomposition

T^{μν} = ε u^μ u^ν − (P + Π)(g^{μν} − u^μ u^ν) + π^{μν},

where ε is the energy density, u^μ is the timelike flow four-velocity (the unique timelike eigenvector of T^{μν}), P(ε) is the equilibrium pressure given by an equation of state, Π is the bulk viscous pressure, and π^{μν} is the symmetric, traceless, transverse shear-stress tensor (u_μ π^{μν} = 0, π^μ_μ = 0).

Pre-equilibrium dynamics generically generate at τ₀ a nontrivial transverse flow velocity field u^μ(x) (the "initial flow") and nonzero dissipative components π^{μν}(x), Π(x), in addition to the energy density ε(x).

Quantify the magnitude and dynamical importance of the initial flow field u^μ at τ₀, and determine how the complete energy–momentum tensor T^{μν}—including its shear-stress components π^{μν} (and bulk Π)—should be used to initialize subsequent viscous hydrodynamic evolution, in such a way that final-state observables (in particular anisotropic flow coefficients v_n and their event-by-event distributions) are correctly reproduced. Specifically:

(a) Estimate the typical size of the transverse components of u^μ at τ₀ relative to the local speed of sound, and characterize their spatial structure on an event-by-event basis.

(b) Determine the quantitative impact on the final flow harmonics v_n of including, versus neglecting, (i) the initial transverse flow u^μ and (ii) the initial shear-stress tensor π^{μν}, when initializing hydrodynamics.

(c) Provide a prescription for matching pre-equilibrium dynamics to hydrodynamics that consistently transfers all components of T^{μν} at τ₀.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: pre-equilibrium frameworks (e.g., KøMPøST and QCD kinetic theory matching) now provide initial conditions for all second-order hydrodynamic variables, including initial flow and shear stress, and recent linear-response frameworks (e.g., 2024 work on initial energy-momentum to final flow) systematically quantify how each component of T^{μν} at τ₀ contributes to final flow harmonics. However, a full consensus on the precise size and importance of initial flow across all collision systems (especially small systems vs. AA) is still being refined, so the question is partially solved rather than fully resolved.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: How can data and modeling constrain the scale and amplitude of initial-state fluctuations in heavy-ion collisions, such as flux-tube radius, Gaussian width, or correlation length, while tying those constraints to a specified physical assumption about the initial state?
self_contained_problem:
In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the spatial profile of energy or entropy density deposited just after the collision fluctuates event by event. Models of these initial-state fluctuations are typically parametrized by a length scale (such as the transverse radius of color flux tubes, the Gaussian smearing width assigned to participant nucleons or partons, or a two-point correlation length of the deposited density) and an amplitude (the variance of the local density fluctuations).

Formulate and carry out a quantitative program with the following requirements:

(a) Fix a definite physical assumption about the microscopic origin of the fluctuations (for example: independent Gaussian sources centered on participant nucleons; color-charge fluctuations in a Color-Glass-Condensate / Glasma flux-tube picture with a transverse scale set by the saturation momentum Q_s; or a hot-spot picture based on constituent quarks).

(b) Within that assumption, define precisely the fluctuation scale parameter σ (e.g. flux-tube radius, Gaussian width, or correlation length) and the fluctuation amplitude parameter A (e.g. the relative variance of the deposited density at a point).

(c) Identify a set of experimental observables in heavy-ion collisions (such as the centrality dependence of anisotropic flow harmonics v_n{2}, v_n{4}, event-by-event v_n distributions, mixed harmonic correlators / symmetric cumulants, or correlations between flow magnitudes and mean transverse momentum) whose dependence on σ and A is monotonic and distinguishable from the dependence on subsequent hydrodynamic transport coefficients (shear and bulk viscosity).

(d) Determine, by combining these observables with viscous hydrodynamic evolution, quantitative confidence regions for σ and A that are consistent with the data, and demonstrate to what extent these constraints depend on, or remain robust against, the choice of physical assumption in (a).

The problem is to provide such a constraint procedure and to state the resulting allowed ranges of σ and A together with their dependence on the underlying physical picture.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made via Bayesian analyses combining viscous hydrodynamics with multi-observable flow data (e.g. Phys. Rev. C 89, 064907 and the Duke/JETSCAPE Bayesian programs), yielding constraints on nucleon Gaussian widths and sub-nucleon hot-spot scales. However, the inferred fluctuation scale and amplitude remain model-dependent (TRENTo vs. IP-Glasma vs. EKRT vs. constituent-quark pictures) and recent works (2024–2025) continue to refine these constraints, so the problem is partially solved rather than closed.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
context_brief: Observable sensitivity and general medium response
original_question: Which aspects of fluctuating initial conditions is each final-state observable most sensitive to, and can a general characterization of hydrodynamic medium response be developed well enough to place significant constraints on both initial conditions and quark-gluon-plasma medium properties?
self_contained_problem:
In ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions, the colliding nuclei produce a hot, dense fireball whose subsequent evolution is well described by relativistic viscous hydrodynamics. The initial state of the fireball, just after the collision, exhibits event-by-event fluctuations of the energy/entropy density in the transverse plane. These fluctuations can be characterized by spatial cumulants such as the eccentricities ε_n e^{i n Φ_n} = − ⟨r^n e^{i n φ}⟩ / ⟨r^n⟩ (n ≥ 2), as well as by higher-order radial and azimuthal cumulants and by finer-grained measures of small-scale structure. After hydrodynamic evolution and freeze-out, the produced hadrons exhibit final-state correlations encoded in the complex anisotropic flow harmonics V_n = v_n e^{i n Ψ_n}, where dN/dφ ∝ 1 + 2 Σ_n v_n cos[n(φ − Ψ_n)], together with their event-by-event distributions, mixed harmonic correlators, symmetric cumulants, principal-component decompositions of p_T-differential flow, and event-plane decorrelation observables.

(a) For each such final-state observable O, determine quantitatively the aspects of the initial state (which spatial cumulant, which length scale, which radial weight, or which combination thereof) to which O is most sensitive, in the sense of providing a response map from initial-state characterizations to O that is approximately linear, weakly contaminated by other modes, and stable across model variations.

(b) Develop a general characterization of the hydrodynamic medium response — i.e., a parameter-independent or controllably parameter-dependent map from initial-state fluctuations to final-state observables — that is precise enough to allow simultaneous quantitative constraints on (i) the properties of the initial conditions (e.g., scale of fluctuations, granularity, geometric cumulants) and (ii) the transport properties of the quark-gluon plasma (e.g., shear viscosity to entropy density ratio η/s, bulk viscosity ζ/s, and equation of state).

Provide such a sensitivity classification and general medium-response framework, or prove that no such characterization with the required precision exists.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on characterizing the hydrodynamic medium response and on identifying which initial-state features dominate each flow observable. Linear and nonlinear response coefficients V_n = κ_n ε_n + ... are now well established for low harmonics, principal-component analyses connect higher-order cumulants of the initial geometry to subleading flow modes, and Bayesian global analyses simultaneously constrain QGP transport coefficients and initial-condition parameters. However, a fully general, model-independent characterization of medium response sufficient to tightly disentangle initial conditions from QGP properties remains an active research goal, with recent works (2023–2025) still proposing new statistical decompositions and using nuclear-structure information to break degeneracies. The problem is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: How should theoretical calculations and experimental analyses define and match centrality classes so that comparisons between heavy-ion data and models yield meaningful quantitative statements about quark-gluon-plasma transport coefficients, especially when impact parameter, initial gluon number, entropy production, and final particle yields must be related?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an ensemble of relativistic heavy-ion collision events characterized by an impact parameter b ≥ 0 (the transverse distance between the centers of the two nuclei). For each event, define the following observables:

  • N_g(b): the number of gluons produced in the early (pre-equilibrium) stage, modeled by a chosen initial-condition prescription (e.g., a saturation-based or Glauber-type model).
  • S_0(b): the initial entropy of the produced matter, computed from the initial energy/entropy density profile.
  • S_f(b): the final entropy after a dissipative hydrodynamic evolution with specified transport coefficients (in particular shear viscosity over entropy density η/s and bulk viscosity ζ/s); in general S_f ≥ S_0 due to viscous entropy production.
  • N_ch(b): the final charged-particle multiplicity obtained from the freeze-out of the evolved fluid.

On the experimental side, events are sorted into centrality classes C_k ⊂ [0,1] (e.g., 0–5%, 5–10%, …) by ranking events according to a measured observable M (typically charged-particle multiplicity in a chosen pseudorapidity window or transverse-energy deposition in a forward calorimeter), and computing the cumulative fraction of the inelastic cross section.

Formulate and solve the following matching problem:

(1) Define a precise mapping Φ between theoretical event classes (parametrized, e.g., by b, N_g, or S_0) and experimental centrality classes C_k that is consistent in the presence of dissipative entropy production, i.e., such that the event-by-event distribution of the chosen sorting observable M predicted by the model agrees in distribution with the experimental one within the same class.

(2) Derive quantitative bounds, as functions of η/s and ζ/s, on the systematic uncertainty introduced into extracted transport coefficients when one identifies centrality via b, via N_g, via S_0, or via N_ch, and show under which assumptions these prescriptions become equivalent.

(3) Specify the minimal set of assumptions relating b ↦ N_g ↦ S_0 ↦ S_f ↦ N_ch that must be verified (and propose verification procedures) so that comparisons between hydrodynamic model output and measured flow harmonics v_n in matched centrality classes yield unbiased estimates of η/s and ζ/s.

The goal is a centrality-matching framework for which one can prove (or numerically demonstrate to a stated precision) that the inferred transport coefficients are independent of the centrality-selection criterion.
status_search_result: This is a methodological open question in relativistic heavy-ion physics. Subsequent literature (Glauber Monte Carlo refinements, Bayesian analyses such as the Duke/JETSCAPE programs, and IP-Glasma+MUSIC studies) has made substantial progress on centrality definition and on extracting η/s and ζ/s, but no universally accepted, rigorously verified mapping between theoretical and experimental centrality classes that controls the dissipative entropy-production bias has been established. The problem is therefore best classified as still open / partially addressed.

context_brief: Future measurements for non-flow and mode mixing

In relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the azimuthal distribution of produced particles is decomposed into Fourier harmonics with coefficients v_n (n = 1, 2, 3, ...) characterizing the anisotropic flow. Define the two-particle correlation harmonic V_{nΔ}(p_T^a, p_T^t) as the n-th Fourier coefficient of the relative-azimuthal-angle distribution of pairs of particles with transverse momenta p_T^a (associated) and p_T^t (trigger); flow factorization is the hypothesis V_{nΔ}(p_T^a, p_T^t) = v_n(p_T^a) v_n(p_T^t). Let Ψ_m denote the event plane of harmonic order m, and let v_n{Ψ_m} denote the n-th flow coefficient measured with respect to Ψ_m (with m ≠ n in general).

Design and propose a program of measurements that:
(a) tests the factorization of V_{nΔ} over a wide range of trigger and associated transverse momenta, and analogously over a wide range of trigger and associated pseudorapidities, in order to discriminate genuine bulk collective anisotropies from non-flow contributions and to characterize event-by-event flow fluctuations;
(b) measures v_n coefficients with respect to event planes Ψ_m of different harmonic order (m ≠ n), thereby probing the nonlinear hydrodynamic response and mode mixing between harmonics.

Identify which specific observables, kinematic regions, and combinations of (n, m) are most effective for separating bulk flow from non-flow effects, for quantifying flow fluctuations, and for isolating hydrodynamic mode-mixing contributions.
status_search_result: This is an open-ended program of proposed future measurements rather than a precise mathematical conjecture. Many of the suggested measurements (factorization breaking of V_{nΔ} in p_T and η, and v_n with respect to Ψ_m for m ≠ n) have been performed by ATLAS, CMS, and ALICE in subsequent years, providing partial information on flow fluctuations and mode mixing, but the broader program of fully disentangling non-flow, fluctuations, and mode mixing remains active research.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: Can untriggered two-particle correlations in events containing a 50–100 GeV jet, compared against minimum-bias events with a consistent centrality selection, provide insight into the interplay between jet-medium response and pure bulk-evolution effects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider relativistic heavy-ion collisions producing a quark–gluon medium whose bulk evolution generates azimuthal two-particle angular correlations C(Δφ, Δη) among soft hadrons (so-called flow / bulk-evolution correlations). In addition, when a hard parton traverses the medium and fragments into a reconstructed jet of transverse momentum in the range 50–100 GeV, the deposition and redistribution of energy in the medium (jet–medium response) contributes additional structure to the soft two-particle correlation function.

Define two event classes at fixed collision centrality:
(a) a "jet-triggered" sample: events containing at least one reconstructed jet with 50 GeV ≤ pT^jet ≤ 100 GeV;
(b) a "minimum-bias" sample: events selected without any jet requirement.

paper_title: Initial state fluctuations and final state correlations: Status and open questions
original_question: What is the physical meaning of the event-plane correlations measured by the ATLAS collaboration, and can additional theory comparisons clarify their interpretation?
self_contained_problem:
In ultrarelativistic heavy-ion collisions, the azimuthal distribution of produced particles in each event is characterized by harmonic flow vectors $\vec{V}_n = v_n e^{i n \Psi_n}$, where $v_n$ is the magnitude of the $n$-th order anisotropic flow and $\Psi_n$ is the corresponding event-plane angle, for $n = 2, 3, 4, \ldots$. Multi-plane correlators are defined as event averages of the form
$$\langle \cos(c_1 n_1 \Psi_{n_1} + c_2 n_2 \Psi_{n_2} + \cdots + c_k n_k \Psi_{n_k}) \rangle,$$
with integer coefficients $c_i$ satisfying $\sum_i c_i n_i = 0$, measured as functions of collision centrality.

Provide a quantitative theoretical interpretation of such event-plane correlators measured in Pb–Pb collisions at the LHC. Specifically:

(a) Determine, within an event-by-event hydrodynamic (or hybrid initial-state plus hydrodynamic) framework, the precise mapping between the initial-state geometric eccentricities $\varepsilon_n e^{i n \Phi_n}$ (defined by $\varepsilon_n e^{i n \Phi_n} = -\langle r^2 e^{i n \phi}\rangle / \langle r^2\rangle$ for $n \ge 2$ in the transverse plane of the energy-density distribution) and the final-state event planes $\Psi_n$, including linear and nonlinear (mode-mixing) response coefficients.

(b) Identify which of these correlators are dominated by linear response (so that they reflect correlations already present in the initial geometry) versus those dominated by nonlinear hydrodynamic mode mixing, and quantify the centrality dependence of each contribution.

(c) Determine whether existing initial-state models (e.g., Glauber-based or saturation-based fluctuation models) combined with viscous hydrodynamics can simultaneously reproduce the centrality dependence and signs of all measured event-plane correlators, and identify which correlators provide independent constraints on the initial-state geometry versus on the transport properties of the produced medium.
status_search_result: Subsequent theoretical work has substantially clarified the interpretation: nonlinear hydrodynamic response formalisms qualitatively reproduce the ATLAS event-plane correlations, and AMPT transport calculations achieve quantitative agreement for many correlators, while pure hydrodynamic calculations achieve only qualitative agreement. The decomposition into linear and nonlinear (mode-mixing) contributions is now established for the lowest harmonics, but no single model framework simultaneously reproduces all measured correlators across centralities, so the interpretation is partially—but not fully—resolved.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
context_brief: periodic stabilization in dimensions two or three
original_question: In dimensions 2 and 3, suppose a control system satisfies small-time reachability together with a Lie algebra condition. Do these hypotheses imply the existence of a periodic stabilizing feedback or periodic stabilization mechanism? The source states that positive answers are already known in the other dimensions from the author's work.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a smooth control-affine system on $\mathbb{R}^n$ of the form
$$\dot{x} = f(x,u), \qquad x \in \mathbb{R}^n,\ u \in \mathbb{R}^m,\quad f(0,0)=0,$$
with $f$ smooth. Recall the following notions:

- The system is small-time locally controllable at the equilibrium $(0,0)$ if for every $T>0$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there exists $\eta>0$ such that for every $x_0,x_1\in\mathbb{R}^n$ with $|x_0|,|x_1|<\eta$ there exists a measurable control $u:[0,T]\to\mathbb{R}^m$ with $\|u\|_\infty<\varepsilon$ steering the state from $x_0$ at time $0$ to $x_1$ at time $T$.
- The system satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition (LARC) at $0$ if the Lie algebra generated by the vector fields $\{f(\cdot,u): u\in\mathbb{R}^m\}$ has full rank $n$ at $0$.
- The system is locally asymptotically stabilizable by means of a periodic time-varying feedback if there exist $T>0$ and a continuous map $u:\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}^m$, with $u(0,t)=0$ for every $t$ and $u(x,t+T)=u(x,t)$ for every $(x,t)$, such that the origin of the closed-loop system $\dot{x}=f(x,u(x,t))$ is locally asymptotically stable (in the sense of Lyapunov, uniformly in the initial time).

It is known that for every $n\notin\{2,3\}$, every smooth control-affine system on $\mathbb{R}^n$ that is small-time locally controllable at $0$ and satisfies the Lie algebra rank condition at $0$ is locally asymptotically stabilizable by means of a periodic time-varying feedback.

Question: Does the same conclusion hold when $n=2$ or $n=3$? That is, for $n\in\{2,3\}$, does small-time local controllability at the origin together with the Lie algebra rank condition imply the existence of a continuous periodic time-varying feedback that locally asymptotically stabilizes the origin?
status_search_result: Search results indicate that Coron established periodic time-varying feedback stabilization of small-time locally controllable systems for all dimensions except 2 and 3, and the cases $n=2,3$ remain a well-known open problem with no announcement of a resolution found in recent literature.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
context_brief: blowup avoidance for nonlinear heat equation
original_question: For a one-dimensional heat equation with a cubic nonlinearity, can the blowup phenomenon be avoided by a suitable control strategy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the one-dimensional semilinear heat equation on a bounded interval $(0,L)$ with a cubic nonlinearity, controlled through the boundary (or through an interior control supported on a subset $\omega \subset (0,L)$):
$$
\begin{cases}
y_t(t,x) - y_{xx}(t,x) + y(t,x)^3 = u(t,x)\,\mathbf{1}_\omega(x), & (t,x)\in (0,T)\times(0,L),\\
y(t,0) = v_0(t),\quad y(t,L) = v_1(t), & t\in(0,T),\\
y(0,x) = y_0(x), & x\in(0,L),
\end{cases}
$$
(or, equivalently, the analogous equation $y_t - y_{xx} = y^3 + u\mathbf{1}_\omega$ with the focusing cubic source term that is known to produce finite-time blowup of uncontrolled solutions for sufficiently large initial data). It is well known that, in the absence of control, suitable initial data $y_0$ lead to solutions whose $L^\infty$-norm diverges in finite time (blowup).

Question: Given an arbitrary initial datum $y_0$ in a natural function space (e.g.\ $L^\infty(0,L)$ or $H^1_0(0,L)$), does there always exist an admissible control (interior locally distributed, or boundary) such that the resulting solution is globally defined for all $t\ge 0$, i.e.\ the blowup phenomenon can always be avoided by an appropriate control strategy? Furthermore, is the equation small-time globally controllable, in the sense that for every pair of states $y_0, y_1$ and every $T>0$ there exists a control steering $y_0$ to $y_1$ in time $T$?
status_search_result: Web search reveals active and partial progress on controllability of semilinear parabolic equations with cubic-type nonlinearities (e.g. local null controllability for parabolic systems with cubic coupling, and feedback controllability of blow-up points), but no definitive resolution of the global blowup-avoidance question or small-time controllability for the one-dimensional heat equation with focusing cubic nonlinearity was found. The problem appears to remain open in its full generality.

paper_title: Some open problems in control theory.
original_question: Is the Navier-Stokes equation controllable?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Omega\subset\mathbb{R}^d$ ($d=2$ or $3$) be a smooth bounded domain, and let $\Gamma\subset\partial\Omega$ be a nonempty open subset of the boundary. Consider the incompressible Navier–Stokes system
$$\partial_t u + (u\cdot\nabla)u - \nu\Delta u + \nabla p = 0, \qquad \nabla\cdot u = 0 \quad\text{in }(0,T)\times\Omega,$$
with the no-slip boundary condition $u = 0$ on $(0,T)\times(\partial\Omega\setminus\Gamma)$, and a boundary control $u = g$ acting on $(0,T)\times\Gamma$ (with $g$ chosen subject only to the compatibility constraint $\int_\Gamma g\cdot n\,d\sigma = 0$).

Question: Is this system globally controllable? That is, given any time $T>0$ and any two finite-energy divergence-free states $u_0, u_1\in L^2(\Omega;\mathbb{R}^d)$ (with $\nabla\cdot u_0 = \nabla\cdot u_1 = 0$ and $u_0\cdot n = u_1\cdot n = 0$ on $\partial\Omega\setminus\Gamma$), does there exist a boundary control $g$ on $(0,T)\times\Gamma$ such that the corresponding solution satisfies $u(0,\cdot)=u_0$ and $u(T,\cdot)=u_1$?

In particular, decide the case $u_1 \equiv 0$ (global null controllability) under the no-slip boundary condition on $\partial\Omega\setminus\Gamma$.
status_search_result: Local exact controllability to trajectories has been established by Fursikov–Imanuvilov and Coron–Fursikov. Small-time global exact controllability is known under Navier slip-with-friction boundary conditions (Coron–Marbach–Sueur, JEMS 2020), and recent works treat curved boundaries with no-slip under additional hypotheses. The general problem of small-time global exact (or null) boundary controllability under the standard no-slip boundary condition, originally posed by J.-L. Lions, remains open.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Continuous measurement-based feedback versus direct coherent feedback
original_question: For a quantum system controlled either by continuous measurement-based feedback or by coherent feedback implemented through direct system-auxiliary coupling, what is the exact relationship between the two control paradigms when both are given the same dissipative resources? Is coherent feedback through direct coupling superior to continuous measurement-based feedback under those conditions, and if it is superior, does the advantage remain when the added dissipative resources are removed?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a primary quantum system $S$ coupled to an auxiliary quantum system $A$, together with a set of dissipative (Markovian) resources—e.g., a fixed collection of Lindblad operators or a fixed bath/probe field with prescribed coupling rates—that may be used to implement control of $S$. Two feedback paradigms are available:

(i) Continuous measurement-based feedback, in which the auxiliary $A$ and the dissipative resources are used to perform a continuous (e.g., homodyne, heterodyne, or photon-counting) quantum measurement of $S$, and the resulting classical record is fed back, in real time and possibly with arbitrary classical processing, to drive the Hamiltonian or Lindblad parameters of $S$.

(ii) Coherent feedback via direct system–auxiliary coupling, in which $S$ and $A$ interact through a unitary (Hamiltonian) coupling, with $A$ also subject to the same dissipative resources, and no measurement is ever performed.

Assume both paradigms are given the same dissipative resources and the same auxiliary Hilbert space.

(a) Determine the precise relationship between the classes of achievable controlled dynamics (e.g., as completely positive trace-preserving maps on $S$, or as steady states, or as input–output transformations) realizable by paradigm (i) and by paradigm (ii) under these matched resources.

(b) Decide whether paradigm (ii) is strictly more powerful than paradigm (i) under these matched resources, in the sense of strict inclusion of the achievable classes for some control objective (such as cooling, stabilization, entanglement generation, or noise suppression).

(c) If (ii) is strictly more powerful in (b), determine whether this strict superiority persists when the dissipative resources are removed, i.e., when paradigm (ii) is restricted to purely unitary $S$–$A$ coupling with no Lindblad terms acting on $A$.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made on comparing coherent and measurement-based feedback. Linear systems theory results (Yamamoto, Phys. Rev. X 4, 041029, 2014) show coherent feedback can outperform measurement feedback for some quantum-information tasks and that no-go theorems exclude measurement-based feedback from achieving backaction evasion, QND-variable generation, and decoherence-free subsystem creation, which coherent feedback can. Further studies (e.g., Phys. Rev. A 97, 062341; arXiv:1606.06507) give task-specific comparisons, sometimes showing coherent feedback matches measurement-based feedback. However, a complete general characterization of the relationship under matched dissipative resources, and a definitive resolution of whether any superiority of coherent feedback persists when dissipative resources are removed, has not been established in full generality, so the problem remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Measurement restrictions and geodesic entropy extraction
original_question: For feedback protocols implemented through irreversible coupling, can one quantitatively characterize how much performance is lost when the controller is restricted to measurement followed by conditional feedback, and can that loss be related to geodesic evolutions in the joint system-auxiliary Hilbert space that extract entropy as quickly as possible?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system $S$ with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$ coupled to an auxiliary system $A$ with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A$, evolving on the joint Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S\otimes\mathcal{H}_A$. Two paradigms of feedback control on $S$ are considered:

(i) Classical feedback control (CFC), in which $S$ is unitarily coupled to $A$ via an interaction Hamiltonian $H_{SA}$ (subject to a fixed operator-norm bound $\|H_{SA}\|\le E$), then $A$ is projectively measured, and a classically conditioned unitary is applied to $S$ based on the outcome.

(ii) Coherent feedback via irreversible coupling (CFIC), in which $S$ is coupled to $A$ (or to a continuum of auxiliary modes) by a one-way, irreversible quantum interaction (e.g., a cascaded / Markovian field-mediated coupling) of comparable energy scale, with no measurement performed and no classical information extracted.

For an initial mixed state $\rho_S$ of $S$, the entropy-extraction task is to drive $S$ to a chosen pure state (equivalently, to reduce the von Neumann entropy $S(\rho_S)$ to zero) in the shortest possible time $T$ subject to the energy bound on the system–auxiliary coupling.

It is known that, under such a Hamiltonian bound, the fastest CFC protocol that extracts all entropy from $S$ corresponds to following a geodesic in $\mathcal{H}_S\otimes\mathcal{H}_A$ (with respect to the Fubini–Study metric).

Problem. Quantitatively characterize the performance gap between CFIC and CFC for entropy extraction. Specifically:

(a) Define a precise figure of merit $\mathcal{P}(\rho_S, E, T)$ measuring how much entropy can be removed from $S$ in time $T$ under either paradigm, and prove a quantitative inequality of the form
$$\mathcal{P}_{\text{CFC}}(\rho_S, E, T) \;\ge\; \mathcal{P}_{\text{CFIC}}(\rho_S, E, T) + \Delta(\rho_S, E, T),$$
or its reverse, with an explicit nontrivial bound $\Delta$.

(b) Express the gap $\Delta$ in geometric terms by relating optimal CFIC trajectories to geodesics in $\mathcal{H}_S\otimes\mathcal{H}_A$, and identify the obstruction that prevents (or permits) a measurement-and-feedback protocol from saturating the geodesic bound achievable by irreversible coherent coupling.
status_search_result: No specific result was found establishing a quantitative inequality between measurement-based feedback and irreversible coherent feedback tied to geodesic entropy-extraction bounds. Related work on measurement-based quantum thermal machines and on geodesic optimal control of entangling operations exists, but does not appear to directly resolve the asked quantitative comparison. Status remains undetermined from available sources.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: Because coherent feedback implemented by unitary system-auxiliary interactions is naturally periodic rather than continuously dissipative, what forms of Hamiltonian are needed to realize continuous or quasi-continuous quantum feedback control, and in which regimes can one derive simple analytic formulas for the resulting steady-state control performance?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system $S$ with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_S$ coupled to an auxiliary quantum system (controller) $A$ with Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}_A$. A coherent feedback protocol is implemented by repeatedly letting the joint system evolve under a unitary $U=e^{-iH\tau/\hbar}$ on $\mathcal{H}_S\otimes\mathcal{H}_A$ generated by a joint Hamiltonian $H$, where the auxiliary $A$ is periodically reset (or refreshed) to a fixed state $\rho_A$ after each interaction interval $\tau>0$. Such a protocol is intrinsically periodic: in the limit of large period it is stroboscopic, while in the limit $\tau\to 0$ with appropriate scaling it should approximate a continuous feedback channel.

Address the following:

(a) Characterize the class of joint Hamiltonians $H$ on $\mathcal{H}_S\otimes\mathcal{H}_A$ (together with reset states $\rho_A$ and scaling of the interaction time $\tau$) for which the discrete, periodic coherent feedback dynamics converges, in a suitable limit, to a continuous-time evolution of the reduced state $\rho_S(t)=\mathrm{Tr}_A[\,\cdot\,]$ on $\mathcal{H}_S$ describable by a time-independent generator (i.e., a Lindblad-type or Hamiltonian-plus-dissipator master equation). Identify additionally those that yield "quasi-continuous" control, in which the periodicity is preserved but the stroboscopic dynamics is well-approximated on coarse-grained timescales by a smooth feedback law.

(b) For the classes identified in (a), derive — wherever possible — closed-form analytic expressions for the steady state $\rho_S^\infty=\lim_{t\to\infty}\rho_S(t)$ and for natural performance measures (e.g., expectation values of target observables, fidelity with a target state, or entropy reduction) as functions of the parameters $(H,\rho_A,\tau)$. Identify regimes (such as weak coupling, fast repetition, or specific symmetry classes of $H$) in which such analytic formulas exist.
status_search_result: A web search returned related work on coherent feedback, Floquet theory, and periodically driven quantum systems, but no result that systematically classifies the Hamiltonians realizing continuous/quasi-continuous coherent feedback together with closed-form steady-state performance formulas. The problem appears to remain open in the general form posed, with only partial progress in specific regimes (e.g., Gaussian/linear quantum systems and weak-coupling limits).

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
original_question: In the regime of good quantum control, what is the optimal protocol for preparing a target state by unitary interaction between the controlled system and auxiliary systems when the interaction strength with any given auxiliary is bounded, and how does the optimum depend on the number of auxiliary systems available?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a quantum system S with Hilbert space H_S and a collection of N auxiliary quantum systems A_1, ..., A_N with Hilbert spaces H_{A_1}, ..., H_{A_N}. Assume "good quantum control": fast, essentially unconstrained local unitary control is available on S and on each A_i individually (and on each A_i one may freely prepare and reset states). The only resource constraint is on the bipartite interactions: for every i, the time-dependent interaction Hamiltonian H_{S,A_i}(t) coupling S to A_i has bounded operator norm,
  ||H_{S,A_i}(t)|| ≤ J,
for a fixed constant J > 0. The full evolution is unitary and given by alternating arbitrary fast local control with interactions H_{S,A_i}(t) (possibly several auxiliaries simultaneously).

Starting from a fixed initial product state |ψ_0⟩_S ⊗ |0⟩_{A_1} ⊗ ... ⊗ |0⟩_{A_N}, the goal is to drive S into a prescribed target pure state |ψ_*⟩ ∈ H_S in minimum total time T (measuring time only during the bounded-norm interaction stages, since local control is free).

Determine the optimal protocol — i.e., the choice of interaction Hamiltonians {H_{S,A_i}(t)} and interleaved local unitaries — that minimizes the preparation time T(N, J) needed to reach |ψ_*⟩ exactly (or to within a fixed fidelity), and characterize the dependence of the optimum T(N, J) on the number N of auxiliary systems and on the interaction-strength bound J. In particular, establish the asymptotic scaling of the minimum preparation time as a function of N.

paper_title: Twenty open problems in quantum control
context_brief: Limits of linear networks for quantum error correction
original_question: For linear quantum systems coupled irreversibly through quantum fields, also called quantum linear networks, can one prove that such linear networks cannot implement quantum error correction, meaning correction of errors on arbitrary unknown quantum states?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of linear quantum networks defined as follows. A linear quantum system consists of a finite collection of bosonic modes with canonical operators (a_1, ..., a_n) (equivalently quadratures (q_i, p_i) with [q_j, p_k] = i δ_{jk}) whose internal Hamiltonian is at most quadratic in the canonical operators. The system is coupled irreversibly to a finite collection of external bosonic quantum field channels (input/output fields satisfying quantum stochastic differential equations) through coupling operators that are linear in the mode operators. Such a system is called a quantum linear network; its Heisenberg-picture dynamics map linear combinations of canonical operators to linear combinations of canonical operators (with added field noise), and its (S, L, H) parameters have S unitary, L linear in the modes, and H quadratic.

A quantum error-correction procedure is a process that, for an arbitrary unknown pure state |ψ⟩ encoded in some subsystem, recovers |ψ⟩ (with arbitrarily high fidelity) after the encoded system has been subjected to errors drawn from a specified noise model acting on the encoded degrees of freedom — in particular, the recovery must succeed without prior knowledge of |ψ⟩.

Prove that no quantum linear network (in the above sense, possibly including measurement of output fields and linear feedback derived from such measurements through the same linear-network class) can implement quantum error correction for arbitrary unknown encoded quantum states against a non-trivial error model. Equivalently, show that the implementation of genuine quantum error correction necessarily requires nonlinear (non-Gaussian) resources beyond the linear-network framework.
status_search_result: A web search did not return a definitive proof that linear quantum networks cannot perform quantum error correction in the general sense posed. Related literature includes passive/averaging-based schemes for linear-optical networks (e.g., Marek 2018, Phys. Rev. A 97, 022324) and earlier no-go style results restricted to Gaussian states/operations (Niset–Fiurášek–Cerf 2009 showing Gaussian errors cannot be corrected by Gaussian operations on Gaussian states), but a complete proof of the general statement does not appear to be established. Status is therefore unclear from available sources.
