original_question: The X-ray spectrum of PMN J0948+0022 shows jet-dominated emission above about 2 keV together with a soft X-ray excess at lower energies, and several distinct models can fit that soft component, including blurred reflection, Comptonisation of thermal disc emission, or a steep power law. original_question: For gamma-ray-emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, only 1H 0323+342 has a clearly detected host galaxy, and its morphology has been interpreted either as spiral structure or as the residual signature of a galaxy merger. Is the development of relativistic jets in these objects driven by strong merger activity, despite mergers being unusual in disk or spiral galaxies?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the class of narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLS1) galaxies that are detected in gamma rays and host relativistic jets. Empirically, among such gamma-ray-emitting NLS1 galaxies, only one (1H 0323+342) has a clearly resolved host galaxy, whose morphology admits two competing interpretations: (i) a one-armed spiral structure, or (ii) a ring-like residual signature of a recent galaxy merger. Galaxy mergers are typically rare in disk/spiral systems, yet powerful relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei have traditionally been associated with merger-built elliptical hosts harboring very high-mass supermassive black holes.

Question: Is the launching and development of relativistic jets in gamma-ray-emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies primarily driven by strong galaxy-merger activity, notwithstanding the fact that their hosts appear to be disk/spiral-like systems in which mergers are unusual?

A small subset is radio-loud, and an even smaller subset has been detected in γ-rays by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT), indicating the presence of relativistic jets. original_question: Are Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 galaxies, an extreme part of the Type 1 active-galactic-nucleus population, a genuinely special class of active galactic nuclei, or are they mainly the low-black-hole-mass end of the broader Type 1 population with properties shaped by host-galaxy secular processes, narrow-line-region conditions, high accretion rates, and orientation?
self_contained_problem:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) of Type 1 are characterized by direct visibility of the broad-line region, exhibiting permitted broad emission lines (e.g., Hβ) with full widths at half maximum typically of several thousand km s⁻¹. Narrow-Line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies form a subclass of Type 1 AGN distinguished by: (i) FWHM(Hβ) ≲ 2000 km s⁻¹, (ii) [O III] λ5007 / Hβ < 3, (iii) often strong optical Fe II emission, (iv) systematically low black-hole masses (typically 10⁶–10⁸ M_⊙), (v) high Eddington accretion ratios, and (vi) extreme positions at one end of the so-called Eigenvector 1 (EV1) correlation space of Type 1 AGN spectral properties. Their host galaxies appear to be more strongly affected by secular (internal) dynamical processes than those of broad-line Seyfert 1s.

Determine whether NLSy1 galaxies constitute a genuinely distinct ("special") physical class of active galactic nuclei, or whether their observational peculiarities can be fully explained as the natural low-black-hole-mass tail of the broader Type 1 AGN population, with their distinguishing characteristics arising from the combination of (a) host-galaxy secular evolution, (b) narrow-line region physical conditions, (c) high accretion rates near or above the Eddington limit, and (d) line-of-sight orientation effects, without requiring an intrinsically separate AGN category.
status_search_result: The classification of NLSy1 galaxies remains an actively debated open question in AGN astrophysics. Recent works continue to investigate whether NLSy1s are simply the low-mass, high-Eddington tail of Type 1 AGN or a genuinely distinct class, with no community consensus. Studies through the 2020s explore their black-hole masses, host secular processes, gamma-ray emission, and X-ray spectra, but disagreement persists on whether their peculiarities reduce to mass/accretion/orientation effects.

original_question: Across active galactic nuclei, how are jets and outflows related to accretion radiative efficiency and black-hole spin, and which combination of black-hole mass, spin, accretion rate, magnetic-field interaction, or other physical parameters determines whether jets and outflows are produced?

paper_title: Nuclei of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs - Central engine & conditions of star formation: Workshop summary and open questions
original_question: What mechanism produces gamma-ray emission in blazars, whose jet emission dominates across wavelengths because the jet axis is aligned close to the line of sight toward the black hole?
self_contained_problem:
Blazars are a class of active galactic nuclei (including BL Lac objects and Flat Spectrum Radio Quasars) characterized by a relativistic jet, launched from the vicinity of the central supermassive black hole, whose axis is closely aligned with the observer's line of sight. Because of this alignment and the resulting relativistic beaming, the jet emission dominates the observed spectral energy distribution at all wavelengths. Many blazars exhibit a high-energy spectral component extending into the gamma-ray band (from MeV up to TeV energies).

Identify the physical radiation mechanism (or combination of mechanisms) responsible for the gamma-ray emission of blazars. In particular, determine whether this emission is produced by:

(a) purely leptonic processes, such as synchrotron self-Compton (SSC) scattering by relativistic electrons in the jet, or external Compton (EC) scattering of photons originating from the accretion disk, the broad-line region, or the dusty torus;

(b) hadronic processes, such as proton synchrotron radiation in strong magnetic fields, or photo-pion / photo-pair cascades initiated by interactions of relativistic protons with ambient photon fields and matter; or

(c) a hybrid lepto-hadronic combination of the above.

Provide a mechanism that consistently reproduces the observed broadband spectral energy distributions, variability time scales, and (where applicable) the associated high-energy neutrino emission across the blazar population.
status_search_result: Recent literature (through 2025) indicates that the origin of the high-energy gamma-ray peak in blazar SEDs remains an active debate between leptonic (SSC/EC) and hadronic (proton synchrotron, photo-pion cascades) scenarios, with lepto-hadronic hybrid models also under consideration. Recent X-ray polarization measurements (e.g., IXPE) and multi-messenger neutrino observations are being used to constrain the models, but no consensus has been reached.

paper_title: Nuclei of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs - Central engine & conditions of star formation: Workshop summary and open questions
original_question: How reliable are the different methods for estimating black-hole masses in active galactic nuclei, including reverberation mapping, single-epoch reverberation-mapping estimates, methods using Balmer lines, methods using the CIV line for objects at redshift greater than about 2, and estimates based on the black-hole-mass–stellar-velocity-dispersion correlation?
self_contained_problem:
In active galactic nuclei (AGN), the mass $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$ of the central supermassive black hole is commonly estimated by several techniques:

(i) Reverberation mapping (RM), which uses the time delay $\tau$ between continuum variability and the response of a broad emission line to derive a characteristic broad-line-region (BLR) radius $R_{\mathrm{BLR}}=c\tau$, and then sets
$$M_{\mathrm{BH}} = f\,\frac{R_{\mathrm{BLR}}\,(\Delta V)^2}{G},$$
where $\Delta V$ is a measure of the broad-line velocity width and $f$ is a dimensionless virial factor (typically $\langle f\rangle\sim 5$) encoding the unknown geometry and kinematics of the BLR.

(ii) Single-epoch (SE) "virial" estimates, which calibrate against RM by using an empirical $R_{\mathrm{BLR}}$–luminosity relation together with a single-epoch line-width measurement.

(iii) Balmer-line based estimates (using $\mathrm{H}\beta$ or $\mathrm{H}\alpha$) within (i) or (ii).

(iv) C IV $\lambda 1549$-based estimates, used for high-redshift quasars ($z\gtrsim 2$) where Balmer lines are not accessible to optical spectroscopy.

(v) Estimates obtained from the $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$–$\sigma_\star$ relation, where $\sigma_\star$ is the stellar velocity dispersion of the host galaxy bulge.

Quantify the reliability of each of these methods. Specifically:

(a) Determine, with rigorous uncertainty propagation, the systematic and statistical uncertainty (in dex of $\log_{10} M_{\mathrm{BH}}$) inherent to RM masses arising from the virial factor $f$, and assess whether the commonly used value $\langle f\rangle\sim 5$ yields masses accurate at the $0.3$–$0.4$ dex level.

(b) Determine the corresponding uncertainty for single-epoch Balmer-line estimates relative to RM masses.

(c) Determine whether C IV-based single-epoch estimates at $z\gtrsim 2$ are biased relative to Balmer-line and RM estimates, and, if so, characterize the bias as a function of luminosity, Eddington ratio, line shape (e.g., blueshift/asymmetry of C IV), and other observables.

(d) Determine the intrinsic scatter and possible systematic offsets of $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$–$\sigma_\star$ based estimates for AGN, especially Type 1 AGN, relative to direct dynamical or RM masses.

Provide a quantitative comparison establishing the relative trustworthiness of methods (i)–(v).
status_search_result: This is a longstanding open question in AGN astrophysics. Recent reviews (e.g., Shen 2013; Peterson 2014; Czerny et al. 2019; SDSS-RM and AGN STORM campaigns through the 2020s) report that RM masses based on Balmer lines are reliable to roughly 0.3–0.5 dex when an average virial factor is adopted, single-epoch Balmer estimates carry ~0.3–0.5 dex scatter, C IV estimates remain controversial with biases that depend on line blueshift and shape, and $M_{\mathrm{BH}}$–$\sigma_\star$ based AGN masses show significant scatter and possible offsets. No consensus calibration eliminating these systematics has been established, so the question remains open.

paper_title: Nuclei of Seyfert galaxies and QSOs - Central engine & conditions of star formation: Workshop summary and open questions
original_question: Do the same kinds of galaxies host active and quiescent black holes, and do the same kinds of galaxies host Type 1 and Type 2 active galactic nuclei, or are these categories phases in an evolutionary sequence whose outcome depends on star formation and active-galactic-nucleus feedback?
self_contained_problem:
Consider galaxies harboring a central supermassive black hole. Such black holes are classified as "active" (actively accreting and powering an active galactic nucleus, AGN) or "quiescent." Active galactic nuclei are further divided into Type 1 (showing both broad and narrow optical emission lines, with a direct view of the central engine) and Type 2 (showing only narrow optical emission lines, with the central engine obscured). Determine which of the following hypotheses is correct for the population of galaxies in the local and intermediate-redshift universe:

(a) Active and quiescent black holes are hosted by statistically indistinguishable populations of galaxies (in terms of stellar mass, morphology, color, environment, and star-formation properties), and Type 1 and Type 2 AGN are likewise hosted by indistinguishable populations, differing only by orientation as predicted by the strict unified model;

(b) These categories instead correspond to distinct phases of an evolutionary sequence, with transitions among quiescent, Type 2, and Type 1 phases governed by ongoing star formation and by feedback from the AGN onto the host's gas content.

Specifically, characterize the host-galaxy properties (morphology, environment, stellar mass, star-formation rate) that do or do not distinguish Type 1 from Type 2 AGN hosts, and from quiescent-black-hole hosts, and decide whether the observed distinctions are consistent with pure orientation effects or require an evolutionary scenario driven by star formation and AGN feedback.
status_search_result: Empirical studies since 2014 have produced partial answers. Star-formation rates of Type 1 and Type 2 AGN appear similar once redshift and X-ray luminosity are controlled, consistent with the unified model. However, statistically significant differences in host stellar mass (Type 1 hosts ~0.2 dex lower), morphology, color, and environment of neighbors of Type 1 vs. Type 2 AGN have been reported, suggesting an evolutionary link rather than pure orientation. The full question — whether these categories are distinct populations or phases of an evolutionary sequence shaped by star formation and AGN feedback — remains an active area of research without consensus.

original_question: At low and high redshift, is the relation between active galactic nuclei and star formation coincidental, causal, self-regulated, or some combination of these, especially when distinguishing galaxy-wide star formation from nuclear star formation near the central black hole?
status_search_result: The character of the AGN/star-formation connection remains an actively debated open question in extragalactic astrophysics. paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
context_brief: AGN class status of gamma-ray radio-loud NLSy1s
original_question: Gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies are Seyfert active galactic nuclei characterized by narrow permitted Hβ lines, [OIII]/Hβ < 3, an Fe II bump, strong X-ray variability, steep X-ray spectra, substantial soft X-ray excess, relatively small central black-hole masses, high accretion rates, and an expected association with spiral hosts. Do the five radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies detected by Fermi-LAT in gamma rays constitute a distinct third class of active galactic nuclei with relativistic jets, in addition to blazars and radio galaxies, and what is the physical nature of that class?
self_contained_problem:
Background and definitions. A narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxy is a type of Seyfert active galactic nucleus (AGN) defined by the following optical and X-ray properties: (i) narrow permitted Balmer emission lines from the broad-line region with FWHM(Hβ) < 2000 km s⁻¹; (ii) a flux ratio [O III] λ5007 / Hβ < 3; (iii) a prominent Fe II emission bump; (iv) strong X-ray variability, a steep X-ray continuum, and a substantial soft X-ray excess; (v) inferred central black-hole masses in the range 10⁶–10⁸ M_⊙; (vi) accretion rates close to or above the Eddington limit; and (vii) host galaxies that are typically spiral. A radio-loud NLSy1 is an NLSy1 whose radio loudness parameter exceeds the standard threshold separating radio-loud from radio-quiet AGN. Among AGN, two well-established classes are known to host powerful relativistic jets pointing close to (blazars) or away from (radio galaxies) the line of sight.

Problem. Consider the population of radio-loud NLSy1 galaxies that have been detected in GeV γ-rays by the Fermi Large Area Telescope (initially comprising five sources). Determine whether these γ-ray-emitting radio-loud NLSy1 galaxies form a genuinely distinct third class of jetted AGN — separate from blazars and from radio galaxies — and characterize the physical nature of such a class. Specifically: (a) establish whether their jet production mechanism, jet power, central black-hole mass distribution, accretion regime, host-galaxy morphology, and cosmological evolution differ in an essential way from those of blazars and radio galaxies; and (b) identify the physical mechanism(s) responsible for the high-energy γ-ray emission in these objects and explain how relativistic jets can be launched and maintained in systems with comparatively low black-hole masses and high (near- or super-Eddington) accretion rates hosted in spiral galaxies.
status_search_result: The classification of γ-ray-emitting radio-loud NLSy1s as a distinct third jetted-AGN class remains an active and unresolved question. Subsequent work has expanded the sample of γ-ray-detected NLSy1s and has revealed that some hosts may be ellipticals or merging systems, blurring the boundary with blazars/radio galaxies; the issues of jet launching at low black-hole masses, near-Eddington accretion, and host morphology remain debated in recent literature.

paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
original_question: In the radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy PKS 1502+036, how can evidence for relativistic boosting—a one-sided radio structure and radio spectral variability—be reconciled with the absence of detected apparent superluminal motion at 15 GHz in VLBA observations from 2002 to 2012?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a radio-loud active galactic nucleus exhibiting the following observational features in its parsec-scale radio jet (as imaged by Very Long Baseline Interferometry at 15 GHz over a decade-long monitoring campaign):

(i) a one-sided core–jet morphology (a bright compact core with a faint jet extending on one side only),
(ii) significant radio spectral variability suggestive of a compact, opacity-evolving emission region,
(iii) no measurable apparent superluminal motion of jet components, with all detected pattern speeds consistent with sub-luminal apparent velocities β_app c (β_app < 1).

In the standard relativistic-beaming framework, a jet with bulk Lorentz factor Γ and viewing angle θ to the line of sight produces an apparent transverse speed
   β_app = β sin θ / (1 − β cos θ),
a Doppler factor δ = 1/[Γ(1 − β cos θ)], and a jet-to-counterjet flux ratio R = ((1 + β cos θ)/(1 − β cos θ))^(2+α) for a continuous jet of spectral index α. One-sidedness and spectral variability typically demand δ ≫ 1, while the absence of superluminal motion bounds β_app.

Problem. Determine a physically self-consistent set of jet parameters (Γ, θ, β) — and, where relevant, a distinction between the bulk flow speed and the pattern speed of moving features — that simultaneously:
(a) produces a jet-to-counterjet brightness ratio large enough to render the counterjet undetectable (consistent with the observed one-sidedness),
(b) yields a Doppler factor δ sufficiently large to account for the observed radio spectral variability (and high gamma-ray luminosity, if applicable),
(c) keeps the apparent component speed β_app ≤ 1 throughout a ≥10-year monitoring baseline.

In particular, identify the regime of (Γ, θ) compatible with all three conditions, and explain how the apparent tension (sometimes called a "Doppler-factor crisis") between strong boosting indicators and the lack of superluminal motion can be resolved (e.g., by a small viewing angle θ ≲ 1/Γ, by a difference between pattern speed and bulk speed, by jet bending or geometry, or by intrinsic variability mimicking variability without large-scale component motion).
status_search_result: Subsequent VLBI monitoring and SED modeling of this source confirmed the apparent tension: the one-sided structure, spectral variability, and high gamma-ray luminosity require a high Doppler factor, yet only sub-luminal pattern speeds have been measured, resembling a "Doppler-factor crisis" similar to that in TeV BL Lacs. Proposed reconciliations include a very small viewing angle (θ ≲ 1/Γ, where the apparent-speed formula yields β_app < 1 even for highly relativistic flows) and/or a pattern speed slower than the bulk-flow speed. The issue has thus been partially understood phenomenologically but no unique parameter solution has been definitively established.

paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
original_question: What physical parameters determine whether a radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxy can form an efficient relativistic jet: is a large central black-hole mass required, or can the relatively small black-hole masses traditionally estimated for gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud NLSy1s, about 10^7–10^8 solar masses, still produce powerful jets?
self_contained_problem:
Active galactic nuclei (AGN) host supermassive black holes that can launch collimated relativistic outflows ("jets"). Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies are a class of AGN identified by optical spectroscopic criteria (FWHM(Hβ) ≲ 2000 km s⁻¹, weak [O III], strong Fe II), and a subset of them are radio-loud and have been detected in GeV gamma rays, indicating the presence of a powerful relativistic jet. Their central black-hole masses, estimated by virial methods from broad-line region kinematics, fall in the range M_BH ≈ 10⁷–10⁸ M_⊙, substantially smaller than the M_BH ≳ 10⁸–10⁹ M_⊙ inferred for blazars and jetted radio galaxies hosted in giant ellipticals.

Determine which physical parameters of the central engine control the formation of an efficient relativistic jet in radio-loud NLSy1 galaxies. In particular, decide whether a large black-hole mass (M_BH ≳ 10⁸–10⁹ M_⊙) is a necessary condition for launching a powerful relativistic jet, or whether the comparatively small masses M_BH ≈ 10⁷–10⁸ M_⊙ inferred for gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud NLSy1s are by themselves sufficient — possibly with other parameters (such as black-hole spin, accretion rate relative to Eddington, magnetic flux threading the horizon as in magnetically arrested disc states, or host-galaxy properties) playing the dominant role.
category_tag: Relativistic jets in active galactic nuclei
status_search_result: Recent reviews and observational studies (e.g., 2019 MDPI review on relativistic jets in gamma-ray NLSy1s, 2021 spectral-index map studies, and 2024–2025 papers on jet triggers) report that the physical parameters controlling jet formation in radio-loud NLSy1s remain under active debate. Some works argue that virial mass estimates underestimate M_BH (e.g., 1H 0323+342, PKS J1222+0413 ≈ 2×10⁸ M_⊙), while others emphasize black-hole spin, Eddington ratio, and magnetically arrested disc states. No consensus has emerged.

paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
original_question: What are the host-galaxy morphologies of gamma-ray-emitting radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies, and can their relativistic jets be explained by strong merger activity rather than ordinary spiral-galaxy evolution, given that only 1H 0323+342 has a clearly detected host and observations of it have been interpreted either as spiral arms or as merger residual structure?
self_contained_problem:
Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies are active galactic nuclei characterized by relatively narrow permitted optical emission lines (FWHM(Hβ) ≲ 2000 km/s), strong Fe II emission, and typically low-mass central black holes. A small subset of NLSy1 galaxies are radio-loud and have been detected at GeV energies, indicating the presence of relativistic jets pointed close to the line of sight. According to the conventional paradigm, powerful relativistic jets are launched almost exclusively by very massive black holes hosted in elliptical galaxies built up through major mergers, whereas NLSy1 galaxies are commonly believed to reside in disk/spiral hosts with pseudobulges.

Determine, on the basis of resolved imaging of the host galaxies of the currently known sample of γ-ray–detected radio-loud NLSy1 galaxies:

(a) The morphological classification (spiral/disk versus elliptical versus merger remnant or interacting system) of these hosts.

(b) Whether their relativistic jets can be plausibly attributed to ongoing or recent strong merger activity (rather than to ordinary secular evolution of a disk/spiral host), in particular for the nearest such object, whose imaging shows a feature that has been interpreted alternatively as a one-armed spiral or as a circumnuclear ring/merger residual.
status_search_result: Subsequent imaging studies of 1H 0323+342 (HST, 2014; deep optical, 2020) favor an asymmetric ring/merger-residual interpretation rather than a regular spiral arm, supporting the hypothesis that the relativistic jet is connected with a recent galaxy interaction. However, host-galaxy imaging of the broader sample of γ-ray–emitting radio-loud NLSy1s remains sparse, and a definitive, sample-wide morphological classification—and a confirmed merger origin for the jets—has not been established. The question is therefore partially answered for the prototype but remains open for the population.

paper_title: Gamma-ray emitting narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies. New discoveries and open questions
context_brief: Rarity and evolutionary duration of radio-loud NLSy1s
original_question: Why is the fraction of radio-loud narrow-line Seyfert 1 galaxies so small compared with radio-loud quasars, and is the rarity explained by only some NLSy1 galaxies experiencing high-accretion episodes that last long enough to spin up their central black holes?
self_contained_problem:
Narrow-line Seyfert 1 (NLSy1) galaxies are a class of active galactic nuclei (AGN) characterized by narrow permitted optical emission lines (FWHM(Hβ) < 2000 km/s), a [O III]/Hβ ratio less than 3, and strong Fe II emission. They are typically powered by relatively low-mass central supermassive black holes (≈10^6–10^8 M_⊙) accreting near or above the Eddington limit. The radio-loudness of an AGN is conventionally defined as R = F_{5 GHz}/F_{4400 Å}, with sources called radio-loud if R > 10 and very radio-loud if R > 100.

Empirically, only a small fraction (≲7%) of NLSy1 galaxies are radio-loud, and only ≈2.5% have R > 100, whereas about 15% of optically selected quasars are radio-loud.

Provide a quantitative astrophysical explanation of the following:

(a) Why is the fraction of radio-loud NLSy1 galaxies substantially smaller than the radio-loud fraction among quasars?

(b) Test the hypothesis that this rarity is explained by the requirement that only those NLSy1 galaxies that undergo high-accretion episodes lasting long enough to spin up their central black holes (to a high dimensionless spin parameter a ≈ 1) become radio-loud. In particular, determine whether the observed black hole mass distributions, accretion histories, and spin distributions of radio-loud versus radio-quiet NLSy1 galaxies are consistent with this scenario, and identify what duration of sustained near-Eddington accretion would be required to produce the observed radio-loud fraction.
status_search_result: The question remains an open issue in AGN astrophysics. Recent reviews and studies (e.g., 2018 review on radio properties of NLSy1 galaxies and 2017 work on radio/gamma-ray-loud NLSy1s) continue to discuss the rarity of radio-loud NLSy1s and the possible role of black hole spin and prolonged accretion episodes, but no consensus quantitative explanation has been established. Individual sources show evidence of high spin (a > 0.6), supporting the spin-up hypothesis, yet population-level confirmation is still lacking.

original_question: Must every Hausdorff countably compact paratopological group G, where the group multiplication G x G -> G is continuous, be totally bounded?
self_contained_problem:
A paratopological group is a group $G$ endowed with a topology such that the multiplication map $G \times G \to G$, $(x,y)\mapsto xy$, is jointly continuous (no continuity of inversion is assumed). A topological space is countably compact if every countable open cover has a finite subcover (equivalently, every infinite subset has an accumulation point). A paratopological group $G$ with neighborhood base $\mathcal{N}(e)$ at the identity is called totally bounded if for every $U \in \mathcal{N}(e)$ there exists a finite set $F \subseteq G$ with $G = FU = UF$.

Question: Must every Hausdorff countably compact paratopological group be totally bounded?

original_question: For a Tychonoff space X, let I(X) be the free topological inverse semigroup over X: a topological inverse semigroup equipped with a topological embedding of X and satisfying the universal property for maps from X into topological inverse semigroups. self_contained_problem:
Recall that an inverse semigroup is a semigroup $S$ such that for every $x \in S$ there exists a unique element $x^{-1} \in S$ (the inverse of $x$) satisfying $x x^{-1} x = x$ and $x^{-1} x x^{-1} = x^{-1}$. A topological inverse semigroup is an inverse semigroup $S$ endowed with a topology making both the multiplication map $S \times S \to S$ and the inversion map $x \mapsto x^{-1}$ continuous. A topological space is called Tychonoff (completely regular Hausdorff) if it is $T_1$ and every closed set can be separated from any point not in it by a continuous real-valued function.

Given a Tychonoff space $X$, the free topological inverse semigroup over $X$ is a topological inverse semigroup $I(X)$ together with a topological embedding $\iota \colon X \hookrightarrow I(X)$ such that for every continuous map $f \colon X \to T$ from $X$ into any topological inverse semigroup $T$, there exists a unique continuous inverse-semigroup homomorphism $\bar{f} \colon I(X) \to T$ with $\bar{f} \circ \iota = f$.

Question: Is $I(X)$ a Tychonoff space for every Tychonoff space $X$?

paper_title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions
original_question: Can the GOE be implemented as a viable and useful theory of nuclear resonance reactions whose theoretically predicted observables are broad enough for practical nuclear-reaction applications, rather than being limited to too narrow a set of quantities?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Consider a model of compound-nucleus resonance reactions in which the internal Hamiltonian H of the compound nucleus is drawn from the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE) of N×N real symmetric random matrices (entries Gaussian, distribution invariant under orthogonal transformations, with variance scaled so that the average level density has a finite limit as N→∞). Coupling to a finite set of open reaction channels a=1,…,Λ is described by real coupling vectors W_a∈R^N held fixed, and the scattering matrix is

   S_{ab}(E) = δ_{ab} − 2π i [W^T (E − H + iπ W W^T)^{-1} W]_{ab},

where W is the N×Λ matrix with columns W_a. Observables of interest include energy-averaged cross sections, S-matrix correlation functions ⟨S_{ab}(E) S_{cd}^*(E+ε)⟩, higher-order cross-section correlation functions ⟨σ_{ab}(E) σ_{cd}(E+ε)⟩ (and their multi-point generalizations), distributions of partial widths and of S-matrix elements, and quantities relevant in the presence of direct reactions, isospin or other symmetry breaking, and overlapping resonances.

Problem. Develop the GOE scattering model above into a viable and practically useful theory of nuclear resonance reactions by deriving, in closed analytic form (or via a tractable computational scheme exact in the GOE average), the full set of observables needed for nuclear-reaction applications. In particular:

(a) Obtain explicit expressions for the n-point S-matrix and cross-section correlation functions ⟨S_{a_1 b_1}(E_1)⋯ S_{a_n b_n}(E_n)⟩ and ⟨σ_{a_1 b_1}(E_1)⋯ σ_{a_n b_n}(E_n)⟩ for arbitrary n, valid in the regime of arbitrary channel transmission coefficients T_a=1−|⟨S_{aa}⟩|^2 (weak to strong absorption) and arbitrary degree of resonance overlap Γ/D.

(b) Extend these expressions to incorporate direct reactions (nonzero ⟨S⟩), partial symmetry breaking (e.g. isospin mixing modeled by a block GOE with coupling), and channel-channel correlations.

(c) Determine the resulting distributions of cross sections, partial widths, and resonance parameters, including deviations from Porter–Thomas, and quantify their dependence on the model parameters.

The question is whether such a comprehensive theoretical framework, with a sufficiently broad set of analytically tractable observables to be useful for practical analysis of compound-nucleus data, can be constructed.
category_tag: Random matrix theory in nuclear scattering
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made: two- and three-point S-matrix correlation functions in the GOE scattering model are known (Verbaarschot–Weidenmüller–Zirnbauer and extensions), and recent work (e.g. Phys. Rev. C 2025/2026 on GOE-S-matrix neutron reaction modeling) embeds GOE into Hauser–Feshbach-type calculations and produces fluctuating cross sections preserving unitarity. However, general n-point cross-section correlation functions and a fully comprehensive analytic framework covering all reaction observables remain incomplete, so the program is partially solved rather than closed.

paper_title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions
original_question: In shell-model calculations for s-d-shell nuclei with spin J = 2 and isospin T = 0 states near the middle of the shell, why does the Mehta-Dyson ∆3 statistic tend to lie slightly above the GOE prediction for very large sequence lengths L even though both the nearest-neighbour spacing distribution and the ∆3 statistic otherwise agree very well with GOE predictions?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let H be a real symmetric Hamiltonian acting on the model space of an s-d-shell nucleus (valence nucleons restricted to the 1s_{1/2}, 0d_{3/2}, 0d_{5/2} single-particle orbits) at a filling near the middle of the shell. Restrict attention to the subspace of states with total angular momentum J = 2 and total isospin T = 0; diagonalisation in this subspace yields an ordered sequence of eigenvalues E_1 ≤ E_2 ≤ … ≤ E_N (with N of order a few thousand). After unfolding the spectrum so that the local mean level density equals 1, denote the unfolded levels by x_1 < x_2 < … < x_N and the nearest-neighbour spacings by s_i = x_{i+1} − x_i.

Two standard spectral statistics are considered:

(i) The nearest-neighbour spacing (NNS) distribution P(s), the empirical distribution of {s_i}, to be compared with the Wigner-like GOE prediction P_{GOE}(s).

(ii) The Dyson–Mehta Δ_3 statistic, defined for an interval of length L by
   Δ_3(L; α) = (1/L) min_{a,b} ∫_α^{α+L} [ N(x) − a x − b ]^2 dx,
where N(x) = #{i : x_i ≤ x} is the staircase counting function, with the average ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ taken over starting points α along the unfolded spectrum. The GOE prediction in the large-L regime is ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩_{GOE} ≈ (1/π^2)[ln(2π L) + γ − 5/4 − π^2/8].

Empirical observation. For shell-model spectra of s-d-shell nuclei restricted to J = 2, T = 0 states near mid-shell, P(s) and ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ both agree well with the GOE predictions for small and moderate L, but ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ systematically lies slightly above the GOE curve when L becomes very large (a sizeable fraction of the available sequence length).

Problem. Provide a quantitative explanation of this systematic large-L excess of the Dyson–Mehta Δ_3 statistic over the GOE prediction in such shell-model spectra. Specifically, identify the mechanism (e.g. residual long-range spectral rigidity violations from approximate constants of motion, finite-N saturation effects, secular variations in the level density not removed by unfolding, or other structural features of the shell-model Hamiltonian) responsible for the deviation, and derive the leading correction to ⟨Δ_3(L)⟩ as a function of L that accounts for the observed upward drift, while remaining consistent with the agreement of P(s) and Δ_3 with GOE at smaller L.
category_tag: Random-matrix spectral statistics in nuclear shell models
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a definitive published explanation of the systematic excess of the Δ_3 statistic over the GOE prediction at very large sequence lengths L for mid-shell s-d-shell J=2, T=0 spectra. Standard references confirm the use of Δ_3 and number variance as long-range rigidity tests and note saturation/finite-size effects, but no source clearly resolves the specific mid-shell excess. The matter appears to remain unresolved.

paper_title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions
context_brief: Separating s-wave and p-wave neutron resonances
original_question: How can low-energy neutron-scattering analyses cleanly separate s-wave neutron resonances from p-wave resonances, including resonances of unknown parity or known p-wave character, so that conclusions about GOE spectral statistics and neutron-width distributions are firm and unbiased?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a low-energy neutron-scattering experiment on a heavy target nucleus that produces a sequence of compound-nucleus resonances at energies $\{E_i\}$ with partial neutron widths $\{\Gamma_i^n\}$. Each resonance carries an orbital angular momentum $\ell$; those with $\ell = 0$ are called s-wave and those with $\ell = 1$ are called p-wave. Random-matrix theory predicts that, for a fixed spin-parity sequence, the rescaled level spacings should follow the Wigner–Dyson statistics of the Gaussian Orthogonal Ensemble (GOE), and that the reduced neutron widths $\gamma_i = \Gamma_i^n / \langle \Gamma^n\rangle$ within a single $\ell$-channel should follow the Porter–Thomas distribution
$$P(\gamma)\,d\gamma = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\gamma}}\,e^{-\gamma/2}\,d\gamma,$$
i.e. a $\chi^2$ distribution with $\nu = 1$ degree of freedom.

In practice, the measured resonance list contains a mixture of s-wave resonances, p-wave resonances (whose mean reduced widths are systematically smaller by a factor proportional to the p-wave penetrability), and resonances of unassigned parity. Including p-wave contaminants in a putative s-wave sample biases tests of GOE level statistics and inflates the apparent low-width tail of the width distribution, leading, e.g., to fitted values $\nu < 1$.

Problem. Devise a procedure that, given only the measured energies $\{E_i\}$ and neutron widths $\{\Gamma_i^n\}$ (possibly augmented by partial parity assignments), cleanly separates the s-wave subset from the p-wave and unknown-parity resonances, so that:
(i) the resulting s-wave subset has a quantifiable, unbiased completeness and purity;
(ii) statistical tests of GOE level-spacing statistics on the extracted s-wave sequence are not confounded by missed s-wave levels or admixed p-wave levels; and
(iii) the inferred reduced-neutron-width distribution can be compared with the Porter–Thomas law in a way that is provably free from selection bias due to the small-width threshold and from p-wave contamination.

Specify both the algorithm and a rigorous statistical framework that quantifies the residual systematic uncertainty in the resulting s-wave sequence.
status_search_result: The problem of cleanly separating s-wave from p-wave neutron resonances remains an active source of uncertainty in tests of GOE statistics and the Porter–Thomas distribution. Subsequent work (e.g., Koehler et al. on Pt isotopes; Weidenmüller and collaborators on realistic neutron-channel models, 2017–2018) shows continuing disagreement between data and the Porter–Thomas prediction, attributed at least in part to imperfect parity separation and threshold/secular effects. No universally accepted unbiased procedure has been established; recent realistic resonance-reaction-model analyses partially mitigate but do not fully resolve the issue.

paper_title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions
original_question: Do neutron widths of isolated compound-nucleus resonances follow the Porter-Thomas distribution predicted by the GOE, or do the small and widely spread maximum-likelihood estimates of the chi-squared degree-of-freedom parameter ν in Pt nuclei and reconstructed-NDE analyses remain inconsistent with the GOE after accounting for cutoff choice, finite sample size, and simulation-calibrated uncertainty in the maximum-likelihood method?
self_contained_problem:
Random Matrix Theory predicts that for an isolated compound-nucleus resonance with a single open neutron channel, the reduced neutron partial width amplitude is a Gaussian random variable, so the reduced neutron widths $\Gamma_n$ follow the Porter–Thomas distribution: a chi-squared distribution with $
u = 1$ degree of freedom,
$$P(x)\,dx =  rac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi x}}\,e^{-x/2}\,dx, \qquad x = \Gamma_n/\langle \Gamma_nangle.$$
More generally one may consider the family $P_
u(x) \propto x^{
u/2-1} e^{-
u x/2}$ (chi-squared with $
u$ degrees of freedom, suitably normalized) and treat $
u$ as a parameter to be estimated from observed resonance widths.

In practice, the data set of measured neutron widths is incomplete: very small widths fall below an experimental detection threshold, so analyses use only widths above a cutoff $c$ and apply a maximum-likelihood (ML) estimator for $
u$ on the truncated sample. Applied to s-wave neutron resonances in platinum isotopes and to a reconstructed Nuclear Data Ensemble, this procedure has yielded ML estimates of $
u$ that are small and widely spread, and apparently inconsistent (at high statistical significance) with $
u = 1$.

Question: After properly accounting for (a) the choice of cutoff $c$, (b) finite-sample bias and variance of the ML estimator, and (c) simulation-calibrated confidence intervals (e.g. Monte Carlo simulations of truncated chi-squared samples of comparable size and signal-to-noise to the data), are the observed ML estimates of $
u$ for neutron widths in Pt isotopes and for the reconstructed Nuclear Data Ensemble genuinely inconsistent with the GOE prediction $
u = 1$, or are they statistically compatible with the Porter–Thomas distribution?
category_tag: Random matrix theory and nuclear resonances
status_search_result: The question remains unresolved. The original ML analyses (Koehler et al.) found small ν significantly below 1 for Pt isotopes, claiming inconsistency with the Porter–Thomas/GOE prediction. Subsequent work (Fanto, Alhassid, Weidenmüller; arXiv:1504.06771, PRL 115, 052501) and a Bayesian reanalysis (arXiv:2106.06311) argue that the ML methodology was flawed — the assumed σ lies outside Bayesian confidence intervals — casting doubt on the rejection of PTD, but they call for reanalysis rather than providing a definitive answer. Theoretical investigations of channel-coupling terms violating orthogonal invariance also have not settled the issue.

paper_title: Open Problems in Applying Random-Matrix Theory to Nuclear Reactions
context_brief: Cross-section correlation functions beyond Ericson regime
original_question: Can one derive practically useful GOE/RMT predictions beyond average cross sections and beyond the Ericson regime, especially theoretical expressions for cross-section correlation functions, when existing analytical results are limited to two-S-matrix-element correlations, selected three- and four-element cases, single-element distributions, and the complete joint distribution only for strongly overlapping resonances?
status_search_result: Subsequent work (Kawai–Weidenmüller and especially Dietz et al., e.g. PRC 92, 044617 (2015), and the PNAS-style "Cross-section fluctuations in chaotic scattering systems" study) has derived analytical expressions for cross-section correlation functions valid across the whole range from isolated to overlapping resonances using a Breit-Wigner-type statistical model and supersymmetric techniques. However, fully closed-form, exact GOE results for the complete joint distribution of all S-matrix elements outside the Ericson regime, and for general higher-order cross-section correlators, remain unavailable. The problem is therefore partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later.
original_question: For a regular language L, call L k-limited if there exists an integer k > 0 such that L* = 1 + L + L^2 + ⋯ = (1 + L)^k; equivalently, when L contains the empty word, L is k-limited exactly when L* = L^k. Decide whether a given regular language is limited, meaning whether such a k exists.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite alphabet and let $\Sigma^*$ denote the free monoid of finite words over $\Sigma$, with empty word $\varepsilon$. For a language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$, define $L^0 = \{\varepsilon\}$, $L^{n+1} = L \cdot L^n$, and $L^* = \bigcup_{n \ge 0} L^n$. Call $L$ $k$-limited (for an integer $k > 0$) if $L^* = \varepsilon + L + L^2 + \cdots = (\varepsilon + L)^k$; equivalently, if $\varepsilon \in L$, then $L$ is $k$-limited iff $L^* = L^k$. A language $L$ is limited if it is $k$-limited for some $k > 0$.

Problem: Given a regular language $L \subseteq \Sigma^*$ (presented, e.g., by a finite automaton or regular expression), decide whether $L$ is limited.
category_tag: Limitedness of regular languages / distance automata
status_search_result: The limitedness problem (also known as the finite power property in this formulation) was shown to be decidable independently by K. Hashiguchi and I. Simon, with a simplified proof later given by H. Leung via the notion of stabilisation. It reduces to (and is essentially equivalent to) the limitedness problem for distance automata, whose decidability is classical and now well established (see e.g. Colcombet's theory of regular cost functions and Toruńczyk's profinite-words approach).

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later.
original_question: Regular expressions over an alphabet A are formed as usual from 0, 1, letters, union, concatenation, and Kleene star, but without complement. The restricted star height of a regular language is the least nesting depth of star among such complement-free regular expressions defining the language. Is there an algorithm that computes the restricted star height of an arbitrary regular language?
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a finite alphabet. Define regular expressions over A inductively by: 0 and 1 are regular expressions; every letter a ∈ A is a regular expression; and if E and F are regular expressions then so are (E ∪ F), (E · F), and E*. (Complement is not allowed.) Each such expression denotes a language L(E) ⊆ A* in the usual way: L(0) = ∅, L(1) = {ε}, L(a) = {a}, with union, concatenation, and Kleene star interpreted standardly. Define the star height h(E) of an expression E recursively by h(0) = h(1) = h(a) = 0, h(E ∪ F) = h(E · F) = max(h(E), h(F)), and h(E*) = h(E) + 1. The restricted star height of a regular language L ⊆ A* is h(L) = min{ h(E) : L(E) = L }.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm which, given (for instance, by a finite automaton or a regular expression) an arbitrary regular language L, computes its restricted star height h(L)?
status_search_result: The restricted star height problem (Eggan's problem) was solved affirmatively by K. Hashiguchi in 1988, who gave an algorithm (of non-elementary complexity) computing the star height of any regular language. A substantially simpler proof and a more efficient algorithm (running in double-exponential space) was given by D. Kirsten in 2005 via a reduction to the limitedness problem for nested distance desert automata.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later.
original_question: For a finite semigroup S, define its group complexity to be the smallest integer n such that S divides a wreath product A0 ∘ G1 ∘ A1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ A_{n-1} ∘ Gn ∘ An, where the Ai are aperiodic semigroups and the Gi are groups. Given the multiplication table of a finite semigroup, is there an algorithm that computes its group complexity?
self_contained_problem:
Let S be a finite semigroup. By the Krohn–Rhodes theorem, every finite semigroup divides a wreath product of the form

  A_0 ∘ G_1 ∘ A_1 ∘ ⋯ ∘ A_{n-1} ∘ G_n ∘ A_n,

where A_0, A_1, …, A_n are finite aperiodic semigroups (semigroups whose subgroups are all trivial) and G_1, …, G_n are finite groups. Here "divides" means S is a homomorphic image of a subsemigroup, and ∘ denotes the wreath product of (transformation) semigroups. Define the group complexity (Krohn–Rhodes complexity) c(S) of S to be the smallest nonnegative integer n for which such a decomposition of S exists.

Question: Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input the multiplication table of an arbitrary finite semigroup S, computes the group complexity c(S)?
status_search_result: A 2024 preprint by Margolis, Rhodes, and Schilling ("Decidability of Krohn-Rhodes complexity for all finite semigroups and automata", arXiv:2406.18477) announces a proof that Krohn–Rhodes (group) complexity is decidable for every nonnegative integer k, building on earlier work establishing decidability of complexity c = 1 (arXiv:2110.10373) and a reduction showing decidability of c = 1 implies decidability for all n ≥ 0. The problem, open for over 50 years, thus appears to be resolved, although the proof is recent and verification by the community is ongoing.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later.
original_question: Fix an alphabet A and an integer n. Let ~_n be the smallest congruence on the free monoid A* satisfying x^n ~_n x^{n+1} for every word x in A*, and let μ: A* → A*/~_n be the natural quotient morphism. For each congruence class m in A*/~_n, is the inverse image μ^{-1}(m) a regular language?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^*$ denote the free monoid on $A$ (the set of all finite words over $A$ under concatenation, with the empty word as identity). Fix an integer $n \geq 1$, and let $\sim_n$ be the smallest congruence on $A^*$ such that $x^n \sim_n x^{n+1}$ for every word $x \in A^*$. Let $\mu : A^* \to A^*/\!\sim_n$ be the canonical quotient morphism.

Question: For every congruence class $m \in A^*/\!\sim_n$, is the inverse image $\mu^{-1}(m) \subseteq A^*$ a regular language (i.e., recognized by a finite automaton)?
category_tag: Free Burnside semigroups and regular languages
status_search_result: The conjecture (Brzozowski's Problem 8) has been resolved positively for many cases: do Lago and others established that for the related identity $x^m = x^{m+n}$ with $m \geq 3$, all classes of the relatively free Burnside semigroup are regular languages and the word problem is decidable. The remaining open case is $n=2$ (the identity $x^2 = x^3$); Plyushchenko and Shur (2011) verified Brzozowski's conjecture for all classes containing an overlap-free or "almost overlap-free" word, but the general case for $x^2 = x^3$ remains neither proved nor disproved.

paper_title: Open problems about regular languages, 35 years later.
original_question: Let X ⊆ A+ be a finite maximal code over an alphabet A. Call X commutatively prefix if there exists a prefix code P whose image under the natural abelianization map α from noncommutative formal series over A to commutative formal polynomials agrees with α(X). Is every finite maximal code commutatively prefix?
self_contained_problem:
Let $A$ be a finite alphabet and let $A^+$ denote the set of nonempty words over $A$. A subset $X \subseteq A^+$ is called a code if every word in $A^+$ has at most one factorization as a concatenation of elements of $X$. A code $X$ is maximal if it is not properly contained in any other code over $A$. A code $P \subseteq A^+$ is a prefix code if no element of $P$ is a proper prefix of another element of $P$.

Let $\mathbb{Z}\langle\langle A\rangle\rangle$ denote the ring of noncommutative formal power series over $A$ with integer coefficients, and let $\mathbb{Z}[[A]]$ denote the corresponding ring of commutative formal series in the variables $A$. Let $\alpha\colon \mathbb{Z}\langle\langle A\rangle\rangle \to \mathbb{Z}[[A]]$ be the natural abelianization homomorphism, which extends the map sending each word $w \in A^*$ to the commutative monomial obtained by forgetting the order of its letters. For a language $L \subseteq A^+$, identify $L$ with the formal sum $\sum_{w \in L} w$, so $\alpha(L)$ is well-defined.

A language $X \subseteq A^+$ is said to be commutatively prefix if there exists a prefix code $P \subseteq A^+$ such that $\alpha(X) = \alpha(P)$.

Question: Is every finite maximal code $X \subseteq A^+$ commutatively prefix?
status_search_result: The general Schützenberger conjecture that every code is commutatively prefix was disproved by Shor, but his counterexample is not a maximal code. The restricted question for finite maximal codes remains open; recent work (e.g., on the factorization conjecture and a 2024 paper on weak structural forms of commutative equivalence in finite codes) continues to investigate it without resolution.

paper_title: Theoretical descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions: open problems & challenges
original_question: How can direct-reaction and compound-nucleus components be described within a single coherent framework so that their respective contributions can be disentangled in reactions involving rare isotopes and in indirect cross-section extraction problems?
self_contained_problem:
In the quantum theory of nuclear reactions, the cross section for a process A(a,b)B is conventionally decomposed into a direct-reaction component (fast, few-degree-of-freedom amplitudes connecting entrance and exit channels coherently, typically described by optical-model, DWBA, coupled-channels, or continuum-discretized coupled-channels methods) and a compound-nucleus component (slow, statistical equilibration of many degrees of freedom, typically described by Hauser–Feshbach theory with width-fluctuation corrections or by random-matrix S-matrix averages of the Engelbrecht–Weidenmüller type). Existing formalisms treat these two contributions with different and largely incompatible mathematical machineries: deterministic coupled-channels equations on one side, and energy-averaged statistical S-matrix theory on the other.

Construct a single coherent reaction-theoretical framework with the following properties:

(1) It produces, for any incident energy E, projectile a, and target A (including rare/short-lived isotopes where excitation of low-lying collective states and breakup channels are non-negligible), a unified scattering operator S(E) acting on the full set of open and weakly bound channels, from which both the energy-averaged direct amplitude ⟨S⟩ and the fluctuating compound amplitude S − ⟨S⟩ are obtained as well-defined projections.

(2) It yields cross-section formulas in which the direct, compound, and direct–compound interference contributions are unambiguously identified, mutually consistent (in particular, unitary as a whole), and reduce in appropriate limits to standard coupled-channels results and to Hauser–Feshbach with Engelbrecht–Weidenmüller transformation.

(3) It is formulated so that, given experimentally measured inclusive or semi-inclusive observables in surrogate (indirect) cross-section extraction settings — where a desired compound-nuclear cross section σ_CN(a,b) on an unstable target is inferred from a different entrance channel that populates the same compound system — the framework provides an explicit, controlled procedure to disentangle the direct contribution from the surrogate data and reconstruct σ_CN(a,b).

Prove the existence of such a framework, specify its governing equations and the operator-theoretic decomposition that separates the direct and compound parts, and establish the conditions on level density, channel coupling, and energy averaging interval under which the disentanglement in (3) is mathematically well-posed.
status_search_result: Unifying direct-reaction and compound-nucleus formalisms into a single coherent framework remains an active and open research challenge in nuclear reaction theory. Progress has been made on partial unifications (e.g., Kawano–Talou–Chadwick work on pre-equilibrium and DWBA-augmented Hauser–Feshbach, Dietrich–Kerman type approaches, and continued development of the Engelbrecht–Weidenmüller transformation), but no fully general, universally accepted framework that simultaneously handles rare-isotope effects and surrogate-reaction extraction has been established.

paper_title: Theoretical descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions: open problems & challenges
original_question: What additional physics is required in preequilibrium reaction models to achieve a general description of preequilibrium reactions in regimes where equilibrium is not reached and a statistical compound-nucleus description is therefore inapplicable?
self_contained_problem:
In nuclear reaction theory, a compound-nuclear reaction proceeds through three conceptual stages after a projectile strikes a target nucleus: (i) a direct stage, in which the projectile interacts with only a few nucleons; (ii) a preequilibrium stage, in which energy is progressively shared among an increasing number of nucleons through successive two-body collisions, generating a hierarchy of particle–hole excitations of growing complexity; and (iii) an equilibrium (compound nucleus) stage, in which the excitation energy is statistically distributed over all available degrees of freedom and the subsequent decay is well described by Hauser–Feshbach statistical theory.

Existing preequilibrium models — including exciton models, hybrid models, and quantum-mechanical multistep direct and multistep compound approaches (e.g., of Feshbach–Kerman–Koonin or Tamura–Udagawa–Lenske type) — describe the intermediate stage by tracking transitions between particle–hole configurations of increasing complexity, typically under simplifying assumptions such as equispaced single-particle levels, average squared two-body matrix elements, factorized state densities, and statistical assumptions on intermediate phases.

Consider an energy and target/projectile regime in which the reaction terminates before full statistical equilibrium has been attained, so that a Hauser–Feshbach compound-nucleus description is not applicable, while the time scales and complexity of the excitations are also too large for purely direct-reaction approaches.

Problem. Identify and formulate the additional physical ingredients that must be incorporated into preequilibrium reaction models so as to provide a general, predictive description of nuclear reactions in this regime. Specifically, determine which currently neglected or schematically treated effects — such as realistic single-particle spectra and shell structure, finite-range and isospin-dependent residual two-body interactions, collective and pairing correlations, angular-momentum and parity conservation, multiple preequilibrium particle emission, coupling between multistep direct and multistep compound chains, quantum interference between reaction paths, cluster (e.g., α, deuteron) and nucleon-transfer degrees of freedom, and a consistent treatment of the transition to and from direct and compound stages — are essential, and provide a unified theoretical framework that consistently incorporates these ingredients and reduces to the standard direct, preequilibrium, and compound-nucleus limits in the appropriate regimes.
status_search_result: The question of formulating a fully general preequilibrium reaction theory is widely regarded as an open challenge in nuclear reaction theory. Recent reviews on compound and preequilibrium reactions continue to list the unification of direct, preequilibrium, and compound-nucleus regimes — and the inclusion of effects such as multiple emission, cluster degrees of freedom, angular momentum, and quantum interference — as outstanding problems, with no comprehensive solution reported.

paper_title: Theoretical descriptions of compound-nuclear reactions: open problems & challenges
original_question: How can low-energy radioactive-beam experiments separate compound-reaction contributions from direct-reaction contributions well enough to yield reliable nuclear-structure information?
self_contained_problem:
In low-energy nuclear reaction experiments performed with radioactive ion beams, the measured cross section for a given exit channel can in general be decomposed as

  σ_total(E,θ) = σ_CN(E,θ) + σ_DR(E,θ),

where σ_CN denotes the contribution from compound-nucleus formation and subsequent statistical decay (described, e.g., by Hauser–Feshbach theory with appropriate level densities, optical-model transmission coefficients, and γ-ray strength functions), and σ_DR denotes the contribution from direct reactions (e.g., elastic/inelastic scattering, transfer, breakup, knockout, described by DWBA, CCBA, CDCC, or related few-body reaction frameworks). Reliable extraction of nuclear-structure information (spectroscopic factors, asymptotic normalization coefficients, single-particle occupancies, level schemes, transition strengths) from such experiments requires an unambiguous separation of σ_CN and σ_DR.

Develop a theoretical and experimental methodology, applicable to low-energy radioactive-beam measurements with limited statistics and broad energy/angle resolution, that allows σ_CN(E,θ) and σ_DR(E,θ) to be separated to a controlled accuracy sufficient to yield reliable nuclear-structure observables. Specifically:

(a) Identify quantitative observables (energy dependence, angular distributions, ejectile spectra, spin distributions, multiplicities, fluctuation analyses, etc.) whose measurement can disentangle the two contributions when only a radioactive beam (typically with low intensity and possibly contaminated) is available.

(b) Provide a unified reaction-theory framework that consistently couples direct and compound channels (e.g., via a generalized optical model with an absorptive imaginary part feeding Hauser–Feshbach decay) so that double counting is avoided and the partition between σ_CN and σ_DR is well defined.

(c) Quantify the residual theoretical and experimental uncertainties on the inferred nuclear-structure quantities resulting from the proposed separation procedure.
category_tag: compound vs. direct nuclear reaction separation
status_search_result: The clean separation of compound and direct reaction components in low-energy radioactive-beam experiments remains an active research challenge. Reviews and recent works on surrogate reactions, Hauser–Feshbach modeling with coupled channels, and (d,p) transfer with rare isotopes continue to identify this separation, and the consistent treatment of pre-equilibrium and direct-semidirect contributions, as an unresolved problem with only partial methodology in place.

paper_title: Progress and open questions in the physics of neutrino cross sections at intermediate energies
original_question: What is the contribution of strange quarks to the nucleon spin, and how can neutral-current elastic neutrino and antineutrino scattering on protons and neutrons determine that quantity in a way that separates it from other nucleon-structure effects?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the nucleon (proton or neutron) viewed as a bound state of quarks and gluons in QCD. The strange-quark contribution to the nucleon spin is defined as

  Δs = ⟨N, s_z = +1/2 | s̄ γ^μ γ_5 s | N, s_z = +1/2⟩ / (2 s^μ),

equivalently the forward matrix element at zero momentum transfer of the strange axial-vector current in a longitudinally polarized nucleon. Equivalently, Δs = G_A^s(Q² = 0), where G_A^s(Q²) is the strange contribution to the nucleon isoscalar axial form factor entering the Z-boson coupling.

Neutral-current elastic (NCE) scattering of neutrinos and antineutrinos on free nucleons,
  ν + p → ν + p,   ν̄ + p → ν̄ + p,   ν + n → ν + n,   ν̄ + n → ν̄ + n,
has differential cross sections that depend on the proton and neutron weak vector form factors (related by isospin to electromagnetic and strange vector form factors) and the weak axial form factor G_A^Z(Q²) = ±(1/2) G_A(Q²) − (1/2) G_A^s(Q²), where the sign is + for the proton and − for the neutron.

Problem. (a) Determine Δs, i.e. the value of G_A^s at Q² = 0, including a quantitative uncertainty. (b) Devise a strategy using measured NCE differential cross sections dσ/dQ² for ν p, ν̄ p, ν n, and ν̄ n (possibly combined with parity-violating elastic electron-scattering form-factor data) that isolates G_A^s(Q²) — and hence Δs through extrapolation to Q² = 0 — from the isovector axial form factor G_A(Q²), the electromagnetic and strange vector form factors, and other nucleon-structure contributions. In particular, identify ratios or combinations of the four NCE channels in which the strange axial contribution is enhanced relative to the dominant isovector axial term, and quantify how well Δs can in principle be extracted in this way.
status_search_result: Recent global fits combine parity-violating electron-scattering data (HAPPEx, SAMPLE, G0, PVA4) with neutral-current elastic neutrino/antineutrino data (BNL E734, MiniBooNE) to constrain the strange axial form factor and Δs, with improving but still model-dependent results (notably nuclear-model dependence for MiniBooNE's hydrocarbon target). The strangeness contribution remains under active investigation, with new constraints reported in 2024 and 2025; a precise, model-independent determination of Δs is not yet established.

paper_title: Progress and open questions in the physics of neutrino cross sections at intermediate energies
original_question: What is the correct q² dependence of the nucleon axial form factor F_A, especially beyond the standard dipole parametrization, so that charged-current quasielastic neutrino cross sections at moderate and high energies can be predicted without large form-factor-driven uncertainties?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current quasielastic (CCQE) neutrino–nucleon scattering, ν_ℓ + n → ℓ⁻ + p (and the antineutrino analogue). In the standard V−A formalism, the hadronic matrix element of the charged weak current between nucleon states is parametrized by vector form factors F₁(q²), F₂(q²) (constrained by electron-scattering data and CVC) together with the axial form factor F_A(q²) and the pseudoscalar form factor F_P(q²) (related to F_A by PCAC). The axial form factor satisfies F_A(0) = g_A ≈ 1.27, fixed by neutron β-decay, and has traditionally been modeled by a dipole ansatz

  F_A(q²) = g_A / (1 − q²/M_A²)²,

with a single axial mass parameter M_A.

Determine the correct functional q²-dependence of the nucleon axial form factor F_A(q²) — beyond the dipole parametrization — for spacelike momentum transfers q² ≤ 0 in the kinematic range relevant to accelerator-based neutrino experiments at moderate and high energies, and quantify it precisely enough that the predicted CCQE cross section σ(E_ν) is free of large form-factor-driven theoretical uncertainties throughout this energy range.

paper_title: Progress and open questions in the physics of neutrino cross sections at intermediate energies
original_question: Are the effective nucleon-nucleon interactions and nonrelativistic approximations used in random-phase-approximation descriptions of neutrino-nucleus scattering still valid when the energy transfer reaches a few hundred MeV, as in MiniBooNE and similar experiments, or do those approximations fail in that regime?
self_contained_problem: In the random-phase-approximation (RPA) treatment of neutrino-nucleus scattering, the nuclear response to the weak current is computed by summing ring diagrams built from particle-hole excitations interacting through an effective nucleon-nucleon residual interaction V (typically a nonrelativistic, possibly density-dependent, finite-range or contact interaction such as those of Landau-Migdal or Skyrme type), and by employing nonrelativistic kinematics and reductions of the weak nucleon current. Such RPA models are known to provide a reliable description of nuclear excitations at low energy and momentum transfer (up to roughly a few tens of MeV).\n\nDetermine whether the effective nucleon-nucleon residual interaction V and the nonrelativistic approximations used in such RPA descriptions of charged-current and neutral-current neutrino-nucleus scattering remain quantitatively valid when the energy transfer omega and three-momentum transfer |q| reach values of a few hundred MeV, as is typical for accelerator-based neutrino experiments in the intermediate-energy regime (e.g., neutrino beams of order 1 GeV). Specifically: identify the regime of (omega, |q|) in which these approximations break down, quantify the resulting error in the inclusive double-differential cross section d^2 sigma / (d omega d|q|), and determine whether a relativistic and/or modified-interaction extension is required to maintain accuracy at the level needed to interpret such experiments.
status_search_result: The validity of nonrelativistic RPA-type approaches and effective NN interactions at energy transfers of several hundred MeV has been a long-standing concern in neutrino-nucleus scattering. Subsequent work has developed relativistic mean-field and SuSAv2 approaches, and continuum/relativistic RPA variants, suggesting nonrelativistic RPA becomes inadequate at high q but no single definitive replacement is universally adopted; the question is generally regarded as still open / partially addressed rather than fully solved.

original_question: How large are two-particle–two-hole and two-body-current interference contributions to quasielastic-like neutrino cross sections under the actual kinematics of modern experiments, and how can their importance be established directly from observable quantities rather than from indirect sum-rule arguments?
self_contained_problem:

(a) For the actual flux-averaged kinematics of modern accelerator-based neutrino experiments, quantitatively determine the magnitude of the 2p2h contribution and of the one-body / two-body current interference contribution to the inclusive quasielastic-like double-differential cross section d²σ/(dT_μ d cos θ_μ), as functions of muon kinetic energy T_μ and scattering angle θ_μ, for both neutrino and antineutrino beams.

(b) Identify a set of directly measurable observables (for example, exclusive or semi-inclusive distributions in hadronic final states, transverse kinematic imbalance variables, or specific regions of the (q⁰, |q|) plane) whose experimental determination establishes the importance of 2p2h and two-body-current interference contributions to the quasielastic-like cross section without relying on indirect sum-rule arguments such as the transverse Coulomb sum rule.

Provide the theoretical predictions and the proposed observables.

paper_title: Progress and open questions in the physics of neutrino cross sections at intermediate energies
original_question: How should neutrino oscillation analyses modify their neutrino-energy reconstruction procedures to account for biases introduced when multinucleon dynamics make a quasielastic-like event look like true quasielastic scattering, given that this misreconstruction can survive even after near-detector constraints are applied?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a long-baseline (or short-baseline) neutrino oscillation experiment that selects charged-current quasielastic-like (QE-like) events on a nuclear target by tagging a single outgoing charged lepton (and, in Cherenkov detectors, no other observed hadronic activity). The incoming neutrino energy E_ν^rec is reconstructed from the lepton kinematics under the kinematic assumption of a true two-body QE process ν + n → ℓ + p on a bound nucleon at rest with a fixed average binding energy:

  E_ν^rec = (2(M_n − E_b) E_ℓ − ((M_n − E_b)^2 + m_ℓ^2 − M_p^2)) / (2(M_n − E_b − E_ℓ + |p_ℓ| cos θ_ℓ)).

In reality, a non-negligible fraction of the QE-like sample is produced by multinucleon (np–nh, "2p2h") interactions in which the neutrino interacts with a correlated pair (or larger cluster) of nucleons, so that the QE kinematic relation between (E_ℓ, θ_ℓ) and the true neutrino energy E_ν^true is violated. The mapping E_ν^true → E_ν^rec is therefore a non-trivial smearing kernel K(E_ν^rec | E_ν^true) that has long, asymmetric tails (predominantly on the low-E_ν^rec side). When oscillation parameters (Δm^2, sin^2 2θ) are extracted by fitting reconstructed-energy spectra at a far detector with constraints from a near detector, this smearing biases the inferred parameters, and the bias does not in general cancel between near and far detectors because the oscillation probability P(E_ν^true) is non-trivial only at the far detector.

Problem. Specify a procedure that an oscillation analysis should adopt for reconstructing the neutrino energy and/or for fitting oscillation parameters so that the bias produced by the multinucleon contamination of the QE-like sample is removed (or controlled to a quantified level), under the constraint that:

(i) the analysis must use only experimentally observable quantities at the detector (e.g., the lepton momentum and angle, plus, where available, hadronic observables);
(ii) the procedure must remain valid even after a near-detector constraint on the event rate as a function of reconstructed energy has been applied;
(iii) the residual bias on (Δm^2, sin^2 2θ) must be smaller than the experiment's statistical uncertainty.

Concretely, determine: (a) the form of the smearing kernel K(E_ν^rec | E_ν^true) that should be folded into the oscillation fit; (b) the additional observables, if any, that must be measured to break the degeneracy between true-QE and multinucleon contributions on an event-by-event or sample-by-sample basis; and (c) the conditions on the nuclear model entering K under which the near-detector constraint suffices to render the far-detector oscillation fit unbiased.
status_search_result: Multiple works (e.g., Martini–Ericson–Chanfray Phys. Rev. D 85, 093012 and D 87, 013009; Lalakulich et al. 1404.5687; and subsequent revisions in 2024–2025) have proposed concrete procedures: folding a multinucleon-inclusive smearing kernel K(E_rec|E_true) computed from microscopic nuclear models into the oscillation fit, and using hadronic observables (proton multiplicity/kinematics, transverse kinematic imbalance) to tag 2p2h events. These mitigate but do not eliminate the bias; experiments (T2K, NOvA, MicroBooNE) now incorporate 2p2h models with sizeable systematic uncertainties, and a fully model-independent prescription that guarantees near-detector cancellation of the bias is still lacking. Hence the question is partially solved.

paper_title: Progress and open questions in the physics of neutrino cross sections at intermediate energies
original_question: What are the correct elementary neutrino-induced pion-production cross sections on nucleons, and which dataset more faithfully captures them, given the tension between the ANL and BNL pπ+ measurements and the resulting uncertainty in the N–Δ axial transition form factors used in theory?
self_contained_problem:
Consider charged-current neutrino-induced single-pion production on nucleons, in particular the channel ν_μ p → μ^- p π^+ at intermediate neutrino energies (roughly 0.5–3 GeV), where the dominant mechanism is excitation of the Δ(1232) resonance. The hadronic amplitude depends on the N–Δ axial transition form factors C_3^A(Q^2), C_4^A(Q^2), C_5^A(Q^2), C_6^A(Q^2), whose Q^2 dependence and overall normalization (especially C_5^A(0)) must be fixed by experiment.

The two principal historical data sets used to constrain these form factors are the Argonne National Laboratory (ANL) 12-ft deuterium bubble chamber measurement and the Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) 7-ft deuterium bubble chamber measurement of the flux-averaged differential and total cross sections for ν_μ p → μ^- p π^+. The reported normalizations of these two data sets differ by approximately 30–40%, producing a corresponding uncertainty in the extracted N–Δ axial form factors and in theoretical predictions used by modern accelerator neutrino oscillation experiments.

Problem. Determine the true elementary cross sections σ(ν_μ p → μ^- p π^+) (and the related channels ν_μ n → μ^- p π^0 and ν_μ n → μ^- n π^+) on free nucleons as a function of neutrino energy, after correcting for nuclear (deuteron) effects, and decide which of the ANL and BNL data sets more faithfully reflects these elementary cross sections. Equivalently, extract the N–Δ(1232) axial transition form factors C_i^A(Q^2) (i = 3, 4, 5, 6) — in particular the value of C_5^A(0) and its Q^2 dependence — in a way that is consistent with both data sets within their stated uncertainties, and quantify the residual systematic uncertainty.
status_search_result: A reanalysis of the ANL and BNL deuterium bubble-chamber pion-production data (Wilkinson et al., 2014; arXiv:1411.4482) showed that, once flux-independent ratios over multiple channels are used, the two data sets are consistent within experimental uncertainties, largely resolving the apparent normalization tension. Subsequent extractions of the N–Δ axial form factors (e.g., Hernández, Nieves, Valverde and follow-ups, arXiv:1001.4416, 1012.4260) have used the combined data to determine C_5^A(0) and its Q^2 dependence, finding a tension with the off-diagonal Goldberger–Treiman relation at roughly 2σ. The discrepancy between ANL and BNL is therefore considered largely resolved at the level of consistency, but the precise elementary cross sections and axial form factors still carry sizeable uncertainties and call for new hydrogen/deuterium measurements.
