paper_title: Additive Combinatorics: A Menu of Research Problems
original_question: For a finite abelian group G, determine the maximum size of a subset A whose specified sumsets are pairwise disjoint in the sum-free sense. This includes determining μ(G,{k,l}), μ(G,[0,s]), μ±(G,{k,l}), μ±(G,[0,s]), μ̂(G,{k,l}), μ̂(G,[0,s]), μ̂(G,N0), μ̂±(G,{k,l}), μ̂±(G,[0,s]), and μ̂±(G,N0), where the defining conditions require kA and lA, or the corresponding signed or restricted variants, to be disjoint for prescribed k and l or for all 0 ≤ l < k in a range.
self_contained_problem:
Let G be a finite abelian group, written additively, and let A ⊆ G. For a positive integer k, define the following sumsets of A:

• kA = { a_1 + a_2 + ⋯ + a_k : a_i ∈ A } (the unrestricted k-fold sumset);
• k_±A = { ε_1 a_1 + ⋯ + ε_k a_k : a_i ∈ A, ε_i ∈ {+1,−1} } (the unrestricted signed k-fold sumset);
• k^A = { a_1 + ⋯ + a_k : a_i ∈ A, all a_i distinct } (the restricted k-fold sumset);
• k^±A = { ε_1 a_1 + ⋯ + ε_k a_k : a_i ∈ A pairwise distinct, ε_i ∈ {+1,−1} } (the restricted signed k-fold sumset);
with the conventions 0A = 0_±A = 0^A = 0^±A = {0}, 1A = 1^A = A, 1_±A = 1^±A = A ∪ (−A).

For nonnegative integers k > l ≥ 0 and a positive integer s, define the following extremal quantities:

μ(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, kA ∩ lA = ∅ },
μ(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, kA ∩ lA = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ_±(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k_±A ∩ l_±A = ∅ },
μ_±(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k_±A ∩ l_±A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ̂(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^A ∩ l^A = ∅ },
μ̂(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^A ∩ l^A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ̂(G,ℕ_0) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^A ∩ l^A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k },
μ̂_±(G,{k,l}) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^±A ∩ l^±A = ∅ },
μ̂_±(G,[0,s]) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^±A ∩ l^±A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k ≤ s },
μ̂_±(G,ℕ_0) = max{ |A| : A ⊆ G, k^±A ∩ l^±A = ∅ for all 0 ≤ l < k }.

Determine, as functions of the finite abelian group G and the parameters k, l, s, exact formulas (or tight bounds) for each of these ten quantities.
status_search_result: These extremal quantities for sum-free–type sets in finite abelian groups (in particular the restricted, signed, and interval/ℕ_0 variants) are known only in special cases (e.g., classical sum-free sets corresponding to μ(G,{1,1}) settled by Diananda–Yap and Green–Ruzsa, and partial results for cyclic and elementary abelian groups). General exact formulas for arbitrary G and all parameters remain open.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Monotonicity and single attractor of free-atom density
original_question: Can one prove from the quantum theory of a free atom that the ground-state one-electron density has a single attractor, a (3,-3) critical point, at the nucleus and decays monotonically away from the nucleus, rather than treating this density topology as a computationally observed but unproved conjecture?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a non-relativistic free atom with N electrons and a single nucleus of charge Z>0 located at the origin in R^3, governed by the standard many-electron Schrödinger Hamiltonian
  H = -∑_{i=1}^N (1/2)Δ_i  - ∑_{i=1}^N Z/|r_i| + ∑_{1≤i<j≤N} 1/|r_i - r_j|,
acting on the antisymmetric subspace of L^2((R^3×{↑,↓})^N). Let Ψ_0 be a (normalized) ground-state wavefunction of H, and define the one-electron density
  ρ(r) = N ∑_{σ_1,...,σ_N} ∫_{R^{3(N-1)}} |Ψ_0(r,σ_1; r_2,σ_2; ... ; r_N,σ_N)|^2 dr_2 ... dr_N.

Prove (or disprove) the following two statements about ρ:

(a) The function ρ has exactly one attractor (i.e. local maximum) on R^3, located at the position of the nucleus r=0, and this critical point is non-degenerate of Morse type (3,−3) (the Hessian of ρ at 0 has three negative eigenvalues).

(b) The density ρ is radially monotonically decreasing away from the nucleus: along every ray emanating from the origin, ρ is a strictly decreasing function of the distance |r|. Equivalently, the spherically averaged density ρ̄(r) = (4π)^{-1} ∫_{S^2} ρ(rω) dω satisfies dρ̄/dr < 0 for r>0, and moreover ρ itself decreases on every radial direction.

Establish (a) and (b) as theorems derived from the underlying many-body quantum mechanics, rather than as numerically observed regularities.
status_search_result: The conjecture that the ground-state one-electron density of a free atom is monotonically decreasing along every ray from the nucleus (and has its unique maximum, of (3,−3) type, at the nucleus) is a long-standing open problem. Rigorous results are known only in special cases: it holds rigorously for hydrogen and for one-electron systems whose external potential increases monotonically from the nucleus, and partial/sufficient conditions have been derived for two-electron and many-electron systems (e.g. Ayers 2003, Angulo–Dehesa 1991). The general many-electron case remains unproven.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: For a Coulombic molecular system with N electrons and q clamped nuclei, is there always a critical internuclear distance for each pair of nuclei such that, whenever all internuclear distances are larger than their critical values, the gradient of the molecular one-electron density has exactly q nuclear (3,-3) critical points and no non-nuclear attractors; and can the statement that most molecules have equilibrium internuclear distances larger than these critical distances be made mathematically precise and proved?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a non-relativistic Coulombic molecular system with N electrons and q clamped nuclei located at positions R_1,...,R_q in R^3, with nuclear charges Z_1,...,Z_q > 0. The electronic Hamiltonian (in atomic units) is

  H = -1/2 sum_{i=1}^N Δ_{r_i} - sum_{i=1}^N sum_{A=1}^q Z_A/|r_i - R_A| + sum_{1<=i<j<=N} 1/|r_i - r_j| + sum_{1<=A<B<=q} Z_A Z_B/|R_A - R_B|.

Let Ψ be a normalized ground-state wavefunction of H (with the nuclear positions fixed as parameters), and let

  ρ(r; R_1,...,R_q) = N ∫ |Ψ(r, r_2,...,r_N)|^2 ds dr_2 ... dr_N

be the associated one-electron density on R^3, where the spin coordinate s and the electron coordinates r_2,...,r_N are integrated out. A point r* ∈ R^3 is called a critical point of ρ if ∇ρ(r*) = 0; it is of type (3,-3) (a local maximum / "attractor") if the Hessian of ρ at r* is negative definite. A nuclear (3,-3) critical point is one located at some R_A; any other (3,-3) critical point is called a non-nuclear attractor.

Question: Prove or disprove the following conjecture.

(a) For every pair of nuclei (A,B) there exists a critical internuclear distance d^c_{AB} > 0 such that, whenever |R_A - R_B| > d^c_{AB} for all 1 <= A < B <= q, the gradient field of ρ has exactly q critical points of type (3,-3), and these are precisely the nuclear positions R_1,...,R_q (in particular, ρ has no non-nuclear attractors).

(b) Formulate in mathematically precise terms, and prove, the statement that for "most" molecules the equilibrium internuclear distances (the local minimizers of the Born–Oppenheimer total energy as a function of (R_1,...,R_q)) exceed the corresponding critical distances d^c_{AB}.
status_search_result: The conjecture concerns when the molecular one-electron density admits only nuclear (3,-3) attractors and no non-nuclear attractors. Non-nuclear attractors are documented in real molecules (e.g., Li_2, Na_3) at certain geometries, and existence/distribution results are mostly numerical or heuristic. No general mathematical proof of the existence of universal critical internuclear distances or of a precise "most molecules" statement appears in the literature; the problem remains an open mathematical conjecture in the quantum theory of atoms in molecules.

original_question: What is the most efficient definition of the state of a topological atom? A satisfactory definition should specify what information constitutes an atomic state and should make the atom’s properties practically deducible from that state, rather than merely listing all atomic properties or invoking a formal existence argument that the atomic one-electron density determines them.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
original_question: Can the literature and formalism of open quantum systems be used to redefine or improve the efficient state description of a topological atom, treating an atom in a molecule as an open subsystem whose properties must be inferred from an appropriate state specification?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a molecule modeled in the Born–Oppenheimer approximation as a quantum system of N electrons in the field of fixed nuclei, with associated electronic state described by a density operator ρ on the antisymmetric Fock/Hilbert space, and with one-electron density ρ(r) = N ∫|Ψ|² dτ' that is partitioned in real space according to the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM): each topological atom Ω is the basin of attraction in the gradient vector field ∇ρ(r) of a nuclear maximum, with interatomic surfaces S(Ω) satisfying the zero-flux condition ∇ρ(r)·n(r) = 0 for all r ∈ S(Ω).

Adopt the framework of open quantum systems, in which a subsystem A coupled to an environment E is described by a reduced density operator ρ_A = Tr_E ρ_{AE} obtained by partial trace, together with an associated dynamical map (e.g., a completely positive trace-preserving evolution or a Lindblad-type master equation) governing its effective dynamics.

Problem. Develop a rigorous formalism in which a topological atom Ω ⊂ ℝ³ (an open spatial subsystem with permeable, zero-flux boundary, exchanging electrons and energy with its complement Ω' in the molecule) is treated as an open quantum subsystem, and use this formalism to give an efficient state specification of the topological atom. Specifically:

(a) Define an appropriate reduced state ρ_Ω that encodes the quantum state of the electrons confined to (or associated with) the basin Ω, obtained by an analogue of the partial trace over the degrees of freedom in Ω', and show that it reproduces the standard QTAIM observables (atomic populations, kinetic and potential energy contributions, atomic multipole moments) as expectation values Tr(ρ_Ω O_Ω) of suitable operators O_Ω restricted to Ω.

(b) Derive the effective (possibly non-unitary) dynamical equation governing ρ_Ω that accounts for the exchange of electrons and energy across the interatomic surface S(Ω), and identify the conditions under which this evolution admits a Markovian (Lindblad) form.

(c) Determine whether such an open-system description provides a more efficient and physically faithful state specification of the topological atom than the standard QTAIM characterization, and, in particular, whether it resolves the issue of inferring atomic properties from a well-defined subsystem state rather than from spatially restricted integrals over the total molecular wavefunction.
status_search_result: A 2019 paper in J. Chem. Theory Comput. by Pendás and coworkers, "Quantum Chemical Topology as a Theory of Open Quantum Systems," explicitly takes up this program: it treats QTAIM basins as open quantum subsystems and derives reduced density operators for real-space regions by tracing out the complementary region. This constitutes substantial progress on parts (a)–(b) of the program, though a fully general dynamical (e.g., Lindblad-type) formulation and the question of whether such a description is genuinely "more efficient" than standard QTAIM remain active research topics. The problem is therefore best classified as partially solved.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: General Gauss-like theorem for all atomic properties
original_question: Can one derive a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms that goes beyond the subsystem hypervirial theorem and covers all conceivable topological-atom properties, including properties such as atomic energy and electron localization or delocalization indices that are not evidently obtained from known property currents on interatomic surfaces?
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let ρ : ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0} be the (one-electron) electron density of a molecular system, viewed as a smooth scalar field with isolated nuclear maxima. The Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM) partitions ℝ³ into disjoint open "topological atoms" Ω_A, where each Ω_A is the basin of attraction (under the gradient flow of ρ) of a nuclear critical point. Each basin is bounded by an interatomic surface S_A consisting of points where the gradient ∇ρ is tangent to the surface, i.e. ∇ρ · n = 0, with n the outward unit normal (the zero-flux boundary condition).

For a quantum-mechanical observable represented by an operator O, the average value over the topological atom Ω_A is ⟨O⟩_A = ∫_{Ω_A} ρ_O(r) dr for an appropriate density ρ_O derived from the system's wavefunction. The subsystem hypervirial theorem states that for a wide class of observables, ⟨O⟩_A can be reconstructed from a "property current" J_O on S_A via a Gauss-like identity of the form
   ⟨O⟩_A = ∮_{S_A} J_O · n dS,
i.e. the basin property is recoverable purely from boundary data (a "holographic" relation).

However, certain properties of topological atoms are not known to admit such a representation. Two important examples are:
 (i) the atomic energy E(Ω_A), defined via the kinetic energy density and an appropriate share of the potential energy of Ω_A;
 (ii) the (de)localization indices λ(Ω_A) and δ(Ω_A, Ω_B), defined for a state with one- and two-electron density matrices ρ₁, ρ₂ by
   δ(Ω_A, Ω_B) = -2 ∫_{Ω_A} ∫_{Ω_B} [ρ₂(r₁,r₂) - ρ(r₁)ρ(r₂)] dr₁ dr₂,
   λ(Ω_A) = δ(Ω_A, Ω_A)/2,
which measure electron sharing between basins.

Problem. Establish (or disprove) a general Gauss-like theorem for topological atoms that strictly extends the subsystem hypervirial theorem and applies to every conceivable property ⟨O⟩_A of a topological atom Ω_A. More precisely: for any reasonable atomic property functional F[ρ, ρ₁, ρ₂, …](Ω_A) — including in particular the atomic energy E(Ω_A), the localization index λ(Ω_A), and the delocalization indices δ(Ω_A, Ω_B) — exhibit a vector (or tensor) field J_F constructible from the wavefunction, defined on (a neighborhood of) S_A, such that
   F(Ω_A) = ∮_{S_A} J_F · n dS,
thereby realizing a fully holographic principle in which all properties of a topological atom are determined by data on its interatomic surface; or else prove that no such universal boundary representation can exist.
status_search_result: Subsequent literature on Quantum Chemical Topology and QTAIM (e.g. reviews on non-covalent interactions and topological coordination numbers from 2022–2025) continues to discuss the subsystem hypervirial theorem and the holographic viewpoint without reporting a general Gauss-like theorem covering atomic energy and (de)localization indices. No proof or counterexample establishing such a universal boundary theorem appears in the available sources, so the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Non-trivial duals of QTAIM and topological atoms
original_question: Does QTAIM, or do topological atoms themselves, have non-trivial dual formulations? Candidate duals include viewing a topological atom’s density in three-dimensional Euclidean space as equivalent to a free-atom density in non-Euclidean space, and viewing property currents of a topological atom as flows on the boundaries of a stationary but non-equilibrium thermodynamic open system.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. In the Quantum Theory of Atoms in Molecules (QTAIM), a molecular system is described by a smooth, everywhere-positive electron density ρ : ℝ³ → ℝ_{>0} obtained from the underlying many-electron wavefunction. A topological atom Ω ⊂ ℝ³ is defined as a basin of the gradient vector field ∇ρ: namely, Ω is a maximal open subset of ℝ³ such that every integral curve of ∇ρ starting in Ω terminates at the same nuclear critical point (a local maximum of ρ). Equivalently, Ω is bounded by a zero-flux surface S = ∂Ω satisfying ∇ρ(r) · n(r) = 0 for every r ∈ S, where n is the outward unit normal. To each one-electron property A is associated a property current j_A on ℝ³, derived from the wavefunction, whose integral fluxes through ∂Ω determine the atomic contribution of Ω to A.

Problem. Determine whether QTAIM, viewed either as a theory of the pair (ρ, {j_A}) or as a theory of its topological atoms Ω, admits a non-trivial dual formulation. In particular, decide each of the following:

(a) Does there exist a non-Euclidean Riemannian (or more general) manifold (M, g), depending functorially on (ℝ³, ρ), and a density ρ̃ on M corresponding to a free (non-interacting) atom, such that the topological atom (Ω, ρ|_Ω) in Euclidean three-space is isomorphic — under a precisely specified equivalence of densities, currents, and basin/zero-flux structures — to (M, ρ̃)? Construct such a duality, or prove that no such non-trivial correspondence exists.

(b) Does there exist a stationary non-equilibrium thermodynamic open system, with a well-defined boundary geometry and boundary flows, such that the property currents {j_A} of a topological atom Ω are equivalent (as vector fields with associated conserved fluxes) to the boundary flows of this thermodynamic system, in a way that recovers all QTAIM atomic observables? Either exhibit such a correspondence or prove its impossibility.

A non-trivial dual is required to give a bijection on observables that is not merely a tautological relabeling.
category_tag: Quantum theory of atoms in molecules
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open conceptual problem about possible dual formulations of QTAIM and its topological atoms. No subsequent literature establishing such a non-trivial duality (either to free-atom densities on non-Euclidean spaces or to boundary flows of stationary non-equilibrium thermodynamic systems) was located, and the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Revisiting the foundations of the quantum theory of atoms in molecules: Some open problems
context_brief: Liquid model and mechanics of charge density
original_question: Can one develop a liquid model of charge density in atoms-in-molecules theory in which a principal parameter is the viscosity experienced by migrating critical points, and can the currently incomplete mechanics of charge density be extended into new models that answer old problems?
self_contained_problem:
In the quantum theory of atoms in molecules, a molecular system is described by its (scalar) one-electron charge density ρ: ℝ³ → ℝ_{≥0}, a smooth function whose critical points (where ∇ρ = 0) are classified by the signature of the Hessian into nuclear attractors (3,−3), bond critical points (3,−1), ring critical points (3,+1), and cage critical points (3,+3). Atomic basins are defined as the connected regions of the gradient field ∇ρ bounded by zero-flux surfaces (surfaces S satisfying ∇ρ(r)·n(r)=0 for all r ∈ S). As nuclear coordinates evolve along a reaction path R(t), the critical points of ρ(·;R(t)) migrate continuously in ℝ³ (away from catastrophe events).

The problem is to formulate a "liquid (continuum) model" for the dynamics of the charge density ρ in which:

1. The migrating critical points {x_k(t)} of ρ(·;R(t)) are treated as transported by an effective velocity field on a viscous medium, governed by a constitutive law of the form
   η(ρ,∇ρ,…) · ẋ_k(t) = F_k[ρ, R, Ṙ],
   where η is a scalar (or tensorial) viscosity functional taken as the principal parameter of the model and F_k is a force functional derivable from the energetic and topological structure of ρ.

2. The model reproduces, in appropriate limits, the established mechanics of the charge density (continuity equation for ρ, atomic-basin force and virial theorems, and stationarity of zero-flux surfaces), and yields a closed evolution equation for ρ along nuclear motion compatible with the catastrophe set of QTAIM.

Construct such a model with a precisely defined viscosity functional η, derive the corresponding equations of motion for ρ and for its critical points, and use it to address at least one of the following standing problems: (a) prediction of bifurcation thresholds at which bond/ring/cage critical points coalesce or annihilate, (b) quantitative characterization of "structural stability" of molecular graphs under nuclear displacement, and (c) extension of the mechanics of the charge density to a complete dynamical theory consistent with the underlying quantum stress-tensor field.

Determine whether such a viscosity-based liquid model of the charge density exists with the above properties, and exhibit it explicitly, or prove that no such consistent model can be formulated within the QTAIM framework.
status_search_result: The question is a programmatic open problem about formulating a new "liquid/viscous" continuum model for the QTAIM charge density. No subsequent work appears to have constructed such a model with viscosity as principal parameter; the broader program of completing the mechanics of the charge density remains open in the QTAIM literature.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: During the normal impact of an inflated ball on a rigid surface, what amount of energy is carried away by sound or a shock wave generated by the rapidly moving ball-ground-air contact line, and are these sound-radiated losses negligible compared with the total energy lost in the impact?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the normal impact of an inflated elastic ball (e.g. a sports ball, modeled as a thin pressurized spherical shell of radius R filled with gas at internal pressure p, mass m) striking a flat rigid surface at vertical velocity V. As the ball deforms against the surface, a circular contact patch forms whose radius l(t) grows in time; from the geometry of a sphere indented by a depth x = Vt, one has l(t) ≈ √(2Rx) so that the lateral expansion velocity of the ball–ground–air contact line is

  dl/dt ≈ V √(R/(2x)),

which diverges as x → 0+. While dl/dt exceeds the speed of sound c_s in the surrounding air, a shock wave is emitted from the contact line, and once dl/dt < c_s ordinary acoustic radiation continues.

Problem. Derive a quantitative estimate of the total energy E_sound radiated as sound and shock waves into the surrounding air during a single normal impact, expressed in terms of the impact parameters (V, R, m, ambient air density ρ_air and sound speed c_s, and any relevant material/pressure parameters). paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: How much impact energy is dissipated by rapid viscoelastic bending and deformation of an inflated ball's shell, and how do the shell material's high-strain-rate viscosity, seams, multilayer construction, and shell thickness affect the coefficient of restitution?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a thin-walled inflated spherical ball (a pressurized elastic shell) of mass $m$, outer radius $R$, shell thickness $h$, and internal gauge pressure $P$, made of a viscoelastic material (e.g., synthetic rubber) with high-strain-rate dynamic viscosity $\eta(\dot\varepsilon)$ for strain rates $\dot\varepsilon \in [10^2, 10^3]\,\mathrm{s}^{-1}$. The ball impacts a rigid flat surface normally with pre-impact speed $U_0$ and rebounds with speed $U_1$; define the coefficient of restitution $e = U_1/U_0$. During contact, the shell undergoes rapid bending and local flattening over a contact patch, producing viscous dissipation $E_{\mathrm{visc}}$ in the shell material in addition to other loss channels (aerodynamic, acoustic, internal-gas, substrate).

(a) Derive a quantitative model that expresses the energy $E_{\mathrm{visc}}$ dissipated by viscoelastic bending and deformation of the shell during a single normal impact as an explicit function of the parameters $(m, R, h, P, U_0, \eta)$, including the dependence on the effective strain-rate spectrum induced by the impact.

(b) Using this model, determine the contribution $\Delta(1-e^2)_{\mathrm{shell}}$ of shell viscoelastic dissipation to $1 - e^2$, and characterize how this contribution depends on shell thickness $h$ in the limit $h \to 0$ (in particular, decide whether $\Delta(1-e^2)_{\mathrm{shell}} \to 0$).

(c) Extend the model to a shell composed of $N$ bonded layers with individual thicknesses $h_i$ and viscosities $\eta_i$, and incorporate the effect of seams (stitched or glued joints of total length $L_s$ and characteristic compliance differing from the bulk shell), and predict how multilayer construction and seams modify $e$ relative to a homogeneous single-layer shell of the same total thickness, mass, radius, and internal pressure.

Provide closed-form scaling laws and, for a basketball-like configuration ($m \approx 0.6\,\mathrm{kg}$, $R \approx 0.12\,\mathrm{m}$, $U_0 = 16\,\mathrm{m/s}$, $\eta \sim 0.2\,\mathrm{Pa\cdot s}$), compute $E_{\mathrm{visc}}$.
status_search_result: No published resolution was found. The question concerns an open modeling/experimental program on viscoelastic shell dissipation in inflated sports balls; the high-strain-rate rheology of synthetic rubber shells in the relevant range and the thickness/seam/layer dependence of the coefficient of restitution have not been definitively characterized in the literature accessible via search.

paper_title: Open questions on the impact of an inflated ball
original_question: Is the momentum-flux force model a valid physical explanation of energy dissipation in inflated-ball impacts, where the proposed dissipative force is Fd = -m xdot^2/(2 R0) for ball mass m, ball radius R0, and indentation speed xdot? A satisfactory answer should supply the missing microscopic mechanism for energy transformation and test the model against systematic coefficient-of-restitution measurements that vary inflation pressure and shell mechanical characteristics.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the normal impact of an inflated spherical ball of mass m, undeformed radius R_0, and internal inflation pressure P_0 against a rigid flat surface, with initial impact speed U_0. Let x(t) denote the indentation (compression) of the ball at time t, and let \dot{x}(t) be the indentation speed. A proposed model for the dissipative force acting on the ball during contact is

   F_d(t) = - m \dot{x}(t)^2 / (2 R_0).

Under this model the equation of motion of the ball's center of mass during contact is m \ddot{x} = F_{el}(x, P_0) + F_d, where F_{el} is the (conservative) elastic restoring force arising from membrane deformation and pressurization.

Resolve the following:

(a) Provide a microscopic physical mechanism (for example, excitation of shell vibrational modes, internal acoustic radiation, viscoelastic membrane losses, or gas-dynamic dissipation) that derives, from first principles, a dissipative force of the form F_d = - m \dot{x}^2 / (2 R_0) for an inflated elastic shell impacting a rigid wall, and identify the regime of inflation pressure, shell stiffness, and impact velocity in which such a derivation is valid.

(b) Using this model, compute the coefficient of restitution

   e(U_0, P_0, \text{shell parameters}) = |\dot{x}(t_f)| / U_0,

where t_f is the moment of separation, and determine whether its predicted dependence on U_0, P_0, and the mechanical parameters of the shell (Young's modulus, thickness, areal density) agrees with systematic experimental measurements of e obtained by varying inflation pressure and shell characteristics over a broad range.

Decide whether the momentum-flux dissipation law F_d = - m \dot{x}^2 / (2 R_0) is a physically valid description of energy loss in inflated-ball impacts.
status_search_result: The question of whether the momentum-flux dissipation law F_d = -m \dot{x}^2/(2R_0) is a correct microscopic model for inflated-ball impacts, and whether it matches restitution-coefficient measurements across inflation pressure and shell properties, appears to remain open: it is posed as an outstanding open problem and no subsequent systematic experimental or theoretical resolution was readily found.

paper_title: Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment: Evaluation Protocols and Open Problems for General Agents
original_question: How can an agent in the Arcade Learning Environment automatically learn a generic internal representation that works across many Atari 2600 games, while being much more sample-efficient than current DQN-like methods, avoiding heavy task-specific tuning, and coping with sparse-reward games such as Montezuma’s Revenge where current methods may occasionally encounter reward without learning to obtain it consistently?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), a reinforcement learning benchmark consisting of a large suite of Atari 2600 games. Each game is modeled as a Markov decision process whose state at time t is given by a raw screen observation s_t (a 210×160 array of pixels with a 128-color palette, optionally stacked over several recent frames), whose action set A is a finite subset of the 18 Atari joystick/button combinations, and whose reward r_t is the per-step change in the in-game score. A general agent is a single learning algorithm (with one fixed set of hyperparameters) that, given only (s_t, r_t, a_t) interaction traces, must learn to play every game in the suite.

Design and analyze a learning procedure that produces an internal representation φ: S → R^d (with d, the architecture, and the training objective fixed across games) and a policy π based on φ such that all of the following hold simultaneously:

1. (Generality) The same algorithm and hyperparameters are used for every game in the ALE; no per-game feature engineering or tuning is permitted.

2. (Sample efficiency) The number of environment interactions required to reach human-level performance on a representative set of ALE games is substantially smaller than the tens of millions of frames required by standard deep Q-network (DQN) style methods. Quantify the achievable sample complexity and prove or empirically establish a separation from the DQN baseline.

3. (Sparse-reward exploration) On games in which extrinsic reward is encountered only after long action sequences—exemplified by Montezuma's Revenge—the procedure must, with high probability, convert isolated reward events into a policy that obtains those rewards consistently, rather than failing to propagate the signal.

State precise assumptions on the environment (e.g., determinism vs. stochasticity, frame-skip, episode termination) under which the guarantees in (2) and (3) hold, and either (a) exhibit an algorithm meeting all three criteria with provable or rigorously measured guarantees, or (b) prove an impossibility result showing that no algorithm satisfying (1) can simultaneously achieve (2) and (3) within a specified sample budget.
status_search_result: The challenge of sample-efficient, general representation learning across ALE—especially in hard-exploration games like Montezuma's Revenge—remains an active open problem. Subsequent works (e.g., Go-Explore, Agent57, MuZero, EfficientZero) have made substantial progress on individual aspects: Agent57 (2020) surpassed human baseline on all 57 Atari games, and EfficientZero (2021) achieved high sample efficiency on the Atari 100k benchmark. However, no single method is widely accepted as simultaneously satisfying generality, DQN-beating sample efficiency, and robust sparse-reward learning without specialized components, so the broader problem is best characterized as partially solved/still open.

paper_title: Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment: Evaluation Protocols and Open Problems for General Agents
context_brief: Exploration under sparse or deceptive rewards
original_question: How can a model-free reinforcement learning agent with function approximation explore the Arcade Learning Environment efficiently enough to discover rewards that are delayed, sparse, or initially negative, as in games such as Montezuma’s Revenge, Private Eye, Pitfall!, and Tennis, potentially by committing to temporally extended decisions at a higher level of abstraction than individual joystick moves and by using intrinsic motivation when scoring appears impossible?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Arcade Learning Environment (ALE), a benchmark suite of Atari 2600 games in which a reinforcement learning agent at each discrete time step observes a frame (or short stack of frames) of raw pixel input, selects one of 18 joystick/button actions, and receives a scalar reward equal to the change in the game's score. Within this benchmark, certain games — including Montezuma's Revenge, Private Eye, Pitfall!, and Tennis — exhibit reward signals that are extremely delayed (thousands of primitive actions may pass before any nonzero reward), sparse, or initially negative/deceptive (the agent receives only negative rewards before discovering any positive ones).

Restrict attention to model-free reinforcement learning agents that use parametric function approximation (e.g., deep neural networks) over the raw observation space and that learn a policy or value function via stochastic interaction with the environment, without access to a learned or hand-coded forward model of the game dynamics, without expert demonstrations, and without game-specific prior knowledge.

Problem. Design and analyze such a model-free function-approximation agent together with an exploration mechanism — possibly based on (i) commitment to temporally extended actions or options at a higher level of abstraction than single joystick inputs, and/or (ii) an intrinsic motivation reward signal that drives the agent to continue exploring when extrinsic scoring appears infeasible — that, using only environment interactions and within a sample budget comparable to standard ALE evaluation protocols, reliably discovers the delayed/sparse/deceptive extrinsic rewards in games such as Montezuma's Revenge, Private Eye, Pitfall!, and Tennis, and attains performance competitive with human play across all of these games simultaneously.
status_search_result: Substantial progress has been made since the problem was posed. DeepMind's Agent57 (2020) is the first agent to surpass the human baseline on all 57 Atari games, including Montezuma's Revenge, Pitfall!, Private Eye, and Tennis, using a model-free distributed agent with a family of intrinsic-motivation policies. Uber's Go-Explore reliably solves Montezuma's Revenge and achieves the first positive learning scores on Pitfall!. However, these successes typically rely on additional machinery (episodic memory/archive of states, meta-controllers over exploratory policies, or restoring to saved states) that arguably goes beyond the strict "purely model-free with function approximation and primitive actions" formulation, so the problem in its narrowest form remains only partially resolved.

paper_title: Revisiting the Arcade Learning Environment: Evaluation Protocols and Open Problems for General Agents
original_question: How can one obtain an off-policy reinforcement learning method for the Arcade Learning Environment that is both stable and practical under function approximation, has theory that actually explains its empirical behavior, can reliably reuse samples generated by policies very different from the current one, and does not depend on brittle heuristics such as replay buffers or target networks merely to avoid divergence?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard reinforcement learning setting in which an agent interacts with a Markov decision process (MDP) M = (S, A, P, r, γ) with state space S, action space A, transition kernel P(s' | s, a), reward function r(s, a), and discount factor γ ∈ [0, 1). The agent's goal is to learn a policy π: S → Δ(A) maximizing the expected discounted return E[∑_{t≥0} γ^t r(s_t, a_t)]. In the off-policy setting, value functions or policies for a target policy π are estimated from trajectories produced by behavior policies μ that may differ substantially from π, and value functions Q_θ: S × A → ℝ are represented by a parameterized function approximator (e.g., a neural network) with parameters θ.

Design an off-policy reinforcement learning algorithm with parameterized function approximation that simultaneously satisfies all of the following requirements, when applied to high-dimensional control tasks of the difficulty of Atari 2600 games (large discrete action spaces, raw image observations, long horizons):

1. Stability: the parameter iterates θ_t generated by the algorithm provably do not diverge under standard regularity assumptions on the function approximator and the data-generating distribution, even when the behavior policy μ differs significantly from the target policy π.

2. Theoretical guarantees that match empirical behavior: the algorithm admits a convergence (or boundedness) analysis whose hypotheses and conclusions actually explain the observed empirical performance, rather than holding only in regimes (e.g., linear function approximation, on-policy sampling) that are absent in practice.

3. Sample reuse: the algorithm can reliably and efficiently reuse transitions (s, a, r, s') generated by behavior policies μ that are very different from the current target policy π, without performance collapse.

4. No reliance on stabilizing heuristics: the algorithm does not require an experience replay buffer or a separately maintained target network solely as a mechanism to prevent divergence; any use of such components must be justified beyond merely ensuring non-divergence.

Either construct such an algorithm and prove it meets requirements 1–4 while demonstrating empirical performance competitive with state-of-the-art off-policy methods on a benchmark suite of high-dimensional control tasks, or prove that no algorithm satisfying all four requirements simultaneously can exist within a specified class of function approximators and sampling regimes.
category_tag: off-policy reinforcement learning with function approximation
status_search_result: The problem is a long-standing open challenge in deep reinforcement learning: combining stable off-policy learning with nonlinear function approximation, theory matching practice, and elimination of replay/target-network heuristics. While significant progress has been made (e.g., Emphatic-TD, Gradient-TD methods, distributional RL, work on the deadly triad, and analyses by Sutton, Maei, and others), no known method jointly satisfies all four requirements at scale. The problem remains open as of available literature.

paper_title: Autonomous Agents Modelling Other Agents: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Can one develop a single representation and modelling approach for autonomous agents that naturally combines multiple agent-modelling capabilities—such as policy reconstruction, type-based reasoning, classification, plan recognition, recursive or epistemic reasoning, and graphical models—so that these different modelling processes inform one another synergistically rather than only being combined in a loose modular way?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an autonomous agent A operating in a multi-agent environment that contains one or more other agents. To act effectively, A must maintain models of the other agents that may capture diverse aspects of their behavior and cognition, including:

(i) Policy reconstruction: estimating another agent's mapping from observation/state histories to action distributions.
(ii) Type-based reasoning: maintaining a (Bayesian) belief over a discrete set of candidate behavioral types and updating it from observed actions.
(iii) Classification: assigning observed agents to behavioral or strategic categories based on features of their interaction history.
(iv) Plan recognition: inferring the goals and (hierarchical) plans of another agent from partial action sequences.
(v) Recursive / epistemic reasoning: representing nested beliefs of the form "A believes that B believes that A believes …" up to some finite depth, as in interactive POMDPs or epistemic logic.
(vi) Graphical models: representing dependencies among agents' actions, types, goals, and observations via probabilistic graphical structures.

Currently, each of these modelling capabilities is typically realized by a distinct formalism, and integrations are achieved only through loose modular pipelines in which the outputs of one component are fed as inputs to another.

Problem. Design a single mathematical representation together with an associated inference and learning procedure for an agent A such that:

(a) The representation simultaneously instantiates all of the capabilities (i)–(vi) above as special cases or as marginal/derived quantities of one underlying model.
(b) Inference performed for any one capability automatically updates the quantities relevant to the others, so that the modelling processes inform one another synergistically rather than independently.
(c) The framework admits a well-defined semantics (e.g., as a probabilistic or decision-theoretic model), permits tractable approximate inference, and reduces, in appropriate limiting cases, to each of the standard formalisms underlying (i)–(vi).

Either construct such a unified representation and prove that it satisfies (a)–(c), or prove that no representation satisfying (a)–(c) can exist under stated assumptions.
status_search_result: The question is posed as a long-term open challenge in agent modelling. No subsequent work appears to provide a single representation that natively unifies policy reconstruction, type-based reasoning, classification, plan recognition, recursive/epistemic reasoning, and graphical models with synergistic mutual inference; existing approaches still combine these capabilities in modular fashion. The problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Autonomous Agents Modelling Other Agents: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can a modelling agent choose exploratory actions that efficiently reveal useful information about another agent's behaviour while remaining safe, in the sense that the exploration does not alter the other agent's behaviour in harmful or unintended ways and does not require computationally intractable look-ahead?
self_contained_problem:
Consider a sequential interaction between a modelling agent A and another agent B, both acting in a shared environment formalized as a stochastic game. At each time step t, agent A selects an action a_t from a finite action set, observes B's action b_t and an environment state s_t, and maintains a probabilistic model M_t over B's policy (a mapping from histories to action distributions). Agent A wishes to perform exploratory actions that yield information about B's policy — that is, actions that reduce the entropy or uncertainty of M_t with respect to B's true (unknown) policy π_B — while satisfying the following constraints:

(i) Safety: the exploratory actions chosen by A must not perturb B's future behaviour in ways that change π_B beyond a prescribed tolerance, i.e. for some predefined divergence measure D and threshold ε ≥ 0, the policy of B conditional on having observed A's exploratory history must satisfy D(π_B^{after} ∥ π_B^{baseline}) ≤ ε, where π_B^{baseline} denotes B's policy in the absence of the exploratory perturbation.

(ii) Tractability: the algorithm used by A to select exploratory actions must run in time polynomial in the size of the state and action spaces and the planning horizon, ruling out exhaustive look-ahead over the joint state-action tree.

Design an action-selection rule (or characterize the existence of one) for agent A that maximizes a measure of expected information gain about π_B over a finite horizon T, subject to the safety constraint (i) and the computational constraint (ii), and provide formal guarantees on its information-gain efficiency relative to the unconstrained Bayes-optimal exploration strategy.
status_search_result: The problem is posed as an open challenge in the literature on agents modelling other agents, where existing safe-exploration methods are noted to either risk altering the modelled agent's behaviour or to require intractable look-ahead. No general algorithm with the described joint safety and tractability guarantees appears to have been established.

paper_title: Autonomous Agents Modelling Other Agents: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
original_question: How can agent-modelling methods be implemented so that they remain computationally efficient enough for real applications—where perception, communication, planning, physics simulation, and rendering already consume most resources—by using techniques such as efficient data structures, parallel architectures, or incremental updates that process only new observations?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an autonomous agent operating in a real-time environment in which the available computational budget per decision cycle is largely consumed by perception, communication, planning, physics simulation, and rendering. Suppose the agent must additionally maintain models of one or more other agents acting in the same environment, where an agent model is a function that, given a history of observations of another agent's behavior, produces a predictive representation (for example, a policy, type distribution, or belief state) used to inform the modelling agent's own decisions.

Develop and analyze general-purpose algorithmic techniques—such as specialized data structures, parallel or distributed architectures, and incremental update schemes that process only newly arrived observations rather than recomputing from full histories—that allow such agent-modelling methods to be implemented with worst-case per-step time and memory complexity small enough to fit within the residual computational budget of a real application. Specifically:

1. Formalize a model of the per-step computational budget and of the agent-modelling task (input: stream of observations of other agents; output: updated predictive model).
2. Identify which classes of agent-modelling methods admit incremental update algorithms whose per-step cost is independent of the length of the observation history, and characterize the achievable trade-offs between update cost, memory, and predictive accuracy.

paper_title: Autonomous Agents Modelling Other Agents: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
original_question: What modifications to existing agent-modelling methods are needed to handle actions that have non-negligible duration, rather than instantaneous effects, and should this challenge be treated within agent modelling itself or instead as part of a lower-level activity-recognition problem that infers temporally extended actions from state data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the standard framework of multi-agent modelling in which an autonomous agent maintains predictive models of other agents' behaviour. Formally, let an environment be described by a state space S, a finite set of agents I, and for each agent i a set of actions A_i. A standard agent model is a mapping π_i : H → Δ(A_i) from interaction histories H (sequences of states and joint actions) to distributions over A_i, with the implicit assumption that each action a ∈ A_i is instantaneous, i.e. its effect on the state is realized in a single discrete time step.

Now drop the instantaneous-action assumption: each action a ∈ A_i has a duration d(a) > 0 (possibly stochastic, possibly state-dependent), during which the agent is committed to a, the action's effect is spread over multiple time steps, and the action may be interrupted. Observations available to the modelling agent consist of state trajectories (s_t)_{t≥0} together possibly with partial action labels.

The problem is to determine:

(a) Precisely which formal modifications must be made to existing classes of agent-modelling methods (e.g. policy reconstruction, type-based reasoning, plan recognition, recursive reasoning, group modelling) so that they remain well-defined, consistent, and predictively accurate when the modelled agents execute temporally extended actions with the above semantics; and

(b) Whether the problem of inferring such temporally extended actions should be handled inside the agent-modelling layer itself (i.e. by enlarging the hypothesis space of π_i to include duration-aware policies over options or semi-Markov decision processes) or whether it should be factored out as a separate lower-level activity-recognition problem that maps raw state trajectories to a sequence of completed extended actions, whose output then feeds an unmodified instantaneous-action modeller.

Provide a rigorous comparison of the two architectural choices in terms of identifiability of the agent's policy, sample complexity of learning, and predictive accuracy under interruption and concurrency of extended actions.
category_tag: Multi-agent modelling with temporally extended actions
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open research direction in the agent-modelling literature. While related frameworks (semi-Markov decision processes, the options framework, plan/activity recognition) provide partial tools, no comprehensive resolution specifying the required modifications or settling the architectural question has been established in the surveyed literature.

paper_title: Autonomous Agents Modelling Other Agents: A Comprehensive Survey and Open Problems
original_question: Can an autonomous agent introspectively assess whether its current modelling method, model class, or model space is adequate for the interaction at hand, diagnose why a model is inadequate or misleading, and then autonomously revise its modelling structures or processes using notions of adequacy that may be weaker and more task-oriented than strict correctness?
self_contained_problem:
Consider an autonomous agent A interacting with one or more other agents in a (possibly partially observable, stochastic) multi-agent environment. Agent A maintains a modelling apparatus consisting of three layers: (i) a modelling method M (an algorithm that maps observed interaction histories to predictions about other agents' behaviour), (ii) a model class C (the parametric or structural family of hypotheses M searches over), and (iii) a model space S (the space of possible model classes A could in principle entertain). Let h_t denote the interaction history available to A at time t, and let τ denote the task or objective A is pursuing.

Define a notion of task-oriented adequacy as a relation Adeq(M, C, S; h_t, τ) that may be strictly weaker than predictive correctness; for example, Adeq could require only that the predictions induced by (M, C) suffice for A to choose actions whose expected return on task τ is within ε of optimal, or that they correctly rank a relevant subset of candidate actions.

Design, and prove guarantees for, an introspective procedure I executable by A that, on the basis of h_t and τ alone (without privileged access to the true models of the other agents), accomplishes the following:

1. Detection: decides whether the current triple (M, C, S) satisfies Adeq(·; h_t, τ); 
2. Diagnosis: when adequacy fails, identifies which layer (the method M, the class C, or the space S) is responsible and characterises in what way the current model is inadequate or misleading;
3. Revision: autonomously produces a revised triple (M', C', S') and provides a criterion under which the revision improves task-oriented adequacy, together with conditions ensuring that the iterative application of I converges (in a precise sense to be specified) to a triple satisfying Adeq.

Formalise the notion of adequacy, the introspection operator I, and the revision dynamics, and determine whether such a procedure with provable detection, diagnosis, and revision guarantees exists for general multi-agent interaction settings, or identify the structural assumptions on the environment, the task τ, and the model space S under which it does.
category_tag: agent modelling and introspective model revision
status_search_result: The problem of an autonomous agent introspectively assessing the adequacy of its own opponent/agent models and autonomously revising its model class or model space using task-oriented (rather than strictly correct) notions of adequacy is identified as an open research direction in surveys on multi-agent modelling. Subsequent work on meta-reasoning, model-class selection, and Bayesian model criticism in multi-agent reinforcement learning addresses fragments (e.g. switching among a fixed pool of models or detecting non-stationarity), but no general framework providing detection, diagnosis, and revision with task-oriented adequacy guarantees appears to have been established.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Let M be a compact 3-dimensional manifold and consider generic vacuum initial data on M for Einstein's equations. Is the maximal vacuum Cauchy development already the maximal vacuum extension, so that the generic solution cannot be continued beyond its Cauchy horizon?
self_contained_problem:
Let $M$ be a compact, smooth, 3-dimensional manifold. A vacuum initial data set on $M$ consists of a Riemannian metric $g$ and a symmetric $(0,2)$-tensor $K$ on $M$ satisfying the vacuum constraint equations
\[
R(g) - |K|_g^2 + (\mathrm{tr}_g K)^2 = 0, \qquad \nabla^j K_{ij} - \nabla_i(\mathrm{tr}_g K) = 0,
\]
where $R(g)$ is the scalar curvature of $g$. Given such data, the maximal vacuum Cauchy development is the unique (up to isometry) globally hyperbolic Lorentzian 4-manifold $(\mathcal{D},\mathbf{g})$ solving the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(\mathbf{g})=0$ in which $(M,g,K)$ embeds as a Cauchy hypersurface, and which is maximal among all such globally hyperbolic developments. A maximal vacuum extension is any inextendible smooth Lorentzian 4-manifold satisfying $\mathrm{Ric}=0$ into which $(M,g,K)$ embeds as an initial data set, with no requirement of global hyperbolicity.

Prove or disprove: For initial data sets $(g,K)$ on $M$ in a generic subset (in a suitable topology) of the space of smooth vacuum initial data, the maximal vacuum Cauchy development of $(M,g,K)$ coincides with a maximal vacuum extension of $(M,g,K)$; equivalently, the generic such solution admits no smooth (or sufficiently regular) extension across its Cauchy horizon.
status_search_result: The problem is the strong cosmic censorship conjecture in vacuum. Substantial progress exists: Dafermos and Luk (2017) showed that for small perturbations of Kerr the Cauchy horizon admits a continuous (C^0) extension, disproving the C^0 formulation in the vacuum setting. The conjecture in stronger formulations (e.g., inextendibility in C^2 or with locally square-integrable Christoffel symbols) remains open and is the subject of ongoing research, as surveyed in 2024–2025 reviews. Hence the precise statement (smooth/regular inextendibility for generic data) is partially resolved.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: For collisionless matter models in general relativity, can one prove global existence of classical spatially inhomogeneous solutions for small initial data, and can one also prove existence and uniqueness for general spatially homogeneous solutions such as Bianchi type IX solutions of the Einstein-Vlasov equations while determining what happens for large initial data?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Einstein–Vlasov system, which couples the Einstein field equations of general relativity to the Vlasov (collisionless Boltzmann) equation describing an ensemble of particles moving on geodesics of the spacetime. Concretely, on a 4-manifold M with Lorentzian metric g of signature (−,+,+,+), the unknown is a pair (g, f) where f: P → [0, ∞) is a non-negative distribution function on the mass-shell P ⊂ T*M (the bundle of future-directed timelike or null covectors of fixed mass), satisfying the Vlasov equation X_g f = 0, with X_g the geodesic spray on P; and g satisfies the Einstein equations Ric(g) − (1/2) R(g) g + Λ g = 8π T(f), where the energy–momentum tensor T(f) is built from the moments of f on the mass-shell.

Address the following two questions for this system:

(a) (Inhomogeneous small-data global existence.) Given asymptotically flat (or otherwise admissible) Cauchy initial data (Σ, h, k, f₀) on a 3-manifold Σ that is sufficiently small in a suitable Sobolev norm and not assumed to possess any spatial symmetry, prove that the maximal Cauchy development of these data, as a classical solution of the Einstein–Vlasov system, exists globally to the future and is geodesically complete.

(b) (Spatially homogeneous case.) For spatially homogeneous initial data of Bianchi type — and in particular for the most delicate case of Bianchi type IX, in which the spatial isometry group acts simply transitively with Lie algebra so(3) — prove an existence and uniqueness theorem for the corresponding solutions of the Einstein–Vlasov equations valid for all initial data (not only those close to special reference solutions), and determine the qualitative dynamical behavior of the resulting cosmologies in the large-data regime, including the structure of any singularities and the asymptotics towards them.
status_search_result: Significant progress has been made: global nonlinear stability of Minkowski space for the massless Einstein–Vlasov system (Taylor, 2017) and for the massive case (Lindblad–Taylor; Fajman–Joudioux–Smulevici, 2019) gives small-data global existence results without symmetry assumptions. For homogeneous models, global existence is known for all Bianchi types except Bianchi IX (and Kantowski–Sachs); the Bianchi IX case and the large-data behavior remain open. Hence the problem is partially solved.

original_question: For a four-dimensional spacetime, when can the spacetime be reconstructed explicitly from its scalar curvature invariants, and what is the minimal collection of such invariants needed to characterize it completely?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a four-dimensional Lorentzian spacetime, smooth and connected. For each $k\ge 0$, consider the scalar polynomial curvature invariants formed by full contractions of the Riemann curvature tensor $R_{abcd}$ together with its covariant derivatives $\nabla_{e_1}\cdots\nabla_{e_k} R_{abcd}$ using the metric $g$ and its inverse. Let $\mathcal{I}(M,g)$ denote the set of all such scalar polynomial curvature invariants. 

(a) Give explicit necessary and sufficient conditions on $(M,g)$ under which the metric $g$ can be reconstructed (locally, up to diffeomorphism) from the values of the invariants in $\mathcal{I}(M,g)$.

(b) For each spacetime $(M,g)$ satisfying the conditions in part (a), determine the minimal cardinality and an explicit minimal collection of invariants from $\mathcal{I}(M,g)$ that suffices to characterize $(M,g)$ completely.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: Can one rigorously derive the geodesic hypothesis of general relativity by proving that sufficiently small test particles, in the negligible-mass limit and including gravitational backreaction issues, move along spacetime geodesics?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Lorentzian 4-manifold satisfying the Einstein field equations. The geodesic hypothesis asserts that a sufficiently small, freely falling test body moves along a timelike geodesic of $(M,g)$.

Formulate and prove a rigorous theorem that justifies this hypothesis. Specifically, give a precise mathematical sense in which the following statement holds: as the size, mass, and self-gravitational backreaction of a material body tend to zero (for instance via a one-parameter family of solutions of the Einstein equations coupled to suitable matter—e.g. a perfect fluid, dust, or a nonlinear Klein–Gordon field—with support concentrating on a timelike curve $\gamma\subset M$), the curve $\gamma$ along which the body's energy concentrates must be a timelike geodesic of the background metric $g$.

The problem is to obtain such a derivation that
(i) starts from the full nonlinear Einstein equations (so that gravitational self-interaction/backreaction is consistently incorporated rather than postulated away),
(ii) avoids ad hoc regularization of singular point-particle stress–energy, and
(iii) yields the geodesic equation for $\gamma$ as a rigorously proved theorem in the negligible-mass limit.
status_search_result: Several rigorous results exist that justify the geodesic hypothesis in restricted settings: Geroch–Jang-type theorems for shrinking world tubes of matter, the Gralla–Wald (2008) rigorous derivation of the motion (and self-force) of a small body via one-parameter families of solutions to Einstein's equations, and Y. Choquet-Bruhat / Stuart / J. Wong-type derivations using concentrated Klein–Gordon matter (e.g. Stuart, Comm. Math. Phys. 2014). However, a fully general theorem covering arbitrary small self-gravitating bodies in generic spacetimes is not established, so the problem is best described as partially solved.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: In spacetime dimensions higher than four, can one classify and prove uniqueness properties for black-hole solutions, despite the much richer family of higher-dimensional vacuum black holes than in four-dimensional general relativity?
self_contained_problem:
Let $(M,g)$ be a $D$-dimensional Lorentzian manifold with $D\ge 5$ that is a smooth, asymptotically flat, stationary solution of the vacuum Einstein equations $\mathrm{Ric}(g)=0$, and suppose $(M,g)$ contains a regular event horizon (so that $(M,g)$ is a stationary, asymptotically flat, vacuum black-hole spacetime). In four dimensions, the classical no-hair/uniqueness theorems imply that any such spacetime is, up to isometry, a Kerr solution and is therefore characterized by its mass and angular momentum. In higher dimensions $D\ge 5$ this fails: explicit families such as the Myers–Perry black holes and the Emparan–Reall black ring (with horizon topology $S^1\times S^2$ in $D=5$) show that mass and angular momenta alone do not determine the solution, and horizon topology is not restricted to spheres.

Problem: Provide a complete classification, up to isometry, of all stationary, asymptotically flat, regular vacuum black-hole solutions in dimension $D\ge 5$, and identify a finite set of geometric/topological invariants (such as mass, angular momenta, horizon topology, and rod/interval structure on the orbit space) that uniquely determine each such solution. Equivalently, prove a uniqueness theorem of the form: any two stationary asymptotically flat vacuum black holes in $D\ge 5$ with the same chosen invariants are isometric, and exhibit the full list of allowed invariant data.
status_search_result: The general classification of stationary asymptotically flat vacuum black holes in dimension D≥5 remains open. Four-dimensional uniqueness fails in higher dimensions, as shown by the Emparan–Reall black ring coexisting with Myers–Perry solutions. Substantial partial results exist: in D=5, uniqueness has been proven within the class of stationary, asymptotically flat vacuum solutions admitting two commuting axial Killing vectors (Hollands–Yazadjiev and others), where the rod/interval structure together with mass and angular momenta determines the solution. The problem is unresolved without such symmetry assumptions and in D≥6.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: The resolution of cosmological and black-hole singularities has been established in symmetry-reduced settings within loop quantum gravity and loop quantum cosmology. Can those singularity-resolution results be proved in a substantially more general setting beyond spatial homogeneity?
self_contained_problem:
In loop quantum gravity (LQG), one quantizes general relativity using holonomies of the Ashtekar–Barbero connection along edges and fluxes of the densitized triad across surfaces, leading to a kinematical Hilbert space built on spin networks. In symmetry-reduced sectors—loop quantum cosmology (LQC) for spatially homogeneous (FRW and Bianchi) cosmological spacetimes and analogous reductions for the interior of Schwarzschild and other black holes—the quantum dynamics replaces the classical curvature singularity by a non-singular bounce: expectation values of geometric operators (such as energy density and curvature scalars) remain bounded, and the quantum state evolves through the would-be singularity to another semiclassical region.

Problem. Establish singularity resolution in loop quantum gravity in a setting that is substantially more general than spatial homogeneity. Concretely, formulate a quantum dynamical framework derived from (or consistent with) the full LQG kinematical Hilbert space which applies to inhomogeneous gravitational degrees of freedom, and prove that for a sufficiently large class of physical states encompassing classically singular initial data (cosmological or black-hole), all classical curvature singularities are resolved—e.g., expectation values and suitable fluctuations of geometric and matter density operators remain finite along the entire quantum evolution, and the state extends across the locus where the classical theory becomes singular.
status_search_result: Singularity resolution is well established in symmetry-reduced LQC (homogeneous and certain anisotropic Bianchi models, plus interior black-hole reductions). Partial progress exists toward inhomogeneous settings (e.g., hybrid quantization of Gowdy models, perturbative inhomogeneities around FRW, and Born–Oppenheimer-type reductions), but a general proof of singularity resolution beyond spatial homogeneity within full LQG remains outstanding as of 2026.

original_question: For the Bianchi type IX dynamical system describing oscillatory cosmological singularities, can one prove that the full past attractor is exactly the Mixmaster attractor rather than merely a subset of it?

Define the Mixmaster attractor M ⊂ X as the union of the three representations of the Bianchi type II vacuum subset together with the Kasner circle (the Bianchi type I vacuum subset). original_question: Do spike structures necessarily occur in generic approaches to spacelike singularities, and if so, what effect do they have on any eventual proof describing generic singularity formation and asymptotics?

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: In modified theories of gravity, are isotropic singularities a typical or generic phenomenon rather than a special feature of particular exact solutions or symmetry classes?
self_contained_problem:
Background. Consider spacetimes $(M,g)$ which are solutions of a modified theory of gravity (for example, $f(R)$ gravity, scalar-tensor theories, higher-derivative gravity such as Gauss–Bonnet or quadratic curvature theories, or other extensions of general relativity). A cosmological singularity at "conformal time" $\tau = 0$ is called an isotropic singularity (in the sense of Goode–Wainwright) if there exists a regular Lorentzian metric $\tilde g$ on a neighborhood of the singular hypersurface and a smooth conformal factor $\Omega(\tau)$ with $\Omega(\tau) \to 0$ as $\tau \to 0$ such that
$$ g = \Omega^2(\tau)\,\tilde g, $$
with $\tilde g$ extending smoothly through $\tau=0$ and $\Omega$ vanishing only at the singular hypersurface. Equivalently, the physical metric becomes conformal to a regular metric at the singularity, which forces the Weyl tensor of $g$ to remain finite (and in fact to vanish in an appropriate conformal sense) as the singularity is approached. This is the mathematical formulation underlying Penrose's Weyl curvature hypothesis.

In standard general relativity coupled to physically reasonable matter, isotropic singularities are known to form a non-generic, measure-zero subclass of cosmological singularities (the generic behaviour being oscillatory and anisotropic of BKL type).

Question. In modified theories of gravity, determine whether isotropic singularities are typical/generic in a suitable sense (for instance, for an open set of initial data within an appropriate function space, or for a positive-measure set of solutions in a natural ensemble of cosmological initial data), as opposed to being a feature only of particular exact solutions, symmetric models, or measure-zero subclasses. Identify modified gravity theories (if any) in which generic cosmological singularities are isotropic, and provide a rigorous proof of genericity, or alternatively show that isotropic singularities remain non-generic in all standard modified gravity theories.
status_search_result: The genericity of isotropic singularities in modified gravity remains an open question. Existing work (e.g., on conformal Weyl gravity and quantum-backreaction analyses) has identified specific modified-gravity models or larger classes of singularities compatible with Penrose's Weyl curvature hypothesis, but no general genericity theorem (or refutation) for isotropic singularities across modified gravity theories has been established.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: What explains the observed small effective cosmological constant and the phenomenon of dark energy, despite the enormous vacuum-energy contributions predicted by standard quantum field theory?
self_contained_problem: In general relativity with a cosmological constant Λ, Einstein's field equations read R_{μν} − (1/2) g_{μν} R + Λ g_{μν} = 8πG T_{μν}, and cosmological observations (Type Ia supernovae, the cosmic microwave background, and large-scale structure) are consistent with a small positive effective cosmological constant corresponding to a vacuum energy density of order ρ_obs ≈ 10^{−47} GeV^4, driving the observed accelerated expansion of the universe ("dark energy"). On the other hand, in standard relativistic quantum field theory the zero-point energy of quantum fields contributes a vacuum energy density which, when regularized with a natural ultraviolet cutoff (e.g. the Planck scale M_Pl ≈ 10^{19} GeV), is of order ρ_QFT ∼ M_Pl^4, exceeding ρ_obs by roughly 120 orders of magnitude. Provide a mathematically and physically consistent theoretical framework that explains the observed value of the effective cosmological constant Λ_eff (or, equivalently, the observed dark-energy density) starting from a quantum theory of matter fields coupled to gravity, reconciling the enormous predicted vacuum-energy contributions with the small observed value, and accounting for the present-day accelerated expansion of the universe.
status_search_result: The cosmological constant problem (and the related dark energy problem) is widely regarded as one of the most important unsolved problems in theoretical physics. Numerous proposals exist (anthropic/multiverse arguments in string landscape, modified gravity, quintessence, sequestering, supersymmetric cancellations), but none is generally accepted as a derivation of the observed value. Recent reviews through 2024–2025 continue to describe it as open.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: For physically relevant inflationary models, how generic is inflation when one starts from generic initial data that may already contain substantial inhomogeneity and anisotropy?
self_contained_problem:
Consider general relativity coupled to a scalar field (the inflaton) with a potential $V(\phi)$ that admits a slow-roll inflationary regime (for example, a plateau-like or chaotic potential of physical interest). Let initial data be specified on a Cauchy hypersurface $\Sigma$ as a triple $(h_{ij}, K_{ij}, \phi, \dot\phi)$ satisfying the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints, where $h_{ij}$ is a Riemannian 3-metric, $K_{ij}$ is a symmetric tensor (extrinsic curvature), and $\phi,\dot\phi$ are the scalar field and its time derivative on $\Sigma$. Allow such initial data to be highly inhomogeneous (large spatial gradients of $\phi$ and large variations in the spatial curvature of $h_{ij}$) and highly anisotropic (large traceless part of $K_{ij}$, comparable to or larger than the inflationary Hubble scale set by $V$).

Define a region of $\Sigma$ to "lead to inflation" if its future Cauchy development contains a connected open set in which the local Hubble parameter remains nearly constant and positive for at least $N \gtrsim 60$ e-folds, with slow-roll conditions satisfied throughout.

Question: For physically relevant choices of $V(\phi)$, quantify in a precise sense (for instance with respect to a natural measure on the constrained initial-data manifold, or via genericity in the sense of open dense subsets in a suitable topology on initial data) how generic the initial data leading to inflation are, when arbitrary substantial inhomogeneity and anisotropy are allowed in the initial data. In particular, determine whether inflation arises from generic such initial data, or only from a measure-zero / non-generic subset, and characterize the threshold of inhomogeneity and anisotropy beyond which inflation fails to occur.
category_tag: Inflationary cosmology / initial-value problem in general relativity
status_search_result: The question of how generic inflation is for inhomogeneous and anisotropic initial data remains an actively studied open problem. Recent numerical-relativity work (e.g., East–Kleban–Linde–Senatore 2016, Clough et al. 2017, and follow-ups through 2022) shows robustness of large-field/plateau inflation to substantial inhomogeneities, while small-field models are far more sensitive; no general, model-independent answer with a precise measure-theoretic notion of genericity has been established.

paper_title: Open problems in mathematical physics
original_question: What is the correct mathematical understanding of critical phenomena in gravitational collapse in general relativity, especially the threshold behavior between dispersion and black-hole formation and the associated critical solutions?
self_contained_problem:
In classical general relativity, consider one-parameter families of asymptotically flat initial data $(g_{ab}(p), K_{ab}(p), \Phi(p))$ for the Einstein equations coupled to some matter model (e.g., a massless scalar field, a perfect fluid, or pure vacuum gravitational waves), parametrized smoothly by a real parameter $p$, such that for sufficiently small $p$ the maximal Cauchy development disperses to flat space, while for sufficiently large $p$ it contains a black hole. Numerical evidence (originating with spherically symmetric massless scalar collapse) suggests that there is a critical value $p_*$ at which:

(i) (Universality) the late-time near-threshold evolution approaches a unique critical spacetime $Z_*$ depending only on the matter model, not on the family;
(ii) (Self-similarity) $Z_*$ is either continuously self-similar (admits a homothetic Killing vector) or discretely self-similar (invariant under a discrete rescaling $(\tau,x)\mapsto(\tau-\Delta,x)$ for a universal echoing period $\Delta$);
(iii) (Scaling) for supercritical data $p>p_*$ near $p_*$, the mass of the resulting black hole obeys $M_{\rm BH}\propto (p-p_*)^{\gamma}$ for a universal critical exponent $\gamma$ depending only on the matter model.

Provide a rigorous mathematical formulation and proof of this picture. In particular:

(a) Formulate precisely, within the Cauchy problem for the Einstein(–matter) system, the notion of the black hole threshold as a codimension-one set in a suitable space of initial data, and the notion of a critical solution as a codimension-one attractor (an attracting fixed point of the renormalization-group-type flow on the threshold surface).
(b) Prove existence, uniqueness, and the conjectured (continuous or discrete) self-similar symmetry of such critical solutions for at least one nontrivial matter model.
(c) Establish the universal mass-scaling law $M_{\rm BH}\sim (p-p_*)^{\gamma}$, deriving $\gamma$ from the spectrum of the linearization of the renormalization flow about the critical solution.
(d) Determine to what extent these phenomena persist beyond spherical symmetry, and in particular whether they occur at the threshold of vacuum gravitational collapse, where the formation of a naked singularity at threshold would constitute a codimension-one failure of cosmic censorship.
status_search_result: A 2025 review (Gundlach, arXiv:2507.07636) and the Living Reviews in Relativity article on critical phenomena in gravitational collapse confirm the picture rests largely on numerical and heuristic dynamical-systems arguments. A rigorous mathematical proof of universality, self-similarity, and the mass-scaling law is not available, and the behavior beyond spherical symmetry — especially at the threshold of vacuum collapse and its relation to naked-singularity formation — remains open.

paper_title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective
original_question: Do current data and mechanisms actually explain the dramatic enhancement effects seen for rare strange particles at sub-threshold heavy-ion collision energies, including observations such as unexpectedly large Ξ−/(Λ + Σ0) and φ/K− ratios?
self_contained_problem:
In heavy-ion collisions at center-of-mass energies below the elementary nucleon-nucleon production threshold for a given strange hadron ("sub-threshold" energies), measurements yield surprisingly large production of doubly strange and hidden-strange hadrons. In particular, in Ar+KCl collisions at E_lab ≈ 1.76 A GeV, the ratio Ξ⁻/(Λ + Σ⁰) is observed to be much larger than the expectation of statistical hadronization (thermal) models, and the ratio φ/K⁻ rises dramatically as the collision energy decreases towards very low energies.

Provide a quantitative microscopic mechanism (for example, multi-step strangeness-exchange reactions of the type Ȳ + B → Ξ + K, Y + Y → Ξ + N, decays of high-mass baryon resonances into φN or Ξ-containing channels, in-medium modifications of strange-particle properties, or other dynamical processes), implemented within a transport or thermal framework, that simultaneously reproduces:
(a) the absolute Ξ⁻ yield and the measured Ξ⁻/(Λ + Σ⁰) ratio at sub-threshold beam energies, and
(b) the energy dependence of the φ/K⁻ ratio, including its strong rise toward sub-threshold energies,
together with the yields of singly strange hadrons (K⁺, K⁻, Λ, Σ) at the same energies, while remaining consistent with elementary p+p and p+A constraints.

Determine whether such a mechanism, supported by present data, accounts for these dramatic sub-threshold enhancements, or identify what additional physics is required.
category_tag: Sub-threshold strangeness production in heavy-ion collisions
status_search_result: Recent literature (HADES experimental reviews, transport-model studies, and a 2023 EPJA systematics paper on strange-hadron yields near threshold) indicates that while strangeness-exchange channels (Ȳ+B, Y+Y → Ξ+K) and proposed high-mass resonance decay channels into φN and Ξ partially explain the sub-threshold Ξ⁻ and φ enhancements seen in Ar+KCl at 1.76 A GeV, no single model simultaneously and quantitatively reproduces the Ξ⁻/(Λ+Σ⁰) and φ/K⁻ ratios together with all singly-strange yields. Standard calculations underpredict the Ξ⁻/Λ/K⁺ ratio by factors of several. The question is therefore still considered open.
