paper_title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective
original_question: Does the charged-particle multiplicity density dNch/dη act as a universal scaling variable for system-size dependence of strange-particle production when comparing proton-proton, proton-nucleus, and nucleus-nucleus collisions across different collision energies?
self_contained_problem:
Consider high-energy hadronic and nuclear collisions of three types: proton–proton (pp), proton–nucleus (pA), and nucleus–nucleus (AA), performed at a range of center-of-mass energies. For each collision event class, define the charged-particle multiplicity density at midrapidity, dN_ch/dη, measured in a fixed pseudorapidity window around η = 0. For each event class, also measure the yields (per inelastic event) of strange and multi-strange hadrons (e.g., K_S^0, Λ, Ξ^-, Ω^-) and form their ratios to pion yields, which quantify strangeness production.

Question: Does the charged-particle multiplicity density dN_ch/dη serve as a universal scaling variable for the system-size and energy dependence of strangeness production? More precisely, when the strange-hadron-to-pion yield ratios are plotted as functions of dN_ch/dη, do the data points obtained from pp, pA, and AA collisions across different collision energies fall on a single common curve, independent of the colliding system and the collision energy?

status_search_result: Experimental measurements (notably ALICE) show that strange-to-pion yield ratios increase smoothly with dN_ch/dη from low-multiplicity pp through p–Pb and into Pb–Pb, with similar trends across systems, suggesting an approximate universal scaling at LHC energies. paper_title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective
original_question: At all collision energies, does the observed multiplicity dependence of strange-particle yield ratios really follow the statistical-model transition from a canonical ensemble to a grand-canonical ensemble, including the expected strangeness hierarchy in which volume dependence grows with increasing strangeness content?
self_contained_problem:
Consider relativistic heavy-ion (and small-system) collisions in which strange hadrons are produced and described by a statistical-thermal (hadron resonance gas) model. In this framework, exact conservation of the strangeness quantum number in a sub-volume V₀ leads to a canonical partition function whose strange-particle yields are suppressed relative to the grand-canonical limit, with a suppression factor that becomes more pronounced as the strangeness content |S| of the hadron species increases. As V₀ grows (parameterized experimentally by the charged-particle multiplicity dN_ch/dη), the canonical description is expected to smoothly approach the grand-canonical limit, producing a "strangeness hierarchy" in which the relative volume (multiplicity) dependence of yield ratios to pions becomes progressively steeper for hadrons of higher |S| (e.g., |S|=1 for K and Λ, |S|=2 for Ξ, |S|=3 for Ω).

Question: Across all available center-of-mass collision energies (from low-energy fixed-target through RHIC and LHC, and across system sizes from pp through p-A to A-A), do the measured multiplicity dependences of strange-to-nonstrange particle yield ratios quantitatively follow the canonical-to-grand-canonical transition predicted by the statistical-thermal model, including the expected ordering in which the slope of the multiplicity dependence increases monotonically with the strangeness content of the hadron?
status_search_result: Studies after 2017 (e.g., Vovchenko et al., 2009.04844) show that the canonical statistical model with strict local strangeness conservation qualitatively reproduces the observed strangeness hierarchy and the trend toward grand-canonical saturation at high multiplicities, but quantitatively over-suppresses (multi-)strange baryons at low multiplicities unless additional ingredients (S-matrix/phase-shift corrections, modified correlation volume) are introduced. The picture works approximately at LHC energies but discrepancies remain at low energies and small systems, so the question is partially settled rather than fully confirmed.

paper_title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective
original_question: Do we have a correct physical description of how strange hadrons are produced and propagate in low-energy heavy-ion collisions, where the relevant medium is hadronic and must be understood before drawing conclusions about any partonic phase?
self_contained_problem:
In relativistic heavy-ion collisions at low center-of-mass energies (roughly a few GeV per nucleon pair), the produced fireball is dominated by a dense hadronic medium rather than a deconfined partonic phase. Strange hadrons (e.g., kaons K^+, K^-, K^0, hyperons Λ, Σ, Ξ, and the φ meson) are produced near or below their elementary nucleon-nucleon thresholds and subsequently propagate through this hadronic medium, where their production cross sections, in-medium self-energies (mass shifts and widths), strangeness-exchange reactions (such as YN ↔ KN, K̄N ↔ πY), and rescattering/absorption all influence the observable yields, spectra, and flow.

Provide a quantitatively predictive theoretical description of the production and propagation of strange hadrons in low-energy heavy-ion collisions that:
(i) specifies the elementary and secondary production channels (including multi-step and sub-threshold mechanisms) together with their cross sections;
(ii) incorporates the in-medium modifications of strange-hadron properties (effective masses, widths, dispersion relations) in dense baryonic matter;
(iii) describes the transport and final-state interactions (including strangeness exchange, regeneration, and absorption); and
(iv) simultaneously reproduces, within a single consistent framework, the measured yields, transverse-momentum spectra, rapidity distributions, and collective flow (directed v1 and elliptic v2) of K^+, K^-, Λ, Ξ, and φ across the available low-energy heavy-ion data.

Determine whether such a consistent description currently exists, or identify the missing physical ingredients required to obtain it.
status_search_result: Recent reviews and experimental programs (HADES at GSI, STAR fixed-target Beam Energy Scan, future CBM at FAIR) continue to highlight discrepancies between transport-model predictions and data on K^±, Λ, Ξ, and φ production and flow at low energies, indicating that a fully consistent description of strangeness production and propagation in dense hadronic matter is still lacking and remains an active research problem.

paper_title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective
original_question: At low collision energies, does the produced hadronic medium behave as a macroscopic system that can be described fully by a statistical model, or are there important low-energy strangeness phenomena that fall outside that description?
self_contained_problem:
Consider relativistic heavy-ion collisions at low center-of-mass energies per nucleon pair (roughly in the range $\sqrt{s_{NN}} \lesssim 10$ GeV), in which a hot and dense hadronic medium is produced and subsequently freezes out into observable hadrons, including strange hadrons such as kaons, hyperons, and multi-strange baryons. The statistical hadronization model postulates that, at chemical freeze-out, the abundances of all hadron species $i$ are determined entirely by a small set of macroscopic thermodynamic parameters — typically a temperature $T$, a baryochemical potential $\mu_B$, a strangeness chemical potential $\mu_S$, an electric charge chemical potential $\mu_Q$, and a fireball volume $V$ (with possible canonical suppression factors for exactly conserved quantum numbers in small systems) — through the grand-canonical (or canonical) partition function of an ideal hadron resonance gas:
$$\langle N_i \rangle \;=\; \frac{V g_i}{2\pi^2}\int_0^\infty \frac{p^2\,dp}{\exp\!\big[(\sqrt{p^2+m_i^2}-\mu_i)/T\big] \pm 1}, \qquad \mu_i = B_i\mu_B + S_i\mu_S + Q_i\mu_Q.$$

Question: At low collision energies in the regime described above, does the produced hadronic medium behave as a macroscopic thermodynamic system whose particle yields — including those of strange hadrons of every strangeness content — are fully and consistently described by a single choice of statistical-model parameters $(T,\mu_B,\mu_S,\mu_Q,V)$ within experimental uncertainties? Equivalently, are all observed low-energy strangeness production phenomena (such as energy-dependent $K^+/\pi^+$ and $\Lambda/\pi$ ratios, multi-strange baryon yields, and possible canonical strangeness suppression) accounted for by such a statistical description, or do there exist robust strangeness observables at low energies that fall outside any consistent statistical-hadronization fit?
status_search_result: The question of whether the statistical hadronization model fully describes hadron (and especially strange hadron) production at low collision energies remains an active and unresolved topic. Recent reviews and HADES/STAR-FXT/NA61 results continue to report deviations (e.g., in $K^+/\pi^+$, $\Xi$ and $\Omega$ yields, and the need for canonical suppression or non-equilibrium strangeness fugacity $\gamma_S$), indicating the issue is still open.

original_question: What is actually established about hyperon-hyperon interactions, especially ΛΛ interactions inferred from two-particle correlation measurements, given that different analyses of the same correlation data favor weakly repulsive versus weakly attractive interactions?
self_contained_problem:
Consider the s-wave low-energy scattering of two Λ hyperons, parameterized in the effective range expansion by a scattering length a₀ and effective range r_eff via k cot δ(k) = 1/a₀ + (1/2) r_eff k² + O(k⁴), where δ(k) is the s-wave phase shift at relative momentum k. In ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, the two-Λ correlation function C(k) is related to the source function S(r) and the relative wave function ψ_k(r) by the Koonin–Pratt formula C(k) = ∫ d³r S(r) |ψ_k(r)|², where ψ_k incorporates quantum statistics, the strong ΛΛ interaction (treated, e.g., via the Lednický–Lyuboshitz analytic formula), and feed-down/residual-source corrections. Two independent analyses of the same Au+Au √s_NN = 200 GeV ΛΛ correlation data have produced conflicting conclusions about the sign of the interaction: one inferring a weakly repulsive ΛΛ interaction and the other a weakly attractive ΛΛ interaction.

Problem: Determine, on the basis of two-particle ΛΛ correlation measurements in heavy-ion collisions, the sign and magnitude of the s-wave ΛΛ scattering length a₀ and effective range r_eff, and decide whether the ΛΛ interaction is attractive or repulsive (and whether it supports a bound or near-threshold state). In particular, identify and quantify the systematic effects (source geometry, collective flow, Σ⁰ feed-down, residual correlations, choice of fit ansatz) responsible for the discrepancy between competing analyses, and provide a self-consistent extraction of (a₀, r_eff) from the available data.
status_search_result: Subsequent analyses of ΛΛ femtoscopic correlations (in Au+Au and later in pp and p–Pb at the LHC by ALICE) have narrowed the allowed region of the ΛΛ scattering parameters, with current STAR-based constraints favoring a weakly attractive, non-binding interaction (roughly −1.25 fm < a₀ < 0, or 1/a₀ in the range −1.8 to −0.8 fm⁻¹ with effective range 3.5–7 fm). However, the precise values remain model- and feed-down dependent, and a fully consistent simultaneous determination of (a₀, r_eff) free of source-shape and Σ⁰ feed-down ambiguities has not been achieved, so the question is partially resolved rather than settled.

paper_title: Open Questions in the Understanding of Strangeness Production in HIC – Experiment Perspective
original_question: Why are yields of very weakly bound hypernuclei such as the hypertriton ³ΛH reproduced so well by statistical-model calculations, even though their tiny binding energies make their survival in a chemical freeze-out environment appear paradoxical, the so-called “snowball in hell” problem?
self_contained_problem:
In high-energy heavy-ion collisions, light (anti-)nuclei and hypernuclei are produced and their integrated yields are typically described by the statistical (thermal) hadronization model, in which particle abundances are fixed at chemical freeze-out at a temperature T_chem on the order of 155 MeV. The hypertriton ³_ΛH is an extremely weakly bound object: it consists of a Λ hyperon bound to a deuteron with a Λ separation energy of only about 130 keV (total binding energy ≈ 2.35 MeV including the deuteron), giving an rms radius of order 10 fm — much larger than the typical inter-hadron spacing in the fireball at freeze-out, and a binding energy orders of magnitude smaller than T_chem.

Naively, such a fragile cluster cannot survive in a hot hadronic medium of temperature T_chem ≫ B(³_ΛH) (the so-called "snowball in hell" situation). Nevertheless, experimental measurements of (anti-)hypertriton yields in Pb–Pb and Au–Au collisions are well reproduced by statistical-model predictions that use the vacuum mass and assume formation at chemical freeze-out.

Provide a quantitative theoretical explanation of this fact: derive, from a microscopic or effective description of the expanding hadronic system, why the chemical-freeze-out statistical model accurately predicts the yield of very weakly bound hypernuclei such as ³_ΛH despite B(³_ΛH) ≪ T_chem, and identify the dynamical mechanism that fixes their abundance at (or near) chemical freeze-out values.
status_search_result: Recent work proposes resolutions of the "snowball in hell" puzzle. A 2024 Phys. Rev. Lett. paper introduces a thermodynamic "contact" density conjugate to the binding momentum, expressing the loosely-bound molecule yield at kinetic (rather than chemical) freeze-out and reproducing the measured ³_ΛH multiplicity. A 2024–2025 study (Phys. Rev. C 111, 054917) further analyzes the hypertriton puzzle. While these provide compelling mechanisms, the broader question of why the statistical hadronization model works quantitatively for such weakly bound objects is still considered not fully settled.

paper_title: Open Problems in Relational Quantum Mechanics
original_question: If relational quantum mechanics rejects observer-independent quantum states and instead treats the state of a system as relative to an observing or interacting physical system, what explanatory work does this relativization of states actually perform, and in what precise sense does it improve our understanding of quantum phenomena rather than merely redescribing them?
self_contained_problem:
Relational Quantum Mechanics (RQM) is an interpretation of quantum theory which denies that physical systems possess observer-independent quantum states. Instead, the quantum state of a system S is defined only relative to a second physical system O that interacts with (or "observes") S; different observing systems may simultaneously assign different states to the same system S, and there is no privileged absolute state. The "third person problem" arises when one considers an external observer P who describes the joint system S+O: P's account of the values realized in S relative to O can come into tension with O's own account of those values, raising the question of how to reconcile the different observer-relative descriptions and what physical content the relativization carries.

Problem. Provide a precise explication of the relativization of quantum states to observing systems in RQM and determine what explanatory role this relativization plays. Specifically:

(a) Formulate, in a mathematically explicit framework (e.g., specifying for each ordered pair (S,O) of physical systems a state-assignment map and rules governing how distinct assignments relative to different observers O, O', P, ... are related), what it means for a quantum state to be "relative to" an observer.

(b) Using this framework, analyze the third person problem: given a system S, an observer O that has interacted with S, and a further observer P describing S+O, state and justify consistency conditions that the state assignments relative to O and relative to P must satisfy, and exhibit whether such conditions can be met without reintroducing observer-independent facts.

(c) Identify in precise terms the explanatory or predictive surplus, if any, that relativization provides over a non-relational description of quantum phenomena (in particular regarding measurement outcomes, the quantum-to-classical transition, and locality/Bell-type correlations), or else show that relativization amounts to a redescription with no additional explanatory content.

Decide whether RQM, so formulated, genuinely advances the understanding of quantum phenomena, or whether the relativization of states fails to perform substantive explanatory work.
status_search_result: The problem is foundational/philosophical concerning the interpretation of quantum mechanics. Subsequent literature on RQM (e.g., debates around the Frauchiger–Renner argument, cross-perspective links proposed by Adlam–Rovelli around 2022–2023, and ongoing critiques) shows that the question of what relativization of states explains, and how observer-relative accounts cohere across observers, remains actively contested with no consensus resolution. It is best classified as still open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Relational Quantum Mechanics
original_question: Can relational quantum mechanics give a justified account of state reduction in measurement, including when all systems are treated quantum mechanically, or does it merely attach observer-relative indices to states while leaving the collapse process unexplained and the measurement problem unresolved?
self_contained_problem:
Within the interpretational framework of Relational Quantum Mechanics (RQM)—in which the state of a physical system S is not absolute but is defined only relative to another system O acting as an "observer," and in which all physical systems (including observers) are to be treated quantum mechanically on equal footing—provide a justified account of the state reduction (collapse) process associated with measurement. Specifically, determine whether RQM can:

(i) explain the occurrence of definite, observer-relative outcomes in a measurement interaction between two quantum systems S and O without presupposing an unexplained collapse postulate inherited from standard quantum mechanics;

(ii) resolve the "third person" problem, i.e., reconcile the descriptions given by an external observer E who treats the joint S+O system unitarily (and would therefore assign an entangled, non-collapsed state) with the description relative to O (for which a definite outcome has occurred); and

(iii) thereby resolve the measurement problem stricto sensu, rather than merely re-labeling quantum states with observer indices while leaving the physical mechanism of state reduction unaccounted for.

Either supply such a justified account, or prove that no consistent account satisfying (i)–(iii) is possible within the axioms of RQM.
category_tag: Foundations of quantum mechanics / measurement problem
status_search_result: The status of state reduction and the measurement problem within Relational Quantum Mechanics remains an actively debated open problem in the foundations-of-physics literature. Subsequent work (e.g., by Rovelli, Di Biagio, Adlam, Brukner, Pienaar, and others through the early 2020s) continues to debate whether RQM successfully accounts for collapse and outcomes; no consensus resolution exists.

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Classify all n-tuples of lattice length-sign sequences of the angles that can occur for integer n-gons, where the lattice length-sign sequence is the complete invariant of an integer angle in the paper’s integer-geometry setting.
self_contained_problem:
Work in the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^2 \subset \mathbb{R}^2$. A point of $\mathbb{R}^2$ is called integer if both of its coordinates are integers; a segment is integer if its endpoints are integer; a polygon is an integer $n$-gon if all of its vertices are integer points. Two integer objects are called integer-congruent if one is taken to the other by an affine transformation of $\mathbb{R}^2$ whose linear part lies in $\mathrm{GL}(2,\mathbb{Z})$ and whose translation part is integer.

The integer length $\mathrm{l}\ell(AB)$ of an integer segment $AB$ is the number of integer points strictly between $A$ and $B$, plus one. Given an integer angle $\angle BAC$ with vertex $A$ and integer points $B,C$ in its interior rays, its sail is the boundary of the convex hull of all integer points lying inside the angle and distinct from $A$, restricted to the part visible from $A$; this sail is a (possibly infinite) integer broken line $A_0A_1A_2\dots$ with consecutive integer edges. For each $i\ge 0$ let $a_{2i+1}=\mathrm{l}\ell(A_iA_{i+1})$ be the integer length of the $i$-th edge, and for each $i\ge 1$ let $a_{2i}$ be the integer (signed) sine of the angle at vertex $A_i$ formed by the two adjacent edges of the sail, with sign equal to $+1$ if the broken line turns left at $A_i$ and $-1$ if it turns right. The resulting sequence
$$\mathrm{LLS}(\angle BAC) = (a_1,a_2,a_3,a_4,\dots)$$
is called the lattice length-sign sequence (LLS-sequence) of the integer angle. It is a complete invariant of integer angles up to integer congruence.

For an integer $n$-gon $P$ with vertices $V_1,V_2,\dots,V_n$ (in cyclic order), let $\alpha_i$ denote the interior integer angle at $V_i$, and define the associated $n$-tuple of LLS-sequences
$$\mathcal{L}(P) = \bigl(\mathrm{LLS}(\alpha_1),\mathrm{LLS}(\alpha_2),\dots,\mathrm{LLS}(\alpha_n)\bigr).$$

Problem. Classify, up to cyclic rotation and reflection of the index $i$, all $n$-tuples $(L_1,\dots,L_n)$ of LLS-sequences that arise as $\mathcal{L}(P)$ for some integer $n$-gon $P$. Equivalently, give necessary and sufficient conditions on an $n$-tuple of finite positive-integer-valued (with signed even entries) sequences for it to be realizable as the tuple of LLS-sequences of the consecutive interior angles of some integer $n$-gon in the plane.
status_search_result: The classification problem (the "IKEA problem") of n-tuples of LLS-sequences realizable as integer n-gons appears in Karpenkov's writings on the geometry of continued fractions and is listed as an open problem. Web searches turn up no published classification result; recent expositions (including Karpenkov's monograph "Geometry of Continued Fractions") describe LLS-sequences as the complete invariant of integer angles but do not present a solution to the global polygon-realization problem.

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Find an adequate complete invariant of cones, up to integer congruence, in the setting of geometric multidimensional continued fractions.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a simplicial cone with apex at the origin whose $n$ edges are spanned by vectors in general position with respect to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^n$ (i.e., the edges do not lie in any rational hyperplane other than those containing them). The sail of $C$ is the boundary of the convex hull of $(C \cap \mathbb{Z}^n) \setminus \{0\}$; the collection of sails associated to all $2^n$ connected components of $\mathbb{R}^n \setminus \bigcup H_i$ (where $H_i$ are the $n$ hyperplanes spanning the faces of $C$) is the $n$-dimensional continued fraction in the sense of Klein associated to $C$.

Two cones $C_1, C_2$ are said to be integer congruent if there exists an affine transformation $A \in \mathrm{GL}(n,\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^n$ such that $A(C_1) = C_2$.

Problem. Construct an adequate complete invariant of such simplicial cones up to integer congruence; that is, exhibit a computable invariant $I(\cdot)$ (for instance, of combinatorial-geometric type generalizing the Lagrange–LLS sequence of an integer angle in dimension two) such that for any two cones $C_1, C_2$ as above,
$$I(C_1) = I(C_2) \iff C_1 \text{ and } C_2 \text{ are integer congruent}.$$
status_search_result: No publication appears to provide a complete integer-congruence invariant for cones in the multidimensional Klein continued-fraction setting. While in dimension two the LLS sequence gives a complete invariant of integer angles, in higher dimensions only partial invariants (face combinatorics, integer areas/volumes, edge lengths and statistical characteristics studied since Arnold) are known. Recent surveys and theses on the geometry of multidimensional continued fractions still treat the construction of an adequate complete invariant of cones as an open problem.

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Classify all combinatorially possible types of faces that can occur in sails, especially for Klein polyhedra arising from geometric multidimensional continued fractions.
self_contained_problem:
Let $C \subset \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ be a simplicial cone with apex at the origin bounded by $n+1$ hyperplanes in general position with respect to the integer lattice $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ (i.e., none of the bounding hyperplanes contains a nonzero lattice point). The associated Klein sail is the boundary of the convex hull
$$\operatorname{Sail}(C) \;=\; \partial igl(\operatorname{conv}(C \cap \mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \setminus \{0\}) igr),$$
which is an $n$-dimensional generalized polyhedral surface. Its faces (compact convex lattice polytopes of dimensions $0,1,\dots,n$) are called the faces of the sail. Two faces are said to be of the same combinatorial type if they are equivalent under the action of the affine group $\operatorname{GL}(n+1,\mathbb{Z}) \ltimes \mathbb{Z}^{n+1}$ on lattice polytopes (equivalently, if there is a lattice-affine bijection between them).

Problem: Classify all combinatorial types of faces (in the lattice/affine equivalence sense above) that can occur as faces of some Klein sail $\operatorname{Sail}(C)$ arising from an $(n+1)$-dimensional simplicial cone in general position with the lattice. In particular, determine which lattice polytopes (up to $\operatorname{GL}\ltimes\mathbb{Z}$ equivalence) are realizable as faces of sails of Klein polyhedra associated with multidimensional geometric continued fractions.

status_search_result: The classification of all combinatorial types of faces of sails of Klein polyhedra is a long-standing open problem in the geometric theory of multidimensional continued fractions. No general classification across all dimensions appears in the literature, and the problem is still posed as open in surveys on the geometry of continued fractions.

original_question: For given integers n and m, determine which n-gons can be realized as faces of an m-dimensional continued fraction.
self_contained_problem:
Setup. Let $m \geq 2$ be an integer and let $A \in GL_{m+1}(\mathbb{R})$ be a real $(m+1)	imes(m+1)$ matrix all of whose eigenvalues are real and distinct. The $m+1$ eigenlines of $A$ partition $\mathbb{R}^{m+1}$ into $2^{m+1}$ open simplicial cones. For each such cone $C$, the Klein sail associated to $(A,C)$ is the boundary of the convex hull
$$\mathrm{conv}\!\left( igl(\mathbb{Z}^{m+1}\setminus\{0\} igr)\cap \overline{C}ight).$$
The union of all $2^{m+1}$ sails is called the $m$-dimensional continued fraction associated with $A$. Each sail is an $m$-dimensional polyhedral surface; its $k$-dimensional faces are convex lattice polytopes, considered up to integer-affine equivalence (i.e., the action of the affine group of $\mathbb{Z}^{m+1}$ that preserves the family of $m$-dimensional continued fractions).

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Describe all finite two-dimensional sails, together with the corresponding continued fractions, for the classes of multidimensional continued fractions considered in the paper.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $A_1,\dots,A_{n+1}$ be $n+1$ hyperplanes in $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ in general position passing through the origin. Their complement decomposes into $2^{n+1}$ open simplicial cones (orthants). For one such orthant $C$, consider the set $C\cap(\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\})$ of nonzero integer points in its closure, and let $\mathrm{conv}(C\cap(\mathbb{Z}^{n+1}\setminus\{0\}))$ be its convex hull. The boundary of this convex hull (with the induced integer polyhedral structure) is called the sail of the orthant $C$. The collection of the $2^{n+1}$ sails associated with the hyperplane arrangement $\{A_1,\dots,A_{n+1}\}$ is the $n$-dimensional continued fraction in the sense of Klein. A sail is called finite if it consists of only finitely many faces.

Take $n=2$, so that the sails are two-dimensional polyhedral surfaces.

Provide a complete classification of all finite two-dimensional sails arising from such hyperplane arrangements in $\mathbb{R}^3$, and for each finite sail describe the corresponding multidimensional continued fraction (i.e., the geometry of the underlying arrangement of three planes through the origin that produces it).

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Does there exist an algorithm that decides whether a prescribed type of fundamental domain can be realized by a periodic multidimensional continued fraction?
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $A \in \mathrm{GL}(n+1,\mathbb{Z})$ be an integer matrix with irreducible characteristic polynomial over $\mathbb{Q}$ and with all eigenvalues real and distinct. The $n+1$ eigenlines of $A$ span $\mathbb{R}^{n+1}$ and partition it into $2^{n+1}$ open simplicial cones (orthants with respect to the eigenbasis). For each such cone $C$, the boundary of the convex hull of the nonzero integer points $\mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \cap \overline{C}$ is an $n$-dimensional polyhedral surface called a sail (in the sense of Klein). The collection of all $2^{n+1}$ sails is the multidimensional continued fraction associated with $A$. The subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}(n+1,\mathbb{Z})$ commuting with $A$ that preserves each eigenline (the Dirichlet group of $A$) is, by Dirichlet's units theorem, free abelian of rank $n$, and it acts freely and discretely on each sail with compact quotient. A fundamental domain of the sail is a compact polyhedral region of the sail whose translates under this group tile the sail.

By the combinatorial type of a fundamental domain we mean the data of its face lattice together with the integer affine equivalence class of each face and the gluing pattern induced by the group action.

Problem. Does there exist an algorithm that, given as input a prescribed combinatorial type $T$ of fundamental domain (as above), decides in finitely many steps whether $T$ is realized as the combinatorial type of a fundamental domain of some sail of the multidimensional continued fraction associated with some matrix $A \in \mathrm{GL}(n+1,\mathbb{Z})$ of the kind described above?

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Describe all torus decompositions that are realized by periodic two-dimensional continued fractions.
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $A \in \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ be a hyperbolic matrix with three real, distinct, irrational eigenvalues, and let $\pi_1, \pi_2, \pi_3 \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ be the three eigenplanes through the origin spanned by pairs of eigenvectors. For each such cone $C$, the boundary of the convex hull of the nonzero integer points of $\overline{C}$ is a polyhedral surface called a sail; the union of the eight sails is the (two-dimensional) Klein continued fraction associated with $A$. The subgroup of $\mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ commuting with $A$ contains a free abelian subgroup of rank $2$ (by the Dirichlet unit theorem) which acts freely and properly discontinuously on each sail; the quotient of a sail by this action is a compact $2$-torus tiled by the images of the faces, edges, and vertices of the sail. This tiled torus is called the torus decomposition of the periodic two-dimensional continued fraction.

Problem. Give a complete classification (combinatorial description) of all tilings of the $2$-torus by convex polygons that arise as torus decompositions of periodic two-dimensional continued fractions in the sense above. Equivalently, characterize precisely which combinatorial torus tilings can be realized by the quotient of some sail of some hyperbolic $A \in \mathrm{GL}_3(\mathbb{Z})$ under the action of its associated rank-$2$ unit group.
status_search_result: This is one of V. I. Arnold's well-known open problems on the geometry of multidimensional continued fractions. The available literature, including surveys of open problems and recent work on decompositions of higher-dimensional continued fractions, treats it as still open: only sporadic examples and partial structural results on torus decompositions of periodic two-dimensional continued fractions are known, with no general classification established.

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: For dimension n ≥ 3, prove that there exists a cone whose sail has a prescribed single non-periodic combinatorial structure.
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 3 be an integer. Consider a simplicial cone C in R^n with apex at the origin, bounded by n hyperplanes in general position passing through the origin (so that C is one of the open orthants determined by these hyperplanes). The sail of C is defined as the boundary of the convex hull of the set of integer points C ∩ Z^n \ {0} contained in the (closure of the) cone. The integer (combinatorial) structure of the sail is the abstract polyhedral complex whose vertices are the extremal integer points of this convex hull and whose faces are its bounded faces, recorded together with the integer-affine equivalence class of each face.

Two sails are said to have the same combinatorial structure if there is a face-preserving isomorphism between their polyhedral complexes that respects the integer-affine types of the faces. The combinatorial structure of a sail is called periodic if it admits a nontrivial automorphism of infinite order (induced, for cones with totally real algebraic irrationality, by the action of the positive Dirichlet group), and non-periodic otherwise.

Problem. Prove that for every n ≥ 3 and every prescribed non-periodic combinatorial structure S that is realizable as a portion of some sail in dimension n, there exists a simplicial cone C ⊂ R^n in general position whose sail realizes exactly the combinatorial structure S. Equivalently, exhibit at least one explicit cone in dimension n ≥ 3 whose sail has a prescribed single non-periodic combinatorial structure.

original_question: For every positive integer constant C, are there only finitely many pairwise integer non-congruent faces whose frequencies exceed C?
self_contained_problem:

For each integer-congruence class [F] of compact faces, one defines its frequency μ([F]) as the total Möbius-invariant measure (with respect to the natural SL(n, ℤ)-invariant measure on the parameter space of such matrices A, suitably normalized) of those operators A whose Klein polyhedron contains a face in the class [F], so that the frequencies form a discrete spectrum of positive real numbers attached to integer-congruence classes of faces.

Question. Prove or disprove the following statement: for every positive integer C, there exist only finitely many pairwise integer non-congruent faces [F] whose frequency μ([F]) exceeds C.

original_question: Assuming the total relative frequency of all possible faces is finite in dimensions n ≥ 3, find an appropriate generalization of the Gauss map and compare the resulting face frequencies with the frequencies coming from Möbius geometry.
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 3. Consider the Klein model of multidimensional continued fractions: for a simplicial cone C ⊂ ℝⁿ⁺¹ with vertex at the origin determined by n+1 linearly independent hyperplanes in general position with respect to the integer lattice ℤⁿ⁺¹, the sail of C is the boundary of the convex hull of the nonzero integer points contained in C. Faces of the sail come with a natural notion of integer-affine equivalence class.

For each integer-affine type T of face, define its relative frequency as the (suitably normalized) limit density of faces of type T appearing among all faces of all sails as one ranges over admissible cones, weighted so that the total measure agrees with the projective-invariant Möbius measure approach (in which an SL(n+1,ℤ)-invariant measure on the space of n-dimensional continued fractions assigns to each face type a frequency obtained as an integral of a top-dimensional projective-invariant form on the corresponding configuration space).

Assume that, in dimension n ≥ 3, the sum of the relative frequencies of all possible integer-affine face types is finite.

(i) the dynamical system admits an absolutely continuous invariant probability measure μ which is ergodic;
(ii) for each integer-affine face type T, the μ-frequency of occurrence of faces of type T along typical orbits is well defined and finite.

Then compare these dynamically defined face frequencies with the Möbius-measure face frequencies, and determine whether the two systems of frequencies coincide (up to a common normalization).

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Let K be a totally real cubic number field, and let y and z be elements of K with 0 < y, z < 1 such that 1, y, and z are linearly independent over Q. Must the Jacobi-Perron algorithm started from v = (1, y, z) produce an eventually periodic continued fraction?
self_contained_problem:
Let $K$ be a totally real cubic number field, i.e., a degree-3 extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ all of whose embeddings into $\mathbb{C}$ have image in $\mathbb{R}$. Let $y, z \in K$ satisfy $0 < y < 1$, $0 < z < 1$, and assume that $1, y, z$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb{Q}$.

The Jacobi–Perron algorithm applied to a vector $v = (v_0, v_1, v_2) \in \mathbb{R}^3$ with $v_0 \neq 0$ is defined as follows. Set $v^{(0)} = v$. Given $v^{(n)} = (v_0^{(n)}, v_1^{(n)}, v_2^{(n)})$ with $v_0^{(n)} \neq 0$, write $\alpha_i^{(n)} = v_i^{(n)}/v_0^{(n)}$ for $i = 1, 2$, let $a_i^{(n)} = \lfloor \alpha_i^{(n)} \rfloor$, and define
$$v^{(n+1)} = \bigl(1,\ \alpha_1^{(n)} - a_1^{(n)},\ \alpha_2^{(n)} - a_2^{(n)}\bigr)$$
after a cyclic relabeling, more precisely:
$$v^{(n+1)} = (\alpha_1^{(n)} - a_1^{(n)},\ \alpha_2^{(n)} - a_2^{(n)},\ 1).$$
The sequence of integer pairs $(a_1^{(n)}, a_2^{(n)})_{n \ge 0}$ is the Jacobi–Perron continued fraction expansion of $v$. The expansion is called eventually periodic if there exist integers $N \ge 0$ and $T \ge 1$ such that $(a_1^{(n+T)}, a_2^{(n+T)}) = (a_1^{(n)}, a_2^{(n)})$ for all $n \ge N$.

Question: For every totally real cubic field $K$ and every choice of $y, z \in K$ as above, must the Jacobi–Perron expansion of the starting vector $v = (1, y, z)$ be eventually periodic?
category_tag: Jacobi-Perron algorithm and multidimensional continued fractions
status_search_result: The conjecture, often called "Jacobi's last theorem," remains open for the original Jacobi–Perron algorithm. Recent work (Karpenkov, 2021–2024) introduced a different multidimensional continued fraction algorithm (the sin²-algorithm) for which periodicity in the totally real cubic case has been established, thereby resolving Hermite's problem in that case for that new algorithm; however, periodicity for the classical Jacobi–Perron algorithm itself on totally real cubic vectors has not been proved.

paper_title: Open problems in geometry of continued fractions
original_question: Generalize continued fractions so that they describe 3-bridge knots, analogously to how ordinary finite continued fractions classify rational, or two-bridge, knots.
self_contained_problem:
A two-bridge (rational) knot or link in the 3-sphere is a knot or link admitting a presentation with bridge number 2; the set of two-bridge knots and links is in bijection (up to ambient isotopy and mirror image) with the set of equivalence classes of rationals p/q ∈ ℚ ∪ {∞} via the classical continued fraction expansion p/q = [a_1; a_2, …, a_n] = a_1 + 1/(a_2 + 1/(a_3 + ⋯ + 1/a_n)), where two such fractions p/q and p'/q' represent the same knot if and only if p = p' and q' ≡ q^{±1} (mod p). In particular, ordinary finite continued fractions provide a complete invariant of two-bridge knots.

Problem. Construct a generalization of continued fractions that plays the same role for 3-bridge knots and links as ordinary finite continued fractions play for 2-bridge knots and links. More precisely, define a class of (multi-dimensional or otherwise generalized) continued-fraction-like algebraic/combinatorial objects together with an explicit equivalence relation on them, and an explicit map from these objects to ambient-isotopy classes of 3-bridge knots and links, such that the induced map from equivalence classes of generalized continued fractions to 3-bridge knot/link types is a bijection (i.e., a complete invariant). Provide an algorithm to compute the generalized continued fraction associated to a given 3-bridge presentation and, conversely, to reconstruct a 3-bridge diagram from the generalized continued fraction.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface any work providing a complete continued-fraction-style classification of 3-bridge knots analogous to the classical p/q parameterization of 2-bridge knots. Existing studies (e.g., Chebyshev/billiard diagrams, Jones polynomial computations for 3-bridge knots) use continued fractions only as auxiliary tools rather than as a complete invariant. The problem appears to remain open.

original_question: Does there exist an infinite finitely generated group with the following property: every action of the group on the real line by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms and without global fixed points is of type (iii), meaning that it is semiconjugate to a minimal action for which every bounded interval can be contracted along suitable group elements?

Let G be a group acting on the real line R by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms. Recall the following terminology. The action is said to have no global fixed point if there is no point x ∈ R fixed by every element of G. Two actions ρ₁, ρ₂ : G → Homeo₊(R) are semiconjugate if there is a non-decreasing surjective map h : R → R (proper at infinity in the appropriate sense) such that h ∘ ρ₁(g) = ρ₂(g) ∘ h for every g ∈ G. An action of G on R by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms is called of type (iii) if it is semiconjugate to a minimal action with the following contraction property: for every bounded interval I ⊂ R and every nonempty open interval J ⊂ R there exists g ∈ G such that g(I) ⊂ J.

Question: Does there exist an infinite, finitely generated group G with the property that every action of G on R by orientation-preserving homeomorphisms without global fixed points is of type (iii)?

context_brief: Minimal conjugacy action on left orders
original_question: Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group for which the conjugation action on the space of all left orders is minimal, that is, every orbit of a left order under conjugation is dense?
self_contained_problem:
A group $G$ is called left-orderable if there exists a total order $\leq$ on $G$ that is invariant under left multiplication: $g \leq h$ implies $fg \leq fh$ for all $f,g,h \in G$. Equivalently, a left order is determined by its positive cone $P = \{g \in G : g > e\}$, which is a subset $P \subseteq G \setminus \{e\}$ satisfying $P \cdot P \subseteq P$ and $G \setminus \{e\} = P \sqcup P^{-1}$.

The space of left orders $\mathrm{LO}(G)$ is the set of all such positive cones, viewed as a subset of $\{0,1\}^{G \setminus \{e\}}$ with the product (Tychonoff) topology; this makes $\mathrm{LO}(G)$ a compact, totally disconnected, metrizable space (when $G$ is countable).

The group $G$ acts on $\mathrm{LO}(G)$ by conjugation: if $P \in \mathrm{LO}(G)$ and $g \in G$, then $g \cdot P := gPg^{-1} \in \mathrm{LO}(G)$.

Question: Does there exist a finitely generated left-orderable group $G$ such that the conjugation action of $G$ on $\mathrm{LO}(G)$ is minimal, in the sense that the orbit $\{gPg^{-1} : g \in G\}$ is dense in $\mathrm{LO}(G)$ for every $P \in \mathrm{LO}(G)$?

The status appears unknown from accessible sources.

original_question: Let G be a finitely generated group of C^2 circle diffeomorphisms with an exceptional minimal set Λ. Is the action of G restricted to Λ topologically conjugate to the action of some group of piecewise-affine homeomorphisms?
self_contained_problem:
Let $S^1$ denote the circle. A homeomorphism $h\colon S^1\to S^1$ is called piecewise affine if there is a finite partition of $S^1$ into arcs on each of which $h$ coincides with the restriction of an affine map (with respect to the standard length/angle parametrization). 

Let $G$ be a finitely generated group acting on $S^1$ by orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphisms. Suppose this action admits an exceptional minimal set $\Lambda \subset S^1$, i.e., a nonempty, closed, $G$-invariant set that is minimal for the $G$-action and is homeomorphic to a Cantor set (equivalently, $\Lambda \neq S^1$ and $\Lambda$ has no isolated points).

That is, does there exist a group $H$ of piecewise-affine homeomorphisms of $S^1$ admitting an exceptional minimal set $\Lambda'$, an isomorphism $\varphi\colon G \to H$, and a homeomorphism $\psi\colon \Lambda \to \Lambda'$ such that $\psi\circ g|_\Lambda = \varphi(g)|_{\Lambda'} \circ \psi$ for all $g \in G$?

paper_title: Group actions on 1-manifolds: a list of very concrete open questions
original_question: For groups of C^2 circle diffeomorphisms, is the restriction of the Godbillon-Vey cohomology class invariant under topological conjugacy?
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Gamma$ be a finitely generated group and let $\rho_1, \rho_2 : \Gamma \to \mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1)$ be two representations of $\Gamma$ by orientation-preserving $C^2$ diffeomorphisms of the circle $S^1$. The Godbillon–Vey cocycle on $\mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1)$ is the 2-cocycle defined by
$$ \mathrm{gv}(f,g) \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}\int_{S^1} \log(f\circ g)'\, d\log g' \;-\; \tfrac{1}{2}\int_{S^1} \log f' \, d\log f', $$
(equivalently, the standard Bott–Thurston Godbillon–Vey 2-cocycle), whose cohomology class $\mathrm{GV} \in H^2(\mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1);\mathbb{R})$ is the Godbillon–Vey class. For a representation $\rho:\Gamma\to\mathrm{Diff}^2_+(S^1)$, denote by $\rho^*\mathrm{GV}\in H^2(\Gamma;\mathbb{R})$ the pullback of this class.

Suppose $\rho_1$ and $\rho_2$ are topologically conjugate, i.e.\ there exists a homeomorphism $h:S^1\to S^1$ such that $\rho_2(\gamma) = h\circ \rho_1(\gamma)\circ h^{-1}$ for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Must one have
$$ \rho_1^*\mathrm{GV} \;=\; \rho_2^*\mathrm{GV} \quad\text{in } H^2(\Gamma;\mathbb{R})\,? $$

In other words: is the restriction of the Godbillon–Vey class to finitely generated groups of $C^2$ circle diffeomorphisms invariant under topological conjugacy?
status_search_result: The topological invariance of the Godbillon–Vey class is a long-standing problem in foliation theory. Partial results are known: Raby and Ghys established invariance under $C^1$ conjugacy, and Hurder–Katok under absolutely continuous conjugacy. For general topological conjugacy of $C^2$ foliations / groups of $C^2$ circle diffeomorphisms, the question remains open, and no resolution appears in recent literature.

original_question: Does Denjoy’s theorem remain true for circle homeomorphisms whose graphs are real-analytic, even when singularities may also occur for the inverse map?
self_contained_problem:
Recall Denjoy's theorem: every orientation-preserving C^2 diffeomorphism of the circle S^1 = R/Z with irrational rotation number is topologically conjugate to the corresponding irrational rotation. In particular, no such diffeomorphism admits a wandering interval (an interval whose forward iterates are pairwise disjoint).

Call an orientation-preserving homeomorphism f : S^1 → S^1 a real-analytic-graph homeomorphism if its graph Γ(f) = {(x, f(x)) : x ∈ S^1} ⊂ S^1 × S^1 is a real-analytic subvariety of S^1 × S^1. Equivalently, f is real-analytic away from a finite set of points where it (and possibly its inverse) may exhibit analytic singularities (vertical/horizontal tangencies, etc.), so that both f and f^{-1} are allowed to fail to be analytic at some points but the graph (which is the same set as the graph of f^{-1} after coordinate swap) is real-analytic.

Question: Does Denjoy's theorem remain valid in this class? Precisely, must every such homeomorphism f with irrational rotation number be topologically conjugate to an irrational rotation, i.e., must f have no wandering interval?

The classical Denjoy theorem requires C^2 (or bounded variation of log derivative) regularity, and known C^∞ Denjoy counterexamples exist, but the real-analytic-graph variant appears to remain open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Symmetry Analysis
context_brief: limits of the classical Lie group method
original_question: Determine, before carrying out a full reduction calculation, which partial differential equations have symmetry reductions that cannot be obtained by the classical Lie group method. The classical Lie group method is the standard infinitesimal-transformation approach to symmetry reductions; the problem asks for an a priori criterion distinguishing equations for which generalized methods such as nonclassical or direct methods are genuinely needed.
self_contained_problem:
Background. Let $\Delta(x,u,u^{(k)})=0$ denote a system of partial differential equations for a function $u(x)$ of independent variables $x=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$, where $u^{(k)}$ denotes the collection of partial derivatives of $u$ up to order $k$. The classical Lie group (infinitesimal) method seeks one-parameter groups of point transformations
$$\tilde x_i = x_i+\varepsilon\,\xi_i(x,u)+O(\varepsilon^2),\qquad \tilde u = u+\varepsilon\,\eta(x,u)+O(\varepsilon^2),$$
whose prolongation leaves the equation invariant on its solution manifold. Invariance of $\Delta=0$ under the prolonged vector field $\mathbf v=\sum_i\xi_i\partial_{x_i}+\eta\,\partial_u$ yields the determining equations for $(\xi_i,\eta)$; the resulting symmetry algebra produces group-invariant (similarity) reductions of $\Delta=0$ to systems with fewer independent variables.

Generalized procedures (the nonclassical method of Bluman and Cole, the direct method of Clarkson and Kruskal, and their further extensions) impose the symmetry condition only on the joint solution set of $\Delta=0$ and an invariant-surface condition $\xi_i u_{x_i}=\eta$, and can produce similarity reductions of $\Delta=0$ that do not arise from any classical Lie point symmetry of $\Delta$.

Problem. Formulate an effective a priori criterion, expressible directly in terms of the partial differential equation $\Delta(x,u,u^{(k)})=0$ itself (its coefficients, structure, or invariants), that decides — without performing the explicit reduction computation — whether $\Delta=0$ admits symmetry reductions that cannot be obtained by the classical Lie group method, and hence for which a generalized (nonclassical, direct, or related) approach is genuinely required.
status_search_result: No general a priori criterion is known. Existing literature provides partial results: criteria for when a nonclassical reduction coincides with a classical one (Arrigo et al.), variants such as the partially nonclassical method, and case-by-case analyses for specific equation families. Recent surveys and papers (2023–2024) continue to introduce new generalized methods that yield reductions inaccessible to classical and nonclassical methods, indicating the general classification problem remains open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Symmetry Analysis
context_brief: symmetry methods for boundary value problems
original_question: Find a general procedure for applying symmetry methods to boundary value problems, rather than only applying the standard classical requirement that both the differential equation and all boundary conditions be invariant under the same one-parameter Lie group.
self_contained_problem:
Consider a boundary value problem consisting of a (system of) differential equation(s)
   E(x, u, u_x, u_xx, ...) = 0
posed on a domain Ω ⊂ ℝ^n with boundary conditions
   B_i(x, u, u_x, ...) = 0  on  Γ_i ⊂ ∂Ω,  i = 1, ..., k.

The classical Lie symmetry approach to such a problem requires that one seek a one-parameter Lie group of point transformations
   x* = x + ε ξ(x,u) + O(ε^2),   u* = u + ε η(x,u) + O(ε^2),
whose infinitesimal generator X = ξ·∂_x + η·∂_u (suitably prolonged) leaves invariant simultaneously:
 (i) the differential equation E = 0,
 (ii) each boundary manifold Γ_i, and
 (iii) each boundary condition B_i = 0 on Γ_i.

This simultaneous-invariance requirement is typically very restrictive and admits only few (often none) nontrivial symmetries even when the underlying equation possesses a rich symmetry algebra.

Problem. Develop a general, systematic procedure for applying symmetry methods to boundary value problems that goes beyond the classical requirement of joint invariance of the equation and all boundary conditions under a single one-parameter Lie group. Specifically, formulate a framework — for example by constructing auxiliary differential equations satisfied by all solutions of a designated subset of the boundary conditions but not by all solutions of E = 0, by allowing symmetries that map solutions of the boundary value problem to solutions while not preserving the boundary conditions individually, or by another mechanism — that
 (a) reduces, in a constructive algorithmic way, to determining symmetries of the boundary value problem (in the sense of mapping solutions to solutions),
 (b) recovers the classical jointly-invariant symmetries as a special case, and
 (c) is capable of producing additional, genuinely new symmetries useful for obtaining exact or invariant solutions of boundary value problems for broad classes of equations and domains.
category_tag: Lie symmetries of boundary value problems
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., Bluman's monographs, Hydon's work on initial-value problems, and articles on Lie symmetries of nonlinear boundary value problems) develops partial techniques — weaker invariance requirements, conditional symmetries, and case-by-case algorithms — but no fully general procedure replacing the classical joint-invariance requirement is known. Surveys explicitly note the lack of a general method for constructing auxiliary equations satisfied by the boundary conditions but not by the full PDE, leaving the question open.

paper_title: Open Problems in Symmetry Analysis
original_question: Develop the study of nonclassical symmetry reductions for differential-difference equations and difference equations.
self_contained_problem:
Background. For a partial differential equation $\Delta(x,u^{(n)})=0$ with independent variables $x=(x_1,\dots,x_p)$ and dependent variable $u$, the classical Lie symmetry method seeks one-parameter groups of point transformations leaving the equation invariant; the corresponding infinitesimal generator $X=\sum_i \xi_i(x,u)\partial_{x_i}+\eta(x,u)\partial_u$ is determined by linear determining equations. The nonclassical (conditional) symmetry method of Bluman and Cole augments the system $\Delta=0$ with the invariant surface condition $Q[u]:=\sum_i \xi_i(x,u)u_{x_i}-\eta(x,u)=0$ and requires invariance only of the joint system $\{\Delta=0,\,Q=0\}$ together with its differential consequences; the resulting determining equations for $(\xi_i,\eta)$ are nonlinear, and the associated $Q$-conditional symmetries yield reductions to lower-dimensional equations and exact solutions not obtainable by classical symmetries.

Setup. Let $u_n(t)$ (or $u_{n,m}$) denote a function defined on a lattice indexed by integers $n$ (and $m$), and consider:
(a) a differential-difference equation of the form
$$F\bigl(t,n,u_n,u_{n\pm 1},\dots,u_{n\pm k},\dot u_n,\dot u_{n\pm 1},\dots,\ddot u_n,\dots\bigr)=0,$$
(b) a (purely) difference equation of the form
$$G\bigl(n,m,u_{n+i,m+j}\bigr)_{(i,j)\in S}=0$$
on a multidimensional lattice, where $S$ is a finite stencil.

Problem. Develop a systematic theory of nonclassical (conditional) symmetry reductions for differential-difference equations and for difference equations. In particular:

1. Formulate an analogue of the invariant surface condition $Q[u]=0$ appropriate for shift operators on a lattice, and derive the corresponding nonclassical determining equations for differential-difference and difference equations.

2. Establish algorithmic procedures (and, where possible, closed-form criteria) for solving these nonlinear determining systems and for constructing the resulting symmetry reductions to lower-dimensional differential-difference, difference, or ordinary differential/difference equations.

3. Apply the framework to obtain new exact solutions of representative integrable and non-integrable differential-difference and difference equations (such as the Toda lattice, Volterra lattice, discrete KdV, and discrete sine-Gordon equations) that are not accessible via classical Lie point symmetries.

paper_title: Open Problems in Symmetry Analysis
original_question: Determine whether nonclassical generalized symmetries exist, and, if they do exist, characterize the kinds of solutions they generate.
self_contained_problem:
Background and setup. Let $\Delta(x,u^{(n)})=0$ be a partial differential equation for an unknown function $u(x)$, $x=(x^1,\dots,x^p)$, where $u^{(n)}$ denotes $u$ together with all its partial derivatives up to order $n$. Two notions of symmetry are recalled.

(a) Generalized (Lie–Bäcklund) symmetry. An evolutionary vector field $\mathbf{v}_Q = Q(x,u^{(k)})\,\partial_u$, with characteristic $Q$ depending on $x$, $u$, and derivatives of $u$ up to some finite order, is a generalized symmetry of $\Delta=0$ if its prolongation satisfies
$$\operatorname{pr}\mathbf{v}_Q[\Delta]\big|_{\Delta=0}=0,$$
i.e. the symmetry condition holds on the solution manifold of $\Delta=0$ together with all its differential consequences.

(b) Nonclassical (conditional) symmetry. An evolutionary vector field $\mathbf{v}_Q$ is a nonclassical symmetry of $\Delta=0$ if its prolongation annihilates $\Delta$ on the joint solution manifold of the system
$$\Delta = 0, \qquad Q = 0,$$
together with all differential consequences of both equations. Equivalently, $\operatorname{pr}\mathbf{v}_Q[\Delta]$ vanishes modulo $\Delta$, $Q$, and their derivatives. When $Q$ is restricted to be linear in first derivatives of $u$ (the classical Bluman–Cole point case), this recovers the usual notion of nonclassical point symmetry.

Combining (a) and (b), a nonclassical generalized symmetry is an evolutionary vector field $\mathbf{v}_Q$ whose characteristic $Q$ is allowed to depend on derivatives of $u$ of arbitrary finite order, and for which the symmetry condition is required to hold only on the joint solution manifold of $\Delta=0$ and $Q=0$ (not on $\Delta=0$ alone).

Problem. 
1. Determine whether there exist partial differential equations $\Delta=0$ admitting a nonclassical generalized symmetry $\mathbf{v}_Q$ that is genuinely new, in the following precise sense: $Q$ depends nontrivially on derivatives of $u$ of order $\geq 1$, and $\mathbf{v}_Q$ is not a generalized symmetry of $\Delta=0$ (i.e. the symmetry condition fails on $\{\Delta=0\}$ but holds on $\{\Delta=0,\,Q=0\}$), and is not equivalent (modulo the equivalence relation $Q\mapsto \alpha\,Q$ for nowhere-zero differential functions $\alpha$, and modulo addition of a generalized symmetry of $\Delta$) to a nonclassical point symmetry.

2. If such genuine nonclassical generalized symmetries exist, characterize the families of exact solutions of $\Delta=0$ that arise as the invariant solutions $\{u : Q(x,u^{(k)})=0\}\cap\{\Delta=0\}$ associated with them, and contrast these solutions with those obtainable from classical Lie symmetries, generalized symmetries, and nonclassical point symmetries.
status_search_result: Recent literature (e.g., reviews and articles on nonclassical/conditional symmetries and connections with classical Lie symmetries, including works through 2023–2025) treats nonclassical symmetries primarily in the point case or for specific equations, and the existence and characterization of genuine nonclassical generalized (higher-order) symmetries is not addressed as a settled matter. No source found resolves the general existence question or provides a structural characterization of the solutions they would produce.

paper_title: Open Problems in Symmetry Analysis
context_brief: choosing useful differential constraints and ansatze
original_question: Find an a priori way to decide which differential constraints are useful for finding special solutions of differential equations, and which ansatz choices will lead to computable solutions.
self_contained_problem:
Let $\Delta(x, u, u_{(1)}, \dots, u_{(k)}) = 0$ be a system of differential equations for an unknown function $u(x)$, where $x = (x^1, \dots, x^n)$ are independent variables and $u_{(j)}$ denotes the collection of all partial derivatives of $u$ of order $j$. A common strategy for producing special (e.g., invariant, similarity, separable, or otherwise structured) solutions is to append to $\Delta = 0$ one or more auxiliary differential constraints $\Phi(x, u, u_{(1)}, \dots, u_{(m)}) = 0$, or to substitute an ansatz $u = F(x, \phi_1(\xi_1), \dots, \phi_r(\xi_r))$ of a prescribed functional form, and then to solve the overdetermined system that results.

Develop an a priori criterion (intrinsic to the differential equation $\Delta = 0$, without first attempting the reduction) that determines:

(a) which differential constraints $\Phi = 0$, when adjoined to $\Delta = 0$, yield a compatible overdetermined system whose general solution is nontrivial and explicitly computable; and

(b) which ansatz choices for $u$ reduce $\Delta = 0$ to a system of equations whose solutions can be found in closed form (or by a finite, effective procedure).

Equivalently, characterize, in terms of structural invariants of $\Delta$ (such as its symmetry algebra, conservation laws, integrability properties, or geometric data of its associated jet-space submanifold), the set of useful differential constraints and computationally tractable ansätze.
status_search_result: The question is posed as an open problem in symmetry analysis concerning the a priori selection of useful differential constraints and ansätze. While many partial frameworks exist (classical and nonclassical symmetry methods, the differential constraints method of Yanenko/Olver/Rozhdestvenskii, compatibility analysis, direct method of Clarkson–Kruskal), no general a priori criterion is known. The problem appears to remain open as a broad research direction.

Let $k \ge 2$ and let $f : \mathbb{P}^k(\mathbb{C}) \to \mathbb{P}^k(\mathbb{C})$ be a holomorphic endomorphism of degree at least $2$. The Fatou set $F(f)$ is the largest open subset of $\mathbb{P}^k$ on which the family of iterates $\{f^n\}_{n \ge 0}$ is locally equicontinuous (equivalently, normal). A Fatou component is a connected component of $F(f)$. A Fatou component $\Omega$ is called wandering if the forward iterates $f^n(\Omega)$, $n \ge 0$, are pairwise disjoint (so $\Omega$ is not preperiodic).

Question: Does there exist a holomorphic endomorphism $f$ of $\mathbb{P}^k(\mathbb{C})$ with $k \ge 2$ that admits a wandering Fatou component? More precisely, characterize the class of holomorphic endomorphisms of $\mathbb{P}^k$ for which wandering Fatou components exist, in contrast to the case $k=1$, where Sullivan's theorem (proved using the Ahlfors–Bers measurable Riemann mapping theorem) asserts that no rational map of $\mathbb{P}^1$ admits a wandering Fatou component.

(Recall, for context, that a domain $U \subset \mathbb{C}^k$ is called a Fatou–Bieberbach domain if $U$ is biholomorphic to $\mathbb{C}^k$ but $U \neq \mathbb{C}^k$.)

Let $F:\mathbb{C}^2\to\mathbb{C}^2$ be a biholomorphism (in particular, one may consider a Hénon map of the form $F(z,w)=(p(z)-aw,z)$ with $p$ a polynomial of degree at least $2$ and $a\in\mathbb{C}^*$). A Siegel domain for $F$ is a maximal connected open set $\Omega\subset\mathbb{C}^2$ containing $p_0$ on which $F$ is conjugate, by a biholomorphism, to a linear rotation, i.e., the iterates $\{F^n|_\Omega\}_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}$ form a normal family with limits also injective and the closure of $\{F^n|_\Omega\}$ in $\mathrm{Hol}(\Omega,\mathbb{C}^2)$ is a compact group acting transitively.

Question: Can such a Siegel domain $\Omega$ have boundary $\partial\Omega$ that is strongly pseudoconvex (i.e., $\partial\Omega$ is a $C^2$ hypersurface near each of its points and the Levi form of any local defining function is positive definite on the complex tangent space)?

Let $M$ be a complex manifold and let $f : M \to M$ be a holomorphic self-map. Recall the following standard notions:

- A point $p \in M$ is periodic of period $k \geq 1$ if $f^k(p) = p$. Such a periodic point is called repelling if all eigenvalues of the differential $Df^k(p)$ have modulus strictly greater than $1$, and a saddle if $Df^k(p)$ has at least one eigenvalue of modulus $>1$ and at least one of modulus $<1$ (this requires $\dim_{\mathbb C} M \geq 2$).
- The non-wandering set $\Omega(f)$ consists of all $x \in M$ such that for every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ there exist arbitrarily large integers $n$ with $f^n(U) \cap U \neq \emptyset$.
- When $M = \mathbb C^n$, the forward orbit $\{f^k(p)\}_{k \geq 0}$ of a point $p$ is called oscillating if it has a subsequence that remains uniformly bounded in $\mathbb C^n$ and another subsequence that tends to $\infty$.

Address the following questions:

(a) Is the closure of the set of repelling periodic points of $f$ always open in $\Omega(f)$?

(b) In the special case where $M = \mathbb C^n$ and $f$ is an entire holomorphic self-map, does (a) admit a counterexample?

(c) For a holomorphic self-map $f$ of $\mathbb C^n$, can there exist a sequence of points whose orbits are oscillating and which converges to a repelling periodic point of $f$?

(d) For a holomorphic self-map $f$ of $\mathbb C^2$, can there exist a sequence of saddle periodic points converging to a repelling periodic point of $f$? (Note that for biholomorphisms this is impossible, since under the inverse map a repelling point becomes attracting.)

An attracting set $A$ is called an attractor if the dynamics $f|_A$ admits a dense orbit (alternatively, is chain transitive, meaning that for every $\delta>0$ the $\delta$-pseudo-orbits of $f|_A$ are dense). $$\{c\in\Lambda : f_c \text{ has a non-trivial attractor}\}$$

Let $\Omega, V \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ be bounded open sets, and let $f: \Omega \to V$ be a biholomorphic mapping. Address the following questions about boundary regularity of $f$:

(a) If both $\partial \Omega$ and $\partial V$ are real-analytic ($C^\omega$), must $f$ extend continuously to $\overline{\Omega}$?

(b) If both $\partial \Omega$ and $\partial V$ are $C^\infty$-smooth, must $f$ extend continuously (or smoothly) to $\overline{\Omega}$?

(c) Do there exist bounded pseudoconvex domains $\Omega, V \subset \mathbb{C}^n$ with smooth boundary and a biholomorphism $f: \Omega \to V$ that does not extend smoothly to $\overline{\Omega}$?

$$\{(z_0,z_1,z_2,z_3,z_4) \in \mathbb{C}^5 : (\operatorname{Re} z_0 + |z_1|^2 - |z_2|^2)^2 + \operatorname{Re} z_4 < 0\}.$$

original_question: How can researchers obtain substantially more age measurements for Milky Way globular clusters, especially the metal-rich bulge clusters that are underrepresented in current HST-based samples because foreground reddening makes them difficult to observe, so that globular-cluster formation models can be constrained more tightly?

The broader goal of a comprehensive, uniform absolute-age catalog for all Milky Way GCs (especially bulge GCs) remains only partially achieved.

paper_title: Globular Cluster Formation and Evolution in the Context of Cosmological Galaxy Assembly: Open Questions
original_question: What causes the approximately 2 Gyr age threshold below which multiple stellar populations have not been found in compact massive clusters, and does that threshold indicate that ancient globular clusters formed through a physically distinct channel from younger massive clusters, or instead that the same formation pathway is operating but the multiple-population signature depends on stellar mass or some other stellar-evolution effect?
self_contained_problem:
In observations of compact, massive star clusters (with masses comparable to Galactic globular clusters, i.e. roughly 10^5 solar masses or greater, and half-light radii of a few parsecs), the chemical-abundance pattern known as "multiple stellar populations" — characterized by star-to-star variations in light elements such as He, C, N, O, Na, Mg, and Al within a single cluster — is found in all sufficiently old clusters but appears to be absent in clusters younger than approximately 2 Gyr. Determine the physical cause of this approximately 2 Gyr age threshold for the onset of detectable multiple stellar populations in compact, massive star clusters. In particular, decide between the following two alternatives (or identify another mechanism):

(a) Ancient globular clusters formed through a physically distinct channel (operative only at high redshift, z ≳ 0.17) that produced multiple populations, while younger massive clusters form through a different channel that does not.

(b) The same formation pathway operates at all cosmic epochs, and the apparent threshold reflects a stellar-evolution or stellar-mass dependence of the observable abundance signatures (for example, the signature being detectable only in stars below a certain initial mass, which corresponds to a cluster age of roughly 2 Gyr on the red giant branch, or an as-yet-unidentified evolutionary effect tied to stellar rotation, magnetic fields, or surface convection).

Provide a quantitative model that reproduces the threshold and predicts which younger clusters should or should not display the signature.
category_tag: Globular cluster formation and multiple stellar populations
status_search_result: Recent literature (2022–2025), including high-resolution spectroscopic studies of intermediate-age clusters such as NGC 1846 and reviews on the driving factors behind multiple populations, continues to state that the cause of the ~2 Gyr lower age threshold for the appearance of multiple stellar populations in compact massive clusters is not yet established. Competing hypotheses (a stellar-mass / evolutionary-effect explanation versus genuinely different formation channels, with cluster mass and retention of enriched gas as additional factors) remain under active investigation, with no consensus resolution.

paper_title: Globular Cluster Formation and Evolution in the Context of Cosmological Galaxy Assembly: Open Questions
original_question: The minimum initial cluster mass needed for a cluster to survive for a Hubble time appears similar to the minimum mass required for a cluster to host multiple stellar populations. Is this similarity just a coincidence, or does it arise from the same underlying physical processes that connect long-term cluster survival to the onset of multiple populations?
self_contained_problem:
Stellar clusters in galaxies are subject to dynamical mass loss processes (two-body relaxation driven evaporation, tidal shocks from interactions with the galactic potential and giant molecular clouds, and stellar evolution mass loss) that, over a Hubble time t_H ≈ 13.8 Gyr, impose a minimum initial mass M_surv below which an initially bound cluster cannot survive as a gravitationally bound system. Independently, observations of old Galactic and extragalactic globular clusters reveal that essentially every cluster more massive than some threshold M_MP exhibits multiple stellar populations (light-element abundance variations such as the Na–O and Mg–Al anti-correlations and He spreads), while clusters less massive than M_MP appear chemically homogeneous; M_MP is empirically of order 10^4–10^5 M_⊙, comparable to the value inferred for M_surv.

Question: Is the approximate equality M_surv ≈ M_MP merely a numerical coincidence between two independent mass scales (one set by long-term dynamical evolution in galactic tidal fields, the other set by the conditions for self-enrichment or retention of polluted ejecta during the cluster's earliest phase), or does it arise as a necessary consequence of common underlying physics linking the formation conditions that allow multiple populations to develop to the structural/dynamical conditions that allow a cluster to survive for a Hubble time? Formulate and justify a physical mechanism (or prove the absence of one) that would force M_surv = M_MP up to a factor of order unity, independent of host-galaxy environment.

paper_title: Globular Cluster Formation and Evolution in the Context of Cosmological Galaxy Assembly: Open Questions
original_question: What role do galaxy mergers play in setting the properties of the present-day globular-cluster population: are mergers mainly a secondary enhancer of globular-cluster formation in already favorable high-redshift discs, do they make an essential contribution by assembling especially massive giant molecular clouds, or do they instead increase cluster destruction strongly enough that their net contribution is modest?
self_contained_problem:
In the cosmological context of hierarchical galaxy assembly, globular clusters (GCs) are dense, gravitationally bound stellar systems with masses typically in the range 10^4–10^6 solar masses, formed predominantly at high redshift. Their present-day (z = 0) population is characterized by observable properties such as the GC mass function, the specific frequency per host galaxy, the spatial and metallicity distributions, and the bimodality between metal-poor and metal-rich subpopulations. Galaxy mergers — major and minor — drive bursts of star formation, can assemble unusually massive giant molecular clouds (GMCs) with masses exceeding 10^7 solar masses through high gas surface densities and turbulent compression, and also produce strong tidal fields that accelerate cluster disruption.

Provide a quantitative determination of the net role played by galaxy mergers in shaping the z = 0 globular-cluster population. Specifically, decide which of the following best describes the merger contribution, and quantify the relative weights of the underlying mechanisms:

(a) Mergers act primarily as a secondary enhancer, boosting GC formation efficiency in high-redshift gas-rich discs where conditions for cluster formation (high pressure, high gas surface density, high turbulent Mach number) are already favorable, without being themselves a necessary ingredient.

(b) Mergers contribute essentially by assembling especially massive GMCs whose collapse produces the most massive bound clusters that survive to z = 0, so that without merger-induced cloud assembly the high-mass end of the present-day GC mass function would not be reproduced.

(c) Mergers increase cluster destruction (through enhanced tidal shocks, disc shocking, and dynamical friction in remnants) sufficiently that their net contribution to the surviving z = 0 GC population is modest, i.e., enhanced formation is largely cancelled by enhanced disruption.

The problem is to quantify, in a cosmological galaxy-formation framework that self-consistently models cluster formation in dense gas and subsequent dynamical evolution, the fractional contribution of merger-triggered formation to the surviving z = 0 GC mass function, specific frequency, metallicity distribution, and spatial distribution, and to identify which of (a), (b), (c) — or which combination — is realized.
status_search_result: The question of the merger contribution to globular cluster formation and survival is widely treated as an open problem in the GC formation literature. Subsequent work using cosmological simulations (E-MOSAICS, EMP-Pathfinder, and related models) has provided partial quantitative estimates suggesting mergers contribute meaningfully but are not the dominant channel, while disruption in merger remnants is significant; however, no consensus quantification has been established.

paper_title: The Planes of Satellite Galaxies Problem, Suggested Solutions, and Open Questions
original_question: For the Great Plane of Andromeda (GPoA), whose 15 on-plane satellites form a thin structure with correlated line-of-sight velocities that are consistent with rotation, do those satellites also have proper-motion components perpendicular to the GPoA, or are their full 3D motions largely confined to the plane? Resolving this determines whether the GPoA is genuinely a rotating plane of satellites rather than only an edge-on line-of-sight velocity pattern.
self_contained_problem:
Consider the Andromeda galaxy (M31) and the subset of 15 of its satellite galaxies that lie in a thin, near-edge-on (as seen from the Milky Way) planar configuration known as the Great Plane of Andromeda (GPoA). These on-plane satellites are observed to have line-of-sight velocities (relative to M31) that are spatially correlated in a manner consistent with coherent rotation about M31: satellites on one side of M31 systematically recede while those on the opposite side systematically approach.

For each on-plane satellite, decompose its three-dimensional velocity vector relative to M31 into a component lying within the GPoA and a component perpendicular to the GPoA. Determine, using precise astrometric proper-motion measurements, whether the perpendicular components of the velocities of the on-plane GPoA satellites are statistically consistent with zero (so that their full 3D motions are largely confined to the plane and the GPoA is a genuine rotationally supported plane of satellites), or whether significant perpendicular motions exist (so that the observed line-of-sight kinematic correlation is only a projected, edge-on signature rather than evidence of a true rotating plane).
status_search_result: Recent HST proper-motion measurements have begun addressing this question for individual on-plane GPoA satellites. NGC 147 and NGC 185 (2020) and Andromeda III (2024) have measured proper motions consistent with co-orbiting along the GPoA, supporting a genuine rotating plane interpretation. However, only a few of the 15 on-plane satellites have measured proper motions to date, so the full question of whether all on-plane GPoA satellites have negligible perpendicular velocity components remains only partially answered.
