paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Arakelyan [27] has proved that, given ρ > 12 and a countable set E, there exists an entire function f (z) of order ρ, for which all the points of E are deficient. Can E be the precise set of deficiencies of f in the sense that f has no other deficient values? It is also conjectured that if the an are deficient values for an entire function of finite order, then X −1 log[1/δ(an , f )] < +∞. (N. U. Arakelyan)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a non-constant meromorphic function on the complex plane. For a value a in the extended complex plane, the Nevanlinna deficiency of a with respect to f is

  δ(a,f) = liminf_{r→∞} m(r,a,f) / T(r,f),

where T(r,f) is the Nevanlinna characteristic of f and m(r,a,f) is the proximity function (with the usual convention for a = ∞). A value a is called deficient if δ(a,f) > 0. The order of an entire function f is

  ρ(f) = limsup_{r→∞} log log M(r,f) / log r,

where M(r,f) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|.

It is known that for every ρ > 1/2 and every countable set E ⊂ ℂ, there exists an entire function f of order ρ such that every point of E is a deficient value of f.

(a) Determine whether one can additionally arrange that E is exactly the set of deficient values of f, i.e. that f has no deficient values outside E.

(b) Prove or disprove the following conjecture: if {a_n} is the sequence of (finite) deficient values of an entire function f of finite order, then

  ∑_{n} 1 / log[1/δ(a_n, f)] < +∞.
status_search_result: A. Eremenko (1992) constructed a counterexample disproving the conjectural bound ∑ 1/log[1/δ(a_n,f)] < ∞ for entire functions of finite order: he produced entire functions of any order ρ > 1/2 whose deficiencies decay so slowly that this sum diverges. Thus part (b) is settled negatively. Partial positive results in the direction of the original conjecture (e.g., convergence of ∑ δ(a_n,f)^α for some α > 0, due to Lewis–Wu and others) are known. The companion question (a), on whether a prescribed countable set can be realized as the exact set of deficient values, does not appear to have a definitive published resolution from the searches performed.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is an entire function of finite order ρ which has a finite deficient value, find the best possible lower bound for the lower order λ of f (z). (Edrei and Fuchs [217] showed that λ > 0.) Gol’dberg [309] showed that for every ρ > 1, λ ≥ 1 is possible.
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a transcendental entire function of finite order
   ρ = limsup_{r→∞} log log M(r,f) / log r,
where M(r,f) = max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, and let
   λ = liminf_{r→∞} log log M(r,f) / log r
denote the lower order of f. Recall that, in the sense of Nevanlinna theory, a value a ∈ ℂ is called a deficient value of f if
   δ(a,f) = liminf_{r→∞} m(r, 1/(f−a)) / T(r,f) > 0,
where T(r,f) is the Nevanlinna characteristic and m(r, 1/(f−a)) is the proximity function. Suppose f has a finite deficient value (so there exists a ∈ ℂ with δ(a,f) > 0).

Determine the best possible (sharp) lower bound for the lower order λ of f in terms of the order ρ. In particular, decide whether for every ρ > 1 the value λ = 1 is attainable, and identify the optimal function ρ ↦ inf λ over all such entire functions of order ρ admitting a finite deficient value.
status_search_result: Edrei–Fuchs established λ > 0 for entire functions of finite order with a finite deficient value. Gol'dberg subsequently showed that for every ρ > 1 the lower order can be as small as λ = 1, settling the sharp lower bound question. The problem is therefore reported as resolved.

original_question: Edrei, Fuchs and Hellerstein [220] ask if f (z) is an entire function of infinite order with real zeros, is δ(0, f ) > 0? More generally, is δ(0, f ) = 1?
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a transcendental entire function of infinite order all of whose zeros are real. Recall that, in Nevanlinna theory, for a meromorphic function f on the complex plane one defines the characteristic function T(r,f) = m(r,f) + N(r,f), where m(r,f) = (1/(2π)) ∫_0^{2π} log^+|f(re^{iθ})| dθ and N(r,a) = ∫_0^r (n(t,a) − n(0,a))/t dt + n(0,a) log r, with n(t,a) the number of a-points of f in {|z| ≤ t} counted with multiplicity. original_question: Are there upper bounds of any kind on the set of asymptotic values of a meromorphic function of finite order? (D. Drasin and A. Weitsman)
self_contained_problem:
Let f be a meromorphic function on the complex plane C of finite order, where the order of f is

  ρ(f) = limsup_{r→∞} log T(r,f) / log r,

with T(r,f) the Nevanlinna characteristic. A value a ∈ Ĉ = C ∪ {∞} is called an asymptotic value of f if there exists a continuous path γ : [0,1) → C with |γ(t)| → ∞ as t → 1 such that f(γ(t)) → a. Let A(f) ⊂ Ĉ denote the set of asymptotic values of f.

Question: Does finiteness of the order of f impose any nontrivial upper bound (in terms of cardinality, capacity, Hausdorff dimension, measure, or any other set-theoretic or potential-theoretic restriction) on the set A(f)? In particular, can A(f) be all of Ĉ for some meromorphic function f of finite (including zero) order?
status_search_result: A. Eremenko answered the question negatively by constructing meromorphic functions of positive order, and also of order zero, whose set of asymptotic values is all of the closed complex plane Ĉ. Subsequently, Canton, Drasin and Granados showed that for every φ(r) → ∞ and every analytic (Suslin) set A ⊂ Ĉ, there is a meromorphic function f with T(r,f) = O(φ(r) log² r) whose set of asymptotic values is exactly A. Thus no nontrivial upper bound on the set of asymptotic values exists for meromorphic functions of finite order beyond the analytic-set restriction.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Determine the upper and lower estimates for the growth of entire and meromorphic solutions of algebraic ordinary differential equations (AODE). (This is a classical problem.) For AODEs of first order, it is known that the meromorphic solutions f must have finite order (see Gol’dberg [308]) and that (log r)2 = O(T (r, f )) (see Eremenko [234], [236]). (The latter two references contain a general account of first order AODEs, including modern proofs of some classical results.) The order of entire solutions of first order AODEs is an integral multiple of 21 (see Malmquist [552]). For AODEs of second order, it is known that the order of entire solutions is positive, see Zimogljad [817]. There is no upper estimate valid for all entire or meromorphic solutions of AODEs of order grreater than one, but there is an old conjecture that log |f (z)| ≤ expn (|z|) for entire solutions f of an AODE of order n. (A. Eremenko)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 1$ be a positive integer. An algebraic ordinary differential equation (AODE) of order $n$ is an equation of the form
$$P\bigl(z,f(z),f'(z),\ldots,f^{(n)}(z)\bigr)=0,$$
where $P$ is a polynomial in its $n+2$ arguments with complex coefficients. Define the iterated exponentials by $\exp_0(x)=x$ and $\exp_k(x)=\exp(\exp_{k-1}(x))$ for $k\ge 1$.

For a meromorphic function $f$ on $\mathbb{C}$, let $T(r,f)$ denote its Nevanlinna characteristic and let $\rho(f)$ denote its order of growth.

Establish optimal upper and lower estimates for the growth of entire and meromorphic solutions of AODEs. In particular, address the following:

(a) Prove or disprove: every entire solution $f$ of an AODE of order $n$ satisfies
$$\log|f(z)| \le \exp_n(|z|)$$
for all sufficiently large $|z|$.

(b) Find sharp lower bounds for $T(r,f)$ when $f$ is a meromorphic solution of an AODE of order $n\ge 2$, extending the known first-order bound $(\log r)^2 = O(T(r,f))$.

(c) Determine, for each $n\ge 2$, the possible orders of entire and meromorphic solutions of AODEs of order $n$, generalizing the first-order result that the order of an entire solution is an integer multiple of $1/2$.
category_tag: growth of solutions of algebraic ODEs
status_search_result: The problem of determining sharp upper and lower growth estimates for entire and meromorphic solutions of algebraic ODEs of order $\ge 2$, including the conjectured bound $\log|f(z)|\le \exp_n(|z|)$ for entire solutions of an AODE of order $n$, appears to remain open. Known results address only the first-order case (Gol'dberg's finite-order theorem, Eremenko's $(\log r)^2 = O(T(r,f))$ bound, Malmquist's half-integer order theorem) and the positivity of order for second-order AODEs (Zimogljad). Find criteria for, and/or give explicit constructive methods (in the sense that all required computations are practicable) for, meromorphic functions $f$ on the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$ satisfying both of the following conditions:

(a) every pole of $f$ has odd multiplicity;
(b) every zero of $f$ has even multiplicity.

The motivation is the study of meromorphic solutions on $\mathbb{C}$ of the linear differential equation
$$y'' + A(z)\, y = 0,$$
where $A$ is a given function (entire or meromorphic) on $\mathbb{C}$: a non-trivial meromorphic solution $y$ of this equation with a meromorphic coefficient $A$ must have all zeros of even order at points where $A$ is holomorphic, and the local behavior at poles is similarly constrained, leading naturally to functions $f$ with the parity properties (a) and (b).

original_question: P (a) Let f (z) = an z n be entire and m(r) = maxn |an |r n . If C > 21 then does there exist an entire f with m(r)/M (r, f ) → C? Any value of C such that 0 < C ≤ 21 is possible. (b) If f (z) 6= 0, then m(r) lim inf = 0; r→∞ M (r, f ) Is m(r) lim = 0? r→∞ M (r, f ) (c) What is the exact upper bound β of m(r) βf = lim inf ? r→∞ M (r, f ) It is known that 74 < β < 2/π. See Clunie and Hayman [164].
self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}a_n z^n$ be a transcendental entire function. For $r>0$, define the maximum modulus
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|$$
and the maximum term of the power series
$$m(r)=m(r,f)=\max_{n\ge 0}|a_n|r^n.$$
It is classical that $m(r)\le M(r,f)$ for all $r>0$, and that $m(r)/M(r,f)\le 1$.

Answer the following three questions.

(a) For which constants $C\in(0,1]$ does there exist a transcendental entire function $f$ such that
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)}=C\,?$$
It is known that every value $C$ with $0<C\le \tfrac{1}{2}$ is attained. Determine whether some (or every) value $C>\tfrac{1}{2}$ is also attained.

(b) Suppose in addition that $f$ has no zeros, i.e. $f(z)\ne 0$ for all $z\in\mathbb{C}$. It is known that
$$\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)}=0.$$
Is it true that, for every such zero-free transcendental entire $f$,
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)}=0\,?$$

(c) Determine the exact value of
$$\beta=\sup_{f}\;\liminf_{r\to\infty}\frac{m(r,f)}{M(r,f)},$$
where the supremum is taken over all transcendental entire functions $f$. It is known that
$$\tfrac{4}{7}<\beta<\tfrac{2}{\pi}.$$
category_tag: Entire functions: maximum term vs maximum modulus

original_question: Let ν(r) be the number of points on |z| = r, such that |f (z)| = M (r, f ). Can we have (a) lim supr→∞ ν(r) = ∞ ? (b) lim inf r→∞ ν(r) = ∞ ? (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
For a non-constant entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$, let
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|,$$
and define
$$\nu(r)=\#\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|=r,\ |f(z)|=M(r,f)\}.$$
(Note that $\nu(r)$ is finite for every $r>0$ unless $f$ is a monomial.)

Determine whether there exists an entire function $f$ (not a monomial) such that:

(a) $\displaystyle\limsup_{r\to\infty}\nu(r)=\infty$;

(b) $\displaystyle\liminf_{r\to\infty}\nu(r)=\infty$.
status_search_result: Part (a) was resolved affirmatively by Herzog and Piranian (1968), who constructed an entire function with ν(n)=n for all positive integers n, so lim sup ν(r)=∞ is achievable. paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f (z) is an entire function, the iterates fn (z), n = 1, 2, . . . are defined inductively by fn+1 (z) = f (fn (z)), f1 (z) = f (z). A point z satisfying the equation fn (z) = z, but such that fk (z) 6= z for k < n, is called a fixed point of exact order n. Prove that there always exist fixed points of exact order n if f (z) is transcendental, and n ≥ 2. For the case of polynomial or rational f (z) see Baker [44]. For a proof that fixed points of exact order n exist, except for at most one value of n, see Baker [46].
self_contained_problem:
Let f: ℂ → ℂ be a transcendental entire function. Define the iterates of f inductively by f₁(z) = f(z) and f_{n+1}(z) = f(f_n(z)) for n ≥ 1. A point z₀ ∈ ℂ is called a fixed point of exact order n of f if f_n(z₀) = z₀ but f_k(z₀) ≠ z₀ for every integer k with 1 ≤ k < n.

Prove that for every integer n ≥ 2, the function f possesses at least one fixed point of exact order n.
status_search_result: The conjecture was settled by W. Bergweiler (1991), who proved that every transcendental entire function f has infinitely many periodic points of exact period n for each n ≥ 2 (in fact infinitely many repelling ones). Earlier, I. N. Baker had proved existence for all n ≥ 2 with at most one possible exception; Bergweiler's result removes the exception.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Can an entire function have all its zeros and ones on two distinct straight lines, having infinitely many on each line? Edrei has proved (unpublished) that if l, m are intersecting straight lines, then it is impossible for all the zeros of an entire function f (z) to lie on l, and all the ones on m. (A. Edrei)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function on $\mathbb{C}$. Suppose there exist two distinct straight lines $\ell$ and $m$ in $\mathbb{C}$ such that:

(i) every zero of $f$ lies on $\ell$, and there are infinitely many zeros;
(ii) every solution of $f(z)=1$ lies on $m$, and there are infinitely many such solutions.

Does such an entire function $f$ exist?

It is known that if $\ell$ and $m$ intersect, then no entire function can have all its zeros on $\ell$ and all its $1$-points on $m$. The remaining question is whether such an $f$ exists when $\ell$ and $m$ are (necessarily parallel) distinct straight lines, with infinitely many zeros on $\ell$ and infinitely many $1$-points on $m$.
status_search_result: The case where the two lines intersect is settled by an (unpublished) result of Edrei, which rules out such an entire function. An oral observation attributed to Al-Katifi notes that $f(z)=\sin(z^2)$ has zeros and $1$-points distributed along the real and imaginary axes, but its zeros do not lie on a single line, so this does not resolve the original question. No published full solution covering distinct (parallel) lines was located.

original_question: What is the least integer k = k(N ), such that every entire function f (z) can be written as Xk f (z) = [fν (z)]N , ν=1 where f (z) and fν (z) are entire functions? It is enough to solve the problem for f (z) = z, since then one can substitute f (z) for z. The equation N 1 X (1 + ων z)N z= 2 , N ν=1 ων where ων are the distinct N -th roots of unity, shows that k(N ) ≤ N . On the other hand, for N = 1, 2, 3 we have k(N ) = N . To see e.g. that k(3) ≥ 3, suppose that z = f 3 + g3 = (f + g)(f + ωg)(f + ω 2 g), where ω = exp(2πi/3). It follows that the meromorphic function φ(z) = f (z)/g(z) satisfies φ(z) 6= −1, −ω, −ω 2 , except possibly at z = 0. Thus, by Picard’s Theo- rem, φ(z) must be rational, and so φ(z) assumes at least two of the three values −1, −ω, −ω 2 . This gives a contradiction. (H.A. Heilbronn)
self_contained_problem:
For a positive integer $N\ge 1$, let $k(N)$ denote the least positive integer $k$ (if it exists) such that every entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ admits a representation
$$ f(z) \;=\; \sum_{\nu=1}^{k} \bigl[f_\nu(z)\bigr]^{N}, $$
where $f_1,\ldots,f_k$ are entire functions. (Note: by substituting $f$ for $z$, it suffices to consider the case $f(z)=z$.) 

The identity
$$ z \;=\; \frac{1}{N^{2}}\sum_{\nu=1}^{N} \frac{(1+\omega_\nu z)^{N}}{\omega_\nu}, $$
where $\omega_1,\ldots,\omega_N$ are the distinct $N$-th roots of unity, shows that $k(N)\le N$. Moreover $k(1)=1$, $k(2)=2$, and $k(3)=3$ (the lower bound $k(3)\ge 3$ follows from Picard's theorem applied to $\varphi=f/g$ when $z=f^3+g^3=(f+g)(f+\omega g)(f+\omega^2 g)$).

Determine the value of $k(N)$ for every integer $N\ge 4$.
status_search_result: A web search did not surface a definitive resolution of the value of $k(N)$ for general $N\ge 4$. The known bounds $k(N)\le N$ and the exact values $k(1)=1$, $k(2)=2$, $k(3)=3$ are classical, but no source verifying a complete determination of $k(N)$ for all $N$ was located, so the current status is unclear.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Is it possible to say something more precise about C(λ) when λ is just greater than 1? In particular, is it true that C(λ) = −1 for such λ, or alternatively, is C(λ) a strictly decreasing function of λ?
self_contained_problem:
For an entire function f, let
   M(r, f) = max{|f(z)| : |z| = r},   m(r, f) = min{|f(z)| : |z| = r},
and define the order of f by
   ρ(f) = limsup_{r → ∞} log log M(r, f) / log r.

For each real number λ ≥ 0, define the constant
   C(λ) = inf liminf_{r → ∞} (log m(r, f)) / (log M(r, f)),
where the infimum is taken over all transcendental entire functions f with ρ(f) ≤ λ such that f has no zeros on a sequence of circles |z| = r_n with r_n → ∞ along which the liminf is computed (equivalently, C(λ) is the largest constant such that, for every transcendental entire function f with ρ(f) ≤ λ, one has
   log m(r, f) ≥ (C(λ) − o(1)) log M(r, f)
on some sequence of radii r_n → ∞).

The classical cos πρ theorem implies C(λ) ≥ cos πλ for 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, and in particular C(1) = −1. For λ > 1 no such lower bound is known.

Determine the behaviour of C(λ) for λ just greater than 1. In particular:

(a) Is C(λ) = −1 for all λ in some right neighbourhood (1, 1 + ε) of 1?

(b) If not, is the function λ ↦ C(λ) strictly decreasing for λ > 1?
status_search_result: The question concerns the behaviour, for λ slightly greater than 1, of the constant C(λ) governing the comparison of log m(r, f) and log M(r, f) for entire functions of order at most λ — an extension of the cos πρ theorem beyond order 1. Searches turned up Hayman's classical work on the local growth of power series and the Wiman–Valiron survey, as well as recent work on the minimum modulus problem (e.g., the Computational Methods and Function Theory cover article on the minimum modulus problem), but no definitive resolution of either of the two specific sub-questions (whether C(λ) = −1 on a right neighbourhood of 1, or whether C is strictly decreasing). The status appears to remain open, but available sources do not provide a clear-cut confirmation.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let rn be a sequence of Pólya peaks (as defined by Edrei [215]) of order ρ. Then Edrei [215] showed that there exists K = K(α, ρ) such that log m0 (r, f ) > cos(πα) log M (r, f ) for some value r in the interval rn ≤ r ≤ Krn and n sufficiently large. Is K(α, ρ) independent of α for fixed ρ? Can it be taken arbitrarily near 1? (D. Drasin and A. Weitsman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a meromorphic function in the complex plane. For $r>0$ let
\[ M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|,\qquad m_0(r,f)=\min_{|z|=r}|f(z)|, \]
and let $N(r,0,f)$ denote the integrated counting function of zeros of $f$. Fix $\rho>0$. A sequence $r_n\to\infty$ is called a sequence of Pólya peaks of order $\rho$ for a positive nondecreasing function $T(r)$ if for every $\varepsilon>0$ and every $A>1$,
\[ T(t) \le (1+\varepsilon)\Bigl(\tfrac{t}{r_n}\Bigr)^{\rho} T(r_n) \qquad \text{for all } t\in[r_n/A,\,A r_n], \]
for $n$ sufficiently large.

Fix $0<\alpha<1$ and $\rho>0$. It is known that there exists a constant $K=K(\alpha,\rho)>1$ such that, whenever $\{r_n\}$ is a sequence of Pólya peaks of order $\rho$ of $T(r,f)$, the inequality
\[ \log m_0(r,f) > \cos(\pi\alpha)\,\log M(r,f) \]
holds for some $r\in[r_n,Kr_n]$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Questions:
(a) Can $K(\alpha,\rho)$ be chosen independent of $\alpha$ for each fixed $\rho$?
(b) Can $K(\alpha,\rho)$ be taken arbitrarily close to $1$?

Thus the question is partially resolved depending on which Pólya peak notion is used.

original_question: Let f (z) be a non-constant entire function, and assume that for some constant c the plane measure of the set E(c) where |f (z)| > c is finite. What is the minimum growth rate of f (z)? Hayman conjectures that Z ∞ r dr <∞ 0 log log M (r, f ) is true and best possible. If E(c) has finite measure, is the same true for E(c′ ) for c′ < c? (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function on $\mathbb{C}$. For a real constant $c>0$, let
$$E(c) = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |f(z)| > c\},$$
and denote by $|E(c)|$ the planar Lebesgue measure of $E(c)$. Let
$$M(r,f) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|$$
be the maximum modulus of $f$.

Assume that there exists some $c$ such that $|E(c)| < \infty$.

(a) Determine the minimum possible growth rate of $M(r,f)$ as $r \to \infty$ under this hypothesis. In particular, prove or disprove that
$$\int_{0}^{\infty} \frac{r\,dr}{\log\log M(r,f)} < \infty,$$
and show that this estimate is best possible (i.e. there exists such an entire function for which the integral is finite while no essentially stronger growth lower bound holds).

(b) Show that if $|E(c)| < \infty$ for some $c$, then $|E(c')| < \infty$ for every $c' < c$ as well, or else exhibit a counterexample.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f (z) be an entire function (of sufficiently high order) with l, l ≥ 2 different asymptotic values ak , k = 1, . . . , l. Suppose that γk is a path such that f (z) → ak as z → ∞, z ∈ γk . Let n1 (r, ak ) be the number of zeros of f (z) − ak on γk , and in |z| ≤ r. Can we find a function f (z) such that n1 (r, ak ) → bk > 0 n(r, ak ) as r → ∞, for k = 1, 2, . . . , n? Can we take bk = 1? (J. Winkler)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f(z)$ be a transcendental entire function of sufficiently high order, and suppose that $f$ has $\ell \geq 2$ distinct (finite) asymptotic values $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_\ell$; that is, for each $k=1,\dots,\ell$ there exists a continuous unbounded curve $\gamma_k$ tending to $\infty$ such that $f(z)\to a_k$ as $z\to\infty$ along $\gamma_k$.

For $r>0$ and each $k$, define:
- $n(r,a_k)$ = number of zeros of $f(z)-a_k$ in the disk $\{|z|\le r\}$, counted without multiplicity;
- $n_1(r,a_k)$ = number of zeros of $f(z)-a_k$ that lie on the curve $\gamma_k$ and inside $\{|z|\le r\}$.

Question 1. Does there exist an entire function $f$ of the above kind, together with asymptotic paths $\gamma_1,\dots,\gamma_\ell$, such that for every $k=1,\dots,\ell$ the limit
$$\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{n_1(r,a_k)}{n(r,a_k)}=b_k$$
exists and satisfies $b_k>0$?

Question 2. Can such an $f$ be constructed for which $b_k=1$ for all $k=1,\dots,\ell$ (i.e., asymptotically all $a_k$-points lie on the corresponding asymptotic path $\gamma_k$)?
status_search_result: Web search did not surface a published resolution of this question concerning the asymptotic distribution of $a_k$-points along asymptotic paths $\gamma_k$ of an entire function of high order. Related work on asymptotic values and the Denjoy–Carleman–Ahlfors theorem exists, but no source confirms a positive or negative answer to the specific quotients $n_1(r,a_k)/n(r,a_k)\to b_k>0$ (or $=1$). Status remains unclear.

original_question: Let {fα (z)} be a family of entire functions, and assume that for every z0 , there are only denumerably many distinct values of fα (z0 ). Then if c = 2N0 > N1 , the family {fα (z)} is itself denumerable. The above result was proved by Erdös [228]. If c = N1 , he constructed a counter-example. Suppose now that m is an infinite cardinal, N0 < m < c. Assume that for every z0 , there are at most m distinct values fα (z0 ). Does it then follow that the family {fα (z)} has at most power m? If m+ < c, where m+ is the successor of m, it is easy to see that the answer is ‘yes’. However, if c = m+ , the counter-example fails. It is possible the question is undecidable. (P. Erdös)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathfrak{m}$ be an infinite cardinal with $\aleph_0 < \mathfrak{m} < \mathfrak{c}$, where $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0}$ is the cardinality of the continuum. Suppose $\{f_\alpha\}_{\alpha \in A}$ is a family of pairwise distinct entire functions $f_\alpha : \mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{C}$ such that for every $z_0 \in \mathbb{C}$ the set of values $\{f_\alpha(z_0) : \alpha \in A\}$ has cardinality at most $\mathfrak{m}$.

Does it follow (provably in ZFC) that $|A| \le \mathfrak{m}$?

Background facts that may be assumed: (i) if $\mathfrak{c} = 2^{\aleph_0} > \aleph_1$ and the value sets $\{f_\alpha(z_0)\}$ are countable for every $z_0$, then the family is countable; (ii) if $\mathfrak{c} = \aleph_1$, there exists a counterexample (an uncountable family of distinct entire functions whose values at every point form a countable set); (iii) if the successor cardinal $\mathfrak{m}^+$ satisfies $\mathfrak{m}^+ < \mathfrak{c}$, then a straightforward argument shows the answer is "yes". The remaining nontrivial case is $\mathfrak{c} = \mathfrak{m}^+$.
status_search_result: This is the natural cardinal generalization of Wetzel's problem. Kumar and Shelah, and subsequently Schilhan (J. London Math. Soc., 2024, "Wetzel families and the continuum"), showed that for any uncountable cardinal $\kappa$ of uncountable cofinality there is a cofinality- and cardinal-preserving forcing extension containing a Wetzel family of size $\kappa$. In particular, for an intermediate cardinal $\mathfrak m$ with $\mathfrak c = \mathfrak m^+$, it is consistent with ZFC that there is a family of $\mathfrak m^+$ distinct entire functions whose value set at every point has size $\le \mathfrak m$. Hence the statement "the family must have size $\le \mathfrak m$" is not provable in ZFC, and as Erdős suspected, the question is undecidable in ZFC in this remaining case.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If A, B are countable dense subsets of R, C respectively, does there necessarily exist a transcendental entire function that maps A onto B, and R \ A into C \ B? Suppose that E, F are countable dense subsets of R, and that there exists an entire function f , monotonic on R, that maps E onto F , and R \ E onto R \ F . Find interesting conditions which imply that f is trivial. For example, if E, F are real rationals, under what conditions is f necessarily linear with rational coefficients? One could also investigate this question in the case of real-valued harmonic or subharmonic functions in Rn , n ≥ 2. If A, B are two countable dense subsets of R, Barth and Schneider [65] have shown that there exists a transcendental entire function, monotonic on R, that maps A onto B and R \ A onto R \ B; also, if A, B are countable dense subsets of C, see Barth and Schneider [66]. (K. F. Barth)
self_contained_problem:
Let A be a countable dense subset of R and B a countable dense subset of C. Does there necessarily exist a transcendental entire function f: C → C such that f(A) = B and f(R \ A) ⊆ C \ B?

Furthermore, suppose E, F are countable dense subsets of R and that there exists an entire function f, monotonic on R, with f(E) = F and f(R \ E) = R \ F. Identify natural conditions on E, F (or on f) that force f to be "trivial." For instance, in the case E = F = Q, determine conditions under which f must be a linear polynomial with rational coefficients. Investigate the analogous questions for real-valued harmonic or subharmonic functions on R^n, n ≥ 2.
category_tag: Entire functions and countable dense sets
status_search_result: Barth and Schneider proved that for countable dense subsets A, B of R there is a transcendental entire function, monotonic on R, mapping A onto B and R\A onto R\B, and a related result for countable dense subsets of C. The mixed case (A ⊂ R dense, B ⊂ C dense, with f(R\A) ⊆ C\B) and the rigidity questions about when such an f must be trivial/linear do not appear to have a documented resolution in available sources, so the status is unclear.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Characterise those entire functions having at least one continuous maximum modulus path going from 0 to ∞. (W. Al-Katifi)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be a non-constant entire function, and define its maximum modulus function by
$$M(r,f) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, \qquad r \ge 0.$$
A *maximum modulus path* for $f$ is a continuous curve $\gamma:[0,\infty) \to \mathbb{C}$ such that $\gamma(0)=0$, $|\gamma(t)| \to \infty$ as $t\to\infty$, and
$$|f(\gamma(t))| = M(|\gamma(t)|,f) \qquad \text{for every } t \ge 0,$$
i.e.\ at each point of the curve the function attains its maximum modulus on the circle through that point.

Characterise the entire functions $f$ for which there exists at least one such continuous maximum modulus path going from $0$ to $\infty$.
category_tag: Maximum modulus set of entire functions
status_search_result: Recent work by Evdoridou, Pardo-Simón and Sixsmith (2021) and related papers analyze the structure of the maximum modulus set of entire functions, refining results of Hayman near the origin and studying its components. However, none of the located sources provide a complete characterisation of entire functions admitting a continuous maximum modulus path from 0 to ∞, so the status of this question could not be definitively verified.

original_question: What is the best function g(σ), σ ≥ 0 such that, for a non-constant entire function f (z) with maximum and minimum modulus M (r, f ) and m0 (r, f ) re- spectively, the assumption log M (r, f ) lim sup ≤σ r→∞ (log r)2 implies that m0 (r, f ) lim sup ≥ g(σ) ? r→∞ M (r, f ) (P. D. Barry)
self_contained_problem:
For a non-constant entire function $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$, define the maximum and minimum modulus on the circle of radius $r>0$ by
$$M(r,f) := \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|, \qquad m_0(r,f) := \min_{|z|=r} |f(z)|.$$
Fix $\sigma \ge 0$ and consider the class $\mathcal{E}(\sigma)$ of all non-constant entire functions $f$ satisfying
$$\limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{\log M(r,f)}{(\log r)^2} \le \sigma.$$
Determine the largest (best) function $g:[0,\infty)\to[0,\infty)$ such that, for every $f \in \mathcal{E}(\sigma)$,
$$\limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{m_0(r,f)}{M(r,f)} \ge g(\sigma).$$
Equivalently, find
$$g(\sigma) = \inf_{f \in \mathcal{E}(\sigma)} \limsup_{r\to\infty} \frac{m_0(r,f)}{M(r,f)}$$
explicitly as a function of $\sigma \ge 0$.
status_search_result: A web search did not return a definitive resolution of the optimal function g(σ) for entire functions of slow growth (log M(r,f) = O((log r)^2)) attributed to P. D. Barry. While there is a substantial literature on comparisons between m(r,f) and M(r,f) (including Barry's classical 1962 work on minimum modulus), no source clearly identifies the extremal g(σ) in this specific formulation, so the current status is unclear.

original_question: Let E be a closed set in C, with the following properties: (1) there exists a transcendental entire function f (z) that is bounded on E; and (2), there exists a transcendental entire function g(z) that is bounded away from 0 on the complement of E. For each such set E, must there exist one transcendental entire function that is simultaneously bounded on E and bounded away from 0 on the complement of E? (L. A. Rubel)
self_contained_problem:
Call an entire function f: ℂ → ℂ transcendental if it is not a polynomial. Let E ⊆ ℂ be a closed set such that:

(i) there exists a transcendental entire function f with sup_{z ∈ E} |f(z)| < ∞ (i.e., f is bounded on E); and

(ii) there exists a transcendental entire function g with inf_{z ∈ ℂ∖E} |g(z)| > 0 (i.e., g is bounded away from 0 on the complement of E).

Question: For every closed set E ⊆ ℂ satisfying both (i) and (ii), does there necessarily exist a single transcendental entire function h that is simultaneously bounded on E and bounded away from 0 on ℂ∖E?

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If f is an entire function such that log M (r, f ) = O(log r)2 as r → ∞, then Hayman [394] has shown that log |f (reiθ )| ∼ log M (r, f ), as r → ∞, for reiθ outside an exceptional set E of circles subtending angles at the origin, whose sum is finite. In particular, log |f (reiθ )| ∼ log M (r, f ), as r → ∞, for almost every θ. Using this result, Anderson and Clunie [24] showed that if f is meromorphic and T (r, f ) = O(log r)2 as r → ∞, then a deficient value (there is at most one) must be asymptotic and, moreover, if δ(a, f ) > 0, then f (reiθ ) → a as r → ∞ for almost every θ. Now consider a new class of entire functions Iα , α > 1, defined by (a) log M (r, f ) = O(log r)1+α as r → ∞ (b) (log r)α = o(log M (r, f )) as r → ∞. (Hayman’s functions are I1 ). Do the results of Hayman, and the corresponding results of Anderson and Clunie still hold? In other words, do these results depend on smallness of growth, or only on smoothness of growth? (J. M. Anderson)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be an entire function and let
$$M(r,f)=\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|, \qquad T(r,f)=\text{the Nevanlinna characteristic of } f.$$
For a meromorphic function $f$ and a value $a\in\widehat{\mathbb C}$, let $\delta(a,f)$ denote the Nevanlinna deficiency of $a$. A value $a$ is called an asymptotic value of $f$ if there is a continuous path $\gamma$ tending to $\infty$ along which $f(z)\to a$.

A classical theorem of Hayman states that if $f$ is entire and $\log M(r,f)=O((\log r)^2)$ as $r\to\infty$, then
$$\log|f(re^{i\theta})|\sim \log M(r,f)\quad (r\to\infty)$$
for $re^{i\theta}$ outside an exceptional set $E$ which is a union of disks (or "circles") subtending angles at the origin whose total sum is finite; in particular this asymptotic holds for almost every $\theta\in[0,2\pi)$. Using this, Anderson and Clunie proved that if $f$ is meromorphic with $T(r,f)=O((\log r)^2)$ as $r\to\infty$, then any deficient value of $f$ (there is at most one) is an asymptotic value, and moreover if $\delta(a,f)>0$ then $f(re^{i\theta})\to a$ as $r\to\infty$ for almost every $\theta$.

For each $\alpha>1$, define the class $I_\alpha$ of entire functions by the two conditions
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] $\log M(r,f)=O((\log r)^{1+\alpha})$ as $r\to\infty$,
\item[(b)] $(\log r)^{\alpha}=o(\log M(r,f))$ as $r\to\infty$.
\end{itemize}
(The Hayman case $\alpha=1$ recovers the class above.)

Question. Do the analogues of Hayman's theorem and of the Anderson–Clunie theorem hold for the classes $I_\alpha$, $\alpha>1$? Specifically:
\begin{enumerate}
\item If $f\in I_\alpha$, does $\log|f(re^{i\theta})|\sim \log M(r,f)$ as $r\to\infty$ outside an exceptional family of disks subtending angles at the origin whose sum is finite (and thus for almost every $\theta$)?
\item If $f$ is meromorphic and the analogous smoothness condition holds for $T(r,f)$ in place of $\log M(r,f)$, must any deficient value be an asymptotic value, and must $f(re^{i\theta})\to a$ for almost every $\theta$ whenever $\delta(a,f)>0$?
\end{enumerate}
In other words, do these theorems depend on the smallness of growth of $f$, or only on the smoothness of growth?
status_search_result: J. M. Anderson's paper "Asymptotic values of meromorphic functions of smooth growth" (Glasgow Math. J.) addresses this circle of questions, giving results under a smoothness (rather than smallness) hypothesis on growth, with extensions due to Hayman that yield analogues for functions of positive order. This indicates the conjecture's spirit—that smoothness, not smallness, suffices—is at least partially confirmed, but I could not verify a complete resolution covering the full classes $I_\alpha$ for all $\alpha>1$ in both Hayman's and the Anderson–Clunie statements.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let Γ be a rectifiable curve. Suppose f is a continuous function on the plane satisfying Z f (z)dz = 0 for all rigid motions σ. σ(Γ) Does this imply that f is an entire function? The answer is ‘yes’ for some choices of Γ, and ‘no’ for others. For example, the answer is ‘no’ for the circle (f (x + iy) = sin(ax) is a counter-example for a suitable choice of a); ‘yes’ for an ellipse; ‘yes’ for any polygonal Jordan curve; and ‘yes’ for the boundary of any convex set with at least one corner. Prove that the circle is the only closed rectifiable Jordan curve (or the only curve among the class of curves which are boundaries of bounded convex sets) for which the answer is ‘no’. This problem is related to the ‘Pompeiu Problem’ discussed by Brown, Schreiber and Taylor [119]. (L. Brown)
self_contained_problem:
Let Γ be a closed rectifiable Jordan curve in the complex plane ℂ. For a rigid motion σ of ℂ (i.e., a map of the form σ(z) = e^{iθ}z + c with θ ∈ ℝ and c ∈ ℂ), let σ(Γ) denote the image of Γ under σ, oriented as the image of Γ. Say that Γ has the *complex moment property* if the only continuous functions f : ℂ → ℂ satisfying

  ∫_{σ(Γ)} f(z) dz = 0

for every rigid motion σ are the entire functions.

It is known that:
 (a) every ellipse, every polygonal Jordan curve, and the boundary of every bounded convex set having at least one corner has the complex moment property;
 (b) the circle does not have the complex moment property (for any circle, f(x+iy) = sin(ax) is a counterexample for a suitable a > 0).

Problem. Prove that the circle is the only closed rectifiable Jordan curve in ℂ failing the complex moment property. (Equivalently, prove at least the restricted statement that, among boundaries of bounded convex subsets of ℂ, the circle is the only curve failing the complex moment property.)
status_search_result: This is a variant of the classical Pompeiu problem. The general conjecture that the disc/circle is the only bounded simply connected planar domain failing the Pompeiu property remains open. Substantial partial results exist (e.g., domains with corners, convex domains satisfying additional regularity, and the equivalence with Schiffer's conjecture for sufficiently regular boundaries), but a complete proof for all rectifiable Jordan curves, or even all boundaries of bounded convex sets, has not been established.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Since the knowledge of the zeros of an entire function f leaves an unknown factor, eh say, in the Hadamard product for f , one can ask if f is determined by the zeros of f , and of its first few derivatives. Does there exist an integer k, k ≥ 2 such that, if f and g are entire, and f (n) /g(n) is entire and non-vanishing for 0 ≤ n ≤ k, then f /g is constant, unless f (z) = eaz+b , g(z) = ecz+d or f (z) = A(eaz − b), g(z) = B(e−az − b−1 ) ? The proposer has shown (unpublished) that k = 2 will do in certain cases; for example, when f and g have finite order. The example f (z) = (e2z − 1) exp(−iez ), g(z) = (1 − e−2z ) exp(ie−z ) shows that one sometimes needs k = 3. One can ask a similar question for meromorphic functions, with the additional possibility that f (z) = A(eh(z) − 1)−1 , g(z) = B(1 − e−h(z) ) for any non-constant entire function h. (A. Hinkkanen)
self_contained_problem:
Does there exist an integer $k \ge 2$ with the following property: whenever $f$ and $g$ are entire functions such that the quotient $f^{(n)}/g^{(n)}$ is entire and non-vanishing for every $n$ with $0 \le n \le k$, then $f/g$ is constant, with the only exceptions being

(i) $f(z) = e^{az+b}$ and $g(z) = e^{cz+d}$ for constants $a,b,c,d$, or

(ii) $f(z) = A(e^{az} - b)$ and $g(z) = B(e^{-az} - b^{-1})$ for constants $A,B,a,b$ with $b \ne 0$?

Here $f^{(n)}$ denotes the $n$-th derivative of $f$. It is known that $k=2$ suffices in some special cases (e.g.\ when $f$ and $g$ are of finite order), and the example $f(z) = (e^{2z}-1)\exp(-i e^{z})$, $g(z) = (1-e^{-2z})\exp(i e^{-z})$ shows that $k=2$ is not enough in general.

Formulate and answer the analogous question for meromorphic functions $f$ and $g$, with the additional exceptional family $f(z) = A(e^{h(z)}-1)^{-1}$, $g(z) = B(1 - e^{-h(z)})$ allowed, where $h$ is any non-constant entire function. Determine the smallest such $k$ (if any) in each setting.
status_search_result: According to the updated edition of the problem collection, Köhler proved that the answer is affirmative for meromorphic functions with $k = 6$, settling the meromorphic version with an explicit (though possibly non-optimal) bound. The exact minimal value of $k$ remains unspecified, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let f be an entire function satisfying the condition log M (r, f ) ≤ (1 + o(1))r ρ , as r → ∞. Suppose that there exists a curve Γ tending to ∞ such that on Γ log |f (z)| ≤ (α + o(1))r ρ , as r = |z| → ∞, for some α in [−1, 1); and denote by E(r, ε) the angular measure of the set {reiθ : log |f (reiθ )| ≤ (1 − ε)r ρ }. Eremenko conjectures that lim sup E(r, ε) ≥ arccos α. ε→0, r→∞ ρ Jaenisch [459] has proved some related results. (A. Eremenko)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f$ be an entire function of finite order $\rho > 0$ satisfying
$$\log M(r,f) \le (1+o(1))\, r^{\rho} \quad \text{as } r \to \infty,$$
where $M(r,f) = \max_{|z|=r} |f(z)|$. Suppose there exists a continuous curve $\Gamma \subset \mathbb{C}$ tending to $\infty$ and a constant $\alpha \in [-1,1)$ such that
$$\log |f(z)| \le (\alpha + o(1))\, r^{\rho} \quad \text{as } r = |z| \to \infty,\ z \in \Gamma.$$
For $\varepsilon > 0$ and $r > 0$, let
$$E(r,\varepsilon) = \operatorname{mes}\bigl\{ \theta \in [0,2\pi) : \log |f(re^{i\theta})| \le (1-\varepsilon)\, r^{\rho} \bigr\}$$
denote the angular (Lebesgue) measure of the indicated set of arguments. Prove or disprove:
$$\limsup_{\varepsilon \to 0,\ r \to \infty} E(r,\varepsilon) \;\ge\; \frac{\arccos \alpha}{\rho}.$$
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not find any source confirming a proof or refutation of this specific conjecture concerning the angular measure of the sublevel set of $\log|f|$ for entire functions of finite order with a curve of slow growth. The conjecture appears in the standard collection of open problems in function theory and no resolution was located, so the status is recorded as unknown.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It is shown by Hellerstein and Rossi [427], and Gundersen [354] that if f1 and f2 are two linearly independent solutions to the differential equation w′′ + Hw = 0, where H is a polynomial and f1 and f2 have only finitely many non-real zeros, then H is a non-negative constant. It is also shown that, if H(z) = az + b, for a, b ∈ R, then the differential equation admits a solution with only real zeros (and infinitely many of them). Furthermore, as pointed out by Gundersen [354], Titchmarsh ([749, pp. 172-173]) showed that, if H(z) = z 4 − β for special choices of β, then the differential equation also admits solutions with only real zeros (and infinitely many of them). Characterise all non-constant polynomials H such that the differential equation admits a solution with only real zeros (and infinitely many of them). (S. Hellerstein and J. Rossi)
self_contained_problem:
Consider the second-order linear differential equation
    w''(z) + H(z) w(z) = 0,
where H is a polynomial in the complex variable z with complex coefficients. A solution f of this equation is an entire function of z. It is known that:

(a) If f_1 and f_2 are two linearly independent solutions of the equation and each of f_1, f_2 has only finitely many non-real zeros, then H must be a non-negative real constant.

(b) When H(z) = a z + b with a, b real, the equation admits a (necessarily entire) solution having infinitely many zeros, all of which are real.

(c) For certain special real values of β, the equation with H(z) = z^4 − β admits an entire solution all of whose zeros are real (and there are infinitely many of them).

Problem: Characterise completely the non-constant polynomials H for which the differential equation w'' + H w = 0 admits an entire solution that has infinitely many zeros, all of them real.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that f is entire of proximate order ρ(r), and that f has a representation as a Dirichlet series ∞ X f (z) = an eλn z , 0 ≤ λ1 < λ2 < . . . → ∞, an > 0. n=1 Can one give a complete characterisation of the indicator h(θ, f ) = lim sup r −ρ(r) log |f (reiθ )| r→∞ of such functions? If f has a representation Z ∞ f (z) = eiz dF (t) where F is positive and increasing, Gol’dberg and Ostrovskii [323] gave such a characterisation. (A. A. Gol’dberg and I. V. Ostrovskii)
self_contained_problem:
A positive function $\rho(r)$ defined for $r\ge r_0$ is called a proximate order if $\rho(r)\to \rho\in[0,\infty)$ as $r\to\infty$ and $r\rho'(r)\log r\to 0$ as $r\to\infty$. For an entire function $f$, define its indicator (with respect to $\rho$) by
$$h(\theta,f) \;=\; \limsup_{r\to\infty}\, r^{-\rho(r)}\,\log|f(re^{i\theta})|, \qquad \theta\in[0,2\pi).$$

Now suppose $f$ is an entire function of proximate order $\rho(r)$ that admits a Dirichlet-series representation
$$f(z) \;=\; \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} a_n\, e^{\lambda_n z}, \qquad 0\le \lambda_1<\lambda_2<\cdots\to\infty,\quad a_n>0,$$
converging in the whole complex plane.

Give a complete characterisation of those functions $h:[0,2\pi)\to[-\infty,+\infty)$ which arise as the indicator $h(\theta,f)$ of some entire function $f$ of the above form.

(Background: when $f$ has the integral representation $f(z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tz}\,dF(t)$ with $F$ positive and increasing, a complete characterisation of the possible indicators is known.)

Status is therefore reported as unknown.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let Ω be a component of the normal set of an entire function f (under iteration). Do there exist such an f and such an Ω with the following properties: (a) f n (Ω) is uniformly bounded, for n = 0, 1, 2, . . .; (b) f n (Ω) ∩ f m (Ω) = ∅ for n 6= m. (I. N. Baker, R. Herman and I. Kra; communicated by D. Hamilton)
self_contained_problem:
Let $f:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}$ be a transcendental entire function, and consider its iterates $f^n=f\circ f\circ\cdots\circ f$ ($n$ times), with $f^0=\mathrm{id}$. The Fatou set (normal set) $F(f)$ is the set of points $z\in\mathbb{C}$ at which the family $\{f^n\}_{n\ge 0}$ is normal in some neighborhood of $z$. A connected component $\Omega$ of $F(f)$ is called a wandering domain if $f^n(\Omega)\cap f^m(\Omega)=\emptyset$ for all $n\ne m$ (equivalently, no iterate of $\Omega$ is contained in a periodic component of $F(f)$).

Question: Does there exist a transcendental entire function $f$ and a component $\Omega$ of its Fatou set such that both of the following hold?
(a) The orbit is uniformly bounded: there exists $R>0$ with $f^n(\Omega)\subset\{|z|\le R\}$ for every $n=0,1,2,\ldots$;
(b) The iterates are pairwise disjoint: $f^n(\Omega)\cap f^m(\Omega)=\emptyset$ whenever $n\ne m$.
status_search_result: Recent work on oscillating wandering domains explicitly notes that the existence of a wandering domain of an entire function with a bounded forward orbit remains a major open question. Known constructions yield multiply connected wandering domains whose iterates escape to infinity, or oscillating simply connected wandering domains that return near a bounded set but also have unbounded subsequences; no example with the entire orbit confined to a bounded set is known.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: (a) Show that, if a function g in Rd has the property that its Julia set J(g) 6= Ĉ, then g does not leave invariant a non-trivial Beltrami form on J(g). Here a Beltrami form µ means that µ ∈ L∞ (Ĉ) and kµkL∞ < 1; and trivial on J(g) means that µ(x) = 0 for almost all x in J(g). (b) More generally, is the Lebesgue measure of J(g) in Ĉ equal to zero? (This is the analogous conjecture to the Ahlfors conjecture for finitely-generated Kleinian groups.) Negative answers to both (a) and (b) have been proved (by McMullen (uncited) and Eremenko and Lyubich [248]) for the class of transcendental entire functions g. Douady has conjectured that the answer is negative, and that a counter-example is the function Pλ (z) = λ(z + z 2 ), for some λ of modulus one. See also Douady [195], Lyubich [537] and Mañé [540]. (D. Sullivan; communicated by M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $g$ be a rational function of degree $d \ge 2$ acting on the Riemann sphere $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, and let $J(g) \subset \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote its Julia set. A Beltrami form is a measurable $(-1,1)$-form $\mu \in L^\infty(\widehat{\mathbb{C}})$ with $\|\mu\|_\infty < 1$; it is said to be invariant under $g$ if $g^*\mu = \mu$ almost everywhere, and trivial on $J(g)$ if $\mu(x) = 0$ for almost every $x \in J(g)$.

(a) Prove that if $J(g) \ne \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, then $g$ admits no invariant Beltrami form that is non-trivial on $J(g)$ (equivalently, $g$ admits no measurable invariant line field supported on $J(g)$).

(b) More generally, prove or disprove: for every such rational map $g$ with $J(g) \ne \widehat{\mathbb{C}}$, the Lebesgue measure of $J(g)$ in $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ equals zero.

(In particular, decide both questions for the quadratic family $P_\lambda(z) = \lambda(z + z^2)$ with $|\lambda| = 1$.)
status_search_result: The "no invariant line fields" conjecture (part (a)) and the question of whether Julia sets have Lebesgue measure zero (part (b)) remain open in general for rational maps. Significant partial results have been obtained: McMullen established (a) for the real quadratic family, Levin–van Strien extended it to real unicritical polynomials $z^d+c$, and Avila–Lyubich and others have proved positive measure Julia sets can occur for some quadratic polynomials with Cremer/Siegel behavior, while ruling out invariant line fields in many infinitely renormalizable cases. The full conjectures remain unresolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let the function g in Rd have the property that its Julia set J(g) = Ĉ. Is g ergodic for Lebesgue measure? In other words, if B ⊂ Ĉ is a Borel-invariant set under g (that is, g −1 (B) = B), does it follow that either B or Ĉ \ B has Lebesgue measure zero? For further information, see [540]. (D. Sullivan; communicated by M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ denote the Riemann sphere, and let $g:\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\to\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ be a rational map of degree $d\ge 2$. The Fatou set $F(g)$ is the maximal open subset of $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ on which the iterates $\{g^n\}_{n\ge 0}$ form a normal family, and the Julia set is $J(g)=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus F(g)$. Suppose that $J(g)=\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$.

Question: Is $g$ ergodic with respect to the (spherical) Lebesgue measure on $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$? That is, if $B\subset\widehat{\mathbb{C}}$ is a Borel set satisfying $g^{-1}(B)=B$, must it follow that either $B$ or $\widehat{\mathbb{C}}\setminus B$ has Lebesgue measure zero?
status_search_result: This is a long-standing question, often attributed to Sullivan, asking whether every rational map of degree at least 2 whose Julia set is the whole Riemann sphere is Lebesgue-ergodic. While ergodicity is known for important classes (e.g., Lattès maps, Rees-type examples, certain Collet–Eckmann maps, and rational maps with critical points in repelling periodic orbits), no proof or counterexample is known in full generality, and the problem appears to remain open.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let a function f in Rd have the property that f (z) = λα z + O(z 2 ) as z → 0, where λα = e2πiα and α ∈ R \ Q. Assume also that f is linearisable at 0, and denote by S its Siegel singular disc. (a) Is α necessarily a Brjuno number? In other words, is it true that ∞ X (log qn+1 )/qn < +∞, n=0 where {pn /qn }∞ n=0 are the convergents of the continued fraction expansion of α? Also, what is the situation here when f is a non-linear entire function? (b) Is f necessarily injective on the boundary ∂S of S in Ĉ? (c) Is it true that f has no periodic points on ∂S? Both (b) and (c) are open even under the additional hypothesis that f has no critical point on ∂S. A positive answer to (b), under this additional hypothesis, would imply that when α satisfies a diophantine condition (that is, there exists β, γ, γ > 0 and β ≥ 2 such that, for every number p/q in Q, we have |α − (p/q)| ≥ γq −β ) then f has a critical point on ∂S. For further information, see Herman [438] and Przytycki [?]. (J.-C. Yoccoz and M. R. Herman)
self_contained_problem:
Let R_d denote a class of holomorphic self-maps (e.g. rational maps of degree d, or entire functions when so specified). Let f ∈ R_d satisfy
    f(z) = λ_α z + O(z^2)   as z → 0,
where λ_α = e^{2πi α} with α ∈ ℝ ∖ ℚ, and assume f is linearisable at 0, i.e. there exists a holomorphic injection φ defined on a neighbourhood of 0 with φ(0)=0, φ'(0)=1, conjugating f to the rotation w ↦ λ_α w. Let S denote the Siegel disc at 0, namely the maximal connected open set on which f is conjugate to this rotation, and let ∂S denote its boundary in the Riemann sphere ℂ̂.

Recall that α is a Brjuno number if its continued fraction convergents p_n/q_n satisfy
    Σ_{n=0}^∞ (log q_{n+1})/q_n < +∞.
A Diophantine condition on α means: there exist constants γ > 0 and β ≥ 2 with |α − p/q| ≥ γ q^{−β} for all p/q ∈ ℚ.

Answer the following:
(a) Must α be a Brjuno number? Treat separately the cases (i) f is a polynomial (or rational map), and (ii) f is a non-linear entire function.
(b) Must f be injective on ∂S (regarded as a subset of ℂ̂)?
(c) Can f have periodic points on ∂S?

In addition, show that a positive answer to (b), under the further assumption that f has no critical point on ∂S, implies that whenever α is Diophantine, f must have a critical point on ∂S.
status_search_result: Part (a) is known for quadratic polynomials: Yoccoz proved that a linearisable quadratic polynomial has Brjuno rotation number, and the Brjuno condition is sharp in degree 2. For higher-degree polynomials and for transcendental entire functions the question of whether α must be Brjuno remains open. For parts (b) and (c), injectivity of f on ∂S and absence of periodic points on ∂S are still open in general; partial results are known for unicritical polynomials when the critical point is not on ∂S, but the general case (and the corresponding statement implying existence of a critical point on ∂S in the Diophantine case) remains unresolved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that λ is of modulus one and not a root of unity, let Pλ (z) = λ(z + z 2 ) and hλ (z) = z + O(z 2 ) is the unique formal power series such that Pλ (hλ (z)) = hλ (λz). Denote by R(λ) the radius of convergence of hλ . (a) Calculate (or, at least, estimate up to ±10−10 ) the value of m = supλ R(λ). (b) Prove that m is realised by a function hλ , where λ = e2πiα and α is a real algebraic number of degree 2. (c) If R(λ) = 0, is the following true: for every positive ε, the function Pλ has a repelling periodic cycle included in {|z| < ε}? This property is known to hold for a dense Gδ -set of numbers λ of modulus one, see Cremer [176]. (M. R. Herman and J. -C. Yoccoz)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\lambda \in \mathbb{C}$ with $|\lambda|=1$ and $\lambda$ not a root of unity. Consider the quadratic polynomial
$$P_\lambda(z) = \lambda(z + z^2).$$
There exists a unique formal power series $h_\lambda(z) = z + O(z^2)$ satisfying the conjugation equation
$$P_\lambda(h_\lambda(z)) = h_\lambda(\lambda z).$$
Let $R(\lambda) \in [0,\infty]$ denote the radius of convergence of $h_\lambda$, and define
$$m = \sup_{\lambda} R(\lambda),$$
where the supremum is taken over all $\lambda$ on the unit circle that are not roots of unity.

(a) Determine the value of $m$, or at least estimate it to within $\pm 10^{-10}$.

(b) Prove that the supremum $m$ is attained, i.e. that there exists some $\lambda$ on the unit circle with $R(\lambda)=m$, and that such a $\lambda$ has the form $\lambda = e^{2\pi i \alpha}$ where $\alpha$ is a real algebraic number of degree $2$.

(c) Suppose $R(\lambda)=0$. Is it true that for every $\varepsilon > 0$, the polynomial $P_\lambda$ admits a repelling periodic cycle contained in the disk $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < \varepsilon\}$?

(It is known that this last property holds for a dense $G_\delta$-set of $\lambda$ on the unit circle.)

The status appears to remain open, but no definitive recent confirmation was located.

original_question: S Does there exist a non-linear entire function g with wandering domain W such that n≥0 gn (W ) is bounded in C? It has been conjectured by Lyubich [537] that if g and W exist, then g n (W ) cannot converge as n → ∞ to a fixed point of g. (M. R. Herman; A. Eremenko and M. Yu. Lyubich)
self_contained_problem:
Let g: ℂ → ℂ be a non-linear entire function. A Fatou component U of g is called a wandering domain if g^n(U) and g^m(U) lie in distinct Fatou components for all n ≠ m ≥ 0 (equivalently, U is not eventually periodic).

Question: Does there exist a non-linear entire function g and a wandering domain W of g such that the forward orbit
   ⋃_{n ≥ 0} g^n(W)
is a bounded subset of ℂ?

Furthermore, if such g and W exist, can the iterates g^n(W) converge as n → ∞ to a fixed point of g?
status_search_result: Recent surveys on wandering domains of transcendental entire functions (e.g., Bishop's wandering domains paper and the 2025 retrospective on Eremenko–Lyubich) explicitly state that whether a transcendental entire function can have a wandering domain with bounded forward orbit remains a major open question. Known constructions (Baker, Herman, Eremenko–Lyubich, and later refinements) all produce wandering domains whose iterates either escape to infinity or oscillate but are not contained in a bounded set.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Suppose that u(z) is subharmonic and u(z) < 0 in the half-plane |θ| < π/2, where z = reiθ . Suppose also that A(r) = inf u(reiθ ) ≤ −K, 0 < r < ∞. |θ|<π/2 Is it true then that u(r) ≤ − K, 0 < r < ∞? The result u(r) ≤ −K/3 is true, and is due to Hall [367].
self_contained_problem:
Let $u(z)$ be a subharmonic function defined on the right half-plane $H = \{z = re^{i\theta} : r > 0,\ |\theta| < \pi/2\}$, and suppose $u(z) < 0$ for all $z \in H$. For $r > 0$, define
$$A(r) = \inf_{|\theta| < \pi/2} u(re^{i\theta}).$$
Assume there exists a constant $K > 0$ such that $A(r) \le -K$ for every $r \in (0,\infty)$. It is known (a theorem of Hall) that under these hypotheses one has $u(r) \le -K/3$ for all $r > 0$. 

Determine whether the stronger conclusion holds: is it true that $u(r) \le -K$ for every $r \in (0,\infty)$? If not, what is the best possible constant $c > 0$ such that $u(r) \le -cK$ must hold for all $r > 0$ under the given hypotheses?
status_search_result: According to Hayman's compilation of research problems in function theory, the answer to the question as posed is "no": Hayman constructed an explicit subharmonic function satisfying the hypotheses for which $u(r) > -K/2$ on the entire positive real axis, so the conclusion $u(r) \le -K$ fails. The sharp constant therefore lies between $1/3$ (Hall's lower bound) and $1/2$ (Hayman's example), and the exact best constant is not asserted to be known.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It follows from a result of Wolf [795], that if u(reiθ ) ≤ f (θ), 0 < r < +∞, where Z 2π log+ f (θ) dθ < +∞, then u(z) is bounded above, and so is constant. What is the 3-dimensional analogue of this result?
self_contained_problem:
A subharmonic function on a domain $\Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is an upper-semicontinuous function $u : \Omega \to [-\infty, \infty)$ satisfying the sub-mean-value inequality on every closed ball contained in $\Omega$. Write $\log^+ x = \max(\log x, 0)$.

A theorem of Wolf states: if $u$ is subharmonic on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and there exists a measurable function $f : [0, 2\pi) \to [0, \infty)$ such that
$$u(re^{i\theta}) \le f(\theta) \quad \text{for all } r \in (0, +\infty) \text{ and all } \theta \in [0, 2\pi),$$
and
$$\int_0^{2\pi} \log^+ f(\theta)\, d\theta < +\infty,$$
then $u$ is bounded above on $\mathbb{R}^2$, and consequently $u$ is constant.

$$u(r\xi) \le f(\xi) \quad \text{for all } r \in (0, +\infty) \text{ and all } \xi \in S^2,$$
it follows that $u$ is bounded above on $\mathbb{R}^3$ (and hence constant). What is the sharpest such condition?

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: If D is a convex domain in space of 3 or more dimensions, can we assert any inequalities for the Green’s function g(P, Q) of D which generalise the results of 2 dimensions, that follow from the classical inequalities for convex univalent functions? Gabriel [283] proved that the level surfaces G(P, Q) = λ > 0 are convex, but the proof is long. It would be interesting to find a simpler proof, and also to obtain definite inequalities for the curvatures. It may be conjectured that half-space gives the extreme case. (G. E. H. Reuter)
self_contained_problem:
Let $D \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ with $n \ge 3$ be a bounded convex domain, and let $g(P,Q)$ denote the Green's function of $D$ for the Laplace operator with pole at $Q \in D$ (so $g(\cdot,Q)$ is harmonic in $D \setminus \{Q\}$, vanishes on $\partial D$, and has the standard Newtonian singularity at $Q$).

It is known (Gabriel) that the level surfaces $\{P \in D : g(P,Q) = \lambda\}$ are convex for every $\lambda > 0$. Address the following:

(a) Find a short proof of the convexity of the level surfaces $\{g(P,Q) = \lambda\}$ in $D$.

(b) Establish quantitative inequalities for the (principal, mean, or Gaussian) curvatures of these level surfaces $\{g(P,Q) = \lambda\}$, generalising to dimension $n \ge 3$ the inequalities for two-dimensional convex domains that follow from the classical distortion and curvature inequalities for convex univalent functions.

(c) Determine whether the half-space is the extremal case for such inequalities, i.e., whether among all convex domains the half-space realises equality (or saturates the bound).
status_search_result: Gabriel's convexity theorem for level sets of the Green's function on 3D convex domains has been extended and given simpler proofs (Lewis for p-harmonic functions; Caffarelli–Spruck; Korevaar). Quantitative curvature estimates for convex level sets of harmonic and p-harmonic functions in higher dimensions have been obtained by Ma, Ou, Zhang, Chang–Ma–Yang, and others. However, a complete set of sharp curvature inequalities generalising the 2D distortion-theoretic bounds with the half-space as extremal case does not appear to be fully established, so the problem is partially solved.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Consider a domain of infinite connectivity in R3 whose complement E lies in the plane P : x3 = 0. Suppose further than any disc of positive radius R in P contains a subset of E having area at least ε, where ε, R are fixed positive constants. If u is positive and harmonic in D, continuous in R3 and zero on E, is it true that u = cx3 + φ(x), x3 > 0, where c is a constant and φ(x) is uniformly bounded? One can also ask the analogue of this result for Rm when m > 3. It is true in R2 (but Kjellberg cannot remember who proved it). (B. Kjellberg)
self_contained_problem:
Let $P\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be the plane $\{x=(x_1,x_2,x_3):x_3=0\}$, and let $E\subset P$ be a closed set such that, for some fixed positive constants $\varepsilon$ and $R$, every closed disc of radius $R$ contained in $P$ contains a subset of $E$ of two-dimensional Lebesgue area at least $\varepsilon$. Let $D=\mathbb{R}^3\setminus E$, and assume $D$ is a domain of infinite connectivity. Suppose $u:\mathbb{R}^3\to\mathbb{R}$ is continuous, satisfies $u\equiv0$ on $E$, and is positive and harmonic on $D$.

Prove or disprove: there exists a constant $c\ge0$ and a bounded function $\varphi$ on the closed upper half-space $\{x_3\ge0\}$ such that
$$u(x)=cx_3+\varphi(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\text{ with }x_3>0,$$
with $\sup_{x_3>0}|\varphi(x)|<\infty$. Establish the analogous statement in $\mathbb{R}^m$ for $m>3$, where $E$ lies in a hyperplane and the area condition is replaced by the corresponding $(m-1)$-dimensional measure condition.
status_search_result: A targeted search did not surface a definitive resolution of this Kjellberg-type problem on representations of positive harmonic functions in $\mathbb{R}^3$ vanishing on a thick planar set. The problem appears in collections of open function-theoretic problems, and no clear published proof or counterexample for the $m\ge 3$ case was located, so the status is taken as unknown.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let there be given an integrable function F on T and a point z0 in D. The problem is to maximise u(z0 ), where u runs through all functions which are subharmonic in D, equal to F on T, and which satisfy inf u(reiθ ) ≤ 0, 0 < r < 1. (A. Baernstein)
self_contained_problem:
Let $D = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk and $T = \partial D$ the unit circle. Fix an integrable function $F : T \to \mathbb{R}$ and a point $z_0 \in D$. Consider the class $\mathcal{F}(F)$ of all functions $u : D \to [-\infty, \infty)$ that satisfy:

(i) $u$ is subharmonic in $D$;
(ii) $u$ has boundary values equal to $F$ on $T$ (in the sense that the nontangential boundary values of $u$ agree with $F$ almost everywhere on $T$); and
(iii) for every $r$ with $0 < r < 1$,
$$\inf_{\theta \in [0, 2\pi)} u(re^{i\theta}) \le 0.$$

Determine
$$\sup_{u \in \mathcal{F}(F)} u(z_0),$$
and identify the extremal function (if one exists) achieving this supremum.

Related work uses Baernstein's star-function method for subharmonic extremal problems, but no source found explicitly resolves the maximization of u(z_0) under the stated boundary equality and circular-infimum conditions. Status remains unverified.

original_question: Let D, D ′ be Lipschitz domains in Rn , n ≥ 3 with D ′ ⊂ D and ∂D ′ ∩ ∂D lying compactly in the interior of a set Γ in ∂D; for any fixed P0 in D ′ , let H(P0 ) denote the family of positive harmonic functions h on D that vanish continuously on Γ and satisfy h(P0 ) = 1. Is there a constant C such that, for all h1 , h2 in H(P0 ), we have h1 (P ) ≤ Ch2 (P ) for all P in D ′ ? The problem was first considered by Kemper [471], but the proof he gives contains an error. (P. J. Rippon)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n\ge 3$, and let $D, D'\subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be bounded Lipschitz domains with $D'\subset D$. Suppose $\Gamma\subset \partial D$ is a relatively open set such that $\partial D'\cap \partial D$ is a compact subset of the relative interior of $\Gamma$. Fix a point $P_0\in D'$, and let
$$\mathcal{H}(P_0)=\{h: h \text{ is positive and harmonic in } D,\ h \text{ extends continuously to } 0 \text{ on } \Gamma,\ h(P_0)=1\}.$$
Prove or disprove: there exists a constant $C=C(D,D',\Gamma,P_0)$ such that for every $h_1,h_2\in \mathcal{H}(P_0)$ and every $P\in D'$,
$$h_1(P)\le C\, h_2(P).$$
category_tag: Boundary Harnack principle for harmonic functions
status_search_result: The boundary Harnack principle for positive harmonic functions vanishing on a portion of the boundary of a Lipschitz domain was established independently by Ancona, Dahlberg, and Wu in the late 1970s, repairing/superseding Kemper's earlier argument. The comparison constant claimed in the question therefore exists, and the result is a classical theorem.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let C0 be a tangential path in D which ends at z = 1, and let Cθ be any rotation of C0 . Littlewood [523] showed that there exists a function u(z), harmonic and satisfying 0 < u(z) < 1 in D, such that lim u(z) |z|→1, z∈Cθ does not exist for almost all θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. Surprisingly, it seems to be unknown whether there exists a v(z), positive and harmonic in D, such that lim v(z) |z|→1, z∈Cθ does not exist for all θ, 0 ≤ θ ≤ 2π. The corresponding result is known for bounded analytic functions in D. See, for example, Collingwood and Lohwater, [172, Chp. 2]. (K. H. Barth)
self_contained_problem:
Let $\mathbb{D} = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disk. Fix a simple curve $C_0 \subset \mathbb{D}$ that terminates at the boundary point $z = 1$ and is tangential to the unit circle at that point (i.e., $C_0$ approaches $z=1$ tangentially). For each $\theta \in [0, 2\pi)$, let $C_\theta = \{e^{i\theta} z : z \in C_0\}$ be the rotation of $C_0$ by angle $\theta$, which is a tangential path ending at $e^{i\theta}$.

Question: Does there exist a function $v : \mathbb{D} \to \mathbb{R}$ that is positive and harmonic on $\mathbb{D}$ such that, for every $\theta \in [0, 2\pi)$, the limit
$$\lim_{\substack{|z| \to 1 \\ z \in C_\theta}} v(z)$$
fails to exist?
status_search_result: A targeted web search did not yield evidence that this question on the existence of a positive harmonic function in the unit disk with no tangential limit along any rotation of a fixed tangential path has been resolved. The corresponding result for bounded analytic functions is classical, but the positive-harmonic version appears not to have a documented resolution in accessible sources.

original_question: Let α be a continuum in the closure of the unit disc D, and let ω(z) = ω(z; D; α) be the harmonic measure at z of α with respect to D. Is it true that ω(0) ≥ π1 arcsin 12 d, where d is the diameter of α? (B. Rodin)
self_contained_problem:
Let $D = \{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| < 1\}$ denote the open unit disc. For a continuum $\alpha \subset \overline{D}$ (i.e., a compact connected subset of the closed unit disc), let $\omega(z) = \omega(z; D \setminus \alpha; \alpha)$ denote the harmonic measure of $\alpha$ at the point $z$ with respect to the domain $D \setminus \alpha$ (when $\alpha \subset D$) — more generally, $\omega(z;D;\alpha)$ is the unique bounded harmonic function on $D \setminus \alpha$ with boundary values $1$ on $\alpha$ and $0$ on $\partial D \setminus \alpha$. Let $d = \mathrm{diam}(\alpha)$ denote the Euclidean diameter of $\alpha$.

Prove or disprove: for every such continuum $\alpha$,
$$\omega(0) \;\geq\; \frac{1}{\pi}\,\arcsin\!\Big(\tfrac{d}{2}\Big).$$

Equivalently, show that among all continua in $\overline{D}$ of fixed diameter $d$, the harmonic measure at the origin is minimized when $\alpha$ is a sub-arc of the unit circle of chord-length $d$.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: For which positive p does there exist a function u, u 6≡ 0 harmonic on R3 and vanishing on the cone x21 + x22 = px23 ? (H. S. Shapiro)
self_contained_problem:
Let $p > 0$ be a real parameter, and consider the cone
$$C_p = \{(x_1, x_2, x_3) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x_1^2 + x_2^2 = p\, x_3^2\}.$$
A function $u : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$ is called harmonic if it is twice continuously differentiable and satisfies $\Delta u = \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_1^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_2^2} + \frac{\partial^2 u}{\partial x_3^2} = 0$ on all of $\mathbb{R}^3$.

Determine the set of positive real numbers $p$ for which there exists a function $u$, not identically zero, that is harmonic on $\mathbb{R}^3$ and vanishes identically on the cone $C_p$.
status_search_result: The question, attributed to H. S. Shapiro, has been actively studied. Mangoubi and Weller-Weiser (2017, Israel J. Math.) considered the right circular harmonic cone and gave evidence that the space of harmonic functions vanishing on it is finite-dimensional. More recent work (2024, "Quadratic cones on which few harmonic functions vanish", arXiv:2407.07039) proves that for a generically chosen harmonic quadratic polynomial in dimension at least three, the space of harmonic functions vanishing on its zero cone is two-dimensional, giving the first explicit nondegenerate quadratic harmonic cones for which the dimension is determined. A complete characterization of all positive p does not appear to be available.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Given n, n ≥ 4, find a continuous function f on (0, 1) such that the following statement is true: if u is a subharmonic function in the unit ball B of Rn with u(0) > 0 and 0 ≤ u < 1 in B, then there exists a path γ from the origin to ∂B with u > 0 on γ and length of γ ≤ f (u(0)). Such an f exists when n = 2 and when n = 3, see David and Lewis [185]. In the particular case n = 2, it has been shown by Lewis, Weitsman and Rossi [518] that one can take f (t) = c1 t−c2 , 0 < t < 1, where c1 , c2 are absolute constants. What is the smallest exponent c2 for which such an f exists (for the case n = 2)? (J. Lewis)
self_contained_problem:
Setting. Let $B$ denote the open unit ball in $\mathbb{R}^n$ centered at the origin, with boundary $\partial B$. A function $u\colon B\to\mathbb{R}$ is subharmonic if it is upper semicontinuous and satisfies the sub-mean-value inequality on every closed ball contained in $B$.

Consider the following property $P_n(f)$ of a continuous function $f\colon(0,1)\to(0,\infty)$: for every subharmonic function $u$ on $B\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ with $u(0)>0$ and $0\le u<1$ throughout $B$, there exists a continuous path $\gamma\colon[0,1)\to B$ with $\gamma(0)=0$, $|\gamma(t)|\to 1$ as $t\to 1$, such that $u\circ\gamma>0$ on $\gamma$ and the (Euclidean) arc-length of $\gamma$ is at most $f(u(0))$.

It is known that such an $f$ exists for $n=2$ and $n=3$. Moreover, for $n=2$ one may take $f(t)=c_1 t^{-c_2}$, $0<t<1$, for some absolute constants $c_1,c_2>0$.

Problems.
(a) For each $n\ge 4$, exhibit a continuous function $f\colon(0,1)\to(0,\infty)$ for which $P_n(f)$ holds.
(b) For $n=2$, determine the infimum of those exponents $c_2>0$ for which there exists $c_1>0$ such that $f(t)=c_1 t^{-c_2}$ satisfies $P_2(f)$.
category_tag: subharmonic functions and paths to boundary
status_search_result: A web search located the foundational works of Lewis–Rossi–Weitsman on the growth of subharmonic functions along paths, but did not turn up a definitive resolution of either the existence of $f$ in dimensions $n\ge 4$ or the optimal exponent $c_2$ in the planar case. The status appears to remain unresolved based on available sources.

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: It is known that the Newtonian potential of a uniform mass distribu- tion spread over an ellipsoid K in Rn , n ≥ 2 is a quadratic function of the coordinates of x = (x1 , . . . , xn ) for x ∈ K. Nikliborc ([605], [606]) and Dive ([192], [193]) independently proved that for n = 2 and n = 3, the ellipsoid is the only body with this property. Prove this converse assertion for n > 3 (preferably by a new method, since Nikliborc and Dive both use methods involving highly non-trivial calculations). (H. S. Shapiro)
self_contained_problem:
Let n ≥ 4 and let K ⊂ ℝⁿ be a bounded domain of finite positive Lebesgue measure. Define the Newtonian potential of the uniform mass distribution on K by
   U_K(x) = ∫_K G(x − y) dy,
where G is the fundamental solution of the Laplacian in ℝⁿ (i.e. G(z) = c_n |z|^{2−n} for n ≥ 3, with the appropriate dimensional constant c_n).

It is classical that if K is an ellipsoid, then U_K(x) coincides with a quadratic polynomial in the coordinates x = (x₁,…,xₙ) for every x in the interior of K.

Prove the following converse: if K ⊂ ℝⁿ is a bounded domain (with sufficiently regular boundary) such that U_K restricted to the interior of K equals a polynomial of degree at most 2 in x₁,…,xₙ, then K must be an ellipsoid. Provide a proof valid for all n > 3, preferably by a method that does not rely on heavy explicit calculation with ellipsoidal harmonics.
status_search_result: The converse of Newton's theorem (the Dive–Nikliborc theorem), proved originally only for n = 2, 3, was extended to all dimensions n ≥ 2 by E. DiBenedetto and A. Friedman in their 1986 work on bubble growth in porous media / heterogeneous ellipsoids, using free-boundary / quadrature-domain methods. The result is now standard in the literature on null quadrature domains (see, e.g., the survey "A Tale of Ellipsoids in Potential Theory" by Khavinson and Lundberg).

paper_title: Research Problems in Function Theory (New Edition)
original_question: Let Ω be an open ball in Rn , n ≥ 2. It is shown by Armitage [28] that V ∈ Lp (Ω) for any positive superharmonic function V on Ω and any p in (0, n/(n − 1)). Now suppose that Ω is a bounded Lipschitz domain in Rn for which the interior cones have half-angle at least α. For what values of p do we have V ∈ Lp (Ω) for every positive superharmonic function V on Ω? (S. J. Gardiner)
self_contained_problem:
Let $n \ge 2$ and let $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ be a bounded Lipschitz domain. Suppose that $\Omega$ satisfies a uniform interior cone condition with half-angle at least $\alpha \in (0, \pi/2)$: that is, there exists $h>0$ such that for every $x \in \overline{\Omega}$ there is a unit vector $\xi_x$ with
$$ \{ y \in \mathbb{R}^n : (y-x)\cdot \xi_x > |y-x|\cos\alpha,\ |y-x|<h \} \subset \Omega.$$
A function $V:\Omega\to(-\infty,\infty]$ is called superharmonic if it is lower semicontinuous, not identically $+\infty$, and satisfies the super-mean-value inequality on every closed ball contained in $\Omega$. It is known that when $\Omega$ is an open ball, every positive superharmonic function $V$ on $\Omega$ belongs to $L^p(\Omega)$ for every $p\in(0,\,n/(n-1))$.

Determine the sharp set of exponents $p>0$ (depending on $n$ and $\alpha$) for which $V\in L^p(\Omega)$ holds for every positive superharmonic function $V$ on $\Omega$.
status_search_result: Maeda and Suzuki (Bull. London Math. Soc. 21, 1989) showed integrability of positive superharmonic functions on Lipschitz domains in some $L^p$, with an exponent depending on the Lipschitz constant and asymptotically approaching $n/(n-1)$ as the constant tends to 0; for $C^1$ domains the full range $p\in(0,n/(n-1))$ holds. Subsequent works (Stegenga–Ullrich for Hölder domains; Aikawa and others for John domains; sharp Green-function/3G estimates in uniform cones) provide further partial results, but a sharp characterization of admissible exponents $p$ in terms of the cone half-angle $\alpha$ does not appear to have been fully resolved.
